notes.explains: Black plays Bb4, pinning the knight and threatening to win the bishop on f4. White's queen is far from the action.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful in open positions. Combine them with threats to win material.
notes.plans: Black will capture the bishop on f4, gaining a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: Black captures on c3, winning a piece. White's queen is still out of play, and Black has a huge lead in development.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, simplify if it maintains your initiative. Keep the pressure on.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing and eventually convert the extra piece.

notes.explains: Black takes the rook on b1, winning more material. White's position is collapsing due to lack of development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no developed pieces, every capture and threat becomes devastating.
notes.plans: Black will consolidate and finish the game with the extra material.

notes.explains: Black's queen goes to a5, threatening both the knight on c3 and the pawn on a2. This double threat is decisive.
notes.teaches: Always look for multiple threats. A single move can attack several weaknesses simultaneously.
notes.plans: Black will capture on a2 and then b2, winning more material.

notes.explains: Black wins the b2 pawn, and White's king is exposed. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: Initiative and development can lead to a quick knockout. Don't let the opponent consolidate.
notes.plans: Black will continue the attack, targeting White's king.

notes.explains: Black captures the bishop on c3, winning another piece. White's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive advantage, look for the most efficient way to convert.
notes.plans: Black will simplify further and win the endgame.

notes.explains: After c3, Qb6 is flexible: it attacks d4 and prepares to recapture on c5 with the queen if White takes. White's b3 is a mistake that loses a pawn, as Black can simply take on d4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent defends a pawn you're attacking, consider whether you can win it by capturing first and then renewing the threat. Flexibility in move order can exploit weaknesses.
notes.plans: Take on d4 with the knight, then develop with Bc5 and castle, exploiting the broken pawn chain and the protected passed pawn on d5.

notes.explains: Black has won a pawn and has a protected passed pawn on d5. White's position is crumbling. Black should develop with Bc5, then consider h5 to exploit the weakened kingside.
notes.teaches: A protected passed pawn in the center is a huge asset; it restricts the opponent's pieces and can be a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Play Bc5, then h5 to open lines against White's king. Avoid rushing to capture material if it allows counterplay.

notes.explains: White's Kh1 avoids a discovered check, but Black can now play h5, threatening to open the h-file. The key is not to rush: Black should consider whether immediate captures are necessary.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, don't force tactics. Prioritize safety and gradual improvement. A safe knight is better than an active one that can be trapped.
notes.plans: Play h5 to open lines, then consider g3 or other moves to maintain pressure. Avoid automatic captures like Bxa1 if they allow counterplay.

notes.explains: After g4, Black's knight is attacked. The correct move is to retreat the knight to a safe square, not to seek an active post. The priority is preserving the piece and winning the rook on a1.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, safety trumps activity. Retreating a piece to preserve it and maintain the material advantage is often the best plan.
notes.plans: Retreat the knight (e.g., Ng6 or Nf5) to safety, then win the rook on a1. After that, consolidate and exploit the extra material.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3 to block the rook's defense. Black can now win the rook by simply retreating the knight (e.g., Ng6) and then taking on a1. The immediate capture Nxg4? would lose the knight.
notes.teaches: Always consider the opponent's resources. A simple retreat can be more effective than a flashy capture. Calculate captures carefully.
notes.plans: Retreat the knight (Ng6 or Nf5), then take the rook on a1. After that, activate the queen and rook, and consider exploiting White's weak king.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to g6, winning the rook on a1. White's king is weak due to g4, and Black can continue with d4 to secure the bishop and prepare Qc6 with threats.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by improving your pieces and restricting the opponent's counterplay. A weak king is a long-term target.
notes.plans: Play d4 to secure the bishop and advance the passed pawn. Then Qc6 to threaten discovered checks and activate the rook. Castle only when necessary.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange and has a decisive material advantage. The game is effectively over; Black just needs to make reasonable moves to convert.
notes.teaches: When you have a large material advantage, avoid unnecessary risks. Simple, solid moves are sufficient to win.
notes.plans: Continue with Qc6, then castle or bring the rook into play. Avoid blundering the advantage back.

notes.explains: The Caro-Kann and French Defenses are structurally similar: both allow White to build a pawn center (d4, e5) while Black attacks it with c5 and f6. The key difference is that in the Caro-Kann, Black develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain (Bf5), but spends two tempi on c5 later.
notes.teaches: Understanding pawn structures is crucial. In closed positions, the side with more pawn breaks (levers) often has the initiative. The Caro-Kann trades a tempo for a better bishop.

notes.explains: A common tactical pattern in the Caro-Kann: when White's king is boxed in on h1 and the h-file is open, a rook lift to h8 can deliver checkmate. This pattern also appears in other openings.
notes.teaches: Keep a mental notebook of tactical patterns. Recognizing patterns like the h-file mate can help you spot winning combinations in similar positions.

notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann, Black often faces development challenges with the kingside pieces. The knight on h6 (aiming for f5) and the dark-squared bishop on e7 or c5 are typical solutions.
notes.teaches: When natural squares are unavailable, consider rim moves or trades to activate pieces. The knight on h6 is not necessarily bad if it can reach f5.

notes.explains: The 'best case scenario test' helps evaluate a plan: imagine the opponent does nothing to stop you. If the plan still doesn't achieve a clear advantage, it's probably not good. For example, playing c4 in the Caro-Kann closes the center and makes it hard to break through, even with b5-b4.
notes.teaches: Evaluate plans by considering the best-case outcome. If the plan is not convincing even then, look for alternatives.

notes.explains: After h3, Black sacrifices the knight with Nxh3+ to open the h-file. White's king is exposed, and Black's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices to open lines against the enemy king are often justified when the king is exposed and the attacker has many pieces ready.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qg5 or Qh4, threatening mate on h2 or g3, and bring the rook to h8.

notes.explains: The attack culminates in a forced checkmate. Black's queen and bishop coordinate to exploit the light squares around White's king.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for ways to combine material gain with mating threats; precision is key to avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Execute the mate with queen checks and bishop support, using the light squares.

notes.explains: The game demonstrates a classic kingside attack against the Hippopotamus setup, using the g3 hook and a knight sacrifice to open lines.
notes.teaches: The Hippopotamus is playable at high levels but dangerous for beginners; it's better to learn classical openings first to build fundamentals.

notes.explains: After some maneuvering, Black plays ...Rd8, a natural move to pressure d4. White's center is solid but Black aims to cause it to collapse.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld, the battle is over the center. Black tries to make White's center collapse, while White tries to expand and control key squares.
notes.plans: Black will look to open the c-file with ...cxd4 and then bring the rook to c8, pressuring the queen on c2. The bishop will go to e6, covering queenside squares.

notes.explains: White pushes d5, attacking the knight. Black retreats to b4, the only good square. The knight on b4 is awkward but necessary to avoid worse alternatives.
notes.teaches: When under attack, use process of elimination to find the least bad square. Sometimes a seemingly passive move is the only way to keep the position together.
notes.plans: Black will try to activate the knight later, perhaps via ...Nd3. Meanwhile, Black looks for tactical opportunities, such as exploiting the undefended bishop on b2.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a knight with …Nfxd5! The idea is to deflect the queen from defending the bishop on b2. After Nxd5 Bxd5, the queen has no safe square to maintain the defense of the bishop.
notes.teaches: When two enemy pieces are aligned and one is defended only by the queen, a sacrifice to deflect the queen can win material. Attacks on the queen are almost as powerful as checks.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, Black will regain the piece with interest, leaving Black up two pawns. The key is to follow up accurately, using intermediate moves like ...Nb6 to attack the queen again.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, Black plays …Nd3, attacking the queen and forcing it to abandon the bishop. Black emerges with two extra pawns.
notes.teaches: In tactical combinations, intermediate moves (like ...Nb6 and ...Nd3) are crucial to maximize gains. Always look for ways to keep the pressure on the opponent's queen.
notes.plans: Black is up two pawns but must consolidate. The king is vulnerable without the fianchetto bishop, so Black should aim to trade queens and simplify to an endgame.

notes.explains: After further complications, Black wins the exchange and remains up two pawns. However, White has active rooks and a vulnerable black king.
notes.teaches: Material advantage is not enough; you must also consider king safety and piece activity. Black must consolidate carefully.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade queens and bring the king to safety. The ideal setup is to centralize the king and rooks, then push the queenside majority.

notes.explains: Black's rook endgame technique: use the rook to attack weak pawns (like f2) and force White's rook to passive defense. Then create connected passed pawns on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king should be active. Use the rook to block lateral checks and advance pawns with the king's support.
notes.plans: Black will advance the kingside pawns (g4, h3, etc.) to create a passed pawn. The rook will block checks and the king will support the pawns.

notes.explains: In the Rossolimo Attack (e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5), Black's choice between g6 and e6 depends on their repertoire against the Open Sicilian. For Accelerated Dragon players, g6 is natural and most popular.
notes.teaches: Your response to the Rossolimo should align with your Open Sicilian repertoire: e6 players often choose e6; Accelerated Dragon players should pick g6.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 4.0-0 Bg7 Re1, Black can play …e5. This move blocks the bishop and creates holes, but it strongly clamps down on d4 and prepares to develop the knight to e7.
notes.teaches: In closed Sicilian structures, e5 can be a powerful central clamp, preventing White's d4 break. The apparent weaknesses (blocked bishop, d5 hole) are manageable with proper piece coordination.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ne7, d6, and later consider f5 or kingside expansion.

notes.explains: After …e5, Black's knight goes to e7, and d6 solidifies the center. Delaying castling can be beneficial: if White plays Bg5, Black can respond with h6 and g5, keeping the king in the center or castling queenside for a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, delaying castling is a valid advanced technique. It allows flexible pawn advances on the kingside without exposing the king.
notes.plans: Consider h6, g5, and later g4 to attack White's kingside, especially if White has played h3.

notes.explains: In the position after …e5, c3 Ne7 d3 d6 Bg5, Black can play …f6. This weakens the a2-g8 diagonal but is safe because the center is closed. The follow-up Be6 covers the diagonal, and Black completes development.
notes.teaches: Moves like f6, which would be suicidal in open positions, become playable when the center is closed. Always compensate for weakened diagonals with proper piece placement.
notes.plans: Play Be6, then castle kingside, and prepare f5 to gain space on the kingside.

notes.explains: After …f6 Be3 Be6 Nbd2 0-0, Black's position is solid. White cannot play d4, and Black has no weaknesses. The knight on e7 and bishop on e6 defend d5. Black's plan is to slowly improve and eventually play f5.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, patience is key. Focus on incremental improvements and avoid rushing. A solid center with no weaknesses often gives Black a comfortable game.
notes.plans: Play f5 to gain space, then consider Bg4 to trade on f3 and occupy d4 with a knight.

notes.explains: The move Bg4 (after ...f5 preparation) aims to exchange on f3, ruining White's kingside pawn structure and planting a knight on d4. This creates threats like Qh3 and checkmate ideas, as White's knight on f3 has few retreat squares.
notes.teaches: Exchanging a bishop for a knight to damage the opponent's pawn structure is a classic idea, especially when the opponent's king is on that side. The resulting outpost for your knight can be decisive.
notes.plans: After Bg4 and exchanges, play Nd4, threatening forks and using the h3 square for the queen.

notes.explains: In the game, after …Bg4 Re3 Nd4, White's rook is awkward. If White retreats the knight to e1, Black can play f5, threatening f4 to trap the rook. The knight on e7 defends d5, allowing Black to ignore that square.
notes.teaches: When a piece has few retreat squares, target it with pawn advances. A trapped rook or knight can decide the game. Defensive pieces can be purely defensive and still valuable.
notes.plans: Play f5, then f4 to trap the rook, or if White avoids, continue with Be6 and queenside play.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, Black wins a piece for a pawn. The conversion is straightforward: activate the rook, centralize the queen, and use the extra material. White's rook on e3 is out of play.
notes.teaches: In won positions, simplify by trading down while maintaining activity. Avoid unnecessary risks; use your extra material to create threats.
notes.plans: Play Be6, Qb6, Rc8, and then push d5 or f5 to open lines.

notes.explains: Black's setup with ...e6, ...d6, ...Bb7, ...c6, ...h6, ...g5 is extremely passive and neglects development. White has built a strong center with d4, e4, and c4, and now must decide how to break through.
notes.teaches: Against passive play, complete your development first before striking in the center. Patience is key; premature pawn breaks can allow the opponent to close the position.
notes.plans: Prepare e5 with Rfe1 to support the break. After e5 d5, recapture with the knight on e5 to keep the center fluid and exploit light-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: After e5 d5 cxd5 cxd5, the position resembles a favorable French Defense structure for White. Black's bishop on b7 is bad, and the knight on g8 cannot develop to f6. White has a clear space advantage.
notes.teaches: When the opponent allows a central pawn break that leaves them with a bad bishop and no counterplay, you should aim to keep the position closed and slowly improve your pieces.
notes.plans: Play Be3 to prepare Rc1, then Nd2 to reroute the knight to c5 or f3, and eventually switch to the kingside with Qh5.

notes.explains: White has completed development and now switches the attack to the kingside with Qh5. The queen pins the g5-pawn and threatens tactical ideas like Nxd5 exd5 e6, or Bxg5. Black is paralyzed.
notes.teaches: When one side has no counterplay, you can often switch the attack from one flank to the other. The principle of two weaknesses: overloading the opponent's defenses by creating threats on both sides.
notes.plans: Threaten Nxg5, forcing the queen back to d8. Then play h4 to open the h-file, or reroute the knight to f3 to renew threats. If Black defends, continue accumulating pressure.

notes.explains: Black blunders the exchange with Rg7, allowing Nxg5. After taking, White must strike while the iron is hot: the kingside is weakened, and the queen is far away.
notes.teaches: After winning material, immediately look for ways to exploit the new weaknesses. Don't relax; the opponent's blunder often creates tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Play h4 to open the kingside. After g6, break through with g6 fxg6 Nxg6, threatening Nxe7+ and Qxe6+.

notes.explains: The final sequence: after g6, Black's kingside collapses. White sacrifices the knight on g6 to remove the defender of f7, then wins with Qxe6+ and Bf4#.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, don't hesitate to sacrifice material to remove key defenders. The queen and bishop coordinate for a mating net.
notes.plans: After Nxg6 Rf7, take on e7 with the knight, then Qxe6+ forces the king to d8, where Bf4 delivers checkmate.

notes.explains: After trading rooks on c8, White plays Qd2, connecting the rooks and preparing to bring the other rook to d1. Black's bishop on c8 is passive, and White's center is solid.
notes.teaches: Trading rooks can be beneficial when it leaves the opponent with a passive piece and you have a space advantage. The queen is well-placed on d2, supporting the center and eyeing the kingside.
notes.plans: White will continue with Rd1, f3, and then consider h4 to create weaknesses on the kingside. The long-term plan is to prepare d5 under favorable conditions.

notes.explains: White plays f3 to reinforce e4 and prepare a future d5. Black's bishop on b7 is passive, and White's pieces are optimally placed. The position is slightly better for White.
notes.teaches: f3 is a useful consolidating move that strengthens the center and prevents Black from occupying e4. It also prepares a later d5 push.
notes.plans: After f3, White can consider h4 to create kingside weaknesses. The idea is to probe Black's position without committing to a central break too early.

notes.explains: With all pieces optimally placed, White plays h4 to create weaknesses on the kingside. This move is not a pawn storm but a probe: it forces Black to decide between h5 (weakening dark squares) or allowing h5-h6 (creating a hook for later attacks).
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and your pieces are well-placed, use pawn moves like h4 to create long-term weaknesses in the opponent's camp. Even on the same side as your own king, such moves are safe if the opponent has no counterplay.
notes.plans: If Black plays h5, White can follow up with Bh6 to trade the dark-squared bishops, exploiting the weakened dark squares. If Black ignores, White pushes h5-h6 to deprive the black king of luft and create tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: Black plays h5, weakening the dark squares. White immediately exploits this by playing Bh6, threatening to trade off Black's powerful fianchettoed bishop. Black cannot save it with Bh8 because the rook is still on f8.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside dark squares, trading off their fianchettoed bishop is often a strategic victory. The timing is crucial: do it before Black can move the rook and save the bishop with Bh8.
notes.plans: After Bh6, White intends to trade on g7, then bring the queen to g5 and the knight to g3 or f4, creating a powerful attack against the weakened black king.

notes.explains: White plays Ng3, preparing to trade on g7 and then bring the queen to g5. The knight on g3 supports the kingside attack and does not block the queen's path to g5 (unlike Nf4).
notes.teaches: When attacking, choose the knight's square to maximize coordination. Ng3 keeps the queen's route to g5 open and allows the knight to later jump to f5 or h5.
notes.plans: White will play Bxg7 Kxg7, then Qg5, threatening Nxh5. Black must defend, but White can then open the center with d5, creating multiple threats.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade and Qg5, Black's king is on h8. White plays d5, opening the center and creating a passed pawn. The knight on g3 and bishop on b3 now have clear paths to join the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, opening the center with a pawn break like d5 can be devastating. The passed pawn also adds pressure and can be pushed further.
notes.plans: After exd5, White recaptures with the rook (or bishop), threatening to push d6. The knight can go to e4 or f5, and the bishop can drop back to c2, pinning the g6 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays f5 to block the knight and bishop, but White pushes d6, reopening the bishop's diagonal and threatening the rook on d8. The pawn on d6 is a powerful passed pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to block your pieces, push the passed pawn further. It creates new threats and forces the opponent to defend passively.
notes.plans: After d6, White threatens Bxf7 (if the knight moves) or simply pushes d7. The immediate threat is Bxf7, winning the queen or checkmating.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng8, hoping to defend, but White plays Bxf7, a deflection sacrifice. Black must take with the queen (Qxf7), after which White captures the rook on d8 with the queen, winning material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is the only defender of a key piece, a sacrifice on a square defended by the queen can deflect it and win material. Always look for such tactical opportunities when the opponent's pieces are overloaded.
notes.plans: After Qxf7 Qxd8, White has a winning material advantage. The simplest continuation is to push the d-pawn to promotion.

notes.explains: After the deflection, White simplifies to a winning endgame. The d-pawn promotes, and Black's king is vulnerable. The final checkmate is Qh8#.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material advantage, simplify by trading pieces while avoiding counterplay. Promoting the passed pawn is often the most straightforward path to victory.
notes.plans: Push the d-pawn to promotion, using checks to avoid stalemate or perpetual check. In this game, the queen delivers checkmate on h8.

notes.explains: This is the prettier mate line, demonstrating how a queen and pawn can deliver mate with the king trapped on the h-file.
notes.teaches: Aesthetic mating patterns often arise from precise king-hunt technique; knowing these patterns helps in practical play.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bg4, White has the classic Bxf7+ and Ng5+ tactic, winning the bishop on g4. This is a common amateur trap.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for tactical motifs like the Greek Gift sacrifice when the opponent pins a knight to the queen.
notes.plans: Play Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+ Kg8 Qxg4, winning a piece.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...e6 instead of ...a5, White can push d4, opening the center and activating the pieces. Black's position becomes cramped and vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent delays development, strike in the center to open lines and increase the initiative.
notes.plans: After d4, if Black captures, recapture with the knight and continue developing with Re1, etc.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bc5, White can play Be3 or simply develop, maintaining pressure. The position is dynamically balanced but White has a slight edge due to better development.
notes.teaches: In open positions, piece activity and king safety are more important than material equality.
notes.plans: Continue developing with Be3, Rad1, etc., aiming to exploit Black's exposed king or weak pawns.

notes.explains: After …O-O, White must avoid the center fork trick: if White castles, Black has Nxe4, Nxe4, d5 forking the knight and bishop. This would dissolve White's central advantage and free Black's light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is on c4 and the center is open, be alert to ...Nxe4 followed by ...d5. The simplest prophylaxis is to move the bishop to b3, keeping it on the active diagonal while defending e4 indirectly.
notes.plans: White can castle next, then prepare d4 or continue development. The bishop on b3 remains safe and maintains pressure on f7.

notes.explains: Black plays a6 preparing b5. White should prevent b5 with a4, because allowing b5 and then meeting it with a4 can lead to complications where Black pushes c5-c4, trapping the bishop. a4 is a direct prophylactic move that stops b5 immediately.
notes.teaches: When Black threatens queenside expansion with ...b5, a4 is often the cleanest way to stop it. Avoid inviting b5 unless you have a concrete follow-up that punishes it.
notes.plans: After a4, White castles and continues development. Black's light-squared bishop remains passive on d7.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to c6, creating tension on d4. White should not rush to trade or retreat; instead, play the improving move Re1, which is useful in many positions. Black then takes on d4, and White recaptures with the queen.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions with no immediate threats, play general improving moves like Re1. Avoid unnecessary trades when you have more space.
notes.plans: After Qxd4, White will decide where to place the bishop (f4 or g5) and continue central pressure.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on c6 is well-placed. White should avoid exchanging it because trades favor the side with less space. Instead, White plays Bf4, developing the bishop to a useful square even if it seems to 'bite on granite' (pawns block its diagonals). The bishop still supports central pressure and coordinates the rooks.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, avoid unnecessary trades. A bishop that appears passive can still be useful for prophylaxis and supporting central pawn breaks.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Qd2 to prevent ...Bf6 with tempo, then consider Nd5 to challenge Black's best piece.

notes.explains: Black defends d6 with Qc7, but White can improve with c3, creating a pawn bulwark that makes Black's bishop bite on granite. The bishop on b3 is undefended, but White should not fear one-move threats like Qb6; the bishop has retreat squares. This is a case where violating the principle of protecting pieces is acceptable because the threat is easily met.
notes.teaches: Do not fear one-move threats that can be parried easily. Sometimes you can leave a piece undefended if the opponent's counterplay is harmless.
notes.plans: White can play h3 to create luft, then consider f4 to push e5 and open lines. The backward d6 pawn remains a long-term target.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng6, attacking the bishop on f4, but this allows White to capture on d6 with tempo (attacking the rook on a8). White wins a pawn and now has a clear advantage. The weakness on d6, created earlier by Black's c6, is now exploited.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a backward pawn in the center, target it immediately. A central pawn weakness is much more serious than a flank weakness because its collapse often leads to a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: After taking on d6, White can push f4 to prepare e5, creating a devastating pawn chain. If Black takes on b2, White can trap the bishop with Kh1 and c3.

notes.explains: After winning the pawn, White pushes d7, threatening to promote. Black defends with Re7. White must find the winning move Qb4, which attacks the knight on f8 and prevents Black from defending the d7 pawn. The key is to induce ...Nf8 first, then Qb4 makes the threat of Qxf8 unstoppable.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a passed pawn, look for ways to attack the defender. Here Qb4 is a quiet move that ties Black's pieces to the defense of the knight, making promotion inevitable.
notes.plans: After Qb4, if Black plays c5, Qxc5 maintains the threat. If Black takes on d7, White recaptures with a new queen. The win is straightforward.

notes.explains: Black castles, walking into a classic Greek Gift sacrifice. White can play Bxh7+ followed by Ng5+, Qh5, etc., leading to a winning attack.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice is a standard attacking motif when the bishop is on d3 and the knight can reach g5. It exploits the weakened kingside after castling.
notes.plans: Execute Bxh7+ Kxh7, Ng5+ Kg6 (or Kg8), Qg4, etc., with a mating attack.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d4, and Black's bishop on c8 remains hemmed in. White has a small but lasting advantage due to superior piece activity and Black's bad bishop.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a bad bishop can be a decisive weakness. White should aim to keep the position closed and exploit Black's lack of space.
notes.plans: Play c3 to support the bishop, then develop the queenside with b3 and Bb2, gradually increasing pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the b2 pawn and preparing to support the queenside pawns. White should respond with a4 to break up Black's pawn chain.
notes.teaches: When Black builds a queenside pawn chain (b5, c4), White can undermine it with b3 and a4. The timing is critical: a4 is strong when the rook on a8 is undefended.
notes.plans: Play a4 immediately, exploiting the undefended rook on a8. If Black plays ...a6, then axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White plays a4, threatening to break the queenside pawn chain. Black cannot play ...a6 because axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend with a piece.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like a4 can be devastating when the opponent's rook is undefended. The threat of winning a pawn or exposing weaknesses forces concessions.
notes.plans: After a4, if Black plays ...Ba6, White can capture on b5 and c4, leaving Black with a weak pawn on c4. Then White will target that pawn with Rb1, Qe2, etc.

notes.explains: White clears the queenside pawns, leaving Black with a weak isolated pawn on c4. White now has a clear target and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Exchanging pawns to create a permanent weakness (isolated pawn) is a key strategic idea. The c4 pawn is a long-term liability for Black.
notes.plans: White will complete development (c3, Nbd2, Rc1, etc.) and then surround and win the c4 pawn. Black cannot easily defend it.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to solidify the center and prepares Nbd2 to target the c4 pawn. Black's rook on d8 does not threaten d4 because the knight on f3 guards it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, solidifying the center with c3 is often necessary before pursuing a queenside plan. The knight on f3 is a key defender.
notes.plans: White will play Nbd2, then perhaps Ne4 or Nf1-e3 to pressure c4. The c4 pawn is a fixed target that cannot be easily defended.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, challenging the e5 pawn and opening the center. White must reassess: the plan to target c4 is now secondary to exploiting the new weakness on e6.
notes.teaches: Flexibility is crucial. When the opponent changes the structure, be ready to switch plans. Here, the opening of the center favors the better-developed side (White).
notes.plans: White should capture on f6 (exf6), opening the e-file and targeting the weak e6 pawn. Then Qe2 or Rfe1 puts pressure on e6.

notes.explains: White captures on f6 and plays Rfe1, putting pressure on e6. Black's king is still in the center, and the e6 pawn is a major weakness.
notes.teaches: After opening the center, the side with better development should target the opponent's weak pawns. The rook on e1 adds pressure and prepares to double on the e-file.
notes.plans: White will play Qe2 or Qd3, attacking e6. Black cannot easily defend it because the king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf7 to defend e6, but this is a decisive mistake. White can now play Ng5+, forcing the king back or to a worse square.
notes.teaches: The king is a poor defender in open positions. Moving it forward often creates new tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: Play Ng5+ Ke7 (or Kg8), then capture on e6 with the rook or knight, winning a pawn and exposing the king further.

notes.explains: White plays d5, winning the knight on c6 because the queen on b6 is pinned to the king. Black's position collapses immediately.
notes.teaches: A pin can be decisive. Here, the queen's pin on the knight allows a simple pawn advance to win material and launch a mating attack.
notes.plans: After d5, Black cannot avoid losing the knight. White will then deliver checkmate with Qd4+ and Bf4, or similar.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qxd6#. The game is a clear example of converting a positional advantage into a direct attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped, a coordinated attack can end the game quickly. Accurate calculation of forcing moves is essential.
notes.plans: The mating sequence is forced: d5 wins the knight, then Qxd5+ forces the king to c7, and Bf4+ Bd6 Qxd6#.

notes.explains: This game illustrates key ideas of the Nimzowitsch French: rapid development, undermining the queenside pawn chain, flexibility in switching plans, and exploiting the opponent's king exposure.
notes.teaches: The Nimzowitsch French is a practical weapon that teaches closed position strategy, pawn breaks, and attacking chess. It is effective up to a high level.

notes.explains: White starts with Nc3 and Bf4, a setup that deliberately blocks the c-pawn to create fresh, imbalanced positions.
notes.teaches: In d4 openings, blocking the c-pawn usually violates the principle of controlling the center with c4, but here it's a calculated risk that leads to unique attacking chances.
notes.plans: White aims to develop quickly, often with ideas like Nb5 targeting c7, and later a kingside pawn storm with g4 and h4.

notes.explains: After Bf5, White can choose between the traditional f3 (preparing g4/h4) or the modern e3, aiming to quickly bring the knight to e5.
notes.teaches: The knight on e5 exerts strong pressure; Black often fails to see the threat of g4, which can trap the bishop or ruin Black's pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play e3, Nf3, then Ne5. If Black castles prematurely, g4 becomes very strong because the king is committed to the kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays Nbd7, which indirectly defends against g4. White should not play g4 here because after Bxe5 dxe5 Nxg4, White loses a pawn.
notes.teaches: When the knight on e5 is attacked, recapturing with the pawn can open lines, but here it's bad because Black's knight captures on g4 with tempo.
notes.plans: Instead of g4, develop the light-squared bishop to d3 or e2. Bd3 is more positional, preparing to recapture with the pawn after Bxd3, opening the c-file and giving the queen access to b3.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d3 with the pawn, accepting doubled pawns. This controls c4 and e4, opens the c-file for the rook, and allows the queen to go to b3.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness; here they control key central squares and create open lines for the heavy pieces.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qb3, Rc1, and later kingside expansion. The pawn on d3 is a strength, not a weakness.

notes.explains: Black plays c6, which is a blunder. White can win a pawn with Nxf7 (attacking the queen) followed by Nxd6, or even Nxc6 with further tactics.
notes.teaches: When the bishop on d6 is undefended, a discovered attack on the queen by the knight can win material. Always check for such tactical shots.
notes.plans: Play Nxf7, forcing the queen to move, then capture the bishop on d6. Alternatively, Nxc6 is also strong, threatening Nb5 after Qc7.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and has a comfortable position. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by improving your pieces and preventing counterplay. Don't rush; build up pressure gradually.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then consider f4 to reinforce the bishop on e5 and open lines for the rook. Also play b4 to stop c5, and a3 to defend the b-pawn.

notes.explains: White plays f4, reinforcing the bishop on e5 and preparing to lift the rook to f3 or g3. This also takes the sting out of ...Nxe5, as recapturing with the f-pawn opens the f-file.
notes.teaches: f4 is a useful multi-purpose move: it supports the bishop, prepares a rook lift, and can open the f-file for attack. The potential weakness of e3 is not a concern because Black cannot easily attack it.
notes.plans: Continue with Rf3, then double rooks on the f-file. Later, consider pushing f5 to open lines, but only after proper preparation.

notes.explains: White has built a strong position: the pawn on d3 controls key squares, the rooks are ready to double on the f-file, and Black is cramped. Black's Nd7 does not threaten anything immediately.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, improve your pieces without rushing. Here, White can bring the last rook to f1 to prepare for the f-file battle.
notes.plans: Play Rf1, then complete the rook lift to f3. Accumulate pressure on the kingside; Black will eventually crack under the strain.

notes.explains: White plays Bd6, chasing the rook from f8 and preparing f5. The bishop is safe here because it's hard to attack, and it can always return to e5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes retreating a piece to a seemingly passive square is actually strong because it prepares future advances and avoids being exchanged.
notes.plans: After Bd6, Black's rook must move (e.g., to e8). Then White can consider f5, opening the f-file. The bishop can later go back to e5 to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: White plays h3 to prevent ...Ng4 and then prepares to push g4, locking out Black's knight. This is a calm, positional approach rather than rushing with f5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a knight that could become active, it's often wise to restrict it with a pawn move like h3, then follow up with g4 to completely shut it out.
notes.plans: After h3, play g4, then consider e4 or f5. The rook on f3 can later go to g3 to target g7. Maintain control of all pawn breaks.

notes.explains: White plays e4, preventing ...Nf5 and keeping the g-file open for the rook. This is better than g4, which would block the rook on f3.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two good moves, consider which one leaves your pieces more active. Here, e4 keeps the rook's path to g3 open, while g4 would block it.
notes.plans: After e4, the rook can go to g3 to attack g7. The bishop on d6 can return to e5 to maintain pressure. White's position is very comfortable.

notes.explains: White returns the bishop to e5, where it pressures g7 and protects d4. Now ...d4 is no longer a threat, and Black's knight on h6 is out of play.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is to return a piece to its best square. The bishop on e5 is a monster, and White should not exchange it without good reason.
notes.plans: Now White can consider f5, which comes with tempo because it attacks the knight on g6. If Black takes on f5, White recaptures with the pawn and continues the attack.

notes.explains: Black exchanges on e5, and White recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file and giving White a powerful pawn center.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the pawn that opens a file for your rooks is often better than recapturing with a piece. Here, the f-file becomes a highway for White's attack.
notes.plans: Now White has a clear plan: double rooks on the f-file, then push f5 to break through. The pawn on e5 also restricts Black's pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh4, forking the rook on f3 and the pawn on f5. White responds with Rf4, defending the pawn and threatening to capture the knight.
notes.teaches: When your piece is forked, look for a move that defends the attacked piece and creates a counter-threat. Here, Rf4 both defends f5 and attacks the knight.
notes.plans: After Rf4, if Black takes on f5, White can play g4, trapping the knight. White's pieces are well-coordinated, and the attack continues.

notes.explains: Black plays Qg6, a tricky move that pins the g-pawn and threatens the rook on f4. White missed this and played Rxf5, but better was Rg3, keeping the pressure.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to pins and counterattacks. Here, Qg6 pins the g-pawn, so White cannot simply play gxf5. Instead, Rg3 would have avoided the pin and maintained the attack.
notes.plans: If White had played Rg3, the knight on f5 would be trapped, and White would win material. In the game, White played Rxf5, giving up the exchange but still winning due to the strong position.

notes.explains: White plays Kh2 to unpin the g-pawn and prepare to capture on f5. Now Black's queen is under attack, and White has a rook and two pieces for the queen.
notes.teaches: When your king is in a pin, moving it away can unlock your pieces. Here, Kh2 allows White to take on f5 and win material.
notes.plans: After Kh2, White will capture the queen with Rxf5, leaving White with a rook and bishop for the queen. The resulting position is winning due to Black's weak king and White's active pieces.

notes.explains: White plays Bg3, a quiet but strong move. It prepares to bring the bishop back to e5 later and avoids giving Black counterplay. The pawns will decide the game.
notes.teaches: In positions with a material advantage, it's important to consolidate and avoid unnecessary complications. Here, Bg3 is a flexible move that improves the bishop and prepares a pawn advance.
notes.plans: White will push the h-pawn to drive away Black's knight, then advance the g-pawn to open lines. The pawns are a decisive force.

notes.explains: White plays Nd2, aiming to bring the knight to f4 to join the attack. The knight has been idle and now becomes a key attacker.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, activate your worst piece. Here, the knight on c3 was doing nothing; bringing it to f4 increases the pressure on Black's king.
notes.plans: The knight will go to f4, then White can push g5 to open lines. The bishop on g3 can later go to h4 to target the rook on e7.

notes.explains: White plays Bh4, threatening to exchange on e7 or chase the rook. This improves the bishop and prepares g5.
notes.teaches: Even a small improvement like moving the bishop to a better diagonal can increase the pressure. Here, Bh4 eyes the rook on e7 and supports the g5 push.
notes.plans: After Bh4, White will play g5, opening lines. The knight on f4 and the pawns will decide the game.

notes.explains: White plays g5, opening lines and threatening g6. This is the decisive breakthrough.
notes.teaches: When you have accumulated enough pressure, it's time to open the position. Here, g5 is the right moment because White's pieces are optimally placed.
notes.plans: After g5, White will play g6, tearing open Black's kingside. The pawns and pieces will create a mating attack or win material.

notes.explains: White plays Qg5, attacking the knight on f6 and threatening h6. Black is forced to give up material.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for moves that create multiple threats. Here, Qg5 threatens h6 and also eyes the knight on f6, forcing Black to defend.
notes.plans: After Qg5, Black will have to move the knight or defend it. White will then play h6, breaking through. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange with Bxe7, leaving Black with a rook and knight against White's queen and bishop. The position is winning.
notes.teaches: In the attack, winning material is often as good as checkmate. Here, White simplifies to a technically winning endgame.
notes.plans: After Bxe7, White will consolidate and use the queen and bishop to target Black's weak king. The pawns will also be a factor.

notes.explains: White forces the win of a rook with Qg6+ and Qxe8+. Black's king is exposed, and White has a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, checks and threats can force the win of more material. Here, the queen's checks exploit Black's weak king position.
notes.plans: After Qxe8+, White will have queen and pawns against rook and knight. The win is a matter of technique.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the pawn (axb3) opens the a-file and secures the bishop on c4, creating imbalance. The doubled b-pawns are not a concern; piece activity matters more.
notes.teaches: In endgames, prioritize active pieces and open files over pawn structure. Doubled pawns are often less important than dynamic factors.
notes.plans: Use the open a-file and active bishop to pressure Black. Aim to infiltrate with the rook on the seventh rank.

notes.explains: White has a rook and two pieces for the queen, but the key is the active rook on e7 and the knight on d5. Black's bishop is hanging, and White threatens Nxc7+.
notes.teaches: In piece imbalances, coordination and threats matter more than material count. Avoid assumptions—keep looking for tactical resources even when ahead.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, threatening Nxc7+ and Bxe5. If Black defends, continue with active rook play and centralize the king.

notes.explains: After Nd5, Black's best defense was Kg7 to protect the bishop, but instead Black blundered with ...Nc6, allowing Ne8+ winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: After a blunder, stay calm and assess the actual threats. The only move to defend the bishop was Kg7; panic leads to collapse.
notes.plans: If Black plays Kg7, White has the bishop pair and initiative, but the game continues. Avoid rushing; untangle pieces methodically.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6, Black plays Bb5 Nxd4? which is a mistake. White recaptures Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Qe2 Qe7 Bg5 h6 Bc4 Qg4 O-O Qxf4 Qh4 Nxe5 Ng4 Nd5 O-O Nxc7 Bxf2+ Rxf2 Qxf2+ Rxf2, White wins the queen and the game.
notes.teaches: In the Four Knights Scotch, Black's early ...Nxd4 is a mistake because it allows White to push e5 with tempo, gaining space and attacking the knight. White should develop naturally and exploit Black's lack of development.
notes.plans: White castles kingside to complete development, then targets the c7 pawn with Nd5, eventually winning material.

notes.explains: After Qh4, White deliberately gives up the e5 pawn to create a powerful attack. Black takes on e5, but White has a follow-up that wins on the spot (though the opponent avoids it by playing Ng4).
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing a pawn for the initiative is stronger than a safe retreat. Qh4 is a master-level idea that sets up threats against f6 and h7, exploiting Black's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: White intends to follow Qxe5 with a rook lift to e1, but since the bishop isn't developed, the immediate threat is less clear; however, the queen on h4 creates pressure that Black cannot easily handle.

notes.explains: After Nxc7, White wins a pawn and threatens the rook. Black is undeveloped and cannot defend properly.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is behind in development, every tactical blow is more effective. The knight fork on c7 exploits the loose pieces and the king's vulnerability.
notes.plans: White will capture the rook on a8 or continue attacking the queen and king, maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: Black plays …Bxf2+? hoping to create counterplay, but White replies Rxf2! Qxf2+ Rxf2, winning the queen. The f2 pawn's absence allows the rook to capture with check, and Black's queen is overloaded.
notes.teaches: When the opponent sacrifices material to open lines, you must calculate carefully. Here, capturing with the rook is winning because it comes with check and wins the queen. The f2 pawn's removal creates a discovered attack.
notes.plans: After Rxf2, White is up a piece and Black's king is exposed. White will consolidate and win.

notes.explains: The move Rxf2 is more elegant than Rd1 because it prevents Black from playing Qxc1+ with check. The rook on f2 also attacks the queen, forcing a win.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, prefer the move that gives the opponent the fewest counter-chances. Rxf2 is 'cultured' because it avoids unnecessary checks and keeps the attack flowing.
notes.plans: White will capture the queen and remain with a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: After Rxf2, White is up a piece and Black's king is exposed. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, simplify and avoid unnecessary risks. The endgame is a matter of technique.
notes.plans: White will activate the king and push pawns, while Black has no counterplay.

notes.explains: White places the bishop on d3 and will follow with c3 and Bf4, resembling a London system. Black's main challenge is finding a good square for the light-squared bishop on c8.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann Exchange, black often struggles to develop the c8-bishop; delaying ...Nc6 in favor of ...Nf6 can allow an early ...Bg4.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop the knight to f6 and then the bishop to g4 before white can play h3.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6 instead of the automatic Nc6, intending to develop the c8-bishop to g4 before white can play h3.
notes.teaches: Sometimes delaying natural moves like ...Nc6 can solve development problems; here ...Nf6 prepares ...Bg4, which is more active than ...Bf5.
notes.plans: After ...Nf6, if white plays c3, black can play ...Bg4; if white plays h3, black can revert to ...Nc6 and aim for ...e5.

notes.explains: White plays h3 to prevent ...Bg4, so black develops the knight to c6. Now white has played c3, and black can play ...e5 to challenge the center and create an IQP.
notes.teaches: When white delays knight development (e.g., playing c3 and h3 instead of Nf3), black can strike in the center with ...e5, often leading to an isolated queen pawn (IQP) for white.
notes.plans: Black plays ...e5, aiming to open the position and give white an isolated pawn on d5.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, the best line. Black must decide which piece to capture on d3. Taking with the knight eliminates the light-squared bishop, which is more valuable than the knight.
notes.teaches: When given a choice of captures, consider which piece is more important to remove. Here, the light-squared bishop is a key attacking piece, so capturing it with the knight is preferable.
notes.plans: Black plays Nxd3+, forcing Qxd3, then develops the dark-squared bishop to d6.

notes.explains: Black develops the dark-squared bishop to d6, a safe and active square. It eyes the kingside and avoids the problems of ...Bc5 (which allows Bb5+ forcing ...Nd7) or ...Be7 (too passive).
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the dark-squared bishop is often best placed on d6, where it is safe and contributes to the attack.
notes.plans: Black will castle, and if white plays Bg5, black will sacrifice the d5-pawn with ...h6 to activate the bishops.

notes.explains: White captures the pawn on d5, giving black the bishop pair. Black now has two bishops against two knights in an open position, which is a favorable imbalance.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is a powerful asset in open positions. Sacrificing a pawn to obtain it is often worth it, especially when the opponent's knights are not well-coordinated.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Rd8, attacking the queen and threatening ...Bh2+ to force the queen away from the center.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rd8, attacking the queen and threatening ...Bh2+ (which would win the queen if it captures on d5). White moves the queen to e3, the best square.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair and an open position, look for tactical threats like ...Bh2+ that exploit the opponent's undeveloped pieces. X-ray attacks on the queen are common.
notes.plans: Black now plays ...Bf5, developing with tempo and threatening to capture on b7. The idea is to keep the initiative and prevent white from completing development.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bf5, developing the bishop and threatening ...Qxb7. White cannot take on b7 because ...Rab8 would trap the queen. This move keeps the pressure on white's position.
notes.teaches: When you have the initiative, develop with tempo. Moves like ...Bf5 force the opponent to react and prevent them from consolidating.
notes.plans: Black will continue to harass the queen and look for ways to exploit white's lack of development, possibly with ...Bd3 or ...Bc7 ideas.

notes.explains: White plays Rd1, a natural move to contest the d-file. Black now has a choice between the direct ...Bd3 and the more subtle ...Bc7. Both are good, but ...Bd3 is more forcing.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple good options, trust your intuition and pick the most aggressive one. Spending too much time on equal alternatives is wasteful.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bd3, attacking the rook and preparing ...Bf4 to harass the queen. The bishop on d3 is untouchable and sets up further threats.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bd3, attacking the rook and threatening ...Bf4. The bishop is immune because ...Bf4 would attack the queen and create mating threats. White's queen is running out of squares.
notes.teaches: Initiative can be maintained by placing pieces on active squares that create multiple threats. The bishop on d3 is a classic example: it attacks the rook and prepares a battery with the other bishop.
notes.plans: After white moves the rook, black will play ...Bf4, forcing the queen to a worse square. The goal is to trap the queen or win material.

notes.explains: White plays Rd2, avoiding the immediate threat. Black now plays ...Bf4, attacking the queen. The queen's only safe squares are e1 and c5; e1 loses to ...Re8 trapping the queen, so c5 is forced.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is short of squares, look for ways to restrict it further. Here, ...Bf4 forces the queen to c5, where it is exposed.
notes.plans: Black will continue to harass the queen, possibly with ...b6 and ...a5, driving it to a3. The ultimate idea is to trap the queen with ...Bd6.

notes.explains: Black chases the queen to a3 with ...b6 and ...a5. The queen is now on the edge of the board, severely restricted. Black's bishops dominate the center and kingside.
notes.teaches: Pushing the opponent's queen to the edge of the board is a strategic success. It reduces the queen's influence and makes it a target.
notes.plans: Black now looks for a way to trap the queen or win material. The key idea is ...Bd6, threatening ...b4 and ...axb4, opening lines against the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bd6, threatening ...b4 and ...axb4, opening the a-file against the queen. White must respond with b4, but then ...axb4 opens the a-file and the queen is trapped.
notes.teaches: A retreating move like ...Bd6 can be powerful when it sets up a tactical threat. Here, the bishop returns to d6 to force b4, after which the queen is trapped.
notes.plans: After ...b4, black plays ...axb4, opening the a-file. The queen on a3 is then attacked by the rook on a8, and white must give up material to save it.

notes.explains: White plays b4 and Qb2, trying to save the queen. Black now has a choice: capture on b1 or keep the bishops. Keeping the bishops with ...Bg6 is stronger, as it maintains pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage (here, the bishop pair), avoid unnecessary piece exchanges. Keeping the bishops increases your winning chances.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bg6, maintaining the bishop pair and keeping the knight on b1 under pressure. White's position is paralyzed.

notes.explains: White plays cxb4, opening the c-file. Black now has a choice between ...Bc7 and ...Bf8. ...Bf8 is better because it keeps the bishop on the long diagonal and maintains pressure on d4.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, keep your bishops on active diagonals. ...Bf8 keeps the bishop on the a3-f8 diagonal, where it can later go to b6 or c7.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bf8, preparing to put the bishop on b6 or c7. The idea is to keep the initiative and eventually win the knight on c3.

notes.explains: White plays Rxd8+ and Nc3, trying to simplify. Black now has a winning tactic: ...Rd3 attacks the knight, and if it moves, ...Bxb4 wins the queen. White's best is ...Rc1, but then ...Bf4 and ...Rc2 follow.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's knight is undefended, look for ways to attack it with your rook. Here, ...Rd3 is a simple move that creates multiple threats.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Rd3, attacking the knight. If the knight moves, ...Bxb4 wins the queen. White's best defense is ...Rc1, but then ...Bf4 and ...Rc2 maintain the pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bf5, a subtle move that prepares ...Rxf3 gxf3 Qg6+ forking the king and rook on c2. This wins material.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet move like ...Bf5 can set up a tactical shot. Here, it clears the g6 square for the queen, creating a fork.
notes.plans: After ...Bf5, if white plays ...Ne1, black plays ...Rd8, attacking the rook on c2. The rook must move to e2, then ...Be5 pins the knight, and ...Rc8 wins the knight on c3.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rc8, attacking the pinned knight on c3. The knight is lost because it is attacked twice and defended only once. White cannot save it without losing more material.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, attack it with another piece. Here, the knight on c3 is pinned by the bishop on e5, and ...Rc8 adds a second attacker, winning the knight.
notes.plans: After winning the knight, black will simplify to a winning endgame with an extra piece.

notes.explains: Black wins the knight and simplifies to a winning endgame with an extra piece. The rest is technique: trade queens, freeze white's pawns with ...b5, and pick them off with the bishop.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, simplify by trading pieces while keeping a material advantage. Use the 'deep freeze' technique (playing ...b5) to immobilize enemy pawns and then capture them.
notes.plans: Black will trade queens, play ...b5 to freeze white's queenside pawns, and then use the bishops to capture them. The extra piece will decide the game.

notes.explains: After Qxg5, Black's king is cut off. Rh1 forces ...Kg8, then Nh5 threatens both Qxg7# and Nf6#. Black's only defense is a meaningless check.
notes.teaches: In mating attacks, cutting off the king's escape and coordinating pieces (queen, rook, knight) is decisive. Look for double threats.
notes.plans: Execute the mate: Nh5, then meet any check by moving the king, as mate is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black's setup with pawns on d5, f5, and e6 (a Maróczy Bind shifted over) makes it hard for White to free himself. Black's strategy is to maintain the clamp and slowly improve.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a clamped center, avoid opening the position prematurely. Instead, make improving moves like Re8 (preventing e5) and centralize knights.
notes.plans: Black can consider Ne4, c6, or even g6, but the most flexible is Re8. Later, the queen can lift to e6 and h6 to start a kingside attack.

notes.explains: White's Ba3 is a good idea, aiming to trade off Black's powerful bishop on d6. Black should avoid c5 (which opens the center) and instead play c6 to maintain the clamp.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to trade a key defender, consider reinforcing your structure rather than opening lines. c6 protects d5 and keeps the position closed.
notes.plans: Black plays c6, then can develop the knight via a6-c7 or move the queen to e6 to free d7 for the knight. The queen lift to h6 is a long-term attacking idea.

notes.explains: White's c4 is too late; Black has already improved his position. Black now launches a kingside attack with Qe6 and Qh6, exploiting White's weakened king safety.
notes.teaches: Positional play and attacking are not mutually exclusive. Once you have a positional grip, you can transition to a direct attack on the king.
notes.plans: Black plays Qe6 (opening d7 for the knight), then Qh6, followed by Ndf6 and Ng4, targeting h3 and f3. The knight on f3 is White's only defender.

notes.explains: White's g3 weakens h3, allowing Black to play Qh3 and then Ng4, creating a deadly threat. The knight on f3 is overloaded, and Black can sacrifice on h2 or simply play Ng5 to distract it.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for weaknesses created by defensive moves. g3 weakens h3, and the knight on f3 becomes a critical defender that can be overloaded.
notes.plans: Black plays Qh3, then Ng4, threatening Nxh2. If White defends with Re1, Black can play Ng5, overloading the f3 knight. The immediate threat is Nxf3 followed by Qxh2# or similar.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng5, threatening Nxf3 and then Qxh2#. White's knight on f3 is the only defender; if it moves, Black crashes through. White's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, identify the key defender and find ways to eliminate it. Here, Ng5 forces the knight to move or be exchanged, leading to mate.
notes.plans: Black continues with Nxf3+ if allowed, then Qxh2#. If White avoids the trade, Black can play Rh6 and Nxh2, or simply take on f3 anyway.

notes.explains: After White takes on g5, Black recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file. Qxg5+ forces Kh1, then Qh6 renews the threat. White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn recapture opens lines for your attack. fxg5 opens the f-file and gives Black a passed pawn.
notes.plans: Black continues with Rh6 and Nxh2, or simply Qxh2# if possible. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the knight on h2, forcing Kxh2, then Qxh2#. This is a classic sacrifice to remove the king's pawn shield.
notes.teaches: When the king is exposed, a knight sacrifice on h2 can be decisive if the queen is nearby to deliver mate.
notes.plans: Black plays Nxh2, and after Kxh2, Qxh2# is mate.

notes.explains: After dxe5 and Qxd8, the exchange variation arises. White's knight on d5 looks strong but is not immediately dangerous. Black cannot play c6 because Nc7 traps the rook. The knight attacks c7, so Black must defend it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a centralized knight can be more of a mirage than a threat if the opponent can challenge it. Look beyond the immediate outpost to the long-term control of central squares.
notes.plans: Play Na6 to defend c7 and prepare to challenge the knight on d5 with c6 later. If Bg5, respond with Rd6 to unpin the knight and protect f6.

notes.explains: White retreated the bishop to b2, which is not the most challenging move. White should have played Be3 to restrict Black's knight on a6 and prepare c5. Now Black can proceed with the plan.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, every tempo matters. White's passive bishop move allows Black to execute his plan without hindrance. Always consider the most active square for your pieces.
notes.plans: Black can now play Nb4 or Ndc5 to reroute the knight toward d4. The immediate Nb4 is tempting, but after Rc1, the knight has no good follow-up. Better to play Ndc5, threatening Nd3 fork and preparing to go to e6 and then d4.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd7, a typical King's Indian maneuver. This move covers c5, opens the diagonal for the bishop on g7, and prepares to reroute both knights toward d4. The knight on f6 was awkward and needed to be repositioned.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, don't hesitate to move a piece multiple times to improve its effectiveness. Nd7 is a regrouping move that enhances coordination and prepares future centralization.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Ndc5, then Ne6, and finally Nd4. The knight on d4 will dominate the board. Meanwhile, Black can also consider trading dark-squared bishops to weaken White's control of d4.

notes.explains: White plays g4, a typical pawn storm move, but here it is a mistake because the queens are off. It creates a permanent weakness on f4 without any attacking prospects. Black can now target f4 with a knight.
notes.teaches: Pawn storms are only effective when the king is exposed and the position is open. In endgames or closed positions, advancing pawns creates weaknesses that the opponent can exploit. Always consider the downside of pawn moves.
notes.plans: Black can now aim to get a knight to f4 via d3 or e6. The knight on d4 can later move to f4, or the other knight can go to f4 via g5 or e6. The weakness on f4 becomes a long-term target.

notes.explains: Black plays Ndc5, threatening Nd3+ and preparing to reroute the knight to e6 and then d4. The knight on b4 also supports this maneuver. Black is systematically improving his pieces.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece improvement is a long-term process. Each move should have a clear purpose, and you should be willing to spend tempos to get your pieces to ideal squares.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne6 next, attacking the bishop on g5 and forcing it to move. Then Nd4 will be established. After that, Black can double rooks on the d-file and consider trading dark-squared bishops.

notes.explains: Black achieves the long-awaited knight on d4. This knight dominates the board, controlling key squares and restricting White's pieces. It is a major strategic victory.
notes.teaches: Centralizing a knight in a closed position is a huge achievement. A knight on d4 controls eight squares and often cannot be easily dislodged. Celebrate small victories and build on them.
notes.plans: Black will now solidify the knight by doubling rooks on the d-file and preparing to trade dark-squared bishops. The knight on d4 is a permanent outpost that will eventually win material or create decisive threats.

notes.explains: Black plays Rcd8, doubling rooks on the d-file and threatening Nxc2+ forking the king and rook. This increases the pressure on White's position. White must be careful to avoid tactical tricks.
notes.teaches: Doubling rooks on an open file is a classic way to increase pressure. Always look for tactical threats like forks when your pieces are centralized.
notes.plans: Black will continue to improve the position, possibly playing Bf6 to trade dark-squared bishops or rerouting the knight on b4 to f4. The pressure will eventually force White to weaken further.

notes.explains: White plays Bf1, a passive move. Black now has a choice: continue with Nc5 to head for f4, or play Bf6 to trade dark-squared bishops. Both are good.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a passive move, you have the luxury of choosing among several good plans. Evaluate which plan is most effective and proceed.
notes.plans: Black can play Nc5, heading for e6 and then f4, or play Bf6, threatening to trade bishops and weaken White's control of d4. The knight on d4 is already strong, so Black can afford to be flexible.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc5, heading for e6 and then f4. This knight will target the weak f4 square created by White's g4 move. The knight on d4 remains a permanent outpost.
notes.teaches: When you have a weak square in the opponent's camp, reroute a knight to exploit it. The knight on c5 can go to e6 and then f4, or directly to d3 and then f4.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne6 next, then Nf4, creating a powerful knight on f4 that attacks the pawn on g2 and restricts White's pieces.

notes.explains: White plays b4, attacking the knight on c5. Black can simply retreat to e6, maintaining the threat to go to f4. White's queenside expansion does not address the central weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Don't be distracted by your opponent's flank operations. If your central control is strong, you can ignore flank pawn moves and continue with your plan.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne6, then Nf4. The knight on f4 will be very strong. Black can also consider Bf6 to trade bishops, further weakening White's control of d4.

notes.explains: Black retreats to e6, maintaining the threat to go to f4. The knight on d4 is still strong. Black is patiently improving the position.
notes.teaches: Patience is key in closed positions. Don't rush; make small improvements and wait for your opponent to weaken further.
notes.plans: Black will play Nf4 next, creating a powerful knight. After that, Black can consider trading bishops or doubling rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: White plays Ng3, a decisive mistake. This allows Black to trade dark-squared bishops with Bf6, after which the weak squares on d4 and f4 become indefensible. White should have taken the knight on d4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a strong knight on d4, you must consider trading it. Allowing Black to keep the knight and trade bishops is fatal. Always evaluate which pieces are most important to trade.
notes.plans: Black will play Bf6, forcing the trade of bishops. After that, the knight on d4 is even stronger, and Black can target the f4 square with the other knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Bf6, forcing the trade of dark-squared bishops. This is a decisive improvement because White's best defensive piece is removed, leaving the weak squares d4 and f4 completely exposed.
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's best piece is a fundamental strategic goal. Here, the dark-squared bishop was White's main defender of the weak squares. Once it's gone, Black's knights dominate.
notes.plans: After the trade, Black will have a knight on d4 and another heading to f4. The position becomes a technical win.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc2+, forking the king and rook. This is the tactical payoff for the positional pressure. The knight on d4 was perfectly placed to exploit the alignment of the king and rook on the d-file.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong positional advantage, always be alert for tactical opportunities. The knight on d4 not only controls squares but also creates tactical threats like forks.
notes.plans: After Nc2+, Black will win the exchange. The resulting endgame is easily winning due to the extra material and Black's dominant knights.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange and a pawn. The position is now a technical win. Black has a rook and two knights against White's rook and bishop, with a dominant position.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, simplify to a winning endgame. Here, Black can trade rooks and use the extra pawn to win.
notes.plans: Black will play Rd2+ to force rook trades, then use the knights to pick off White's pawns. The endgame is straightforward.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd2+, forcing the trade of rooks. This simplifies to a winning endgame where Black's knights dominate White's bishop.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. Here, trading rooks leaves Black with a material advantage and no risk.
notes.plans: After the rook trade, Black will use the knights to attack White's pawns and promote a pawn.

notes.explains: Black wins the rook and now has a decisive material advantage. The knights will easily pick off White's remaining pawns.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, use your pieces to target the opponent's weaknesses. Here, the knights can attack the pawns on the kingside.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne4 or similar to attack the f-pawn, then win more pawns. The game is over.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6 attacking b2. White should not defend b2 with b3 because that blocks the b3 square for the knight. Instead, ignore the pawn and continue development.
notes.teaches: If Black captures on b2, opening the b-file with Rb1 gives White a strong attack due to Black's poor development. Intuitively, this is bad for Black, so you don't need to calculate.
notes.plans: Play Nbd2, then Nb3, and later Rc1, targeting the d4 pawn at leisure.

notes.explains: White takes on d4 with the f-knight, not the b-knight. This keeps the b-knight on b3 to potentially jump to c5, and prepares a kingside pawn push with f4-f5.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which knight to use based on future plans: the b-knight stays for queenside pressure, the f-knight clears the way for f4.
notes.plans: Play Be3, then consider f4-f5 to attack Black's kingside. The d4 square is controlled by the knight.

notes.explains: If Black plays Nxe5, White has the brilliant move Nc6, attacking the queen and threatening the knight. The queen cannot protect the knight without walking into an x-ray.
notes.teaches: Look for double attacks and x-ray tactics when the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated. Even if you miss the best move, simpler continuations like Qh5 still give White a strong attack.
notes.plans: After Nc6, Black's queen must move, and White can capture on a7 or continue the attack.

notes.explains: Black captures on a2. White can ignore this pawn and play Qe2, preparing to shift the queen to g4 to target g7, or play f4 to start a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for long-term positional pressure and attacking chances is a key concept. The a2 pawn is irrelevant for the next 20 moves; White's initiative is worth more.
notes.plans: Play f4, then f5, opening lines on the kingside. The queen on e2 can later go to g4.

notes.explains: White launches a demolition sacrifice: sacrificing a piece to destroy Black's king cover. After f4-f5, White opens the e-file and delivers a quick checkmate.
notes.teaches: A demolition sacrifice is used to rip open the pawn shield around the king. Once the king is exposed, the remaining pieces can deliver a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After f5, capture on e6, then play Qe6+ followed by Bd4+ and Qf6+ etc., forcing mate.

notes.explains: The attack from f4 to checkmate took only seven moves. White's intuition to sacrifice the a2 pawn and then the exchange was justified by the overwhelming attack.
notes.teaches: When you have the initiative, you don't need to calculate every line. Intuition, built from pattern recognition, tells you that the attack is worth the material.

notes.explains: If Black plays c4, White should not be afraid. c4 takes pressure off the d4 pawn, allowing White to focus on kingside play. The closed center gives White time to attack.
notes.teaches: In the Steinitz, c4 actually benefits White because it diverts Black's resources from attacking d4. White can then invest tempi in a kingside assault.
notes.plans: Develop with Bd3, then prepare f4-f5. The center is closed, so White's attack is not easily countered.

notes.explains: If Black plays Bc5, White has a powerful attacking continuation: Rxc5! This sacrifices the exchange but opens lines. After Nxc6 (double attack on queen), White captures on g7 and has overwhelming compensation.
notes.teaches: Positional sacrifices like the exchange can be justified by long-term pressure. Even if you are down material, if your opponent is passive and uncoordinated, you have full compensation.
notes.plans: After Nxg7, drop the knight back to f5 and build up against Black's king. The attack may take several moves but is crushing.

notes.explains: White plays f4 before Nc3, which allows …d5. This is a legitimate but slightly inaccurate move order; the Grand Prix Attack usually starts with Nc3 to prevent d5.
notes.teaches: Punish inaccurate move orders by striking in the center immediately. …d5 challenges White's center and exploits the absence of the knight on c3.
notes.plans: After …d5, if White takes on d5, Black should not recapture with the queen but instead play Nf6, offering a pawn for rapid development and central control.

notes.explains: After exd5, Black plays …Nf6, not Qxd5. If White tries to hold the pawn with c4, Black plays e6, and after the trade on d5, Black gets tremendous positional compensation—better development and control of the center.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for rapid development and central control can be more valuable than material. The queen on d5 would be vulnerable without the knight on c3 to defend it.
notes.plans: Black will recapture the pawn on d5 later, enjoying a lead in development and pressure against White's center.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, threatening the knight on d5. Black should retreat the knight to b6, not take on f4. Taking on f4 would allow Qf3, creating awkward threats and blocking Black's dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: Don't grab pawns at the cost of piece activity and king safety. The pawn on f4 is actually beneficial for Black because it restricts White's bishop and king-side play.
notes.plans: Play Nb6, forcing the bishop to move. After Bb3, play c4, trapping the bishop and forcing Bb5+ (or Bc4). Then trade light-squared bishops with Bd7, simplifying into a favorable position.

notes.explains: Black forces the trade of light-squared bishops. White's dark-squared bishop is terrible because the pawn on f4 hems it in. Black gains control of the d4 square, a key outpost.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a bad bishop, trade the good one to leave them with the bad one. The c5 pawn controls d4, preventing White from playing d4 to free their position.
notes.plans: After the bishop trade, develop with Nc6, castles, and prepare to win back the pawn on d5. Black has a comfortable position with a clamp on d4.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, threatening Ng5 or Ne5. Black's priority is to get the king to safety and complete development. The long-term plan is 'castling by hand': move the king to g8 manually.
notes.teaches: When you cannot castle conventionally, you can manually castle by moving the king to g8 and the rook to f8 or e8. This is a common technique when the king has moved or the path is blocked.
notes.plans: Short-term: develop king-side pieces and avoid tactics. Long-term: play g6, Bg7, Rf8, and Kg8. The knight on f3 threatens e5, so Black must be careful not to allow a strong knight outpost.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, preparing Bg7 and manual castling. This is more important than developing the queen-side knight. White's attack is unsound; Black should not fear the exposed king.
notes.teaches: Prioritize king safety and development over material. Even if the king looks exposed, if the opponent lacks firepower, it is safe. Don't be intimidated by aggressive but unsound sacrifices.
notes.plans: Continue with Bg7, Rf8, Kg8. If White gives check on g5 or e5, Black can move the king to e8 or g8, and White's attack fizzles due to lack of pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Rf8, continuing manual castling. White now plays f5, trying to open lines. Black must decide how to recapture: with the pawn or with the bishop?
notes.teaches: When a pawn captures another pawn, consider which squares become newly accessible to the opponent. After gxf5, the h5 square becomes available to White's queen, which could lead to dangerous checks.
notes.plans: Black can take with the pawn (gxf5) or ignore the pawn and continue with Kg8. Taking with the pawn is principled but requires care against Qh5+ and Nf7 forks. Ignoring the pawn is also possible if Black calculates that White's attack is harmless.

notes.explains: Black takes on f5 with the pawn. Now White plays Ng5+ and Black must choose the correct king retreat. King to e8 would allow Qh5+ and a fork on f7. King to g8 is safer.
notes.teaches: In king safety, the square you retreat to matters. Avoid squares that allow the opponent to create double threats. Always consider checks and forks when moving the king.
notes.plans: After Kg8, if White plays Qh5, Black can defend f7 with Qf8. Then play h6 to drive the knight away. Black's king is safe and White's attack fizzles.
