notes.explains: Black plays Kg8, avoiding the fork. White now plays Qh5, threatening Qxf7#. Black can defend with Qf8, then h6 to kick the knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent threatens mate, look for defensive moves that also counterattack. Qf8 defends f7 and prepares to trap the knight with h6.
notes.plans: Play Qf8, then h6. After the knight retreats, Black is safe and can complete development. Black is up a piece and will soon win the pawn on f5.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf8, defending f7 and preparing h6. White's attack is over. Black is up a piece and will soon consolidate.
notes.teaches: Once the immediate threats are parried, the defender's material advantage becomes decisive. Don't rush to counterattack; first ensure king safety.
notes.plans: Play h6, forcing the knight to move. Then recapture the pawn on f5 with the queen or bishop. Black will have a winning position.

notes.explains: Black plays h6, forcing the knight to retreat. White's attack is completely refuted. Black is up a piece and will soon win the pawn on f5.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to drive away attackers. Once the attacker is repelled, the defender's material advantage becomes decisive.
notes.plans: After the knight moves, play Qxf5 or Bxf5, then complete development with Nc6, etc. Black's king is safe and White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: White retreats the knight to f3. Black can now simply take the knight on f3, as White has no compensation. Alternatively, Black could play Qg4, trading queens, which is simplest.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplification is often the easiest path to victory. Trading queens reduces White's attacking chances and leaves Black with a decisive material advantage.
notes.plans: Play Qxf3 or Qg4 (forcing queen trade). Then develop the queen-side knight and rook. Black's king is safe and White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: Black takes the knight on f3. White has no attack left. Black is up a piece and will soon win the pawn on f5. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's attack is refuted, the defender should calmly capture material and consolidate. There is no need for risky counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Qxf5, then develop the queen-side. Black's king is safe and White's king is exposed. Black will soon launch a mating attack.

notes.explains: Black recaptures the pawn on f5. Now Black is up a piece and a pawn. White's king is exposed. Black should now look for a direct attack.
notes.teaches: Once material is secured, transition to a king hunt. The exposed white king is a target. Use checks and threats to force mate or win more material.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, then bring the rook to f8. Black can also consider Qd4+ to force the king to g2, then Qg4+ or other checks. The key is to calculate accurately to avoid counterplay.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to c6, preparing to bring the rook to f8. White's king is still on g1, vulnerable. Black should now consider checks like Qd4+.
notes.teaches: Keep your pieces active and coordinate them for an attack. The queen and rook can work together to exploit the exposed king.
notes.plans: Play Rf8, then Qd4+ to force the king to g2. Then Qg4+ or other checks. Black must calculate carefully to avoid letting White's king escape.

notes.explains: Black plays Rf8, activating the rook. White now plays Qh5, threatening Qxf7#. Black can defend with Qf8 again, but also has a tactical idea: Qd4+.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is on h5, the rook on f1 is undefended (type 2 undefended piece). A check on d4 can force the king to move, creating a discovered attack on the rook.
notes.plans: Play Qd4+! If Kg2, then Qg4+ forcing queen trade. If Kh1, then Bxe4+ wins. Black must calculate the line: Qd4+ Kg2 Qg4+ Kh1 Qxf5 Rxf5, and Black is up a piece.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd4+, forcing the king to g2. Now Black can play Qg4+, forcing queen trade. After Qxg4 hxg4, Black is up a piece and a pawn with a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, trading queens simplifies the position and reduces counterplay. The check on d4 also exploits the undefended rook on f1.
notes.plans: After Qg4+, White must trade queens. Then Black has a winning endgame. Alternatively, Black could play for mate, but simplification is safer.

notes.explains: Black plays Qg4+, forcing queen trade. White cannot avoid it without losing material. After the trade, Black is up a piece and a pawn.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, the simplest path is often the best. Forcing a queen trade removes all counterplay and leaves you with a technically winning endgame.
notes.plans: After Qxg4 hxg4, Black has a rook and knight for a rook and pawn, with an extra piece. Develop the queen-side and push pawns.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black is up a piece and a pawn. The endgame is winning. Black should develop the queen-side and activate the king.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, activate your king and centralize your pieces. Avoid unnecessary risks and use your material advantage to create passed pawns.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, then bring the rook to f8. The king can go to g7 or h7. Push the queen-side pawns. White has no counterplay.

notes.explains: Black has castled queenside and is pushing kingside pawns to create a mating attack. White's knight on h1 is trapped, and Black's bishop on d6 is powerful. The key is to open lines without allowing White counterplay.
notes.teaches: When attacking, coordinate pieces to exploit weaknesses. Here, Black uses the g2 square as a hook to tie down White's pieces, then switches to the e-file when White defends.
notes.plans: Black should continue pushing the h-pawn to open the h-file, while keeping the e-file closed to restrict White's rooks. If White plays f4, Black can occupy the e3 square with a rook.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd4 to defend the e3 square, preventing White's knight from jumping there after h3. This ensures that h3 will be a crushing move, as the knight cannot escape to e3.
notes.teaches: Before executing a pawn break, check if the opponent has a defensive resource that could neutralize it. Here, Nd4 eliminates the knight's escape square, making h3 decisive.
notes.plans: After Nd4, Black plays h3, threatening mate on g2. White must respond with Nh4, after which Black can eliminate the knight with Be7, forcing f4, then take on h4 and occupy the e-file.

notes.explains: Black has sacrificed material to create a mating attack. White's king is exposed, and Black's rook on h2 ties down White's pieces. The immediate threat is Rh1#.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use a rook to create a 'hook' that ties down the defender. Here, the rook on h2 prevents White from moving the f2 rook, as it would allow mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press the attack, possibly by bringing the queen to the h-file or opening the center. White's only defense is to block with the rook on f2, but Black can then infiltrate on the e-file.

notes.explains: Black has won material and is converting the advantage. The queen and rook coordinate to create mating threats, while White's king is exposed. Black's pawns on the queenside are also a threat.
notes.teaches: In converting a winning position, avoid unnecessary risks. Use the queen to control key squares and prevent counterplay. Here, Black's queen infiltrates and forces mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue to harass the white king with checks, while advancing the queenside pawns. The immediate plan is to deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: Black has pushed the h-pawn to h4, creating a potential mating square on g2. White's knight is trapped on h1, and Black's bishop on d6 is powerful. The position is ripe for a breakthrough.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are passive, pushing pawns to create weaknesses is effective. Here, h4 threatens h3, which would open the h-file and create mate threats.
notes.plans: Black should play Nd4 to prevent White's knight from escaping to e3, then play h3. After White's knight goes to h4, Black can eliminate it with Be7, forcing f4, then take on h4 and occupy the e-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxg3, sacrificing the bishop to open the h-file. After fxg3, Black has Rxh2+ and Reh8, creating a decisive attack. The sacrifice is sound because White's king is exposed and Black's rooks dominate.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is worth sacrificing a piece to open lines against the enemy king. Here, the bishop sacrifice removes a defender and opens the h-file, allowing Black's rooks to deliver mate.
notes.plans: After Bxg3, Black plays Rxh2+ and Reh8, threatening Rh1#. White must give up material to avoid immediate mate, but Black's attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: Black's queen and rook coordinate to deliver checkmate. The queen chases the white king across the board, while the rook on h2 prevents escape. The final checkmate is Qa4#.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, use checks to drive the king to a mating net. Here, the queen's checks force the king to the edge, where the rook and queen deliver mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue checking until the king is trapped. The rook on h2 controls the h-file, while the queen covers the a4 square for mate.

notes.explains: Black's final move Qa4# delivers checkmate. The queen is supported by the rook on h2, and the white king has no escape squares.
notes.teaches: Always look for the most efficient checkmate. Here, Qa4# is a classic mate with queen and rook against a lone king.

notes.explains: Black's setup with e6 and g6 creates dark-square weaknesses on the kingside. White's h4 is a provocative move that exploits these weaknesses by threatening to open lines or create a stronghold on g5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates a complex of weaknesses (like dark squares), open the position and create tension to exploit them. A pawn push like h4 can provoke further weaknesses or set up attacking ideas.
notes.plans: If Black plays h5, White can occupy g5 with a bishop or knight. If Black castles, White can play hxg6 and open the h-file for a mating attack. If Black plays h6, White can continue with h5 and g4 to blast open the kingside.

notes.explains: After Black plays h5, White's g5 forces Nh7, then h6 dislodges the bishop. Black's king is exposed, and White's queen on d2 threatens Qg5#. The key is to notice that g5 is the only mating square and to prepare it with a battery.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is short of squares, identify the potential mating squares and find a way to deliver a piece there. Sometimes a quiet move like Qd2, building a battery, is more effective than a flashy sacrifice.
notes.plans: White's plan is to play Qg5 with checkmate. Black can delay with ...f6, but then Bg5 is still deadly. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black allowed h5 and then White played h6, attacking the bishop on g7. The double threat of hxg7 and h7 is devastating because Black cannot contain all the weaknesses.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pawn on h5, the pawn can be used to dislodge the defender of the kingside (h6) or to open the h-file (hxg6) after castling. These are two key ideas in such structures.
notes.plans: White will play hxg7 or h7, opening lines or promoting. Black's position collapses due to the multiple threats.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White's queen on d2 threatens Qg5#. Black's only try is ...f6, but then Bg5 is still mate. The attack is clean and winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a mating threat, look for the simplest way to deliver it. Don't overcomplicate with sacrifices if a quiet move like Qd2 sets up an unstoppable threat.
notes.plans: White plays Qg5 next move, checkmate. Black cannot prevent it.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...f6 to block the mate, White simply plays Bg5, renewing the threat. Black's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: When a mating threat is blocked, look for another piece to deliver the same mate. The idea of transferring the mating piece to the key square is common.
notes.plans: White will play Bg5, and Black cannot stop Qg5# or Bxf6.

notes.explains: After Bg5, if Black takes, White recaptures with check and then mates. The attack is straightforward.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the simplest recapture leads to a winning attack. Don't overlook basic checks and captures.
notes.plans: White plays Qg5+ and then mates. Black's king has no escape.

notes.explains: The final checkmate: Qh6#. The attack succeeded because White exploited the dark-square weaknesses created by Black's e6 and g6 setup.
notes.teaches: A well-prepared pawn storm can lead to a decisive mating attack. The key is to identify the weaknesses and commit to the attack with precise moves.
notes.plans: White delivers checkmate. The game is over.

notes.explains: Black's best response to h4 is probably h5, accepting the weakness on g5 but avoiding a direct attack. Even so, White gets a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When facing a provocative pawn push like h4, the lesser evil is often to accept a small weakness (like h5) rather than allowing a devastating attack. Sometimes you must choose the least bad option.
notes.plans: Black will try to defend the kingside, but White's pressure on the dark squares remains. Black's position is difficult but defensible.

notes.explains: After Bg5, Black's position is hopeless. The attack is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, don't hesitate. Play the most forcing moves to convert.
notes.plans: White will play Qg5# or Bxf6 next. Black cannot prevent mate.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 g6 Bf4 Bg7, White's Bf4 is standard but the choice of fianchetto and d6 leads to a decision: prepare e5 or c5. Here, Black should orient toward e5 because White's bishop on d3 is inaccurately placed, making e5 a threat with tempo.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, choose your pawn break (e5 or c5) early and be consistent. Bishop d3 is inaccurate because it allows e5 with tempo and exposes the bishop to a fork.
notes.plans: Prepare e5 by playing Nc6 and then e5, or first play Re8 to induce a prophylactic move like Bc2.

notes.explains: Black plays h6 to ask the bishop's intentions. White's bishop retreats to h4. Black develops harmoniously with Be6 and Qe7, then plays Nd5, putting the knight on a protected square and preparing f5.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, ask your opponent's pieces questions with moves like h6. Place knights on safe, central squares like d5 to prepare pawn breaks.
notes.plans: After Nd5, Black is ready to play f5, which will attack White's center and potentially trap the bishop on g3 if White castles kingside.

notes.explains: After White castles, Black plays g5 and then f5. White's bishop on g3 is now trapped by the pawn on f4. White's knight on e4 is also under attack. Black wins a piece.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is on g3 and you have a pawn on f5, pushing to f4 can trap the bishop. Always be alert for such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After f5, if White moves the knight, Black captures the bishop on g3. If White tries to save the bishop, Black wins material.

notes.explains: After the sequence, Black wins the queen and is two pieces up. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simplify and avoid unnecessary risks. Protect your king and consolidate.
notes.plans: Play Qxg7, then centralize the knight and support it with c6 to prevent counterplay.

notes.explains: The Armenian variation (or similar) involves playing Nfd7 instead of Nc6. This blocks the bishop but accelerates e5 and allows f5 later. After e5, White's best is Bg5, but Black gets two bishops and a good position.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian against the London, Nfd7 is a flexible move that prepares e5 and f5. Blocking the bishop is not a drawback if it speeds up your pawn breaks.
notes.plans: After Nfd7, play e5, then f5, and later return the knight to f6 to open the diagonal for the bishop.

notes.explains: After White plays Bg5 and Black plays h6, White should take on f6 to avoid losing a piece. If White retreats to h4, Black can play g5 and then e4, winning the piece.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is pinned, be careful not to overextend. Sometimes giving up the bishop pair is better than losing a piece.
notes.plans: If White takes on f6, Black recaptures with the queen or bishop and then pushes f5 and g5 to attack.

notes.explains: If White plays Bxf6 before retreating to g3, Black's f5 push is less effective because White can play e4 to block. The difference is crucial: White gains a tempo to stop Black's attack.
notes.teaches: Timing matters in pawn breaks. A preparatory move like Bxf6 can neutralize Black's f5 advance.
notes.plans: White should consider Bxf6 before Bg3 to prevent Black's f5. Then Black might play h5 to start a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After g5, White's best is to maneuver the knight to g3 and then f5, creating pressure. Black must respond with Bd5 to prevent Qf3 and the collapse of the kingside.
notes.teaches: Even after sacrificing a piece, look for positional ideas. Maneuvering knights to strong squares can compensate for material deficit.
notes.plans: White should play Ng3-f5, threatening to invade. Black should play Bd5 to cover f3 and prepare exchanges.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh5, but White can now play Bxh6, opening the h-file. If Black recaptures, White has Ng5+ and a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent blockades with a knight, look for sacrifices to open lines. The knight on h3 supports g5 and a potential Ng5.
notes.plans: White can take on h6, then follow up with Ng5, forcing weaknesses.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop to open the h-file and bring the knight to g5 with tempo. Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack, sacrificing material to open lines is often worth it if you can bring pieces quickly to the king.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qxh6 or O-O-O, bringing more pieces into the attack.

notes.explains: White captures on e5, opening both the e-file and f-file. Black's king is completely exposed, and White's queen and rook deliver mate.
notes.teaches: Once files are opened against an exposed king, the attack is often unstoppable. Use your queen and rook to deliver checks and force mate.
notes.plans: White plays Qf7+ followed by Qg7#. Black's king has no escape squares.

notes.explains: After both kings move to b1 and b8, White's next step is to trade off Black's strongest piece: the bishop on e5. Bf4 is a good move because it exchanges a powerful bishop for a passive one, and the tactics work (Nxd4 is impossible due to pin).
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's best piece is a key positional idea. Here, the bishop on e5 controls many squares; removing it leaves Black with a bad bishop on e6.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, then after the trade, bring the rook to e1 to pressure the e6 bishop, and continue improving pieces.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade, White has a pleasant position. The next step is to bring the rook to e1, putting pressure on the e6 bishop. Black's pieces are passive, and White can continue accumulating pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, keep making improving moves. Bring rooks to open files, target weak pieces, and avoid rushing. The opponent will eventually run out of good moves.
notes.plans: Play Rde1, then consider tactical ideas like Bxe6 followed by Qd6 trade, exploiting the alignment of rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd6, offering a queen trade. White can transform the positional advantage into a tactical one by noticing the alignment of rooks on the d-file and the undefended rook on d6. The sequence Bxe6 (defending the queen), then Qxd6, then Nxe6 exploits this.
notes.teaches: When all your pieces are on perfect squares, look for tactics. Here, the undefended rook on d6 and the alignment of heavy pieces create a tactical opportunity. Don't be afraid to change the pawn structure to shift the target of attack.
notes.plans: Play Bxe6, then Qxd6, then Nxe6, winning a pawn. The resulting endgame is winning due to the weak e6 pawn and active pieces.

notes.explains: After Nxe6, White has won a pawn. The knight on e6 is strong, controlling d8 and attacking the d5 pawn. Black's pieces are passive. White's plan is to consolidate and win more pawns.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, keep your rooks on open files and use your knight to create threats. Avoid tunneling on one weakness; look for ways to create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Play Ba4 (to later go to b3, attacking d5), then c3 to immobilize d5, and eventually win the d5 pawn. If Black tries counterplay, use tactics like Ng7 to fork rooks.

notes.explains: After …Nb4, White has a winning tactic: Ng7 forks the rooks. This move is easy to miss because the knight goes to an unusual square (g7), but it exploits the undefended rook on e8 and the pinned knight on e7.
notes.teaches: Avoid tunnel vision on one plan (e.g., winning the d5 pawn). Look for geometric moves like knight forks. When your pieces are well-placed, always check for tactical blows that win material immediately.
notes.plans: Play Ng7, winning the exchange. After that, use the extra material to win the game.

notes.explains: The Danish Gambit sacrifices one or two pawns (here c3 offers a second pawn after …exd4) to gain a lead in development and the initiative.
notes.teaches: Gambits require a mentality ready to sacrifice material for rapid development and attacking chances. Prioritize piece activity over pawns.
notes.plans: Develop quickly with Bc4, Nf3, and castle, aiming bishops at the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, not recapturing the pawn, maintaining the gambit mentality. Black's knight on e4 is undefended and the king is still in the center, making the knight a tactical target.
notes.teaches: A piece in the center is not automatically good if it is undefended and the opponent's king is exposed. Avoid forcing it away; instead, prevent Black from stabilizing it with d5.
notes.plans: Develop Nf3, castle, and consider Qb3 to control d5 and threaten f7.

notes.explains: Black's a6 is a waste of time; he should have played d5 immediately to attack the bishop and secure the knight. Violating opening principles (control center, develop) without good reason is punished.
notes.teaches: If you are not controlling the center or developing, you need a very good reason. Preparing b5 is not sufficient.
notes.plans: White should play Qb3, building a battery with the bishop and threatening f7, while also controlling d5.

notes.explains: After Bxf7+ and Rxe1, Black can play c4, intercepting the queen's protection of the bishop. This is a common tactical resource: a pawn move that breaks the connection between pieces.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned or under attack, look for intermediate moves (like c4) that disrupt the opponent's coordination. This is a form of 'desperado' – if you will lose a piece, get as much material as possible in return.
notes.plans: If Black plays c4, White should capture the knight on e4 (taking something) rather than losing the bishop for nothing.

notes.explains: After …Kf7, both queens are hanging. This is a highly tactical situation. The key is to move your queen with check (e.g., Qb3+ or Qd5+) so that after the king moves, you can capture the opponent's queen.
notes.teaches: When both queens are en prise, look for a check that moves your queen away safely. This is a common tactical motif.
notes.plans: Play Qd5+ (or Qb3+) to force the king to move, then capture the queen on e4.

notes.explains: Black's king is on f6, exposed. White has a rook and queen active. The goal is to hunt the king, often by sacrificing pieces to lure it further into the open.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, consider sacrificing material (like a rook) to force the king into a mating net. Look for checks and threats that restrict the king's escape squares.
notes.plans: Play Rg4+ (rook lift) to check the king. After Kf5, consider Rg5+ or Qf7+ leading to mate.

notes.explains: Rg4+ is a rook lift that checks the king. The king cannot go back to f7 (queen covers) or f6 (bishop covers), so it must go to f5. Now White has a faster mate than Rg5+.
notes.teaches: When hunting the king, don't automatically play the most obvious check. Look for a sacrifice that forces the king into a worse position. Here, the rook on g4 can be a lure.
notes.plans: After Kf5, play Qf7+ (forcing the king to g5 or e5) then Qg5# or similar. Alternatively, Rg5+ leads to mate in a few moves.

notes.explains: Black takes on c3, but white recaptures with the knight, maintaining a strong center and good piece activity.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the knight is better than with the pawn because it keeps the pawn structure intact and the knight can later move to e4 or d5.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b2, then consider pushing b4 or playing f4 to open the center.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa6, a strange move trying to prevent b5, but the queen is offside and can be harassed.
notes.teaches: Don't place the queen on a6 in this setup; it becomes a target and hinders black's development.
notes.plans: Play a4 to reinforce b5, then continue with Bb2 and prepare b4.

notes.explains: White plays Qe1 to avoid the pin and prepare to chase the bishop with h3. This is a flexible move that also supports the center.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is pinned, moving the queen out of the pin can be a good way to neutralize it without weakening your pawn structure.
notes.plans: After Qe1, play h3 to force the bishop to decide, then continue with Bb2 and b4.

notes.explains: Black's bishop moves to f5, where it eyes e4. White must be careful not to allow e4, but it's not immediately possible due to defenders.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop lands on f5, watch for the e4 break. Count attackers and defenders before allowing it.
notes.plans: Continue development with Bb2, and if black tries e4, be ready to capture or counterattack.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to b2, completing the fianchetto setup. The bishop eyes the long diagonal and pressures e5.
notes.teaches: The bishop on b2 is powerful in this setup, especially after the knight on c3 moves, creating a battery with the queen.
notes.plans: Consider moving the knight to e4 or d5, then play Qc3 to create a battery threatening mate on g7.

notes.explains: White plays b4-b5, opening the position. Black captures on b5, but white recaptures with the bishop, threatening Qc3 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: In this setup, the b4-b5 break is a key plan to activate the bishop. Even if material is temporarily sacrificed, the initiative and threats can be overwhelming.
notes.plans: After Bxc4, play Qc3 threatening mate on g7, forcing black to weaken with f6 or lose material.

notes.explains: White plays Qc3, creating a battery with the bishop on b2. Black must respond to the mate threat on g7.
notes.teaches: Building a battery on the long diagonal is a powerful idea when the opponent's king is castled kingside. It forces weakening moves like f6.
notes.plans: After black defends, continue pressuring the weakened dark squares, possibly with Rc1 or doubling rooks.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to block the diagonal, but this weakens the e6 pawn and dark squares. White can exploit this.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their pawn structure to block a diagonal, look for ways to exploit the new weaknesses, especially on the same color complex.
notes.plans: Play Bb3 or Bd3 to target e6, or consider opening the center with d5.

notes.explains: White places the bishop on d5, dominating the board and threatening e6. Black's position is collapsing.
notes.teaches: A centralized bishop on a strong outpost can be decisive. It restricts the opponent's pieces and creates multiple threats.
notes.plans: Continue pressure on e6, possibly with Rfe1 or Qd3, and prepare to break through.

notes.explains: White plays Qd3, threatening Qxe6+ and further pressure. Black is helpless.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pawns are weak, concentrate your pieces on the weak points. A queen and bishop duo can be lethal.
notes.plans: Capture on e6 or play Re6 to double rooks, forcing resignation.

notes.explains: White captures on e6, winning a pawn and maintaining a crushing attack.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive advantage, simplify by capturing material while keeping the initiative.
notes.plans: After Rxe6, continue with Re1 or Qd5+ to force mate or further material gains.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qe8#, exploiting the weak dark squares and exposed king.
notes.teaches: The fianchetto bishop setup can lead to a swift mate when the opponent weakens their kingside. Always look for mating patterns.

notes.explains: Black trades knights and plays Bh6 to target the weakened e3-pawn after f3. This is an unconventional but logical way to pressure White's center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens a pawn (here e3), redeploying a bishop to attack it can be more effective than routine development, even if it means moving a fianchettoed bishop.
notes.plans: Black will continue pressuring e3 with ...Qb6 or ...Bxg2 ideas, while preparing queenside expansion with ...b5 to discourage White from castling queenside.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 preemptively, gaining space on the queenside and preparing to open lines if White castles queenside. This move gains a tempo if White castles queenside.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, every tempo matters. Starting your attack early, even before the opponent commits their king, can be crucial.
notes.plans: If White castles queenside, Black will open the b-file with ...b4 and ...c5. If White castles kingside, Black will continue with ...Bb7 and ...e5.

notes.explains: Black opens the queenside with b4 and c5, forcing White to recapture on c3. This prevents White from castling queenside safely, as the b-file is now open.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, opening lines can be more effective than a direct attack. Here, Black opens the b-file to target the king.
notes.plans: Black will now redeploy the knight to d7 to chase the bishop and prepare ...e5, opening the center while White's king is vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb7, a patient preparatory move. It protects the d5-pawn before pushing e5, preventing White from exploiting the d5 weakness after the center opens.
notes.teaches: Before executing a central break, ensure your pawns are protected. A seemingly passive move like Bb7 can be essential to avoid tactical refutations.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...e5, opening the center. The bishop on b7 will support the d5-pawn and later become active on the long diagonal.

notes.explains: Black strikes in the center with e5 after White's g4. This is timely because White's kingside attack is not yet coordinated, and Black opens lines to exploit White's exposed king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent launches a pawn storm, countering in the center can be more effective than defending passively. The center break often disrupts the attack.
notes.plans: After ...e5, Black will open the center with ...dxe5 or ...exd4, activating the rooks and bishops. The knight will later target weak points like g4.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8, maintaining the tension. There is no need to capture immediately; the rook supports the e5-pawn and prepares to recapture if White takes.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, keeping the tension can be better than resolving it. Patience forces the opponent to make the first concession.
notes.plans: Black will wait for White to commit. If White castles kingside, Black will target the g4-pawn with ...Nf6. If White does nothing, Black will eventually push ...e4.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, attacking the g4-pawn. This is possible because White's bishop cannot capture on e5 due to tactical lines: ...Nxg4, Bxg7, Qxh4 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: When attacking a pawn, always check if the opponent's counter-capture leads to tactics. Here, the threat of ...Qxh4 forces White to defend passively.
notes.plans: Black will win the g4-pawn, then use the open h-file and central control to launch a decisive attack. The knight will later go to g4 or e5.

notes.explains: Black captures the g4-pawn with the knight. This is safe because White's counterplay is insufficient; the knight is well-placed to attack e3 and later f3.
notes.teaches: Winning a pawn is good, but ensure the resulting position gives you active play. Here, the knight on g4 is a powerful outpost that ties down White's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will target the e3-pawn with ...Nxe3 or ...Qc7, and later bring the queen to the kingside. The open h-file and central pressure will decide the game.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc8 instead of the more natural Rc8. This subtlety avoids a tactical line where White's rook checks on d8 after ...Nxe3, winning material.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, every move must be calculated precisely. A seemingly equivalent move can have a hidden tactical flaw. Always check for checks and captures.
notes.plans: Black will recapture on c5, then use the queen and rook to pressure White's weak pawns. The knight on g4 will continue to threaten e3 and f2.

notes.explains: Black plays e4, opening the diagonal for the bishop and creating a path for the knight to f3. This move exploits White's weak dark squares and the pinned knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a central pawn break can be devastating. Here, e4 forces White's bishop to a passive square and gives Black a decisive outpost.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Nf3, threatening ...Qh3 and ...Rxe4. The knight on f3 is a monster, and White cannot defend all threats. The game will end quickly.

notes.explains: Black's attack culminates in winning material. The knight on f3 is unstoppable, and White's king is exposed. Black simplifies to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: A successful attack often ends not with checkmate but with winning material. Use the king's vulnerability as a springboard to gain a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Black will convert the extra material by activating the rooks and pushing the queenside pawns. The king is safe, and White has no counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on b4 pins the knight on c3 and pressures e4. White's Bd3 develops and defends e4, neutralizing the pin.
notes.teaches: Against early ...Bb4 in Owen's Defense, develop Bd3 to defend e4 and prepare to break the pin without wasting time on a3.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ne2 to connect knights and prepare to castle kingside, ignoring the bishop on b4.

notes.explains: Black voluntarily gives up the bishop pair by capturing on c3, which is a positional mistake. White recaptures with the b-pawn, keeping the e4 pawn defended and gaining the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading your bishop for a knight without compensation, especially when you have the bishop pair. White's doubled c-pawns are not a weakness here because they control central squares.
notes.plans: Continue development with Ne2, castle kingside, and prepare e5 to gain space and attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays h6 to prevent Bg5, which would pin the knight and create kingside weaknesses. White now has a choice between developing or expanding.
notes.teaches: When the opponent prevents a pin, consider whether to switch to a different plan. Here, expanding with e5 is more ambitious than routine development.
notes.plans: Play e5 to gain space and prepare Qg4, targeting the weak g7 pawn and exploiting Black's lack of kingside development.

notes.explains: White plays Qg4, threatening the g7 pawn and forcing Black to weaken the kingside. Black cannot castle because of the pin on h6, and g6 creates a hole on f6.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's kingside is undeveloped, a queen sortie to g4 can create decisive threats. The weakness of g7 is a common target in such positions.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ne4, c4 to chase the knight from d5, and then Nf6+ if possible. If Black plays g6, the f6 hole becomes a permanent weakness.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, further weakening the kingside. White can now open the f-file with f4, exploiting the pawn on g5 as a hook.
notes.teaches: A pawn like g5 can be used as a hook to open lines for an attack. f4 is a typical break to open the f-file against an uncastled king.
notes.plans: Play f4, and if ...gxf4, recapture with the bishop and then target g7 with Qg7. If ...Nxf4, consider taking on d5 first to prevent counterplay.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the bishop on f4, maintaining pressure. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White threatens Qg7, winning the rook on h8.
notes.teaches: After opening the f-file, the rook on f1 and queen on g4 combine to create mating threats. The bishop on f4 also eyes h6, adding to the attack.
notes.plans: Play Qg7, forcing ...Rf8, then Bxh6, breaking through. If Black defends with ...Qe7, consider Ne4 or other consolidating moves.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, ignoring the kingside threat, and White opens the g-file with g6. This exploits Black's lack of development and exposes the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent ignores your attack, punish them by opening more lines. g6 is a typical pawn sacrifice to open the g-file and accelerate the attack.
notes.plans: Recapture on g6 with the queen or rook, then double rooks on the g-file and bring the bishop to f4 or e5 to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays Rf7, skewering the king and the bishop on b7. The rook on the seventh rank is devastating, as it attacks everything on that rank.
notes.teaches: An open file allows the rook to penetrate to the seventh rank, where it can create decisive threats. Rf7 is a natural move that cannot be bad.
notes.plans: Continue with simple captures and checks, such as Nxd5 or exd6, to win material while maintaining the attack. Do not overcomplicate.

notes.explains: White plays Be5, defending the d4 pawn with tempo and cutting off the king's escape squares. Now White threatens b3 followed by c4#.
notes.teaches: When the king is trapped, look for mating constructions. Be5 is a quiet move that sets up a deadly pawn mate, demonstrating the power of restricting the king.
notes.plans: Play b3, threatening c4#. If Black plays ...Rxg6, then Re1 deprives the king of e4, and c4 is mate. If Black plays ...Nc6, then Rd7#.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Rd7#, exploiting the pin on the knight and the king's lack of escape squares.
notes.teaches: After restricting the king, a simple rook check can be mate. Always consider all legal moves of the opponent to ensure no hidden defenses exist.

notes.explains: Black plays ...d5, transposing to a French-like structure. White must be careful because ...c5 is a serious threat, as there is no c3 pawn to defend the chain.
notes.teaches: In this line, after e5, Black's ...c5 can be dangerous because White cannot play c3. White must respond actively, typically with Nf4 or a tactical shot.
notes.plans: Play Nf4, and if ...c5, then Nxc6! forcing ...dxc6, then Qh5+ g6, Bxg6+ Ke7, and Bg5+ winning. This line exploits Black's weak dark squares.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a knight to open lines and deliver a devastating checkmate attack. The key is the bishop on g5 check, forcing ...Nf6, then exf6+ and Bxf6+ Kxf6, followed by a skewer.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for sacrificial combinations to open lines. The skewer at the end (Bg5+ ...Kxf6, then Qg5+? no, actually after Bxf6+ Kxf6, Qh4+ wins the queen) is a common tactical motif.
notes.plans: After Bg5+, if ...Nf6, then exf6+ Kxf6, and Qh4+ winning the queen. If ...Ke8, then Qxg6+ hxg6, Bxg6#.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White wins the queen with Qh4+, as the king is forced to move and the queen is lost.
notes.teaches: Always check for checks and captures at the end of a combination. Here, Qh4+ is a double attack that wins the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ne4, a typical idea in the Caro-Kann. White must respond with the counterintuitive Nb1, preparing to trap the knight with f3.
notes.teaches: When a knight jumps to e4, the idea of retreating the knight to b1 to play f3 is a known concept. This prevents the knight from escaping via ...Nxc3 and allows White to trap it.
notes.plans: Play Nb1, then if Black plays ...c5, play c3 to solidify the center. Then f3 wins the knight. If Black plays ...Bg4, then f3 still wins.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to prevent ...c4 and then f3 traps the knight on e4. Black's knight is stranded and will be lost.
notes.teaches: After Nb1, the idea is to solidify the center with c3 before trapping the knight. This prevents Black from counterplay with ...c4.
notes.plans: After c3, play f3 winning the knight. If Black tries ...Bg4, f3 still wins. The position is winning for White.

notes.explains: White chases the knight with h4, trapping it on g5. Black will have to give up the knight.
notes.teaches: When a knight is out of squares, use pawns to trap it. h4 is a typical move to trap a knight on g5.
notes.plans: After h4, the knight is trapped. White can capture it next move, winning a piece.

notes.explains: White captures the trapped knight, winning a piece. The position is clearly winning.
notes.teaches: Simple tactics like trapping a knight can lead to a decisive material advantage. Always look for ways to exploit an opponent's overextended pieces.
notes.plans: Continue developing and consolidate the advantage. The extra piece should be enough to win.

notes.explains: White castles and then plays Nf4, aiming at the kingside. Black's king is still in the center, and White's pieces are well-placed for an attack.
notes.teaches: After developing, look for ways to transfer knights to attacking squares. Nf4 is a typical maneuver to target g6 and h5.
notes.plans: Play Nh5, threatening Nf6+ and Qg4. If Black plays ...Re8, then Qg4 wins on the spot. If Black plays ...Ne8, then Nf4 still keeps pressure.

notes.explains: White plays Qg4, threatening Qxg7#. Black cannot defend adequately because the knight on h5 prevents ...g6.
notes.teaches: The combination of Nh5 and Qg4 creates a deadly threat. The knight on h5 controls g7 and f6, making the queen's attack unstoppable.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Bf8, then Nf6+ wins the exchange. If Black plays ...Ne8, then Nf4 still maintains pressure.

notes.explains: White wins the queen with a fork, leading to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to defend, look for tactical shots like Nf6+ forking king and queen.
notes.plans: The resulting endgame is winning due to the extra queen. Simply consolidate and promote.

notes.explains: White plays Qh4, threatening Qxh7# and keeping the attack alive. Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: After winning the queen, continue to press the attack. Do not relax; look for immediate threats like checkmate.
notes.plans: Play Qxh7+ Kf8, then Qh8+ Ke7, and Qxg7 winning. Alternatively, simple moves like Re1 also win.

notes.explains: White wins another pawn and the attack continues. Black's king is still in danger.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, keep taking material while maintaining threats. This is the most efficient way to convert.
notes.plans: Bring the rook into the attack with Re1 or Re7, and look for checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays Qf5, threatening Qxc5+ and keeping the king in the center. The queen is well-placed.
notes.teaches: After winning material, centralize your queen to maximize threats. Qf5 attacks multiple targets and restricts the king.
notes.plans: Play Re1, threatening Re7+ and mate. If Black plays ...Kb5, then a3 or b4 traps the king.

notes.explains: White plays a3, preventing ...b4 and preparing b4+ to trap the king. The king is running out of squares.
notes.teaches: When the king is on the run, use pawns to restrict its movement. a3 is a quiet but deadly move.
notes.plans: Play b4+ Ka4, then Qc2+ Kb5, and c4+ Ka4, Qa2#. Alternatively, Re1 also wins.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qa2#, a classic king-hunt mate.
notes.teaches: A king hunt often ends with a queen mate on the edge of the board. The key is to restrict the king's escape squares with pawns.

notes.explains: The game ends with a beautiful checkmate after a king hunt.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to involve all your pieces in the attack. Here, the queen and pawns coordinated perfectly to trap the king.

notes.explains: The Glek System arises after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 g3. White fianchettoes the bishop to pressure the center and prepare a kingside attack. Black's response determines the specific setup.
notes.teaches: The Glek System is an underrated weapon that avoids heavy theory and leads to fresh positions where Black often misplaces pieces.
notes.plans: Complete kingside development with d3, castle, then choose between the traditional plan (h3, Kh2, Nd2, f4) or the Bishop e3 plan.

notes.explains: After Black plays ...d6 and develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, White completes development with d3 and castles. Black often plays ...h6, which is harmless as White never intended Bg5.
notes.teaches: Delay committing to a plan until Black reveals their setup. The move ...h6 is a common but unnecessary precaution.
notes.plans: Continue with h3, Kh2, Nd2, and prepare f4 to attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: The traditional Glek plan involves h3, Kh2, Nd2, and f4. The king moves to h2 to unpin the f-pawn, and the knight retreats to d2 to clear the f-file. This prepares a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: The core idea is to push f4 and launch a kingside attack. The fianchettoed bishop on g2 supports the attack and can block checks on h3.
notes.plans: After f4, if Black takes, recapture with the g-pawn and continue with f5, creating a kingside clamp. If Black doesn't take, push f5 and play like a King's Indian setup.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...Ng6, they relinquish control of d4. A thematic response is d4, striking in the center. After d4 exd4 Nxd4, Black can play ...d5, which liquidates the center and leads to a slightly better endgame for White.
notes.teaches: When an opponent moves a piece backward, look to occupy the squares they abandoned. The d4 break is a common idea in the Glek.
notes.plans: Consider d4 to gain central space, but be aware of ...d5 counterplay. Alternatively, stick with the f4 plan.

notes.explains: After f4, Black plays ...exf4 gxf4, and then ...Nh4 attacks the bishop on g2. White must not allow the trade, as it weakens the king. The correct response is Bh1, protecting the bishop and keeping the king safe.
notes.teaches: The fianchettoed bishop is crucial for king safety. Never give it up lightly, as it exposes the king and weakens the h3 pawn.
notes.plans: After Bh1, Black may play ...Qd7, threatening Qxh3. White can meet this with f5, cutting off the battery and trapping the knight on h4.

notes.explains: When Black plays ...g5 to support the knight on h4, White should trade knights with Nf3. After Nf3 Nxf3+ Qxf3, White's queen enters the attack, and Black's kingside pawns become targets. The pawn on f5 acts as a plug, preventing Black from bringing pieces to the defense.
notes.teaches: Trade off pieces that hinder your attack. The f5 pawn restricts Black's pieces and gives White a lasting initiative.
notes.plans: Use the queen and pawns to target h6 and g5. Consider pushing h4 to shatter Black's kingside pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ng6, threatening Qxh3# because the g1 square is covered by the bishop on c5. White must first play d4 to chase the bishop away before capturing on g6. After d4 Bb6, White can play fxg6, but Black gets dangerous counterplay with Qxh3+ Kg1 Qg3+ and ...Bh3. It's safer to avoid this and instead sacrifice a knight on g5.
notes.teaches: When calculating captures, consider if the opponent has a mating threat. If so, look for prophylactic moves first. A knight sacrifice for two pawns is a low-risk investment if the attack is strong.
notes.plans: Play Nxg5, ripping open Black's kingside. After hxg5 Bxg5, White has a crushing attack with the bishop on g5 and the f5 pawn.

notes.explains: After the sacrifice Nxg5, Black plays ...Nh7. White should not try to be fancy with Nd5 but simply move the bishop to safety, e.g., Bh6, keeping the g-file open for a rook. The key is to threaten fxg6, forcing the knight to move, and then deliver a check on g1.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, prefer simple, functional moves over flashy tactics. Keep lines open for your rooks and queen.
notes.plans: Play Qd3 to protect the h3 pawn and the d4 pawn, preventing Black's bishop from entering the defense. Then threaten fxg6.

notes.explains: After Qd3, Black plays ...gxf5. White recaptures with the pawn and then plays Nd5, threatening Nf6+ forking king and queen. Black's pieces are all on the queenside, unable to help. White can convert the attack into a material advantage by winning the exchange or checkmating.
notes.teaches: An attack doesn't always need to end in checkmate. Winning material using the king as a target is often easier and just as effective.
notes.plans: Play Nf6+ to win the exchange, or look for a mating pattern. The black king is short of squares, so consider Qh5 or Rg1.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...d5 instead of ...d6, the game becomes more open. After exd5 Nxd5 Bg2, Black often plays ...Nxc3. White recaptures with the b-pawn, accepting doubled pawns in exchange for open b-file and easier d4 push.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness. Here they give White central control and attacking chances on the b-file.
notes.plans: Play d4 to control the center, and use the b-file to pressure b7. The bishop on g2 becomes very powerful.

notes.explains: After ...Nxc3 bxc3, Black may play ...e4, trying to disrupt White's development. The correct response is Qe2, which pins the pawn and threatens to win it. If Black plays ...Qe7, White can play Nd4, and if ...Nxd4 cxd4, the pawn on e4 falls.
notes.teaches: The move Qe2 is a standard idea against ...e4 in such structures. It pins the pawn and prepares to win it.
notes.plans: After Qe2, if Black defends with ...Qe7, play Nd4, threatening Nf5 or simply winning the e4 pawn.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bc5 instead of ...e4, White castles and then plays Re1, pressuring the e5 pawn. Black's natural ...Re8 is a mistake because White can play d4, and if exd4, White trades rooks on e8 and recaptures on d4 with a good center.
notes.teaches: Pressure on the e-file can force concessions. The d4 break is often available when Black's knight is not on d4.
notes.plans: After d4, if Black takes, recapture with the queen or knight, maintaining central control. If Black doesn't take, White has a strong center.

notes.explains: In the line with ...Bc5, Black's best move is ...Bg4, pinning the knight. White can play h3, and if ...Bh5, then g4, forcing the bishop to g6. Then Nxe5 Nxe5, and White should play d4 first to open the bishop's diagonal before recapturing.
notes.teaches: When recovering a piece, consider move orders that improve your position. d4 opens lines and chases the bishop before recapturing.
notes.plans: After d4, if Black plays ...Bxd4, recapture with cxd4, gaining the bishop pair and a strong initiative.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bd6 instead of ...Bc5, White can play d4 immediately, as Black's control of d4 is weaker. This leads to a favorable center for White.
notes.teaches: When Black's pieces are less active, seize the center immediately. d4 is a thematic break in the Glek.
notes.plans: After d4, maintain the center and look for kingside expansion with f4.

notes.explains: Black may try ...e4 and ...f5, creating a pawn chain. White can undermine it with g4, opening lines. After hxg4 Bxg4, White has the better structure and active pieces.
notes.teaches: Undermining a pawn chain with a flank pawn break can expose weaknesses. The resulting open lines favor the side with better piece activity.
notes.plans: Play g4 to break open the kingside. After the exchange, White has pressure on the b-file and better central control.

notes.explains: In the ...d5 line, after Bg2, Black's most common move is ...Nxc3. But Black can also play ...Be7. White's plan is still to play Re1 and then d4 if possible, or else play Rb1 to pressure b7.
notes.teaches: The basic plan in the ...d5 line is to control the center and use the b-file. Rb1 ties Black's rook to b7.
notes.plans: If d4 is not immediately possible, play Rb1 to create pressure, then look for d4 or kingside expansion.

notes.explains: After ...d6 and ...a5, White can play Na4, targeting the bishop on c5. If Black retreats to b6, White can trade on b6, ruining Black's pawn structure. Then White continues with h3, Kh2, and the standard kingside plan.
notes.teaches: Na4 is a strong move to eliminate Black's dark-squared bishop, which is a key defender. The resulting pawn weaknesses benefit White.
notes.plans: After Nxb6 axb6, play h3 and Kh2, preparing f4. The bishop pair and Black's weak pawns give White a lasting edge.

notes.explains: In the position after Na4 Bb6 Nxb6 axb6, White can play Re1 as prophylaxis against ...d5. This prevents Black from opening the center and allows White to execute the kingside plan undisturbed.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like Re1 can prevent counterplay and allow you to pursue your own plan without interruption.
notes.plans: Continue with h3, Kh2, and prepare f4. Alternatively, play c4 to permanently prevent ...d5, then aim for d4.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Ng6, White can consider d4 immediately. After d4 exd4 Nxd4, Black may play ...d5, leading to complications. White should calculate carefully but often emerges better.
notes.teaches: When a knight moves away from the center, consider occupying the vacated square with a pawn or piece. d4 is a natural response.
notes.plans: After d4, if ...d5, play exd5 Nxd5 and then Nb3, forking bishop and knight. This wins material.

notes.explains: In the game, after f4 exf4 gxf4 Nh4 Bh1, Black played ...Qd7, threatening Qxh3. White played f5, cutting off the battery and trapping the knight. This is a key defensive and attacking move.
notes.teaches: When your opponent sets up a battery against your king, use pawn moves to block the diagonal or cut off the attack.
notes.plans: After f5, the knight on h4 is trapped. White can then play Nf3 to trade it off and bring the queen into the attack.

notes.explains: After ...g5, White played Nf3, forcing the trade of knights. Black's kingside pawns become weak, and White's queen enters the game with Qxf3. The f5 pawn restricts Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: Trade off pieces that block your attack. The resulting pawn weaknesses are easy to target with the queen and pawns.
notes.plans: Push h4 to shatter Black's kingside pawns. The open g-file and Black's passive pieces make the attack decisive.

notes.explains: Black played ...Ng6, threatening Qxh3#. White responded with d4 to chase the bishop away, then Nxg5, sacrificing a knight for two pawns. This rips open Black's kingside and gives White a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When facing a mating threat, look for a prophylactic move that also improves your position. A knight sacrifice for two pawns is a low-risk investment if the attack is strong.
notes.plans: After Nxg5 hxg5 Bxg5, White has a powerful attack. Play Qd3 to protect h3 and d4, then threaten fxg6.

notes.explains: After the sacrifice, Black played ...Nh7. White played Bh6, keeping the g-file open. Then Qd3 protected h3 and d4, preventing Black's bishop from entering the defense. White threatened fxg6, forcing the knight to move.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, keep lines open for your rooks. Protect key pawns with your queen to free your other pieces.
notes.plans: After Qd3, play fxg6, then use the open g-file to bring the rook to g1. The attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: White played Nd5, threatening Nf6+ forking king and queen. Black's pieces are all on the queenside, unable to defend. White can win the exchange or checkmate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are far from the action, a simple fork can win material. Use the king as a target to gain an advantage.
notes.plans: Play Nf6+ to win the exchange, or look for a mating pattern. The black king is short of squares.

notes.explains: In the final position, White has multiple ways to win. The simplest is to play Qe8+, forcing the queen trade, or to play Rg1, threatening mate. The game ended with White winning all of Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, choose the simplest and most forcing continuation. Avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Play Qe8+ or Rg1 to force a decisive material advantage. The attack has succeeded.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ng4, threatening ...Ne5. White can consider Qc2 to support e4 and prepare development of the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent threatens a knight outpost, reinforcing the center with Qc2 is a solid response that also connects rooks.
notes.plans: Continue with Rc1, then b3 and Bb2, or consider trading the light-squared bishop for Black's fianchetto bishop to ease development.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to d7, which makes it harder for Black to play ...e6 later. White now has a choice for the light-squared bishop: keep it on c4, move to f1, or try Bb5 to induce ...a6 then retreat.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you can use provocative moves like Bb5 to gain a tempo or force a weakness, even if you plan to retreat.
notes.plans: Play Bb5, then after ...a6, retreat to f1 to keep the bishop and prepare a4 to fix the a-pawn.

notes.explains: White plays a4 to fix the a5 pawn and prevent Black from playing ...a4 to block b3. Now the rook can go to a3 and then to d3 to pressure the center, or simply play b3 and Bb2.
notes.teaches: Fixing a pawn with a4 prevents Black from using it to hinder your queenside expansion. The rook can be rerouted via a3 to d3 for central pressure.
notes.plans: Play Ra3, then after ...e6, trade on e6 and play Rd3 to attack d6. Alternatively, if Black doesn't play ...e6, proceed with b3 and Bb2.

notes.explains: Black trades bishops on a6. White should accept because keeping the bishop would allow ...Nb8-c6-a5, attacking the weak a4 pawn. After Bxa6, White's rook on a3 can go to d3.
notes.teaches: When a fianchettoed bishop is under attack, consider trading it if the alternative allows the opponent to target a weakness. Flexibility in rook placement is key.
notes.plans: Play Bxa6, then Rxa6, then Rd3 to pressure d6. Follow up with b3 and Bb2.

notes.explains: White's rook on d3 pressures the d6 pawn. Black has two center pawns but they are weak and require constant defense. White's plan is to trade Black's dark-squared bishop and then attack the king.
notes.teaches: Having more center pawns doesn't matter if they are weak and your pieces are passive. The rook on d3 is more useful than on b1 because it attacks the center.
notes.plans: Play b3, then Bb2 to trade bishops. After the trade, White can use the e-file and the weakened dark squares around Black's king to create mating threats.

notes.explains: Black pushes d5, opening the center. White recaptures and now the e-file is open. White's plan is still to trade the dark-squared bishops and use the e-file for attack.
notes.teaches: When the center opens, the importance of trading the opponent's fianchettoed bishop increases because it exposes the king. The e-file becomes a highway for your rooks.
notes.plans: Play Bb2 to trade bishops, then use the e-file and the weakened dark squares to create threats.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qe7 instead of ...d5. White continues with b3 and now has the option of Bb2 or first improving the knight with Nf3, threatening to go to g5 or trade on e5.
notes.teaches: Patience is key. Instead of rushing to trade, improve your pieces first. The knight on f3 is more flexible than on g3, and it can later go to g5 or support a trade on e5.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then after ...Nd7, decide whether to trade on e5 or play Rd1 to increase pressure on d6.

notes.explains: Black plays c4 to trade knights. White recaptures and plays Qe2, attacking the knight. Black blunders with ...Rb2, allowing Qxc4 and then Qxf2+ Kh2, when the rook on g3 defends g2.
notes.teaches: Always check if your opponent's move creates a tactical opportunity. Here, Black assumed Qxd4 was impossible, but the queen fork wins material.
notes.plans: After Qxc4, Black's best is ...Ne5, but White is better with a pawn up and pressure.

notes.explains: The Benko Gambit is an underrated opening that gives Black serious queenside counterplay when it works. However, White can avoid it with Nf3 or play the main line with Nc3, Bxa6, e4, which is considered better for White.
notes.teaches: Even if a gambit is theoretically dubious at the highest level, it can be very effective at club level. The key is to understand the typical attacking ideas: pressure on the b-file, the fianchettoed bishop, and the a6-c4 pawn structure.
notes.plans: If playing the Benko as Black, be prepared for White's avoidance lines. If playing White, the Nc3/Bxa6/e4 line is a reliable way to get an advantage.

notes.explains: Black's ...Rb2 is a blunder because Qxc4 leaves the queen on f2 check defended by the rook on g3. Black resigns.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, players often make false assumptions. Always double-check if your opponent's queen can be captured or if there are checks.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Bc4, Black should not panic. The threat to f7 is not immediate because d6 is already played. Developing with Nc6 is flexible, and e6 can wait.
notes.teaches: Against early Bc4 in the Sicilian, develop naturally without rushing to defend f7. The pawn on d6 already covers e5, so Nc6 is safe.
notes.plans: Continue development with Nf6, then consider e6 to challenge the knight on g5 if White plays Ng5.

notes.explains: When White plays Ng5 and Qh5, the knight on g5 is undefended except by the queen. Black can kick the queen with g6, then fork or pin to win the knight.
notes.teaches: Always check if an attacking piece is defended. If the defender can be chased away, the piece may become vulnerable.
notes.plans: Play g6, then after Qg4 play d5 forking queen and knight, or after Qh4 play Be7 followed by h6.

notes.explains: Black is up two pieces and two pawns. The simplest plan is to trade pieces and simplify. The idea of Nxe4 (or similar) to land a piece on e4, then d5 wins back material with interest.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, look to trade pieces and simplify. In Sicilian positions with Bc4, watch for sacrifices to plant a piece on e4.
notes.plans: Play Nxe4, then after dxe4, d5 wins back the piece. Continue developing and trade down.

notes.explains: With a huge material advantage, the traditional plan is to create a passed pawn and push it. Here, open files allow rook trades to ease the process.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, create a passed pawn and advance it. Use rook trades to clear the path.
notes.plans: Play Rfb8 to create luft, then trade rooks and push the d-pawn. Place bishops to cover squares in front of the pawn.

notes.explains: After e4 Nc6, White can play d4 (independent) or Nf3 (transposing to Ruy Lopez/Italian). A solid positional approach is c3, making the center 'bite on granite', then develop with Bd3, Nbd2, and later Nf1-g3.
notes.teaches: Against the Nimzowitsch, a solid setup with c3, Bd3, and Nbd2 controls the center without overextending. The pawns act as bodyguards for the bishop.
notes.plans: Play c3, Bd3, Nbd2, O-O, then Re1 and consider a4 to pressure Black's queenside if he plays b5.

notes.explains: Black's pawn on b5 is a weakness. White can play a4 to pressure it, potentially opening files for the rook. If Black takes on a4, Qxa4 gives White a strong position.
notes.teaches: In positions with a fixed pawn chain, look to attack the base of the chain. A pawn that sticks out like a sore thumb can be targeted.
notes.plans: Play a4, threatening to capture or open the a-file. If Black plays bxa4, recapture with the queen. Then consider Bb5 to build a battery with Qa4.

notes.explains: After a4, Black played f6, which weakens the light squares. White noticed a check on b3, which becomes relevant if Black captures on b2. The move Bb5 builds a battery and prepares a7 to trap the knight.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a weakening move like f6, note new tactical possibilities (e.g., checks on b3). Always look for ways to exploit weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play Bb5, threatening Qa4 and a7. If Black plays Na6, Bxa6 Rxa7 wins the pawn. If Black misses this, capture on b5 and continue.

notes.explains: White is up a piece and has a strong center. The move c4 glues the bishop and ties down Black's pieces. Later, Rook d3 attacks the weak d6 pawn, and the game simplifies.
notes.teaches: When ahead, use pawns to defend your pieces permanently ('pawns are the best defenders'). Target opponent's weak pawns to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play c4 to secure the bishop, then Rd3 to attack d6. After winning the pawn, trade down and push the passed pawn.

notes.explains: After e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5, White can play d4, but Black often plays d5 leading to sharp lines similar to the Scandinavian. White can avoid theory with Nf3 and develop naturally.
notes.teaches: Against Alekhine's, playing Nf3 and developing solidly avoids the sharp theoretical lines. Don't give Black what he wants if you're not prepared.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then c3 to support d4, Bd3, and develop with Nbd2. Consider a4 only if necessary; prophylaxis should be purposeful.

notes.explains: Black's pawn on b5 is a weakness. White plays a4 to strike at it. After Black plays Nc4, axb5 wins the knight. The move Bb5 was found by noticing the light-square weaknesses after c5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens a complex of squares, look to place your bishop on that color. Use the queen to create a battery and pressure.
notes.plans: Play a4, then after Nc4, axb5 wins a pawn. Continue with Bb5 and Qa4 to maintain pressure. If Black plays Na6, consider a7 to trap the knight.

notes.explains: After winning material, White plays c4 to glue the bishop and prevent counterplay. The queen on b6 exerts an x-ray on the king; instead of playing Kh1 (symptom), White plays Qa7 (cause) to eliminate the threat.
notes.teaches: When dealing with a threat, ask if you can target the cause (the attacking piece) rather than just the symptom (the check). This often leads to more effective moves.
notes.plans: Play c4 to secure the bishop, then Qa7 to neutralize the queen's x-ray. After exchanges, push the passed pawn.

notes.explains: After Nc3, Black often plays Bb4 pinning the knight. White can play a3, threatening to win the bishop because the rook on a1 is not hanging (Black has no pieces developed to exploit it).
notes.teaches: A move like a3 can be strong even if it looks like it hangs a rook, because the opponent lacks the coordination to take it. Always consider the opponent's development before assuming a tactic works.
notes.plans: Play a3, and if Bxc3+, recapture with bxc3, opening the b-file and giving White a strong pawn center.

notes.explains: Black takes on c3, and White recaptures with the pawn. This ruins White's queenside pawn structure, but the knight on d6 (after Nd6+) will be a monster, completely paralyzing Black's development.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to ruin your pawn structure if it gives you a powerful outpost for a knight. The knight on d6 in the Sicilian can be worth more than a clean pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play Nd6+ Kf8 (or Ke7), then Qd6, and Black cannot develop his kingside pieces. White will castle kingside and attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, trying to develop. White can now play Nd6+ and then Qd6, or even play Bc4 and castle, building up pressure slowly. The knight on d6 is a permanent blockade.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominant knight on a weak square, you don't need to rush. Develop your other pieces and increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, O-O, then f4 to open lines. Black's pieces are stuck and White's attack will be overwhelming.

notes.explains: After Qd6+, Black's king is stuck in the center. White has a huge advantage. The game ended quickly with a checkmate after Qd6+ Kf8? (a blunder) but even with Ke8, White is winning.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, look for immediate checks and mating threats. The queen and knight can create a deadly attack.
notes.plans: If Ke8, White can play Bc4, O-O, and then f4, breaking open the center. Black's king will be exposed.

notes.explains: White fell into the trap: after dxc5, Black trades queens and wins a rook with Bxc3+. White is down material and Black has a winning position.
notes.teaches: Always check if a pawn capture leads to a tactical sequence. In the Grünfeld, taking on c5 can be deadly if the bishop on f4 is undefended.
notes.plans: Black is up a rook. Develop quickly, castle, and use the extra material to win.

notes.explains: Black is up a rook. White has some compensation with the two bishops and a pawn, but Black's position is winning. Black should develop and consolidate.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading pieces and avoid unnecessary risks. Develop your pieces and get the king to safety.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, O-O, and then bring the rook to d8 or c8. The extra rook will decide the game.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, trying to develop. Black should now play Bg4 or Nc6, developing with tempo. The bishop on a1 is safe for now.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld, even when winning, keep developing. Don't let White's pieces become active.
notes.plans: Play Bg4, pinning the knight, then Nc6, O-O, and eventually push e5 or f5 to open lines.

notes.opening: Four Knights Scotch, Deferred Latvian Gambit
notes.explains: Bg5 pins the knight on f6 and threatens Qe5+ again. Black's best is Nf6, but then White can simply take on f6 and continue the attack. The position is winning.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful in king hunts. Use them to restrict the opponent's pieces and create threats.
notes.plans: After Nf6, Bxf6 gxf6, Qxf6+ Ke8, O-O-O and the attack is decisive. Alternatively, if Black plays Be7, then Bxe7 Kxe7, O-O-O and the king is still exposed.

notes.explains: White plays Rc1, threatening to trap the bishop on a1. Black can save it by playing Bb2 or Bg7, but Black is still winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, don't be greedy; consolidate. The bishop on a1 can retreat to b2 or g7.
notes.plans: Play Bb2, then Nc6, O-O, and use the extra rook to attack.

notes.explains: White avoided the Stafford by not taking on e5, so we didn't get the gambit. The Stafford is a tricky weapon for club players, but at GM level it's considered refuted.
notes.teaches: The Stafford Gambit is a practical surprise weapon below master level, but objectively White can get a clear advantage with precise play.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 d5, the Elephant Gambit is considered dubious but tricky. White's best is exd5 or Nxe5, but many club players don't know the refutation.
notes.teaches: Offbeat openings like the Elephant Gambit can be effective against unprepared opponents, even if objectively inferior.

notes.explains: Ng5 is a mistake because the d5-pawn blocks the bishop on c4, so Nxf7 is not a real threat. Black can simply play ...h6 and ...Bg4 to gain tempo.
notes.teaches: Don't assume discovered checks are scary; if the opponent's pieces are undeveloped, the king can often escape. Always check if the threat is real.
notes.plans: Play ...h6, chase the knight to h3, then develop with ...Bg4 to trap the queen or force weaknesses.

notes.explains: After Nh3, Black has a choice: immediately capture the knight on h3 or first play ...Bg4. The move ...Bg4 is stronger because it forces White to weaken his position (f3 or Be2) before Black captures.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to improve your initial idea. Don't rush into a capture; first see if you can force the opponent to make additional concessions.
notes.plans: Play ...Bg4, threatening the queen. If White plays f3, capture with the e-pawn and win a piece. If Be2, then capture on h3 and take on d5 with a dominant position.

notes.explains: After …exf3, White is lost. The pawn on g2 is overloaded, and Black threatens ...fxg2 and ...f2+. White must give up a piece to avoid immediate mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and you have a material advantage, prioritize king safety and development over grabbing material. Castle first, then attack.
notes.plans: Castle kingside (0-0) to secure the king, then develop the remaining pieces and use the extra queen to checkmate.

notes.explains: After Rg1, Black should not rush to take on g2. Instead, prioritize development and king safety: play ...Be7 and castle. This avoids unnecessary risks like ...Bc5 which allows Rc1+.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, don't get greedy. Focus on completing development and securing your king. The win will come naturally.
notes.plans: Play ...Be7, castle, then use the extra queen to launch a decisive attack. Avoid moves that give counterplay.

notes.explains: After castling, Black can play ...Bc5, pinning the knight and preparing ...Nf4. White's position is collapsing. Black should continue developing and avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material advantage, practice precision. Cement good habits by playing accurately even when the game is already won.
notes.plans: Play ...Nc6, ...Nf4, and eventually win back the d5 pawn. Keep the king safe and avoid counterplay.

notes.explains: …Nf6 is the Marshall Defense, which is not good. White should play cxd5 Nxd5 e4, but must avoid the natural Nc3 because of …e5!, which is very unpleasant.
notes.teaches: In the Marshall Defense, White's best is e4 followed by Bd3, which prevents ...e5 and keeps a strong center. Avoid Nc3 due to ...e5!.
notes.plans: Play e4, then Bd3, and develop naturally. Black's early knight moves have lost time, so White can afford slow moves like h3.

notes.explains: White has a perfect position: full center control, all pieces developed, and Black's pieces are passive. The only undeveloped piece is the c1-bishop.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and the opponent is passive, place your bishop actively. Here Bg5 is better than Be3 because it pressures Black's position and can trade off the fianchettoed bishop.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, then Qd2 to trade bishops on h6, weakening Black's kingside. Follow up with central expansion (d5) and a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After d5, Black's counterplay is stopped. White now threatens to take on f6 and then play e5. Black's knight on d7 is misplaced.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to undermine your center with ...c5, advance d5 to maintain the space advantage. Do not capture on c5, which would open the file for Black.
notes.plans: Continue with Qd2, trade bishops on h6, then prepare a kingside attack with f4, Ne2-g3, etc.

notes.explains: After trading bishops, White has a dominating position. Black's kingside is weakened, and White's pieces are ready for an attack. The rook on d1 controls the only open file.
notes.teaches: When you have control of the only open file, that is a huge positional advantage. Use it to infiltrate the opponent's position.
notes.plans: Play Ne2-g3, then f4, breaking open the kingside. If Black plays ...e6, capture and use the d-file to attack the queen.

notes.explains: White's knight is heading to g3 to join the attack. Black's ...a6 is harmless; White can ignore it because the threat of ...b5 is not dangerous (it leaves c5 undefended).
notes.teaches: Don't automatically stop your opponent's threats. Evaluate if the threat is real. If it's not dangerous, continue with your own plan.
notes.plans: Play Ng3, then f4. If Black plays ...b5, capture on c5 with the bishop, exploiting the undefended pawn and the vulnerable king.

notes.explains: After Rd7, Black is lost. The rook invades with checkmate threats. The knight on f6 is pinned, and the queen is on the same rank as the king, allowing a decisive tactic.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, look for the most direct winning continuation. Here, the rook lift to d7 ends the game immediately.
notes.plans: Play Rxd7, winning the queen. Black cannot avoid material loss and checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays Bishop c5 to avoid the main lines and keep the game offbeat, hoping to transpose into the Stafford Gambit if White plays Nc3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent avoids your intended gambit, stay flexible and choose a solid developing move that keeps tension.
notes.plans: Continue development with d6 and Nc6, preparing to challenge White's center and possibly play Bg4.

notes.explains: Black confused the move order: after ...Qh4, White can play g3, and the queen takes on a4, but White's king defends the knight on d2. The correct order would have been ...Bxd2 first, then Qh4 forking king and knight.
notes.teaches: Move order is critical in sharp openings; a single misstep can turn a winning line into a losing one.
notes.plans: White is up a piece; consolidate by developing and tucking the king to c1.

notes.explains: After simplifying queens, White has a material advantage. The king is safe on e2, and White can focus on development and exploiting Black's weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify if it doesn't relinquish the initiative, but here development is more important than trading queens.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g2 or prepare e4 to open lines and threaten Black's king.

notes.explains: e4 threatens to open the diagonal for the bishop and goads Black into castling, after which White can attack the weakened dark squares around Black's king.
notes.teaches: When Black lacks a fianchettoed bishop, the dark squares around the king become vulnerable; target them with Qh6 and Ng5.
notes.plans: Play Qh6, threatening Ng5; if Black pushes f6, exploit the weakened diagonal with Bc4.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to block Ng5, but this weakens the e6 pawn and the c4 diagonal. White can now aim for Bc4 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: Every pawn move creates weaknesses; f6 opens the c4 diagonal for a devastating bishop.
notes.plans: Chase the queen from c6 (e.g., with Bb5 or Nd4) to clear the way for Bc4, then deliver mate.

notes.explains: After Bb5 and Qh6, White forces the queen away and creates threats. Ng5 is decisive, threatening mate on h7.
notes.teaches: Combine piece pressure with direct threats; once the king is exposed, bring in the knight for the kill.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, and after ...Qe7, continue with Nf5 or other moves to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: Black plays …e5, which looks like a mistake but is a move-order trick to lure White into a French Defense. However, Black can avoid the French by developing the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before playing e6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to force a transposition you dislike, look for a move that sidesteps it while improving your position. Here, developing the bishop to g4 or f5 before playing e6 gives an improved French.
notes.plans: Play Bg4 (or Bf5), then e6, reaching a French structure with the bishop outside the pawn chain.
