notes.explains: Black plays …d5, entering a line against the Elephant (…d5). The idea is to meet d4 with …e6, reaching a French with the bishop outside the pawn chain. If White plays exd5, Black can play …Qxd5 and then Bg4, gaining compensation for the pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Elephant Gambit, the line …d5 followed by ...e6 and ...Bg4 gives Black active piece play and a weak White king, at the cost of a pawn. This is a practical alternative to the main lines.
notes.plans: After exd5 Qxd5 c4 Qd6, play Bg4, then castle queenside and pressure the center.

notes.explains: Black plays …e6, reaching a French structure with the bishop on g4 (or f5). The bishop is outside the pawn chain, which is a significant improvement over a standard French.
notes.teaches: Getting the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before playing e6 is a key idea in the French Defense. It gives the bishop more activity and avoids it being hemmed in.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to e7, then to f5, and prepare queenside castling.

notes.explains: Black plays …Qc7, reinforcing the knight on c6 and preventing Bxc6+ from doubling the pawns. The queen on c7 also eyes the e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent threatens to capture on c6 and ruin your pawn structure, you can often defend with the queen (or bishop) to avoid the doubled pawns. Here, Qc7 is solid and keeps the structure intact.
notes.plans: Follow up with ...e6, ...Nge7, ...Nf5, and ...Bg4 or ...Bf5.

notes.explains: After d4, Black has a choice: play tactically with ...cxd4 or solidly with ...e6. The tactical line involves ...cxd4, Bxf3, Qxf3, cxd4, but White can castle and gain time against the queen. The solid ...e6 is simpler and keeps a good position.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between a sharp tactical line and a solid positional continuation, consider whether the tactical line gives your opponent counterplay. Here, the simple ...e6 is better because it avoids unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Play ...Nge7, ...Nf5, and develop the bishop to b7 or g4.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to f5, a typical square in the Caro-Kann and similar structures. The knight pressures d4 and eyes the kingside.
notes.teaches: In structures with a pawn on d4 and e5, the knight often goes to f5 (or g6) to pressure the d4 pawn and prepare kingside attacks. This is a standard maneuver in many openings.
notes.plans: Continue with ...Bb7, ...O-O-O, and possibly ...g6 and ...h5 to attack the white king.

notes.explains: Black plays …Bh5, pinning the knight. White may try to win a piece with h3 and g4, but Black can retreat the bishop to g6, leaving White with weakened kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is pinned, don't panic. If the opponent tries to chase it with pawns, you can often retreat and leave them with weaknesses. Calculate whether the pawn advance actually wins a piece.
notes.plans: If White plays h3, retreat the bishop to g6. Then consider ...h5 to use the pawn as a hook for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Black plays …c4, closing the queenside and making White's rook on c1 look misplaced. This move also restricts White's pieces and prepares a queenside pawn advance.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a move that doesn't improve their position (like Rc1), you can often punish it by closing the file and making that rook useless. This is a typical way to exploit a mis-timed move.
notes.plans: Follow up with ...b5, ...a5, ...b4, creating a queenside attack. The pawn on c4 also restricts White's bishop and knight.

notes.explains: Black plays …b5, starting a typical queenside pawn storm. This is a standard plan in such structures.
notes.teaches: In positions with a closed center and a space advantage on the queenside, advancing the pawns (b5, a5, b4) is a common and powerful plan. The pawns can create weaknesses and open lines.
notes.plans: Continue with ...a5, ...b4, and possibly ...Ba3 to trap the rook on a1.

notes.explains: Black plays …bxa4, opening the b-file. Normally, opening the queenside like this is risky, but here White is so passive that Black gains more from the open file than White does.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you should violate general principles (like not opening the file for your opponent) when the specific position justifies it. Here, White's pieces are poorly placed, so the open b-file favors Black.
notes.plans: Play ...Rb8, ...O-O, and then ...Ba3 to target the rook on a1.

notes.explains: Black plays …Ba3, attacking the rook on a1. This is a common idea when the rook has few squares. If the rook moves to a1, then Bb2 forks the rook and the a-pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's rook is confined (e.g., by a pawn on a2 and the queen on d1), a bishop on a3 can trap or win the exchange. This motif appears in many openings.
notes.plans: After Ba3, if the rook moves to a1, play Bb2 forking rook and pawn. If the rook moves to c2, then Bg6 creates an x-ray that traps the rook.

notes.explains: Black wins the a4 pawn with the fork Bb2. This is a concrete result of the pressure created by Ba3.
notes.teaches: When you have a fork or a threat, follow through with it if it wins material. Don't delay unnecessarily.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, double rooks on the b-file and infiltrate.

notes.explains: Black exchanges bishops and then plays Rxb8, winning the exchange. White's pawn structure is ruined, and Black has a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: Transforming one advantage (a pawn) into another (the exchange) is a common way to simplify to a winning endgame. Here, the ruined pawn structure makes White's position hopeless.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the b-file, then infiltrate with the queen and rooks.

notes.explains: Black plays …Qb6, attacking the d4 pawn. White's knight on f1 is the only defender, and Black can increase pressure with ...Rxb1 and ...Qxb1.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is defended only once, you can often win it by adding pressure. Here, the queen joins the attack on d4, and White cannot defend it adequately.
notes.plans: Play ...Rxb1, then ...Qxb1, winning the d4 pawn. Alternatively, double rooks on the b-file.

notes.explains: Black wins the queen and enters a winning endgame. The rest is technique.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, simplify to an endgame and convert. Don't take unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Push the queenside pawns and create a passed pawn. Use the king actively.

notes.explains: Black's most common response is Bc5. White develops naturally with Bg2, d6, and d3. A key prophylactic move for Black is a6 or a5; without it, White can play Na4, forcing the exchange of Black's dark-squared bishop and securing the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: In the Glek system, Na4 is a positional threat that gives White the bishop pair and prepares the d3-d4 pawn break.
notes.plans: White can continue developing (castling, h3) before capturing on b6, then aim for d4 to open the center.

notes.explains: After Na4, Black's bishop on b6 is not going anywhere. White can delay the capture and play other improving moves like castling and h3 (to prevent Bg4). When ready, Nxb6 gives White the bishop pair and prepares d4.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to capture an inactive piece; use the time to improve your position first.
notes.plans: Play h3 to restrict Black's light-squared bishop, then capture on b6 and prepare d4.

notes.explains: Black's Nh7 prepares f5, creating urgency. White should push d4 immediately to prevent Black's counterplay. d4 threatens d5, forking the knight and pawn, and forces Black to give up the e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent prepares a dangerous pawn break, preempt it with your own central break.
notes.plans: Push d4, recapture on d4 with the knight, and continue development (Bb2).

notes.explains: After d4, Black played Bd7 (passive) and then f5 (decisive mistake). White has completed development (Bb2) and has a central advantage. f5 weakens Black's king and opens the diagonal for White's light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: A pawn break that weakens your king and opens lines for the opponent's bishops is often a serious positional error.
notes.plans: White can capture on c6 to get two bishops vs two knights, or play more slowly. The key is not to rush with one-move threats but to improve piece coordination.

notes.explains: White chose to capture on c6 (Bxc6, then Qxd8+ and Rxd8) to maintain the bishop pair and avoid loosening the kingside. This is a long-term positional decision.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, avoid trades that give the opponent active pieces or weaken your king. Prefer to keep the bishops in an open position.
notes.plans: After Bxc6, White has two bishops vs two knights. The plan is to centralize the queen (Qd3) and activate the rooks, avoiding flashy threats.

notes.explains: White played Qd3, which threatens Bxf5 (skewer) but more importantly centralizes the queen and connects rooks. Black blundered with ...Rxf5?, allowing Bb4 skewering the rook to the knight.
notes.teaches: When winning material, don't grab the first piece you see. Look for ways to win even more material. Here, g4 wins a piece instead of just the exchange.
notes.plans: After Bb4, Black's best is ...Rf8, but White can play g4, winning a piece. The skewer is a key tactic.

notes.explains: After winning material, White needs to consolidate. The bishop on h7 is vulnerable; it should be moved to a safe square with tempo (Bf5). The queen should not be tied to defending it.
notes.teaches: After winning material, reassess priorities: consolidate by moving vulnerable pieces to safe squares and activating passive pieces.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, then activate the rook (Ra1-e1) and look for queen trades or back-rank mates.

notes.explains: Against the Philidor, Bc4 is a good alternative to the main line d4. It transposes to a passive Italian for Black, who has committed to Be7 or g6. White develops naturally with d3, Nc3, and h3 (to prevent Bg4).
notes.teaches: You don't need to memorize sharp theory; choose flexible moves that lead to comfortable positions with simple plans.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3, d3, h3, then castle. Black's main options are ...c6 (preparing d5) or ...Nc6. White can meet ...c6 with a4 to prevent b5, or castle first to save a tempo.

notes.explains: Black played ...Kh8, a prophylactic move preparing f5. White should prevent b5 with a4, then wait for Black to undevelop (Ng8) before striking in the center with d4.
notes.teaches: Punish passive play by opening the center. When the opponent's pieces are on the back rank, it's a good time for d4.
notes.plans: Play a4 to stop b5, then d4 when Black's pieces are poorly placed. If Black plays f5, consider Bxg8 to eliminate the knight and win a pawn.

notes.explains: After d4, Black played f5. White can play Bxg8 (sacrificing the bishop pair) to win a pawn: Kxg8, dxe5, fxe4, Nxe4, and White is up a pawn with better development.
notes.teaches: Sometimes giving up the bishop pair is worth it to win a pawn and leave the opponent with poor development.
notes.plans: After Bxg8, White has an extra pawn. Consolidate by completing development and exploiting Black's weak king.

notes.explains: Black played d5, attacking the knight. White retreats to g3, which is a good square: it protects the king and allows future jumps to h5 or f5. The open f-file makes Bxh3 a constant threat.
notes.teaches: In open f-file positions, always be aware of Bxh3 tactics. The knight on g3 is well-placed for defense and future attacks.
notes.plans: After Ng3, White plans to complete development and eventually push e4 to open the center.

notes.explains: Black played Bc5, the only developed piece. White trades on e3, accepting doubled pawns but gaining the f-file and eliminating Black's active piece. The doubled pawns are not weak; the e5 pawn is strong and the e3 pawn can advance to e4.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always bad. They can control key squares and open lines. Here, the trade gives White a lasting initiative.
notes.plans: After Bxe3, fxe3, White has the f-file and can play e4 to open the center. Black's pieces are undeveloped and clumsy.

notes.explains: White played e4, ripping open the center. Black's queen checks on b6, but White's king moves to h1 (better than h2 to avoid pins on the knight). White is now threatening e6 and other invasions.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, open the center to exploit the opponent's uncoordinated pieces. King safety considerations: h1 avoids future checks on e5.
notes.plans: After e4, White can play e6, Qd6, or other aggressive moves. The key is to keep the initiative and not allow Black to consolidate.

notes.explains: White played e6, then e7, then Ng5, creating multiple threats. Black's ...Nxe4 allows a back-rank mate: Rxf8+ Kxf8, Qd8#. The key is to keep the rook on f1 active.
notes.teaches: When attacking, bring all pieces into the attack. A back-rank mate can occur even with a pawn on h6 if the king's escape is blocked.
notes.plans: After Ng5, White threatens Nxf7 and other tactics. If Black defends, White can play Qd3 or other moves to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: In the critical line after e7 Re8, White played Ng5. If Black plays Nxe4, Rxf8+ leads to mate. If Black plays Qe5, White should not play Qd8? but instead Qf3, sacrificing the e7 pawn to bring the rook to e1 with a winning attack.
notes.teaches: When calculating, consider sacrificing material to activate your pieces. Transforming a material advantage into a positional or attacking one is a key skill.
notes.plans: After Qf3, White threatens Rae1 and the black king is exposed. Black's pieces are undeveloped and cannot defend.

notes.explains: g4 is a strong positional move that permanently prevents Black from playing c5, giving White a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: When Black cannot achieve the c5 break, White's space advantage and control become decisive. g4 fixes the pawn structure and denies Black any counterplay.
notes.plans: Follow up with Rc1 and Ne5, pressuring the c-file and targeting c6. The knight on e5 can later go to c6 or support an attack.

notes.explains: e3 is a patient prophylactic move that prepares Nd2 to attack the c4-pawn. It also solidifies the center and prevents any tactics on d4.
notes.teaches: Before executing a plan, consider preparatory moves that neutralize potential counterplay. e3 ensures that Nd2 does not leave the d4-pawn hanging.
notes.plans: After Nd2, White will capture on c4, winning a pawn. Black's bishop trade is fine; White's king is safe and the queenside weaknesses remain.

notes.explains: White wins a pawn and now has a two-on-one queenside majority. Black's c5 break is too late; White opens the d-file and captures on c4.
notes.teaches: Converting an advantage often involves winning a pawn and then exploiting the resulting pawn majority. Patience and precise calculation are required.
notes.plans: Use the outside passed pawn on the queenside to create further weaknesses. Black's time trouble may hasten the end.

notes.explains: After winning a second pawn, White has a decisive material advantage. Black's time trouble and lack of counterplay make the conversion straightforward.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a two-pawn advantage with an active rook is usually winning. Use the rook to infiltrate and create threats.
notes.plans: Play b3 to defend the knight, then infiltrate with Rd7. Black's a5 push can be met by Qd2, attacking a5 and preparing Nb2 to win the a4-pawn.

notes.explains: Nb2 wins the a4-pawn, exploiting the overworked rook on a8. This is a clean tactical finish.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for tactics that win additional material. The knight retreat to b2 is a classic example of exploiting a pinned or overloaded piece.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, White's material advantage is decisive. The game ends shortly.

notes.explains: After e5 c3 Nc6 cxd4 exd4, White can play Bc4, transposing to an Alapin line. Black should play Nf6, and if White plays Ng5, Black has the defensive resource Qb4+ to enable castling and protect f7.
notes.teaches: In Fried Liver-type attacks, a queen check can be a unique defensive resource to get the king to safety.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, and if Ng5, Qb4+ followed by O-O.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn: after cxd5, Nxd5, Nxe4, Bxe4, Bf3, Bb7, Rc1, Qb6 attacks b2 and d4. White cannot defend both.
notes.teaches: Calculate tactical sequences to the end. Here, the skewer on the b-file wins material. Always look for double attacks.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, consolidate by defending b7 and activating the rooks.

notes.explains: Black captures on b2, ruining White's queenside pawns. White has no compensation for the pawn deficit.
notes.teaches: When you win a pawn, look to further damage the opponent's structure. The b2 pawn is a common target in Benoni structures.
notes.plans: Defend the b7 pawn with Qd7, then bring rooks to the c-file and centralize.

notes.explains: Qd7 defends b7 and connects the rooks, a multi-purpose move. White's queen on c2 is passive.
notes.teaches: Prefer moves that accomplish multiple goals: defense, development, and coordination.
notes.plans: Play Rac8 and Rfd8, then consider a5 to pressure c4 or b5 to open lines.

notes.explains: a5 is a thematic move: it threatens to open the a-file or fix White's queenside pawns. If White takes axb5, the pawn structure is ruined; if White plays b5, the queen on a4 becomes active.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage on the queenside, pushing a5 is a standard way to increase pressure. It can create weaknesses or open lines.
notes.plans: Follow up with b5 or Qa4 to target the c4 pawn and the rook on c1.

notes.explains: After bxa5, Rxa5, Qa4 attacks the rook and the a7 pawn. Black's queen is well-placed, and White's queenside is weak.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pawn structure is compromised, target the weaknesses with your queen and rooks. Qa4 is a strong multi-purpose move.
notes.plans: Continue with Rb5 or Qxa7, or prepare d4 to break in the center.

notes.explains: d4 is a central break, threatening e5 and e4. White must respond carefully; the best defense is Qe4, blocking the pawns.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, opening the center can accelerate the win. Push d4 to create passed pawns and activate pieces.
notes.plans: After d4, follow with e5 and e4, crushing White's position.

notes.explains: e5 pushes the pawns forward, threatening e4. White's pieces are tied down, and the central pawns are unstoppable.
notes.teaches: Once the center is opened, advance your pawns with tempo. The pawns become a battering ram.
notes.plans: Play e4, then f5, and the pawns will tear through White's position.

notes.explains: White played Bb4 instead of the critical Qe4, allowing e4. Now Black's pawns are crushing, and White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Always prioritize stopping the opponent's central pawn break. Qe4 was the only defense; missing it leads to a quick loss.
notes.plans: Push d3, then the pawns create tactics and win material.

notes.explains: d3 pushes the pawn forward, creating threats. White's rook on c1 is under attack, and there are pins and back-rank threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a powerful pawn roller, push them forward. They create tactical opportunities and restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: After d3, look for the most clinical win: Rxc4 or Qb3, winning the rook on a2.

notes.explains: White plays Rxd3, but Black has multiple winning continuations. Rxc4 threatens Rxb4, and Qb3 wins the rook on a2.
notes.teaches: Always look for the most clinical continuation. Here, Qb3 is cleaner than Rxc4, but both win. Calculate to avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Play Qb3, winning the rook on a2, or Rxc4 with threats.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Bb4, the main line. White must not play Bd3 immediately (drops the knight on d4) or f3 (weakens the king, allows d5). Correct is Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3, overprotecting e4.
notes.teaches: In the Four Knights Scotch, the move order is critical: capture on c6 first to free d3 for the bishop, and avoid weakening pawn moves like f3.
notes.plans: After Bd3, Black often castles, and White can continue with 0-0, preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop to g5 or f4.

notes.explains: After Bd3 0-0, Black's best is …d5, leading to sharp theory. Instead, …d6 is a common inaccuracy: it blocks the dark-squared bishop's retreat, making the pin Bg5 very troublesome.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is on b4, avoid closing its retreat with d6; d5 is more active and keeps the bishop flexible.
notes.plans: After …d6, White plays Bg5, pinning the knight. Black must either play g5 (weakening) or tolerate the pin, which White can exploit with f4 and e5.

notes.explains: After Bg5, White's plan is to increase pressure on f6. The immediate Qf3 is less accurate; better is f4, preparing e5. But before pushing e5, White should play Kh1 to avoid ...Qd4+ tactics on the a7-g1 diagonal.
notes.teaches: When attacking on the kingside, prophylactic king moves can prevent counter-tactics along open diagonals. Don't rush the breakthrough if a single preparatory move makes it safe.
notes.plans: After Kh1, White can continue with Qf3 and Re1, building up for e5. The immediate e5 is also possible but requires care.

notes.explains: In the game, after Kh1, Black played ...Bc5, and White chose Qf3. However, the immediate e5 was winning: after e5 dxe5 fxe5, Black's knight is pinned, and …Rxe5? loses to Bxf6 gxf6 Bxh7+! Kxh7 Qh5+ Kg8 Qxe5, winning a rook.
notes.teaches: When a pinned piece is overloaded, a pawn break can open lines and create tactical shots. Always check if the breakthrough is immediately winning before making preparatory moves.
notes.plans: If Black avoids the rook capture, White still has a strong attack. The key is to notice that the queen x-rays c6, and the bishop on c5 is undefended.

notes.explains: After Qf3, Black played ...Kh8, and White could still play e5. The best follow-up is Ne4!, attacking the bishop on c5 and the knight on f6. If ...Bd7, then exd6 and Black's position collapses.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are active, a knight jump to a central outpost can create multiple threats and force concessions.
notes.plans: After Ne4, White threatens Nxf6+ and exd6. Black's pinned knight makes it hard to defend.

notes.explains: Later, White could have played Qg6, threatening Qh7#. The king cannot escape via f8 because of the f-file control. This shows the power of a queen on g6 in such positions.
notes.teaches: In kingside attacks, the queen often finds a powerful post on g6 or h5, especially when the f-file is open and the king lacks escape squares.
notes.plans: After Qg6, Black must give up material to prevent mate, e.g., ...Rg8, but then White wins the exchange or more.

notes.explains: Black's attempt ...Bg4 is not scary: White can simply take on f6 first, then if ...Bxf3, Bxf3 wins a piece. The queen can also retreat to g3, a good attacking square.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to break a pin with a bishop sortie, you can often ignore it or trade down to a winning endgame. The g3 square is a safe haven for the queen in many openings.
notes.plans: If ...Bg4, White plays Nxf6+ or Qg3, maintaining the attack.

notes.explains: After Bd3, Black's best is …d5. Then exd5 cxd5 leads to a main line. White's recommended setup is h3! (flexible, controls g4), then Qf3, and later develop the bishop to g5 or f4 depending on Black's response.
notes.teaches: In the Four Knights Scotch main line, h3 is a useful prophylactic move that prevents ...Bg4 and prepares Qf3. It keeps options open for the dark-squared bishop.
notes.plans: After h3, White plays Qf3. If Black plays ...Bd6, White can trade bishops with Bg5 or fianchetto with g3 and Bg2. The key is to maintain pressure on d5 and the f6 knight.

notes.explains: In the main line after h3 c6 Qf3, Black often plays ...Bd6. White can then play Re1, and if ...Rb8, b3! prepares Bb2, targeting the dark squares. The bishop can also go to f4, and if Black trades, White gets control of c5 and pressure on the queenside pawns.
notes.teaches: The dark-squared bishop in the Four Knights Scotch is flexible: it can go to g5, f4, or b2. Trading it often favors White because of the resulting dark-square weaknesses on the queenside.
notes.plans: After b3, White can play Bb2, then Na4 to target c5, immobilizing the c6 pawn. The rook on b1 supports the b4 break.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...d6 instead of ...d5, White should play Bg5 immediately. Black's best response is ...g5, but that weakens the kingside. White can then play f4, blasting open the position. The g5 pawn becomes a target.
notes.teaches: When Black plays ...d6, the bishop on b4 is trapped; White exploits this with Bg5, forcing ...g5 or enduring a permanent pin. The resulting pawn weaknesses give White a lasting attack.
notes.plans: After ...g5, White plays f4, opening lines. If Black plays ...Rg8, White can continue with Qf3 and Re1, building up for e5.

notes.explains: In the game, after f4, Black played ...a5, a neutral move. White responded with Kh1, a prophylactic move to avoid ...Qd4+ tactics. This allowed White to later play Qf3 and Re1 without worry.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong attack, don't rush the breakthrough if a single prophylactic move makes it safe. Patience can increase the success rate of your attack.
notes.plans: After Kh1, White can continue with Qf3 and Re1, then e5. The immediate e5 was also winning, but Kh1 is safe and methodical.

notes.explains: After Kh1, Black played ...Bc5. White played Qf3, but the immediate e5 was winning: …dxe5 fxe5 Rxe5? Bxf6 gxf6 Bxh7+! Kxh7 Qh5+ Kg8 Qxe5, winning a rook. White missed this because he didn't notice the x-ray on c6 and the undefended bishop on c5.
notes.teaches: Always scan the entire board for undefended pieces and x-rays. Even in a dominating position, a simple tactical shot can be the quickest win.
notes.plans: If Black avoids the rook capture, White still has a strong attack. The key is to notice that the queen x-rays c6, and the bishop on c5 is undefended.

notes.explains: After winning material, White converted by mopping up pawns and delivering checkmate. The key was to avoid unnecessary complications and trade queens when advantageous.
notes.teaches: When converting a winning position, simplify by trading pieces, especially queens, to reduce counterplay. Keep your king safe and advance passed pawns.
notes.plans: White can play Qxc7, then take on f4, and eventually promote a pawn or deliver mate.

notes.explains: After the e5 break and exchanges, Black has a comfortable position. The rook on e8 pressures the e5 bishop, and Black is ready to develop the queenside bishop.
notes.teaches: After opening the center with e5, developing with Re8 is a natural way to pressure the opponent's pieces and prepare further activity.
notes.plans: Black will develop the bishop to b7 or g4, then consider central pawn breaks like f5 or c5.

notes.explains: Black plays b6 and Bb7, fianchettoing the light-squared bishop to aim at the e4 square. This is a slow but solid plan, though it allows White to generate counterplay with Ng5.
notes.teaches: Fianchettoing the light-squared bishop against the Stonewall can be effective, but it must be timed carefully to avoid tactical shots like Ng5 targeting f7.
notes.plans: Black intends to complete development with Bb7 and then possibly play c5 or f5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: White plays Ng5, threatening Nxf7. Black must be careful; the immediate Nxe4? is a mistake because after Qh4 Bxe4, White has Qb3 threatening smothered mate. Black should instead consider h6 or other defensive moves.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a knight to g5, always check if it threatens f7. A common defensive idea is h6, giving the king an escape square on h7 and preventing smothered mate threats.
notes.plans: Black should play h6 to kick the knight, or if that is not possible, find a way to protect f7 without weakening the king's position.

notes.explains: Black mistakenly captures on e4, leading to a critical position. White's Qb3 creates a devastating threat of smothered mate via Nf7+ and Nd6+ followed by Qb3#. Black must now find a defense or face immediate loss.
notes.teaches: In chaotic positions, break down the threats: the queen is hanging, the knight on e4 is attacked twice, and White's queen on b3 threatens smothered mate. Always consider all threats, especially those involving the king's safety.
notes.plans: Black's best defense is to play h6 or Re7 to protect f7, or to enter an endgame with Qxe4, which leads to a drawish opposite-colored bishop endgame.

notes.explains: Black trades queens and enters an opposite-colored bishop endgame. White has a slight edge due to better piece activity, but the position is objectively drawn with correct play.
notes.teaches: When facing a dangerous attack, simplifying to an endgame can be a safe haven. Opposite-colored bishop endgames are notoriously drawish, even with a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade rooks and activate the king, while White will try to create winning chances by exploiting the bishop pair and weak pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, undermining the d4 pawn and opening lines for the queen and bishop. This is a strong move to activate the pieces and create winning chances in the endgame.
notes.teaches: In endgames with an extra pawn, opening files and diagonals for your pieces is crucial. Undermining the opponent's pawn chain with c5 can give your queen and bishop more scope.
notes.plans: After c5, Black will capture on d4 and use the open e-file and long diagonal to pressure White's position.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg7-e5, using the pin on the f2 rook to attack the h2 pawn. This is a second-order tactic: the pin means the king defends the rook, so attacking h2 overloads the king.
notes.teaches: When you see a pin, don't just stop there. Ask yourself how you can exploit the pinned piece's immobility to create additional threats, such as overloading the defender.
notes.plans: Black will capture on h2 or use the threat to win material, eventually converting the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black has many good setups (e6, d6, g6, a6) depending on one's preferred Sicilian variation. Here, the fianchetto (g6) is chosen as it fits the Accelerated Dragon style.
notes.teaches: Choose your setup based on the type of Sicilian you play; consistency helps in understanding typical plans.
notes.plans: Develop with g6, Bg7, and later consider d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: Bd2 intends Bc3 to pressure the kingside, but Black should not trade bishops; instead, continue development.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading your fianchettoed bishop for a less active piece; it is a key defender.
notes.plans: Continue with Bg7, Nf6, and castle, preparing to open the center with d5.

notes.explains: c3 is a poor move because it does not develop and restricts White's knight; White's lack of development is becoming critical.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary pawn moves that hinder your own pieces; prioritize development.
notes.plans: Black continues developing normally, aiming to open the center soon.

notes.explains: Nf6 is chosen over e6 and Bg7 because here rapid development and opening the center are more important than preserving the fianchetto bishop's diagonal. The d6 square is also a concern.
notes.teaches: Prioritize development speed over rigid setup when the center is fluid; sometimes a knight on f6 is more active than a pawn on e6.
notes.plans: Castle next, then prepare d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: Black castles, completing development and ensuring king safety before pushing d5.
notes.teaches: Always secure your king before launching central operations, especially when the opponent is underdeveloped.
notes.plans: Now ready to play d5, opening the center while White is still undeveloped.

notes.explains: e5 is a terrible move for White, overextending without development. Black's knight should go to d5, keeping central control, though Nh5 is also possible.
notes.teaches: When a pawn advances, look for the square it vacates and consider occupying it with a piece.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, centralizing the knight and preparing further pressure.

notes.explains: White's queen on e4 is vulnerable. Black should take the e5 pawn with the knight (Nxe5), not the bishop, because Nxe5 threatens a fork on d3 and keeps the queen exposed.
notes.teaches: When capturing, consider which piece leaves the opponent's queen most vulnerable; avoid moving your bishop from its strong diagonal without good reason.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, threatening Nd3+ and winning the queen.

notes.explains: Black chooses Qc7 over Qb6. Qc7 is not just a threat (Nd3+ wins queen) but also useful if White castles queenside (x-rays c3) and helps coordinate rooks.
notes.teaches: A good move should be useful even without the immediate threat; avoid 'one-move-tricks' that have no follow-up.
notes.plans: Play Qc7, threatening Nd3+ and preparing further development.

notes.explains: Nd3+ forks king and queen, winning the queen. White's lack of development made this possible.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is exposed and the king is vulnerable, look for forks and discoveries.
notes.plans: Win the queen and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: After winning the queen, Black is up massive material. Instead of grabbing more material (Qxf2), Black should open the center with d5 to exploit White's poor development.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, prioritize opening lines and activating pieces over grabbing more pawns; speed up the attack.
notes.plans: Play d5, opening the d-file and bringing the rook to d8, targeting the knight on d2.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, sacrificing a pawn to open the d-file. The rook will go to d8, and the bishop can go to h6 to target the knight on d2.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing material to accelerate the attack is often correct when the opponent is undeveloped.
notes.plans: Play Rd8, then Bh6, and look for ways to eliminate the knight on d2.

notes.explains: Black must be careful: after Bh6, if White plays Kb1, the knight on f3 can be captured but the d2 knight recaptures. So Black should play Bf5 first, preventing Kb1 and preparing Rc8 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prevent the opponent's king from escaping; a moving target is harder to hit.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, then Rc8, threatening sacrifices on c3 and a hidden mate threat.

notes.explains: Black has a hidden mate threat: Qe4, threatening Qb1# because the knight on d2 is pinned to the king. The knight cannot capture the queen.
notes.teaches: Always consider pins; a piece that appears to defend a square may be immobilized. If you see a good move (like taking the free knight), look for a better one (like Qe4 with mate threat).
notes.plans: Play Qe4, threatening Qb1#. White's only defense is Re1, but then Black can win material or checkmate.

notes.explains: If White had played correctly (Nf3, Nc3, Be2, O-O), the position would be close to equal. But White's inaccuracies (Bd2, c3, e5) gave Black a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: Even after a poor opening, accurate development can keep the balance; one must not panic.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing and look to open the center.

notes.explains: If White plays Bc3, Black should not fear it. Nd5 is a strong response, pressuring the bishop. If White takes on d5, Black recaptures with the knight and can 'castle by hand' (Rf8, Kg8) to safety.
notes.teaches: When your king is exposed, you can often 'castle artificially' by moving the rook and king manually. Don't fear exchanges that open lines if you have active pieces.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, and if Bxd5, exd5, then Rf8, Kg8, and later d5.

notes.explains: After artificial castling, Black is safe and can push d5. If White plays e5, Black has Ng4 winning the e5 pawn. If exd5, Nxd5 gives Black a massive initiative with potential sacrifices on c3.
notes.teaches: Once the king is safe, open the center to exploit your lead in development.
notes.plans: Play d5, and if e5, Ng4 wins the pawn; if exd5, Nxd5 with strong attack.

notes.explains: If White plays e5, Black should play Ng4, attacking the e5 pawn three times against one defender. This wins the pawn.
notes.teaches: Count attackers and defenders before capturing; if you have more attackers, you win the pawn.
notes.plans: Play Ng4, winning the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: After exd5, Nxd5 gives Black a powerful knight in the center. Black can then play Bf5, and if White plays Nf3, Black can push e5-e4-e3, collapsing White's position.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight supported by pawns can be devastating; use pawn advances to restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, then e5, e4, e3, or consider sacrifices on c3.

notes.explains: If White plays Bg3, Black should not play Nxe5? because of Qb5 skewering the knights. Instead, Black should first take on c3? No, the correct move is to create a double attack: Qe4, attacking both undefended pieces (knight on d5 and bishop on g3). The knight cannot defend the bishop because it's on a light square.
notes.teaches: When you see two undefended pieces, look for a fork or double attack. Be aware of skewers and pins that might defend them.
notes.plans: Play Qe4, forking the knight and bishop.

notes.explains: If Black blunders with Nxe5, White has Qb5 skewering the knights. But Black can save the game by creating a counter-threat: Qb6 attacking b2. If White takes the knight, Black takes the rook. This shows the importance of counterplay when behind.
notes.teaches: When you blunder, look for counter-threats using your lead in development or active pieces. Don't panic; find the best move.
notes.plans: Play Qb6, threatening Qxb2 and creating complications.

notes.explains: After Qb6, if White plays Qxe5, Black has Qxb2, winning the rook. White may have compensation but Black is not losing. This is better than panicking and giving up the knight.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to create threats that force the opponent to defend, rather than accepting material loss.
notes.plans: Play Qb6, and if Qxe5, Qxb2 with counterplay.

notes.explains: White gives up the knight for Black's dark-squared bishop, preserving the bishop pair. This is preferable to Bf4 because Black could then play Qe7 and trade bishops, reducing White's attacking potential.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, avoid unnecessary trades that remove one of them; exchanging a knight for the opponent's bishop is often a good deal.
notes.plans: After Qxd6, consider where to place the light-squared bishop. Bb3 is prophylactic, discouraging e5 by pinning the f-pawn.

notes.explains: Bb3 is a prophylactic move: it discourages Black from playing e5 because after e5, White has Bg5 attacking the queen, and f6 is illegal due to the pin on f7. This keeps Black's light-squared bishop locked in.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet-looking move that prevents the opponent's best plan is more valuable than a direct attack. Ask: 'What does my opponent want to do, and can I stop it?'
notes.plans: If Black plays b6 to develop the bishop, respond with Bg5 to provoke f6, then drop back to f4, exploiting the weakened e6 pawn.

notes.explains: Bg5 provokes f6, which weakens the e6 pawn and prevents Black from playing e5. After f6, White drops the bishop back to f4, now with the added benefit that e6 is a permanent weakness.
notes.teaches: Provoke a pawn weakness before placing your piece on its ideal square. This pattern (provoke, then retreat) can be used in many positions.
notes.plans: After Bf4, continue developing with Rc1, targeting the queen and the weak e6 pawn. Keep the initiative by making threats every move.

notes.explains: Rac1 brings the last piece into the attack. The rook on c1 eyes the queen on d6 and the weak e6 pawn. All White's pieces are active, and Black is struggling to develop.
notes.teaches: In an initiative-based position, bring every piece into the game. Do not waste time; each move should create a threat or improve your position.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bb7, take on e6. If Bd7, consider Qd3 or Qd2 to attack the bishop, exploiting the fact that it is only defended by the queen (a type-2 undefended piece).

notes.explains: White captures on e6, entering an endgame up a pawn with active pieces. Black's minor pieces are poorly placed: the knight on a5 is on the rim, and the bishop on a6 is awkward.
notes.teaches: When queens come off, do not relax. Keep the initiative by maintaining pressure on the opponent's poorly placed pieces. Use pins and pawn advances to restrict them further.
notes.plans: Preserve the pin on the knight on f7. Play Nd4 to create a secondary threat (e.g., Bc5 or Bf7). Avoid trading pieces unnecessarily; keep the rooks active.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange with Rc7, forking the bishop on c8 and the knight on f7. After the dust settles, White is up a rook for a bishop, with active rooks and a safe king.
notes.teaches: In endgames, prioritize piece activity over material. Do not waste time saving pawns; instead, get your rooks to the seventh rank and create threats.
notes.plans: Play h4 to create luft and discourage Black's kingside pawns. Then play Rcc7, doubling rooks on the seventh rank. This will win all of Black's pawns and lead to mate or a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: White creates an outside passed pawn on the a-file and promotes it. The technique is simple: push the pawn, use the rook to support it, and trade rooks when advantageous.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, creating an outside passed pawn is a standard winning method. Use your rook to support the pawn's advance and trade rooks to simplify into a won pawn endgame.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn to promotion. If Black's rook tries to block, use your rook to give checks and force the king into a bad position.

notes.explains: After Nc7+ Rxc7 Bxc7, White is up a rook and has a winning position. The game is effectively over. Black's position collapsed due to passive defense and lack of development.
notes.teaches: When you are a pawn up and have the initiative, don't let up. Keep creating threats and forcing concessions. Black's attempt to defend passively (Nd5) only made things worse.
notes.plans: Finish the game by developing the remaining pieces and converting the material advantage.

notes.explains: After Bc4, Black's knight on c5 attacks e3. White can sacrifice the c5 pawn with h3, leading to a complex position where White's light-square control and pawn majority give an advantage.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's worth giving back the extra pawn to gain positional trumps: bishop pair, light-square control, and a mobile pawn majority. Compare pawn majorities to assess the position.
notes.plans: Play h3, and if Black takes on c5, continue with g4, then develop the knight to d2 or c4. Push the queenside pawns (a4, b4) to create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: After h3, Black cannot take on g2 because of the open lines. White's plan is to keep the bishop pair and push the queenside pawns. The knight on c6 is restricted by the pawns on b4 and c5.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pawn majority, avoid blockading your own pawns. Push the unopposed pawn first (a4 before b5) to prevent the opponent's knight from blocking.
notes.plans: Play a4, then b4, gaining space. If Black plays a5, then b5 is bad because of Na5 blockading. Instead, push a5 first to soften up the knight on c6.

notes.explains: The final sequence shows a classic winning attack. White's pieces coordinate perfectly: the bishop on h3 (via g3) controls c8, the rook on d1 pins the knight, and the knight on b5 delivers the final blow.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is stuck in the center, look for tactical blows like Nc7+ that win material. The bishop on h3 is crucial for preventing the king's escape.
notes.plans: Convert the material advantage by developing the remaining pieces and avoiding counterplay.

notes.explains: Black plays Qg5, threatening Qxg2 mate and also preventing White from taking on e4 because of the fork on g2. This forces White to deal with the threat.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on e4, Qg5 can be a powerful move that creates multiple threats and ties down White's pieces.
notes.plans: After Qg5, Black threatens Qxg2# and also prepares to bring the rook to f6 or h6 for a mating attack.

notes.explains: After Kh1, Black can deliver checkmate with Nxg3+ followed by Rf6 and Rh6. White cannot prevent it; even giving up the rook on f2 only delays the mate.
notes.teaches: This is a classic mating pattern: a knight sacrifice on g3 opens the h-file, and the rook swings over to deliver mate. White's king is trapped.
notes.plans: Execute the mate: Nxg3+, hxg3, Rf6, and Rh6#.

notes.explains: The Nimzo-Indian is not just a positional opening; it can lead to powerful attacks, especially with the setup shown (knight on e4, queen on g5, rook lift to h6).
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian is a gateway to sharp attacks. Knowing typical attacking patterns (like the one with Qg5 and Rf6-h6) can lead to brilliant wins.

notes.explains: If White avoids the immediate mate with a move like Nf3, Black can still maintain pressure. The key is to keep the knight on e4 and build up the attack.
notes.teaches: Do not be lulled into creating a threat just because it's tempting; always calculate. In this position, taking on e4 with the knight would allow Bc4, giving White a good knight vs bad bishop scenario.

notes.explains: In the line where White plays d5, Black should recapture with the bishop, not the knight, to avoid a bad bishop vs good knight scenario. The knight on e4 is a strong outpost.
notes.teaches: When choosing between captures, consider the resulting piece quality. A knight outpost is often worth more than a bishop, so keep the knight and trade the bishop.

notes.explains: If White avoids the mate with a move like Nf3, Black can still maintain pressure. The key is to keep the knight on e4 and build up the attack.
notes.teaches: In positions with a knight on e4, look for ways to bring the rook to the kingside (e.g., Rf6-h6) and combine with queen and bishop for a mating attack.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4 (Bowdler Attack) and then Qh5, an early queen sortie that violates opening principles. Black must defend both the e5 and f7 threats.
notes.teaches: When White plays Bc4 against the Sicilian, e6 is a natural response that blunts the bishop and prepares development.
notes.plans: Develop knights and bishop, chase the queen with tempo, and aim for d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: After Qh5, Black should not panic. Moves like Nf6, e6, or d6 are all fine; the key is to develop while harassing the queen.
notes.teaches: Against an early queen sortie, prioritize development and use tempo-gaining moves to drive the queen back.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then d5 to open lines and exploit White's lagging development.

notes.explains: White's queen on h4 is awkward. Black can consider Be7, preparing d5 and threatening ...Ne4 to trap the queen.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is misplaced, look for ways to trap it or gain time by threatening it with developing moves.
notes.plans: Play Be7, then d5, and after exchanges, Ne4 will attack the queen.

notes.explains: Another strong option is Nd4, attacking c2 and threatening the bishop. White struggles to defend both the pawn and the bishop.
notes.teaches: In open positions, centralizing the knight with tempo can create multiple threats that are hard to parry.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, then if Bb3, continue with c4 or d5 to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: After Nd4, White's best is Kd1 (avoiding e5 which would allow ...Nxb3). Black should now play d5 before Be7 to prevent White's e5.
notes.teaches: Order of moves matters: play the most forcing move first (d5) to deny the opponent counterplay (e5).
notes.plans: Play d5, exd5, then cxd5, followed by Be7, developing with tempo and opening the center.

notes.explains: Black can also consider Ne4, forcing queen trade. Concrete calculation shows that after Qxe4, Kxe4, C3, Nxf2+, Ke1, Nd3+, Kd1, Bg4 leads to a winning attack.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically reject queen trades when you have a development lead; concrete calculation may reveal a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Calculate Ne4 line; if White avoids it, continue with d5 and Be7.

notes.explains: In the game, White played Kd1, and Black played d5, opening the center. After exchanges, Black's development advantage is crushing.
notes.teaches: When ahead in development, open the center to exploit the opponent's uncastled king and undeveloped pieces.
notes.plans: Play d5, then after exchanges, develop bishops and rook to deliver checkmate or win material.

notes.explains: Black's knight on d4 is powerful. White cannot easily dislodge it; if Ne2, Black plays Ne5, threatening the bishop and maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight supported by pawns is a long-term asset; avoid trading it off without compensation.
notes.plans: Keep the knight on d4, play Ne5 if needed, and target c2 and f2.

notes.explains: White's best try is e5, but Black can simply take on b3 and then d5, leaving White's pawns weak and pieces uncoordinated.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries a pawn break, calculate carefully; often you can ignore it and continue with your own plan.
notes.plans: After e5, take on b3, then play d5, exploiting the loose e5 pawn.

notes.explains: The game ended quickly after Black's d5 and Ne4, winning material. White's early queen sortie left them hopelessly behind in development.
notes.teaches: Violating opening principles (bringing queen out early) is punished by simple, principled play: develop, gain tempo, open the center.
notes.plans: Continue developing, trade queens if advantageous, and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black's d6 is somewhat passive, restricting his bishop and leaving the knight on a6 on the rim. White should consider d4 even without the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: Even when down material, central pawn breaks can be correct if they create imbalance and activity.
notes.plans: Play d4 to open the center and prepare opposite-side castling.

notes.explains: If Black takes on d4, White should recapture with the queen, not the knight. This clears the queen for quick development and allows castling long.
notes.teaches: When planning opposite-side castling, prioritize clearing the queen from the center and developing quickly.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nc3, Bg5, and O-O-O, possibly with e5 to gain space.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 pins the knight and attacks d4. White must defend the pawn without trading queens, as that would reduce attacking chances when down material.
notes.teaches: When down material, avoid unnecessary queen trades. Defend central pawns with other pawns when possible.
notes.plans: Play c3 to support d4, then develop with Be3 and Nbd2.

notes.explains: White has developed and now must decide where to place the queen and whether to castle long. Castling long is risky due to c3 weakening, but it's necessary to generate a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: When down material, you cannot afford luxury in king safety. Opposite-side castling is a standard way to create attacking chances.
notes.plans: Play h3 to prepare g4 and a pawn storm, then castle long and push g4-g5.

notes.explains: After h3, Black traded bishop for knight. White recaptured with the knight, keeping the g-pawn for the pawn storm. The g-file alone is not enough; the pawns are needed to open lines.
notes.teaches: An open file alone is insufficient for an attack. Pawns are needed to create further weaknesses and break open the king's cover.
notes.plans: Continue with g4, g5, and h4-h5 to open the h-file.

notes.explains: Black's c5 is a mistake. It creates a hole on d5 and weakens the center. White should not close the center with d5, as that would give Black a free hand on the queenside.
notes.teaches: Avoid creating holes in your pawn structure. When the opponent has a space disadvantage, keep the center open to emphasize piece activity.
notes.plans: Castle long and aim to use the d5 square for a knight.

notes.explains: White castles long, committing to a kingside attack. The king is safer on the queenside despite the c3 weakness, because the attack is on the other side.
notes.teaches: Opposite-side castling allows you to throw pawns at the opponent's king without exposing your own.
notes.plans: Push g4, g5, h4, h5 to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: Black's Qa5 attacks a2. White must defend without creating a hook. Kb1 is better than a3, which would give Black a target on b4.
notes.teaches: Avoid creating pawn hooks on the side you are castled. Defend with the king or pieces instead.
notes.plans: Play Kb1, then continue the pawn storm on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black's Rfe8 is a waste of time. He should be attacking on the queenside with b5 immediately. The rook move does nothing to speed up his attack.
notes.teaches: When you have an attack, do not waste time on prophylactic moves. Every tempo counts, especially when the opponent is also attacking.
notes.plans: Continue with g4, g5, h4, h5 to open the kingside.

notes.explains: Black's g6 is a decisive mistake. It creates a hook that allows White to open the h-file quickly. Black should have played c4 and b4 to speed up his own attack.
notes.teaches: Do not create pawn hooks on the side you are being attacked. Pushing pawns in front of your king only helps the opponent open lines.
notes.plans: Play h5, then Qh3 to double on the h-file before capturing on g6.

notes.explains: h5 attacks the g6 pawn. White should not capture immediately; instead, he should prepare with Qh3 to double on the h-file and prevent Black from defending with Rf7.
notes.teaches: Delay the capture that opens the file until you have maximum force ready. The threat is often stronger than the execution.
notes.plans: Play Qh3, then hxg6 and Rxh7 with a mating attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Nxg3, but White should ignore it and continue the attack. Taking the knight would waste time and let Black defend.
notes.teaches: When you are on the verge of checkmate, do not be distracted by material. Focus on delivering the final blow.
notes.plans: Play Rxg3 or Qh3, then hxg6 and mate.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the exchange (bishop for rook) to keep the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal. Black plays Na5 attacking the bishop, but White can respond with Be6, keeping the bishop active and preparing Ng5.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing, evaluate what you gain: here, White keeps a powerful attacking piece (the light-squared bishop) and has a pawn plus long-term attacking chances. The material deficit is minimal.
notes.plans: Play Be6, then Ng5, threatening Nf7 or Nh7. The queen can later join via e4 or h4. The attack is worth more than the exchange.

notes.explains: Black grabs material with Nxb2, but this is greedy. White now has Ng5 with multiple threats: Nf7+ and Qh4. Black's king is exposed and White's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When defending, don't grab material if it gives the opponent a decisive attack. Prioritize king safety over material.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, threatening Nf7+ and Qh4. If Black tries to defend with h6, White can continue with Qh4 or other attacking moves. The attack is winning.

notes.explains: Black panics with Qxf4, but White has a decisive check: Nd6+! This knight move severs the connection between Black's queen and bishop, allowing Qxe5+ with mate threats. The key is to consider all possible knight checks.
notes.teaches: When you have a discovered check, methodically examine every possible square for the knight. One of them may win immediately.
notes.plans: After Nd6+, if Kf8, Qxe5 is mate. If Kg7, Qxe5+ leads to mate or wins the queen. The game is over.

notes.explains: After Nxc6, Black can recapture with the d-pawn (dxc6) to open the d-file and develop quickly, accepting doubled pawns that are not easily attacked.
notes.teaches: When deciding between recaptures, consider which one accelerates development and opens lines, especially if the opponent's king is still in the center.
notes.plans: Develop rapidly: castle, bring the knight to e5 via g6, and place the queen on g5. Then occupy the open d-file with a rook.

notes.explains: With White's king castled and Black's pieces ideally placed (knight on e5, queen on g5, rook on d3), Black has total positional domination. The rook on d3 attacks weak pawns and restricts White's pieces.
notes.teaches: Once you have a positional advantage, convert it by targeting weak pawns. Use an outpost (like e5) to anchor your pieces and prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: Take White's pawns one by one, starting with c3 or e3. Keep the rook on d3 to maximize pressure. Watch for tactical motifs like forks (e.g., Nd3).

notes.explains: After Nc4, Black takes with the bishop (Bxc4) to keep the knight on e5. If bxc4, then Rxc3 wins a pawn while maintaining the strong rook on d3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to trade off an active piece, consider recapturing with a piece that preserves your positional trumps (here, keeping the knight on e5).
notes.plans: Continue taking pawns (e.g., Rxe3) and then create luft with g6 and h5 to prevent back-rank mates. Be aware of potential forks (e.g., Nd3).

notes.explains: With a winning material advantage, Black can aim for a checkmate by advancing the h-pawn to h4 to control g3, then play Qg3 threatening mate. White's checks can be sidestepped by moving the king to h6.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive advantage, look for the most direct winning plan. Here, advancing the h-pawn to control g3 sets up a mating net. Always calculate checks carefully to find a safe king hiding square.
notes.plans: Play h4, then Qg3. If White gives checks, move the king to h6 (not h8) to avoid further checks. Then capture White's remaining pieces.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn with Qxa2, but must be careful not to trap the queen. White can play Ra3, but the queen returns safely to e6.
notes.teaches: Before capturing a pawn, always check if your queen can be trapped. If the queen can retreat safely, the capture is often good.
notes.plans: After Qe6, Black is up a pawn and should consolidate, avoiding rook infiltration.

notes.explains: Re8 prepares to meet Rd7 with Re7, forcing a trade of rooks. This is a standard technique to neutralize rook infiltration on the seventh rank.
notes.teaches: When an opponent threatens to put a rook on the seventh rank, meeting it with your own rook on the same file can force a favorable trade.
notes.plans: After Re7, Black can simplify further and push the b-pawn.

notes.explains: Qb5 is a good square, attacking b7 and avoiding tactics. Black must be careful not to allow rook doubling on the c-file.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, preventing the opponent from doubling rooks on an open file is crucial. Active queen placement can deter threats.
notes.plans: Continue to push the b-pawn and create luft with g6 or h6.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a rook with Rxb7, but Black can recapture and the resulting endgame is a draw if White plays correctly (e.g., Kf3).
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a rook on the seventh rank can be dangerous, but if the opponent has active counterplay, it may lead to a draw.
notes.plans: Black should aim to activate the rook and push the b-pawn, but must avoid losing all pawns.

notes.explains: After fianchettoing the bishop and playing Re8, we have successfully castled by hand, bringing the king to g8. However, we have spent many tempi and need to catch up in development and central activity.
notes.teaches: After a slow start, you must immediately challenge the opponent's center to prevent them from building a lasting positional advantage.
notes.plans: Play c5 to break open the center and undermine White's pawn structure.

notes.explains: After c5, White may play h5, but our pawn structure on g6 and e6 is solid; if hxg6 we recapture with the h-pawn, so there is no real threat.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks on the flank, a solid pawn structure can absorb the pressure; don't panic and stick to your central plan.
notes.plans: Continue with cxd4, then consider taking on c4 to create an isolated queen pawn for White.

notes.explains: Developing the knight to c6 is more direct than d7; it attacks d4 and prepares b6 and Bb7. However, we must be careful: b6 immediately fails to Nxc6 Bb5 pinning the queen to the rook.
notes.teaches: When a natural developing move is prevented by a tactical trick, look for a preparatory move that addresses the threat while maintaining your plan.
notes.plans: Play Qd6 to defend the knight on c6 while keeping pressure on d4, then follow with Nb4 to chase away the queen and finally b6.

notes.explains: Instead of playing b6 passively, we play b5 with tempo, attacking the bishop on b3. This gains time and completes development.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between a quiet move and an aggressive move that does the same thing, choose the aggressive one if it gains tempo.
notes.plans: After b5, we have all pieces developed except the knight on e5, which is not a major problem. We can continue improving piece placement, e.g., Ne4 or Rbc8.

notes.explains: With all pieces developed, we look for the most active square for each piece. The knight on f6 can jump to e4, which is a natural outpost and improves its activity.
notes.teaches: In positions without clear tactics, simply improve your worst-placed piece. Look for outposts and active squares.
notes.plans: Continue with Rbc8 to prepare infiltration on c2, and be aware of the queen's overload: it guards g2 and the knight on e2, so Nf6 is a threat.

notes.explains: Rxg2+ is the decisive blow. If Qxg2, then Nf6 is mate. If Kf1, we can move the queen away with check (Qc4+) to win the queen.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, look for the most forcing continuation. Checks and captures that create threats are usually best.
notes.plans: After Rxg2+, White is lost. The game ends shortly.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh5, threatening to take on g3 and also eyeing f4. White must calculate carefully. The key is to see that after Bxb6 Nxg3, White can move the bishop with tempo (Bd4) to win a piece.
notes.teaches: When both queens are hanging, follow a checklist: 1) Can I move my queen with check? 2) Can I desperado? 3) Can I take the opponent's queen and then move my piece with tempo?
notes.plans: Play Bxb6, and after Nxg3, play Bd4, attacking the rook and winning at least a minor piece.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, trying to trap the bishop. White can now push d6, opening lines and creating a square for the knight on e5. The pawn push also weakens black's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is threatened, use pawn breaks to create escape squares and open lines for your other pieces.
notes.plans: Play d6, threatening to open the e-file. If black takes, recapture with the knight and use the e5 square for the knight. If black doesn't take, the pawn on d6 is a powerful passed pawn.

notes.explains: White's knight checks on d6, forcing the king to f8. Now White can play g4, trapping the knight on h5. The knight has no escape squares.
notes.teaches: Use pawn advances to trap enemy pieces; the knight on h5 is vulnerable because it lacks retreat squares.
notes.plans: Play g4, winning the knight. After black moves the king, White captures the knight and remains with a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: Black's knight escapes to f4. White can play Nxf4, opening the g-file and exposing the black king. The bishop on d4 is powerful.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are scattered, simplify by trading into a winning endgame or continue the attack with piece activity.
notes.plans: Play Nxf4, then after gxf4, use the open g-file to attack the king. Alternatively, play Bc4+ to force the king to e7 and then bring the rook to d1.

notes.explains: Black's king is driven back to d8. White has a winning attack. The simplest win is to trade queens and push the passed d-pawn.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a far-advanced passed pawn is a decisive asset. Use it to promote or force material gains.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, threatening Qe8#. If black defends, trade queens and push the d-pawn to promotion.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2, threatening Qe8#. Black must give up material to prevent mate. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use threats of mate to force concessions. Simple, direct moves are often the most effective.
notes.plans: After black blocks or moves, capture the rook on h8 or promote the d-pawn.

notes.explains: Black blocks with Bg8. White can simply take on h7, then promote the d-pawn. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, focus on the most direct plan: promote the passed pawn. Use your pieces to support it.
notes.plans: Play Bxh7, then advance the d-pawn to d7 and d8=Q.

notes.explains: Black plays b5, a flexible Najdorf-style move, keeping options open. White's h3 is slightly inferior to f3 because it doesn't protect e4, allowing Black to develop more freely.
notes.teaches: In the Dragodorf, b5 is a flexible move that doesn't commit the king. White's h3 is a tempo loss compared to f3, as it fails to defend e4.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Bb7, O-O, and then decide between Nbd7 or Nc6 based on White's next move.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2, a slow move that allows Black to complete development. Black castles kingside, a risky but principled decision. The alternative Nbd7 would allow g5 Nh5 Bf3, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: When White plays slowly, Black should complete development and prepare counterplay. Castling kingside in the Dragodorf is risky but can be justified if White cannot generate a quick attack.
notes.plans: Black will play Nbd7, Rc8, and prepare the exchange sacrifice on c3.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange on c3. After bxc3 Nxc4, White's light-squared bishop is gone, leaving light-square weaknesses. Black gets a pawn and tremendous compensation: the knight on d7 will go to e5, and White cannot castle safely.
notes.teaches: The exchange sacrifice on c3 is a classic Sicilian theme. It destroys White's pawn structure, eliminates a key defender, and gives Black long-term positional pressure, often worth more than the material.
notes.plans: Black will recapture on c3 with the knight, then target White's weak pawns and light squares, while preventing White from castling.

notes.explains: After the exchange sacrifice, Black retreats the bishop to a8, a safe square that avoids potential forks and keeps the bishop on the long diagonal. White castles, but Black's compensation is clear.
notes.teaches: After a sacrifice, piece placement matters. The bishop on a8 is safe and still exerts pressure. Avoid placing pieces on squares where they can be forked or attacked.
notes.plans: Black will play Qc7, preparing e5 and d5 to create a powerful pawn center, then target White's queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7, a flexible move that avoids the trade of dark-squared bishops. If White plays Bd4, Black can respond with e5 followed by d5, creating a massive pawn center that restricts White's pieces.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading your fianchettoed bishop unnecessarily. A waiting move like Qc7 can provoke White into Bd4, after which e5 and d5 give Black a dominant center.
notes.plans: Black will play e5 and d5, then use the pawn center to restrict White's pieces and attack the queenside weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black trades queens, entering an endgame with two pawns for the exchange. White's rooks have no open files, while Black's knight and bishop are active. The pawn on d6 is a target, but Black's pieces dominate.
notes.teaches: In some positions, trading queens simplifies to a winning endgame. Two pawns for the exchange is often enough compensation, especially when the opponent's rooks are passive.
notes.plans: Black will push the d-pawn, activate the knight to c4 or e3, and target White's weak pawns.

notes.explains: Black methodically improves the position: g5 prevents f4, f6 solidifies the center, h6 stops back-rank issues, then d4 opens the bishop. The knight maneuvers to e3 via c5, creating a decisive threat.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, prevent counterplay first (g5, f6, h6), then improve your pieces. The knight belongs on e3, attacking weak pawns and supporting promotion.
notes.plans: Black will play Nc5, then Ne3, targeting f1 and g2. White's desperation sack with Rxf6 is met by careful king moves and a tactical fork (Nf4+).

notes.explains: Black now has the queen on f6. White plays Nh5, attacking the queen. Black can safely take the pawn on b2: after Qxb2 Rb1, the queen retreats to e5, where it is safe because f4 would weaken White's pawns and allow Qxe3+.
notes.teaches: Taking a pawn with the queen requires concrete calculation. Here Qxb2 is safe because the queen has a good retreat square (e5) and White's counterplay is insufficient.
notes.plans: After Qe5, Black is up a pawn with a strong position. Black should aim to consolidate, possibly by castling and developing the light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd4, a strong central square. The queen is safe here because White cannot easily attack it. It also prevents White from castling, as Bxg3 would win a piece due to the pin on f2.
notes.teaches: A centralized queen can be very powerful if it is not easily attacked. Here Qd4 ties White down and prevents castling, creating a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Black's next moves can include pushing the a-pawn or playing Rfd8 to prepare e5. White's king is stuck in the center and Black's pieces are more active.

notes.explains: Black's c6 is unusual; the standard move is Be7. After d4 b5 Bb3, Black's c5 is a decisive mistake because it opens the diagonal to the rook on a8. White can play Bd5, winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is underdeveloped, look for tactical shots that exploit the lack of coordination, especially ideas that win the rook in the corner.
notes.plans: After winning the exchange, White castles and then transforms the advantage by trading the d4 pawn to open squares for the knight and bishop, leading to a quick attack on the king.

notes.explains: White has a large material advantage (exchange and pawn) and Black is undeveloped on the kingside. The simplest win is to push e5, exploiting the pin on the e-file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is still on e8, pawn advances in the center can create decisive pins and win material.
notes.plans: Play e5, and if Black captures twice, recapture with Rfe1, pinning the bishop and winning it with f4.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bg4. White must be careful: if the pawn were on c4, Black could play ...Bxf3 gxf3 Ne5, exploiting the queen's alignment on the d-file to win the d4 pawn. With c3, White can simply ignore the pin or play h3 later.
notes.teaches: A pawn on c4 can be a liability when the opponent pins the knight, as it opens tactics on d4. The move c3 is safer, preventing ...Nb4 and keeping the center solid.
notes.plans: White can continue with Nbd2, preparing to challenge the pin with h3 or Re1.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5, developing and pinning the knight. Black could play ...h6 to ask the bishop's intentions, but White can retreat to e3 or d2. The immediate c3 was also possible, but Bg5 is flexible.
notes.teaches: Developing the bishop to g5 can be a good way to maintain pressure, but be aware of potential ...h6 and the need for a retreat square.
notes.plans: After Bg5, White can consider h3 to break the pin, or simply castle and prepare central play.

notes.explains: White captures on f6, doubling Black's pawns. However, this gives up the dark-squared bishop and allows Black to generate play on the g-file with ...Kh8 and ...Rg8. The trade is not always beneficial.
notes.teaches: Exchanging a good bishop for a knight to double pawns can backfire if the opponent gets attacking chances on the open file. Consider the long-term value of the bishop pair.
notes.plans: White might instead avoid the trade and continue development with Nbd2, keeping the bishop pair.

notes.explains: Black castles queenside and prepares to double rooks on the e-file, targeting White's bishop on e2. White's knight on d2 is passive, and the pin on the e-file is annoying.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has an open file and a pin, it's important to relieve the pressure by either breaking the pin or reinforcing the pinned piece.
notes.plans: White can consider moves like Re1, h3, or even g4 to break the pin, but must be careful not to weaken the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays Nh4, threatening to trade bishops and gain control of f5. If Black accepts the trade, White's knight goes to f5, dominating the position. If Black retreats, White plays Bd3 and Qh5 with a strong attack.
notes.teaches: The knight maneuver to h4 is a classic idea to contest the light-squared bishop and gain the f5 outpost. This often leads to a powerful attacking setup.
notes.plans: After Nh4, if Black trades, play Nf5 and Qf3 or Qh5. If Black retreats, play Bd3 and Qh5, threatening ...Bxh7+ and Qc2+.

notes.explains: Black captures on e4, but White has a tactic: after dxe4, Black's bishop is hanging, and White can win a piece or the exchange. The key is to calculate the sequence accurately.
notes.teaches: When the opponent captures a pawn, look for intermediate moves that exploit loose pieces or pins. Here, recapturing with the pawn opens lines and attacks the bishop.
notes.plans: White should play dxe4, then if ...Bxe4, Nxg6 wins the exchange. If ...Bxe2, Nxd7 wins the exchange as well.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange after a tactical sequence. Now White is up material but must be careful of Black's counterplay on the g-file and the exposed king.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by simplifying or neutralizing the opponent's active pieces. Avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: White can consider trading queens or rooks to reduce Black's attacking potential, then push the passed pawn.

notes.explains: After trades, White has a queen and knight against Black's queen and rook. White is up a pawn but Black has active pieces. White must avoid blunders like ...Rg6 pinning the knight.
notes.teaches: When up material, be wary of pins and tactics that could turn the tables. Prophylactic moves like Rg3 can neutralize threats.
notes.plans: White can play Rg3 to defend the g2 pawn and prepare to push the c-pawn. Alternatively, trade queens to enter a winning endgame.

notes.explains: White plays Rg3 to defend against ...Rg6 and prepare to push the c-pawn. This move neutralizes Black's only active piece and allows White to advance the passed pawn.
notes.teaches: Identify the opponent's most dangerous piece and neutralize it. Here, the rook on g8 is the main source of counterplay, so blocking it with Rg3 is effective.
notes.plans: After Rg3, White can push c4-c5-c6-c7, using the rook to support the pawn. If Black blockades with the queen, offer a queen trade; if with the rook, use the bishop to chase it away.

notes.explains: White pushes the c-pawn and Black blockades with the queen. White plays Qe3, threatening a queen trade. Since White is up material, trading queens is favorable.
notes.teaches: When a queen blockades a passed pawn, offering a queen trade is a powerful technique to remove the blockade. The side with extra material benefits from simplification.
notes.plans: If Black avoids the trade, White can continue pushing the pawn. If Black trades, the rook and pawn endgame is winning.

notes.explains: White trades queens and pushes the pawn to c5. Black blockades with the rook on c8. White plays Bh3, threatening to chase the rook away or support the pawn's advance.
notes.teaches: When a rook blockades a passed pawn, use the bishop to attack the rook from a distance, forcing it to move or allowing the pawn to advance.
notes.plans: After Bh3, if ...Rc8, White can play c6 and then c7, supported by the rook. The pawn will promote.

notes.explains: Black captures the c-pawn, but White recaptures and then wins the f5 pawn. Now White has a rook and bishop against a rook, with a passed pawn on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity is key. White's rook is active, and the extra pawn can be converted by creating a passed pawn on the kingside.
notes.plans: White can push the g-pawn or use the rook to attack Black's pawns. The bishop can help support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: White wins the g-pawn and now has a bishop and rook against a rook. The bishop and rook coordinate well to deliver checkmate or win more material.
notes.teaches: In bishop and rook vs rook endgames, the bishop can control squares the rook cannot, often leading to a forced win. Look for tactics like pins and forks.
notes.plans: White can play Qd3, forcing ...g6, then Rf8+ and ladder mate. Alternatively, trade rooks and win with the bishop and king.

notes.explains: White's c4 creates a permanent hole on d4, as neither the c- nor e-pawn can defend it. This gives Black long-term dark-square control.
notes.teaches: A hole is a square that cannot be defended by any pawn. Such weaknesses are strategic targets, especially once development is complete.
notes.plans: Exploit the d4 outpost later, after developing pieces. Do not rush to occupy it immediately.

notes.explains: Playing g6 here allows White to push d4 and transpose to a Maroczy Bind, which is theoretically fine but not the most punishing response. A more critical move is e6 or Nf6, pressuring e4 and preventing d4.
notes.teaches: When White plays c4 early, Black should consider preventing d4 to avoid the Maroczy Bind, which is comfortable for White. Punish the c4 move by targeting e4.
notes.plans: If White plays d4, accept the transposition; if White plays d3, Black gets a comfortable advantage.

notes.explains: Trading the light-squared bishop for the knight on f3 increases Black's control over d4. The knight on f3 is a key defender of d4; removing it makes d4 even more accessible.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, trading a bishop for a knight that defends a key square can be a good strategic exchange, even if it costs a tempo.
notes.plans: After the trade, consider developing the g8-knight to e7 (the 'Botvinnik setup') to avoid obstructing the dark-squared bishop's control of d4.

notes.explains: Developing the knight to e7 rather than f6 keeps the dark-squared bishop's diagonal unobstructed and adds pawn control over d5 and f5. The closed center makes e6 and g6 safe together.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, the rule against playing both e6 and g6 does not apply because the center is blocked. The knight on e7 is a flexible, non-obstructing square.
notes.plans: Complete kingside development with castling, then prepare the queenside pawn break b5.

notes.explains: Playing h6 before castling prevents White from playing Qd2 and Bh6, which would trade off Black's powerful dark-squared bishop. If White takes on e7, Black recaptures with the queen to keep the knight on e7.
