notes.plans: Black will continue with Rc8 or Bb7, preparing to double rooks on the c-file or target the c2 pawn. The knight can later maneuver to c4 via b8-d7-b6.

notes.explains: White's b4 is a panic move that weakens the queenside and leaves the knight on c3 undefended. Black can immediately exploit this.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn move, look for ways to exploit the undefended pieces or weakened squares. Here, Rfc8 attacks the knight and threatens tactics.
notes.plans: Black plays Rfc8, and after White's Rb3, Black can play Nb8 to reroute the knight to b6 and eventually c4, exploiting the weak c4 square.

notes.explains: Nb8 is a retreating knight maneuver inspired by Nimzowitsch's famous Nh1. The knight will go to b6 and then c4, occupying the weak square.
notes.teaches: Retreating knight moves can be powerful when part of a longer maneuver to reach an outpost. Don't be afraid to move a piece backward if it improves its future prospects.
notes.plans: Black's knight goes to b6 and then c4, while the other knight stays on f6 to pressure e4. White's position is cramped and passive.

notes.explains: Black exchanges on f3, ruining White's kingside pawn structure. Although Black's kingside looks ugly, it is solid and White has no attacking pieces.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically reject a move that weakens your pawn structure if it is unexploitable. Here, the doubled f-pawns are not a target because White lacks the pieces to attack.
notes.plans: Black will play g6 to further solidify the kingside, then continue the knight maneuver to c4. White's only counterplay would be a4, but it's too late.

notes.explains: Nh5 is a surprising move that places the knight on the rim, but it controls key squares g3 and f4, restricting White's knight on e2.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim can be effective if they control critical squares. Here, Nh5 prevents White from generating kingside play and opens a path for the queen to join the attack.
notes.plans: Black's queen will go to d8 and then h4, targeting the weakened kingside. The knight on h5 is annoying for White and can later be redeployed.

notes.explains: Black's Qd8 prepares Qh4, threatening mate on h3. The knight on h5 and the open g-file give Black a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's kingside is weakened, transfer your queen to the attack. The queen on d8 is well-placed to go to h4, exploiting the dark-square weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will play Qh4, forcing White to defend. The tactical blow Nxf4 is possible, but Qh4 is simpler and more effective.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a knight on f4 to open lines against the king. After Bxf4, Qxh3 is mate, so White must play Kh2, but Black's attack continues.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be alert to tactical sacrifices that open lines. Here, Nxf4 is a standard sacrifice to expose the king, even if it's not the only winning move.
notes.plans: After Kh2, Black plays Qxh3+ and then e5 to open the center and bring the knight into the attack. The rook on c6 can lift to f6 or double on the c-file.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, opening the center to bring the knight on b8 into the attack via d7 and e5. This is more effective than a direct knight move.
notes.teaches: When attacking, open the center to involve your pieces. The pawn break e5 gives Black's knight access to e5 and opens the e-file for the rook.
notes.plans: Black plays dxe5, then Nxe5, and the knight on e5 is powerful. The rook on c8 can go to e8 or lift to f6, targeting f2.

notes.explains: Black's Rc6 is a flexible move that keeps the rook on the c-file while preparing to lift it to f6 or double on the c-file. It also eyes the c2 pawn.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, keep your pieces flexible. The rook on c6 can go to f6 to target f2, or stay on the c-file to pressure c2. This adaptability is key.
notes.plans: Black will play Rf6 or double rooks on the c-file, depending on White's response. The immediate threat is Rxf3, winning the pawn on f3.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn with Qxd5, and then Rc8-d8 traps the queen. White's queen has no good squares and must retreat to g2, after which Black picks off the c2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, look for tactics that win material. Here, the queen on d5 is safe because of the threat of Rc8-d8, and White's queen is overloaded.
notes.plans: Black plays Rd8, forcing the queen back, then takes on c2. The game is technically winning, but Black should avoid unnecessary complications.

notes.explains: Black wins the c2 pawn and is up two pawns. The game is technically winning, but Black must be careful not to allow counterplay.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify if possible, but avoid moves that give the opponent counterplay. Here, the simplest win is to take on c2 and consolidate.
notes.plans: Black will trade rooks if possible and use the extra pawns to win. The king should be kept safe, and Black should avoid pawn weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black plays Rxf2, a queen sacrifice that forces checkmate or wins more material. White must take the rook, after which Black's queen delivers mate.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning position, look for the most forcing and beautiful finish. Here, the queen sacrifice is decisive and avoids any technical difficulties.
notes.plans: After Kxf2, Black plays Qf3+ and Qg3#. If White doesn't take, Black is simply up a rook.

notes.explains: Be5 is a powerful move: it threatens Bxf6, which would ruin Black's kingside pawns, and if Black takes the bishop with ...f6, the knight on c4 is trapped. Black's best is ...g6, but then White has a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When a bishop threatens to destroy the opponent's pawn structure, it can be worth more than a rook; such sacrifices are often winning.
notes.plans: After ...g6, continue with Qf3, then g4 to open lines against the black king. Castle kingside and prepare to exploit the weakened dark squares.

notes.explains: Qf3 increases the pressure on f6, threatening Bxf6 followed by Qxf6. Black cannot take the queen because of Bb5 winning the exchange. White maintains the tension and prepares to castle.
notes.teaches: Piling up on a weak point with multiple pieces is a classic attacking technique; do not rush to capture if you can increase the pressure first.
notes.plans: Castle, then consider Rc1 to support the c-pawn, and look for ways to open the f-file or exploit the pinned knight.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White wins a second pawn. The doubled f-pawns are not a problem because White's structure is otherwise solid, and the extra pawns on the queenside are decisive.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness; assess the overall position. Here the doubled pawns clamp down on central squares and White has a clear material advantage.
notes.plans: Trade rooks to simplify, then use the queenside pawn majority to create a passed pawn. Bring the king into the game in the endgame.

notes.explains: White wins a third pawn with Qxa7. The knight on b7 is poorly placed, and White's queen is active on a6, pressuring the queenside.
notes.teaches: When up material, look to win more pawns by targeting weak points, but avoid unnecessary complications. Simplify by trading pieces when possible.
notes.plans: Trade queens and rooks, then advance the queenside pawns while keeping the black knight restricted. Bring the king to the center.

notes.explains: White is up two pawns in the rook endgame. The winning plan is to create a passed pawn on the queenside while keeping the black king passive. A classic technique is to stalemate the black king, forcing Black to give up pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames with extra pawns, advance your majority, trade rooks if advantageous, and use king activity to support the pawns. Avoid stalemate by leaving the opponent a move.
notes.plans: Push the a- and b-pawns, bring the king to c5, and if necessary, sacrifice a pawn to break through. Ensure the black king cannot become active.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc5, increasing pressure on d3 and threatening to capture it. White cannot easily defend both d3 and e4. Black avoids taking on d3 immediately to keep the tension and maintain multiple threats.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to capture a weak pawn if it relieves the pressure. By keeping the tension, you create an ultimatum: White must either give up the pawn or weaken their position further.
notes.plans: If White plays dxc4, recapture with the knight and then take on e4, leaving White with a bad pawn structure. If White defends e4, continue targeting d3.

notes.explains: White plays e5 to open the center, but this is a mistake. Black must choose the correct order of captures: first Bxg2 to eliminate the bishop, then decide between dxe5 or cxd3.
notes.teaches: In critical positions, order of operations is crucial. Evaluate each capture's consequences before committing. Here, taking on g2 first simplifies and removes a defender of White's king.
notes.plans: Play Bxg2 first. If White recaptures with the king, then play dxe5. If White plays exf6, then Bxf1 is winning. After Bxg2, consider cxd3 to keep the center intact and gain a pawn.

notes.explains: Black captures on d3, winning a pawn and keeping the center intact. After Qxe5, Black has a pawn mass in the center that protects the king, while White's king is exposed on the g-file.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, simplifying into a position with a safe king and active pieces is often best. The central pawn mass provides excellent king shelter.
notes.plans: After Qxe5, consider taking on f6 with the pawn rather than the bishop to open the g-file and create an outpost on e4. Play f5 to cement the knight on e4.

notes.explains: Black plays f5, creating an outpost on e4 for the knight. The doubled pawn on f6 is actually beneficial: it provides king safety, opens the g-file, and the front pawn can be pushed without compromising the king.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always bad. Here, the f-pawns shield the king, open a file for attack, and the front pawn can be used as a battering ram. The outpost on e4 becomes a powerful asset.
notes.plans: Play Ne4 to occupy the outpost. Follow up with Rg8 to pressure g3. If White plays Ng5, chase it away with f6 or exchange with Bxg5.

notes.explains: Black exchanges on g5 and then plays Rg5, crashing through on the g-file. The pressure on g3 is overwhelming, and White is already losing.
notes.teaches: Once you have an outpost and an open file, coordinate your pieces to target the weakest point. Here, the rook on g5 and knight on e4 create unbearable pressure on g3.
notes.plans: Play d5 to improve the knight and open the queen's diagonal. Then play h4 to attack g3, or simply take on g3 with the rook.

notes.explains: Black simplifies by exchanging rooks and queens, leaving a winning endgame with a knight and three pawns against a bishop and pawn. The h-pawn is not dangerous because the king can stop it.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplification is often the easiest path to victory. Don't fear giving the opponent a passed pawn if it is far from promotion and your king can handle it.
notes.plans: Activate the rook with Rc8, then push the central pawns with f6 and e5. If White tries to create counterplay, use the extra material to simplify further.

notes.explains: Black pushes the central pawns, creating an unstoppable passed pawn on d4. The knight on e4 supports the pawns, and White's bishop is helpless.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, passed pawns are powerful, especially when supported by a knight. Push them forward and use the knight to control key squares.
notes.plans: Play d4, then d3, and promote. If White tries to block with the bishop, use the knight to cut off its diagonal or sacrifice to promote.

notes.explains: Black plays f4, cutting off the bishop's diagonal and preventing it from stopping the d-pawn. The pawn on d4 is now unstoppable.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, use your own pawns to block the opponent's pieces. Here, f4 traps the bishop and ensures the d-pawn's promotion.
notes.plans: Push d3 and d2, then promote. If White's h-pawn becomes dangerous, use the knight to block or checkmate the king.

notes.explains: White's c4 aims for a Maroczy Bind structure by preparing d4. Black should avoid a6 early, as it allows this setup.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, playing a6 prematurely can let White enter a favorable Maroczy Bind. Instead, develop with Nf6 first.
notes.plans: Black can adopt a Hedgehog setup with e6, a6, b6, Bb7, Nbd7, and Qc7 to counter White's space advantage.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight and prevents d4 because if d4, Black takes on f3 and White must recapture with the pawn, weakening the center.
notes.teaches: Use pins to prevent your opponent's key pawn breaks. Here, Bg4 stops d4 and creates a hole on d4 for Black.
notes.plans: After Bg4, play e6 to protect d5, then develop naturally. Avoid e5, which would weaken d5.

notes.explains: White finally pushes d4, but it's a blunder because Black can take on f3 and then capture on d4, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's only idea is stopped, they may panic and make a mistake. Stay patient and punish premature breaks.
notes.plans: Take on f3 with the bishop, then recapture on d4 with the c-pawn (cxd4) to create a protected passed pawn after e5.

notes.explains: White plays e5? which is a panic move. Black can simply take on e5 with the pawn (dxe5) and be up two pawns. But the clinical choice is d5xc5, keeping the pawn mass.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify to a winning endgame. Avoid flashy moves that give counterplay.
notes.plans: After dxc5, Black has two extra pawns. Castle and then use the pawn majority to advance.

notes.explains: After Black's dxc5, White has Rb1, defending b2 and threatening to attack Black's b7 pawn. Black must be careful not to lose the b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When simplifying, watch for counterplay against your own weaknesses. Rb1 is a strong defensive move that also creates threats.
notes.plans: Black should castle first to secure the king, then deal with the b2 pawn. Priority is king safety over material.

notes.explains: Black plays Rc8 to prepare b6, undermining the bishop on d6. The bishop is White's only active piece, so removing its support collapses White's position.
notes.teaches: Identify your opponent's strongest piece and target its support. Here, the bishop on d6 is supported by the c5 pawn; undermine it with b6.
notes.plans: Play b6, then Qd7 to defend the knight, then bxc5. After that, the bishop becomes a target and White's position falls apart.

notes.explains: After b6 and Qd7, Black removes the c5 pawn. The bishop on d6 is now vulnerable. Black's queen goes to c7 to avoid pins and support the b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: Avoid walking into pins. Qb7 would allow Rd6, forking the knight and queen. Qc7 is safe and supports the b2 pawn.
notes.plans: Continue to pressure the bishop. The b2 pawn is crucial; keep it defended with the bishop on f6.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd4, attacking the bishop and creating multiple threats: Rc1, and the fork Nc2+ followed by Nc3 forking queen and rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's rook moves, look for back-rank weaknesses and forks. Nd4 exploits the x-ray on the bishop and the loose queen and rook.
notes.plans: After Nd4, White cannot defend all threats. The fork Nc2+ wins material.

notes.explains: The Classical Variation (Be2) is a calm developmental approach favored by Karpov. It avoids tactical complications and aims to convert superior central control into a tangible advantage. Both sides castle kingside, so the battle revolves around central control rather than opposite-side attacks.
notes.teaches: Don't confuse calm development with lack of ambition. The Classical Variation is a dangerous weapon that gives White a lasting edge without needing to memorize sharp lines.

notes.explains: After e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Be2 Bg7 Nf3 O-O O-O, Black's main ideas are ...c5, ...e5, or ...c6. Against ...c5, White can play d5 (Benoni-style) or dxc5. Both are playable, but d5 is principled, keeping a central pawn majority.
notes.teaches: In closed center positions, White's key maneuver is Nf3-d2-c4, targeting the weak d6 pawn. This is a standard idea from the Benoni structure.
notes.plans: Play d5 to close the center, then maneuver the knight to c4. Prevent Black's expansion with ...b5 by playing a4 if Black plays ...a6.

notes.explains: Black played ...Qb6, attacking b2. White played Nd2, seemingly blundering the b2 pawn, but after ...Qxb2, Nb5 creates a double threat (Nc7+ and Nxd6) and the queen is in trouble. The knight on d2 also defends e4, a crucial point.
notes.teaches: When your opponent grabs a pawn on b2 with the queen, don't panic. Look for counterplay that exploits the queen's exposed position. A knight on b5 can be devastating.
notes.plans: After Nb5, Black's queen is trapped. The immediate threat is Nc7+, winning the rook. Black's best is ...Nbd7, but White is winning.

notes.explains: To trap the queen on b2, first identify its escape routes (b4, a5, d8). Cover b4 with a3, then play Rb1, forcing the queen to a2. Finally, Bc4 traps it. This requires precise coordination of multiple pieces.
notes.teaches: Trapping a queen is a complex process that often requires many pieces. Don't assume it's easy; look for escape squares and ensure you have enough material to keep the queen trapped without giving up too much in return.
notes.plans: Play a3, then Rb1, then Bc4. Black's best defense is ...Bg4, but f3 repels it. The queen is lost.

notes.explains: After trapping the queen, Black played ...Bh5, which also becomes trapped. White can win it with g4. This shows the importance of making mental notes: while focusing on the queen, don't overlook other hanging pieces.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for additional weaknesses. When your opponent is in trouble, look for secondary targets. A quick mental note can lead to winning more material.
notes.plans: Play g4, winning the bishop. Then simplify and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Up a queen for a rook, White can play Nxd6, deflecting the rook from d6. If ...Rxd6, Qxb7 forks the knight on a6 and the rook on b8. Black can try ...Rb8, but Qxa7 keeps the pressure, and White wins the knight back.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, look for tactics that simplify or win more material. Deflection and forks are common themes. Always calculate until you are sure the tactic works.
notes.plans: Play Nxd6, then Qxb7, winning the exchange and more pawns. Alternatively, play Nc4 for a more symbolic finish.

notes.explains: With a huge material advantage, White's simplest plan is to trade pieces and promote the d-pawn. Alternatively, look for checkmate. Here, Nd6 threatens Qxg6+ and Bf5#. The knight on d6 blocks the king's escape to h5.
notes.teaches: When up massive material, first look for checkmate. If none exists, simplify by trading pieces and pushing passed pawns. Don't get fancy; clinical play is fastest.
notes.plans: Play Nd6, threatening Qxg6+ and Bf5#. If Black defends, simplify and promote the d-pawn.

notes.explains: The choice of Be2 over Bc4 or Bd3 is tactical. Bc4 allows ...Nxe4!? with a fork trick, while Bd3 invites ...Bg4, pressuring d4. Be2 avoids these issues and is more solid.
notes.teaches: In the Pirc, Be2 is the safest and most principled square for the bishop. It avoids tactical tricks and prepares a solid kingside setup.

notes.explains: A common trap: if White plays Bd3 and Black plays ...Bg4, White may try h3, but after ...Bxf3, Qxf3, Nc6, and ...Nd7, White's d4 pawn comes under pressure. A known trick is ...Ne5! hitting the loose bishop on d3, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: Be aware of loose pieces. If your bishop is undefended, your opponent may exploit it with a knight fork or other tactic. Always check for such opportunities.

notes.explains: After Be2, O-O, O-O, a critical tabiya arises. Black's main moves are ...c6, ...e5, and ...c5. Against ...c6, White should play a4 to prevent ...b5 expansion. This is a standard prophylactic idea.
notes.teaches: In the Pirc, if Black plays ...c6, immediately play a4 to stop ...b5. Allowing ...b5 gives Black counterplay and weakens White's center.
notes.plans: After a4, Black often plays ...Nbd7. White can then play h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and later aim for Bc4, trading queens and leaving Black with development problems.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...e5, White can capture twice, leading to an endgame where Black wins back the pawn with ...Nxc4. However, White can avoid this by playing Bg5, pinning the knight and maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: In the ...e5 line, don't automatically recapture. Bg5 is a strong move that prevents Black from equalizing easily. If Black grabs the b2 pawn, White gets a huge attack.
notes.plans: After ...e5, play Bg5. If ...Qxb2, play c3, cutting off the bishop's retreat, and White's attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: In the Benoni-like structure after d5, the knight maneuver Nf3-d2-c4 is essential. It targets the d6 pawn and puts pressure on Black's position. If Black plays ...a6, White should respond with a4 to prevent ...b5.
notes.teaches: The knight on c4 is a monster in these structures. It attacks d6 and supports central expansion. Always look for this maneuver when you have a pawn on d5 and Black has a pawn on d6.
notes.plans: Play Nd2, then Nc4. If Black plays ...a6, play a4. Then continue with moves like f3, Bg4, or other improvements.

notes.explains: A cautionary tale: in a similar position, the player tried to trap the queen but overlooked that Black could sacrifice the queen for three pieces and a dangerous passed pawn. The resulting material imbalance (queen vs. rook and two minor pieces) was insufficient because Black's pieces were active.
notes.teaches: When trapping a queen, ensure you don't give up too many pieces for it. A queen is worth about 9 points, but three minor pieces (9 points) with coordination can be better. Always evaluate the resulting material balance and activity.

notes.explains: In the game, after trapping the queen, White also won the bishop on h5 with g4. This is a classic example of picking low-hanging fruit: when your opponent is in trouble, look for additional hanging pieces before executing more complex tactics.
notes.teaches: Always scan for undefended pieces. Winning a free piece is often better than a flashy tactic. Simplify when possible.

notes.explains: The final mating idea: Qxg6+ and Bf5# requires the knight on d6 to block the king's escape to h5. This pattern (queen sacrifice on g6 followed by bishop to f5) is a common checkmate motif when the king is trapped by its own pawns.
notes.teaches: Recognize mating patterns where a queen sacrifice opens lines. The knight's role in covering escape squares is crucial. Always consider such patterns when the king is boxed in.

notes.explains: c6 is a rare waiting move that invites White to develop the knight to f3, after which Black plays d5, exploiting the knight's vulnerability to e4 and gaining a strong center.
notes.teaches: A waiting move can provoke a useful development from the opponent, then strike at the newly placed piece.
notes.plans: After d5 and e4, recapture with the knight on e4, then develop with Nf6 and Bc5, aiming to castle quickly.

notes.explains: After Nxe5, Black should not panic; the knight on e5 is vulnerable to ...e4, winning back the pawn and leaving Black with a monster pawn center.
notes.teaches: When a knight lands on e5 early, look for ...e4 to kick it and reclaim the pawn with central dominance.
notes.plans: Play ...e4, then ...Nxe4, followed by ...Nf6 and ...Bc5, with the king castled short.

notes.explains: White castles into a discovered attack: the bishop on b5 is loose, and ...Qb6 wins it because the knight on c4 blocks the queen's defense.
notes.teaches: When the opponent castles, check if any of their pieces are undefended or if a discovered attack is possible.
notes.plans: Play ...Qb6, winning the bishop, then consolidate the extra piece.

notes.explains: White's Bd2 pins the knight on c4 to the queen, threatening Nxe4. Black can break the pin with ...Bb4, exchanging the bishop for the knight and freeing the queen.
notes.teaches: When pinned, consider exchanging the pinning piece or using a bishop to block the pin and then trade.
notes.plans: Play ...Bb4, then ...Bxc3, ...Bxc3, and move the queen to safety (e.g., ...Qb6).

notes.explains: Black cannot castle because the bishop on c3 pins the f-pawn. The plan is to dislodge the bishop with ...a5, then take with the knight to cover c5 and allow castling.
notes.teaches: When a bishop prevents castling, use a pawn to chase it away, and recapture with a piece that controls key squares.
notes.plans: Play ...a5, then ...axb4, recapturing with the knight to cover c5, then castle short.

notes.explains: Black can force a queen trade with ...Qc6, leading to a winning endgame up a piece. Taking on d4 instead would grab a pawn but open lines for White's counterplay.
notes.teaches: When up material, prefer simplifying to a safe endgame over grabbing extra pawns that might give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play ...Qc6, trade queens, then consolidate the extra piece in the endgame.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black's plan is to activate the king and rook. Playing ...f5 allows the king to go to f7 and then e6, protecting the knight and preparing rook infiltration via the a-file.
notes.teaches: In endgames, bring the king to the center to support pieces and prepare rook activity on open files.
notes.plans: Play ...f5, then ...Kf7, ...Ke6, and ...Ra8-a2, doubling rooks on the second rank.

notes.explains: Black should avoid taking on a3 prematurely because it hangs the knight on b4. Instead, ...Rc8 forces a rook trade or drives the rook back, then Black can capture on a3 safely.
notes.teaches: In endgames, prioritize piece safety and forcing favorable trades before grabbing pawns.
notes.plans: Play ...Rc8, then after the rook trade or retreat, capture on a3 and push the e-pawn or activate the rook.

notes.explains: After winning the exchange, Black can accelerate the win by cutting off White's king with ...Ra2, then doubling rooks on the second rank or pushing the e-pawn.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, restrict the opponent's king and create mating threats or decisive infiltration.
notes.plans: Play ...Ra2, then ...e3, and bring the knight to e4 or double rooks for checkmate.

notes.explains: The game is effectively over; Black has a decisive material advantage and can checkmate with rook and knight.
notes.teaches: Once the advantage is overwhelming, convert efficiently without allowing counterplay.
notes.plans: Push the e-pawn or bring the rook to h1 for checkmate.

notes.explains: Black's queen is attacked and must move. Qh5 is a good square, x-raying the knight on f3 and less common than Qa5, potentially taking the opponent out of theory.
notes.teaches: When choosing a queen retreat, consider safety and additional threats. Qh5 is safe and creates a pin on the f3 knight.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development with Be7 or Bb7, and consider both kingside and queenside castling. The pawn on d4 is a long-term asset.

notes.explains: White plays Rxe4, which is less common than Nxe4. Black must think independently. Both kingside and queenside castling are options.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar move, rely on general principles: complete development, secure the king, and exploit weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black can play Be7 or Bb7. If White offers a queen trade with Nxd4, Black can consider a tactical sequence: ...Be7 Nxd4 Qxd1 Nxd1 f5, chasing the rook and winning the exchange.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black plays f5, attacking the rook. The rook cannot go to h4 because Be7 guards it, so it must go to f4. Then g5 traps the rook, winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: Rooks are poor defenders of other pieces because they are easily attacked. Use pawns to chase away the rook and win material.
notes.plans: After g5, White is forced to give up the exchange. Black will have a rook and two bishops for a rook and knight, with a strong pawn on d4.

notes.explains: Bb7 is a strong move, preparing to castle queenside and putting pressure on the center. The engine approves of both Bb7 and Be6.
notes.teaches: Develop bishops to active squares that support your plans. Bb7 eyes the center and the kingside, and prepares long castling.
notes.plans: Black aims to reinforce the d4 pawn and complete development. If White plays Nxd4, Black can recapture with the rook and then play ...c5 or ...f5 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: White plays Nce2, preparing to take on d4 with the knight. Black must find a move that reinforces the d4 pawn. Qd5 is a good choice: it attacks the rook on e4 and adds a defender to d4.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is under pressure, use your queen to both attack and defend. Centralizing the queen can be very effective.
notes.plans: After Qd5, White's best is Nc3, forcing a repetition. If White plays something else, Black can castle and then play f5 to chase the rook.

notes.explains: Black castles kingside. The d4 pawn is still hanging, but if White takes it, Black will pin the knight with ...Re8, creating a compromised position for White.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to ignore a threat and focus on your own plans. Castling is a priority, and the pawn can be sacrificed for long-term compensation.
notes.plans: Black can play f5 to chase the rook from e4, then win the knight on d4 or a pawn. Alternatively, Black can reinforce the pawn with ...Rd8 or ...Be6.

notes.explains: Black pushes d3, a strong move that makes the pawn difficult to attack. Even if White wins it back, the tempo spent allows Black to develop and activate pieces.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn on d3 can be a huge asset. Don't be afraid to advance it; the energy White spends to capture it will benefit your other pieces.
notes.plans: Black should reinforce the pawn with ...Rd8 or develop the bishop to e6. The pawn is a long-term strength, and Black has the two bishops.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd8, reinforcing the d3 pawn and completing development. The rook on d8 also x-rays the queen on d1.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong pawn, use your rooks to support it. Rd8 is a natural developing move that also defends the pawn.
notes.plans: Black can now consider ...Bf5 or ...Be6. If White plays c4, Black may have the option of a queen sacrifice on e4 for long-term compensation.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the queen on e4 for a rook and a piece. The idea is that the pawn on d3 is so strong and well-supported that it will prevail over the queen. White's position becomes passive, and Black has excellent long-term compensation.
notes.teaches: A positional queen sacrifice can be justified when you have a powerful passed pawn, active pieces, and the opponent's queen is a poor blockader. The queen is easily attacked and cannot effectively restrain the pawn.
notes.plans: Black does not need to rush. Improve piece placement: develop the bishop to f6, put the rook on e8, and aim to advance the d-pawn. The pawn on d3 is the key; White will struggle to contain it.

notes.explains: After the queen sacrifice, Black plays Bf6, putting the bishop on the long diagonal and preparing to double rooks on the e-file. White's queen is on d2, leaving the knight on g3 undefended.
notes.teaches: After a sacrifice, activate your pieces to maximum effect. Bf6 is a natural developing move that also creates threats.
notes.plans: Black can take the knight on g3, ruining White's pawn structure, and then bring the knight to d4. However, immediate Nd4 is a blunder due to Qxd3. Instead, play ...Re8 first, seizing the open file.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8, seizing the open e-file. White's rook on d1 is passive. Black threatens to infiltrate with ...Re2.
notes.teaches: In open-file positions, the rook belongs on the open file. Re8 is a natural and strong move, putting pressure on White's position.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Re2, attacking the pawn on d2. White's queen is tied to defense. Black should avoid rushing; instead, improve piece placement and prepare to advance the d-pawn.

notes.explains: Black pushes d2, threatening to promote. The pawn is extremely dangerous. White's queen is tied to the back rank, and Black's pieces are very active.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn near promotion, advancing it can create decisive threats. The queen is a poor blockader because it can be chased away.
notes.plans: Black should not rush with ...Re1+ immediately, as Kg2 gives White counterplay. Instead, improve piece placement: play ...Nd4 to centralize the knight, then ...Rd8 to support the pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, attacking the bishop on f4. If the bishop takes on d2, Black recaptures with the rook and has overwhelming material for the queen. If the bishop retreats, Black plays ...Ne3+ winning the rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, use pawns to chase them away. g5 is a strong move that forces a favorable outcome.
notes.plans: After g5, White's best is to give up the bishop for the pawn, but Black then has rook, knight, and bishop for the queen, with a weak white king. Black can aim for a checkmating attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne3, threatening to take the rook on d1. This is a stronger threat than defending the rook on e2. The knight is pinned to the king, so it cannot be captured.
notes.teaches: When your rook is attacked, consider if you have an even stronger threat. Ne3+ is a check that wins the rook, ignoring the threat to your own rook.
notes.plans: After Ne3+, White's king moves to g3. Black then takes the rook on d1, and after White recaptures on e8, Black can promote the pawn with ...Nxb2, winning.

notes.explains: Black captures on b2, threatening to promote. White's queen is tied to the back rank. Black's pawn on d2 is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a passed pawn supported by active pieces is often decisive. Here, Black's knight and rook are perfectly placed to assist the pawn.
notes.plans: Black will promote the pawn to a queen, giving Black a rook, knight, and queen for the queen. White's king is exposed, and Black has a winning attack.

notes.explains: White's setup with g3 and e3 is passive, allowing Black to seize the center with d5. Black develops naturally, avoiding premature pawn pushes like e4 which could become weak after d3.
notes.teaches: In the Reversed Sicilian, Black should prioritize central control and development over speculative pawn advances. Completing development before attacking is key.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming for a kingside attack with h5 and opening the h-file.

notes.explains: After closing the center with e4, Black launches a pawn storm on the kingside with h5-h4, aiming to open the h-file. White's f3 is too slow; Black captures on f3 to open lines, then continues with h4.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, an attack on the flank can be decisive. Opening the h-file with pawn sacrifices is a typical attacking method in such structures.
notes.plans: Black will play Bh3 to target the rook on h1, winning the exchange or more. The rook will infiltrate on the h-file.

notes.explains: White panics with Rh1, overlooking Bh3 which wins the exchange. Black's attack is overwhelming; the king is exposed and the h-file rook infiltrates decisively.
notes.teaches: Once the h-file is open, the attacker's rook and queen can combine for a quick mate or material gain. Defensive moves like Rh1 can be punished by exploiting the pin on the h-file.
notes.plans: Black will continue to bring more pieces to the attack, with the queen and rook creating mating threats.

notes.explains: After …Nf6 Nc3 Bb4, Black often takes on d4, but Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 d5 exd5 cxd5 O-O O-O Bg5 c6 Qf3 Be7 Rae1 Be6 Qh3 g6 Bh6 Re8 Bxg7 Kxg7 Qh6+ Kg8 Re3 Qf6 Rg3+ Kf8 Qh8# is a forced mate.
notes.teaches: In the Four Knights Scotch, if Black takes on d4, White gets a strong initiative. The key is to develop quickly and target the kingside.
notes.plans: White's plan is to attack the black king with queen and rook, using the open g-file.

notes.explains: In the Queen's Gambit Declined, after d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Nf3 Nbd7 Rc1 c6, Black's setup with ...c6 and ...Bd6 is solid. The move ...c6 is crucial to support d5 and avoid blocking the c-pawn.
notes.teaches: Do not automatically develop knights to c6 in d4 openings; ...c6 is often better to support the center and keep the c-pawn flexible.
notes.plans: Develop the light-squared bishop to f5 or maneuver it via g4-h5-g6 to avoid weakening with g6.

notes.explains: After winning a pawn, White has a knight on d4 and Black's king is exposed. The knight and queen coordinate well; Qf7 is a major threat.
notes.teaches: A knight and queen can create a powerful tandem. Look for moves like g5 to open lines or create mating threats when the opponent's king is in the center.
notes.plans: Play g5 to threaten Qf7, then if Black defends with Nh6, take on h6 and continue the attack. Later, take on g7 and then decide between taking the rook or giving a check on c8.

notes.explains: White is up material and has a strong center. The priority is king safety and completing development. Castling is better than trying to save the knight immediately.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, first secure your king and finish development. Don't panic about minor threats; the bigger picture is winning the game safely.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then bring the knight to d5 or f6, centralize the queen, and use the pawns to steamroll Black's position.

notes.explains: The e3 line is more positional and often leads to an isolated queen pawn (IQP) structure. Black's main response is c5.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, both sides have typical plans: White attacks with pieces, Black tries to blockade and trade down. Understanding the typical pawn structure is key.
notes.plans: White can aim for e4 to challenge the center, or play Nf3 and develop harmoniously.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 exd4, Black's best is Nf6, not Bg4. Bg4 is a mistake that allows Qb3 with strong threats.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, one mistake can be fatal. Know the correct responses to avoid falling into traps.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bg4, White should play Qb3, threatening f7 and b7. Black's best defense is Bb6, but White still wins a pawn.

notes.explains: The idea of pushing e5 in response to e4 is a common theme in many openings, using the extra pawn as a bargaining chip to force a queen trade and leave the opponent's king in the center.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn, you can often use it to open lines and trade queens, leaving the opponent's king exposed. This is a recurring idea in the QGA, Blackmar-Diemer Gambit, and c3 Sicilian.
notes.plans: After e5 dxe5, Black plays Qxd1+ and gets a comfortable endgame with a lead in development.

notes.explains: The order of moves matters: playing Nf3 first prevents Black's ...e5 push, while e3 allows it but is more flexible. The e3 e5 line is very theoretical.
notes.teaches: Move order can be crucial in the opening. Understand the differences between similar lines to choose the one that suits your style.
notes.plans: If you want to avoid theory, play Nf3 first. If you want to play ambitiously, play e4.

notes.explains: White plays d4, opening the center. Black should capture with …cxd4 to avoid an unfavorable queen trade after Qxd4, which would expose the king.
notes.teaches: In Sicilian structures, avoid trading queens early when your king is still in the center, as it often leaves you vulnerable to a lasting initiative.
notes.plans: After …cxd4 Qxd4, Black will develop with ...Nf6, ...e6, and ...Be7, accepting a slight weakness on d5 but aiming to catch up in development.

notes.explains: Black is seriously behind in development. The immediate …Nf6 runs into e5, leading to a poor endgame. Black must first prevent e5 by playing …e5, a typical positional concession to block the center.
notes.teaches: When behind in development, avoid opening the center. A pawn move like ...e5 can be a necessary evil to buy time for development, even if it creates a weakness on d5.
notes.plans: After …e5 Qd3, Black will play ...Be7, ...Nf6, and ...0-0, accepting the d5 weakness as a long-term problem but prioritizing king safety.

notes.explains: Black needs to develop but must avoid the 'Smyslov idea': if Black plays …Nf6 immediately, White can play Bg5, exchanging the knight and then occupying the d5 outpost with a knight. This is a classic strategic pattern.
notes.teaches: When a key outpost (like d5) is contested, be wary of allowing your defender to be exchanged. The Smyslov idea is to remove the defender and then occupy the square.
notes.plans: Black should first play …Be7 to prevent Bg5, then follow with ...Nf6 and ...0-0. If White plays Bg5 anyway, Black can respond with ...h6 to break the pin.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5 anyway. Black must avoid the exchange by playing …h6, forcing the bishop to retreat. This prevents the Smyslov idea and keeps the knight on f6 to contest d5.
notes.teaches: When facing a pin that threatens to exchange your defender, a pawn move like ...h6 can be a useful prophylactic, especially if the bishop has no good retreat that maintains the pin.
notes.plans: After …h6 Bh4, Black will play ...Nf6, ...0-0, and then aim to activate the light-squared bishop and challenge White's center.

notes.explains: Black finally develops the knight to f6. White now has a strong move: Qb4, threatening Qxb7 and also preparing Bb6 to attack the d6 pawn. This puts Black under severe pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a lead in development, they can often create threats that force concessions. Here, Black must deal with the queen's entry on b4.
notes.plans: Black should play …Qd7, defending b7 and preparing to contest the b4 square. Alternatively, …Qe7 is possible but more awkward. The key is to avoid allowing Bb6.

notes.explains: Black played …Qd7, but White has the crushing reply Rd1, threatening Nxe5. If Black plays …Qc6, then Nxe5 dxe5 Rd8# is mate. Black must move the queen again.
notes.teaches: When your queen is attacked and the opponent has a rook on an open file, be alert to back-rank mate threats. Sometimes you must retreat the queen to an awkward square to survive.
notes.plans: Black's only move is …Qe6, blocking the e5 pawn but allowing ...0-0 next. White then plays Bc7, attacking the queen and forcing further concessions.

notes.explains: White plays Bc7, attacking the queen and threatening Nxe5. Black must play …d5 to avoid losing the d6 pawn, but this opens the center and White's attack becomes overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When you are behind in development, a pawn break like ...d5 can be forced, but it often leads to a losing position if the opponent's pieces are better coordinated.
notes.plans: Black plays …d5, hoping to complicate. White can simply capture Nxd5, and after …Nxd5 Qxd5, Black cannot recapture because of mate on d8. Black is lost.

notes.explains: After Qxd5, Black cannot recapture because of mate. The only move is …Qa5, but White has d4, and Black's position collapses. The opening phase is a complete disaster for Black due to the development deficit.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, a single misstep can lead to a decisive disadvantage. It is crucial to know the specific tactical nuances of your repertoire to avoid such catastrophes.
notes.plans: Black will try to survive by giving up material and hoping for counterplay, but White's attack is overwhelming. The game is effectively lost.

notes.explains: Black has traded knights to eliminate White's active knight on e5 and now develops the bishop to c6, putting pressure on g2 and forcing White to react.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a well-posted knight, exchanging it efficiently (here Nbd7) can be better than chasing it with the queen, which would allow White to support it with d4.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with e6 to block the bishop on c4, then Bc6, and castle kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays e6 to make the bishop on c4 'bite on granite' – it no longer attacks anything important. Castling is then natural.
notes.teaches: When facing a bishop on c4, playing e6 is a solid way to neutralize it; g6 would leave the bishop active on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Black will complete development with Be7 and O-O, then consider queenside expansion or central breaks.

notes.explains: Black plays a6 to prevent both Nb5 and Bb5, keeping the light-squared bishop on c6 where it is a key piece pressuring g2.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like a6 can be important to preserve a well-placed bishop. Don't fear Nb5 – the bishop can drop back to b8 and remain effective.
notes.plans: Black will continue with b5 to restrict White's pieces and prepare queenside expansion.

notes.explains: b5 gains space on the queenside and restricts White's minor pieces, especially the knight on a3 and the bishop on b3.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, expanding with pawns can suffocate the opponent's pieces. But avoid overextending – keep the pawn chain solid.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with Bd6, preparing kingside play or a Greek Gift sacrifice.

notes.explains: Bd6 develops the bishop, aims at h2, and sets up potential kingside attacking ideas. The bishop on c6 and the bishop on d6 create a battery against White's king.
notes.teaches: When in doubt, default to reasonable developing moves. Bd6 is natural and keeps the tension, preparing tactics like the Greek Gift sacrifice.
notes.plans: Black will consider h5 to anchor the g4 square for a knight, then possibly play Ng4 or the Greek Gift sacrifice Bxh2+.

notes.explains: h5 prepares the Greek Gift sacrifice by anchoring the g4 square for the knight, and also threatens Ng4 directly. It is a classic preparatory move before sacrificing on h2.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh2+ followed by Ng4+) often requires preparation: the g4 square must be controlled. h5 is a standard way to secure that square.
notes.plans: Black will play Bxh2+ if White allows, or else continue with Ng4 and then Qc7 to set up a mating net.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 to keep the queen near the kingside, preparing a mating attack. The queen on c7 supports the idea of Bh2+ and Bg1, threatening mate from two directions.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack, keep your queen close to the action but not exposed. Qc7 is safer than Qh4 because it avoids White's defensive resources like d5.
notes.plans: Black will play Bh2+ and Bg1, threatening mate on h2. If White defends, Black can play ...gxh3 and ...Qh2#.

notes.explains: Black plays Bh2+ and then Bg1, threatening mate on h2 from both the bishop and the knight. This is a classic mating pattern: the bishop on g1 and knight on g4 combine to threaten ...Qh2#.
notes.teaches: The bishop on g1 and knight on g4 create a deadly mate threat. This pattern is common in many games – recognize it and look for ways to set it up.
notes.plans: After White defends (e.g., Nxg4), Black recaptures with hxg4 and then ...gxh3, threatening ...Qh2#. White's only defense is to give up material or allow mate.

notes.explains: After hxg4, Black plays gxh3, opening the h-file and threatening Qh2#. White cannot prevent mate without losing material.
notes.teaches: When you have a mating attack, keep adding pressure. Opening lines (here the h-file) is often decisive. The threat of mate forces the opponent to give up material or get mated.
notes.plans: Black will play Qh2# if White does not block. If White plays g3, then ...h2#. Otherwise, Black can take on g2 and then deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange (rook for bishop) to keep the attack going. After ...Bxd5, Black has two pawns for the piece and a continuing attack. The king is exposed and Black's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: In a sacrificial attack, material is secondary to king safety and piece activity. Two pawns for a piece is often sufficient compensation if the attack persists.
notes.plans: Black will activate the rook on a8 via ...Kf8 and ...Re8, bringing more pieces to the attack. White's king is stuck in the center and vulnerable to checks and discovered attacks.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf8 to tuck the king away safely and prepare to bring the rook on a8 into the game via e8. This is a typical defensive/offensive maneuver: secure the king and activate the rook.
notes.teaches: When your king is safe, you can focus on activating all your pieces. Kf8 is a useful move to avoid forks (like Bf5+) and to connect the rooks.
notes.plans: Black will play Re8, putting pressure on the e-file and supporting the attack. The rook on e8 is a powerful piece even if not immediately threatening anything.

notes.explains: Black plays c4 to open lines against White's king. The pawn break is decisive because it creates threats like Ba4+ and allows the rook to join the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, pawn breaks like c4 can open files and diagonals for your pieces. Look for ways to expose the king further.
notes.plans: After c4, Black will play Ba4+ and then Rxb3 or other captures, winning material. The attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: Black uses checks and threats to drive the king to a4, then plays Rb8 threatening ...Rxb3+ and mate. The king is exposed and Black's pieces coordinate perfectly.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, use checks to force the king into a worse position. Then bring in all your pieces to deliver the final blow. The b-file becomes the main avenue of attack.
notes.plans: Black will play Rxb3+ or Qxb3+ followed by mate. White's king has no escape.

notes.explains: Black simplifies to a winning endgame by trading rooks. With a queen and pawns against a queen, Black's extra pawns and active king decide the game.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and are short on time, simplifying to a winning endgame is a practical approach. Trade pieces but keep the pressure.
notes.plans: Black will push the passed pawns and use the queen to create threats. White's king is exposed and cannot stop the pawns.

notes.explains: After …cxd5, Black has a knight developed, controls the center, and White has moved the queen three times—a clear violation of development principles.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize piece development over pawn moves. Moving the same piece repeatedly wastes time and hands the initiative to the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue developing with ...Nc6 or ...e5, aiming to complete kingside castling and activate the bishops.

notes.explains: Playing Bg4 attacks the queen and provokes f3, which weakens White's kingside. The bishop is safe because the knight on c3 defends it, and if White plays Nf3, Black pins the knight.
notes.teaches: Provoking weaknesses is a powerful concept: place a piece where it can be attacked, force a weakening pawn move, then retreat. The two tempi spent are worth the structural damage.
notes.plans: After f3, retreat the bishop to f5, eyeing the weakened light squares. Black can follow up with e6 and develop the other bishop.

notes.explains: Qa5+ forks the bishop on c4 and the king. If White plays Nc3 to defend, the knight is pinned and attacked by the pawn on d5—a classic case where a pawn attacking a pinned piece leads to material loss.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical opportunities like forks. When a pinned piece is attacked by a pawn, the defender is often in trouble because the pawn cannot be captured by the pinned piece.
notes.plans: Capture the knight on c3, then the bishop on c4, leaving White's kingside shattered. Black will be up a piece with a winning position.

notes.explains: After winning the piece, Black should not look for flashy continuations. Instead, complete development with e6, Bc5, and castle. The position is winning; simple, solid moves preserve the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a big material advantage, avoid unnecessary complications. Focus on finishing development, securing the king, and trading down to a technically winning endgame.
notes.plans: Play e6, develop the bishop to c5 or d6, castle kingside, and then start targeting White's weak pawns.

notes.explains: After trading queens, Black is up a piece and several pawns. Even in the endgame, complete development: bring out the bishop and centralize the king. Playing f6 prevents the bishop from being trapped on g7.
notes.teaches: Never neglect development, even in the endgame. A piece left on its starting square is a liability. Use pawn moves like f6 to give the bishop a safe square.
notes.plans: Play Bd6 or Bc5, then centralize the king to d7 or e7. Target White's weak pawns and trade down to a winning pawn endgame.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black spots that White's king and rook are on the same diagonal. The bishop can maneuver to c4 to skewer the rook. When facing an unexpected check, remember the three defenses: capture, block, or move the king.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical motifs like skewers, even in simplified positions. When surprised by a check, pause and consider all three ways to meet it.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, skewering the rook. After the rook moves, capture it. Then mop up White's remaining pawns.

notes.explains: …f6 is a terrible move because it weakens the kingside and doesn't develop. White can immediately exploit it with Nxe5, winning a pawn and more.
notes.teaches: Never play f6 in the opening unless absolutely necessary. It weakens the king's position and neglects development. The Damiano Defense is a classic example of how to punish such moves.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, and if Black recaptures with ...fxe5, then Qh5+ wins the rook. If Black doesn't recapture, White is up a pawn with a better position.

notes.explains: After winning the rook, White should not rush to capture everything. Instead, complete development: bring out the knight, castle, and centralize. The position is winning; simple moves suffice.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material advantage, focus on development and king safety. Don't get greedy; consolidate your position before launching further attacks.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to c3 or d2, castle kingside, and then advance the center pawns. Black's king is exposed, so any further attack will be easy.

notes.explains: Black's king is exposed and White has a crushing attack. The game ends in a quick checkmate. This demonstrates the consequences of weakening the kingside early.
notes.teaches: A single bad move like f6 can lead to a swift defeat. Always prioritize king safety and development in the opening.
notes.plans: Deliver checkmate with the queen and bishop coordination.

notes.explains: The Fantasy Variation (f3) is recommended because it is less studied than main lines and leads to sharp tactical positions where black cannot improvise.
notes.teaches: Choose openings that are less theoretical and force opponents to think early.
notes.plans: After …dxe4 fxe4 e5, white should develop with Nf3, meeting ...Bg4 with Bc4 or c3.

notes.explains: After e4 c6 f3 d5 e5 e6 Nf3 Bg4, the correct move is Bc4, targeting f7 and threatening Bxf7+ followed by Nxe5. Black cannot take the knight because …Bxf3 Qxf3 gives White a massive attack on f7.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, prioritize active piece development and immediate threats over material. The bishop on c4 creates a tactical threat that forces Black to defend precisely.
notes.plans: After Bc4, if Black plays …Nf6?, White wins with Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ (forking king and bishop) and regains the piece with a winning attack.

notes.explains: Black's setup with ...Qe7 prepares queenside castling and threatens ...h5-h4, leading to opposite-side attacks.
notes.teaches: Recognize when the opponent is preparing opposite-side castling and plan your own attack accordingly.
notes.plans: White should complete development with Nbd2, then consider Qa4 or Qb3 to pressure the queenside.

notes.explains: Qa4 provokes ...Kb8, after which the queen drops back to b3 with an x-ray on the b-pawn. This is a practical way to create problems for a well-prepared opponent.
notes.teaches: Use provocative moves to force the opponent out of preparation; even if not objectively best, they create practical difficulties.
notes.plans: After …Kb8 Qb3, white threatens Ba6 and Nc4, pressuring the queenside and the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's ...Nh5 aims to eliminate the dark-squared bishop to relieve pressure on e5. White should not panic with Bxf7; instead, stick to the queenside plan.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a threat, evaluate if it can be ignored or met with a stronger counter-threat.
notes.plans: White should play Ba6, threatening to force ...b6 and then jump the knight to c4, creating serious pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: After …Nb6, white must calculate concretely. The bishop on a6 is hanging, so white needs a tempo-gaining move. Nxe5 is strong because if black recaptures, Nc6 forks the king and queen.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, look for forcing moves that exploit the opponent's loss of control over key squares.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, threatening Nc6+; if black avoids the fork, white wins a pawn and maintains the attack.

notes.explains: Black's ...Be6 is a strong defensive move that white underestimated. It pins the knight and threatens to win material. White must now cut losses and find the best way to give up a piece for maximum compensation.
notes.teaches: When you have miscalculated, accept the loss and look for the most graceful way to minimize damage—often by sacrificing a piece for pawns and long-term pressure.
notes.plans: Play Nxc6+ to force bxc6, then Bxd6+; white gets two pawns and continued pressure against the black king.

notes.explains: White has two pawns for the piece and practical attacking chances. The queen retreats to c2, a flexible square that keeps rooks coordinated and avoids immediate threats.
notes.teaches: When down material, give your opponent as many decisions as possible; open-ended moves can be more effective than forcing lines.
notes.plans: Start pushing the a-pawn (a4-a5) to drive away the knight on b6 and open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: White plays b4 to gain space on the queenside and prevent ...c5. This also gives black more rope to make mistakes.
notes.teaches: When attacking, use pawns to restrict the opponent's options and create targets.
notes.plans: Follow up with a5 to chase the knight away, then consider Bxc8 or Nc4 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Nc4 brings the knight into the attack and threatens tactical ideas. Black must decide where to place the queen.
notes.teaches: Every move should pose a new problem for the opponent, especially when they are short on time.
notes.plans: After black's queen move, play Bxc8 to eliminate the bishop and continue the queenside assault.

notes.explains: White plays g3 to kick the knight from f4 and then capture the f7 pawn. This weakens the king slightly but with reduced material, it's not a problem.
notes.teaches: When down material, look for ways to win back pawns; a minor piece is only three points.
notes.plans: After ...Nh5, play Rxf7, winning a pawn and creating a passed e-pawn. Then use the rook on the seventh rank to generate tactical threats.

notes.explains: After Rxf7, white threatens Nb6+ forking king and queen. The combination of the rook on the seventh rank and the x-ray on the a-file creates a winning tactic.
notes.teaches: Look for tactical motifs like forks, discovered checks, and x-rays when you have a rook on the seventh rank.
notes.plans: Play Nb6+; if ...Nxb6, axb6 wins the queen. If ...Kb8, then Rxf8+ and axb6 is winning.

notes.explains: White's attack culminates in Qa4, threatening mate on a7. Black's king is exposed and white's pieces coordinate perfectly.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, use your queen and rook together to create mating threats; don't be afraid to sacrifice material for a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After ...Kb8, play Qa6 followed by Qb7#. If black tries to block, simply capture the blocking piece.

notes.explains: Black's Nd4 is an old sideline aiming to disrupt normal Ruy Lopez play. White should not panic; the knight is a target.
notes.teaches: Against early knight sorties, the simplest approach is often to challenge or capture it, but here Bc4 is the principled retreat, keeping pressure on e5.
notes.plans: Develop with d3, then Nbd2, and later consider f4 to build a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After Nxd4 exd4, White's bishop retreats to c4 (not a4) to keep an eye on f7 and support d3. Black's d4-pawn is isolated and weak.
notes.teaches: In the Bird, White's bishop belongs on c4 to maintain pressure; the d4-pawn is a long-term weakness that Black must defend.
notes.plans: Play d3, develop the knight to d2, and later target the d4-pawn with moves like Re1+ and Bg5.

notes.explains: d3 is solid, protecting e4 and preparing development. Black's best is d5, challenging the center.
notes.teaches: When the center is fluid, solidifying with d3 is often better than committing to e5, which would allow ...d5 with tempo.
notes.plans: After ...d5, capture on d5, then Re1+ to exploit Black's uncastled king.

notes.explains: Re1+ is natural, forcing Black to block with Be7 or Be6. This gains time and keeps the king in the center.
notes.teaches: Checking with the rook when the opponent's king is exposed is a standard way to gain tempo and disrupt coordination.
notes.plans: After ...Be7, play Bg5 to trade dark-squared bishops, leaving Black with a bad bishop on e6.

notes.explains: Bg5 is a positional move, aiming to trade bishops. After ...f6 or ...Be6, White gets a favorable exchange.
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's good bishop (here the dark-squared one) can leave them with a passive piece, especially when the center is open.
notes.plans: After ...Be6, capture on e7, then develop Nbd2 and target the d4-pawn.

notes.explains: After the trade, Black's queen is on e7, and the d4-pawn is weak. White should now play Nd2, but Bxd5 was even stronger, doubling Black's pawns and leaving a monster knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between a good positional move and a decisive one, calculate carefully; here capturing on d5 gives a nearly winning advantage.
notes.plans: If Nd2, then ...0-0-0 is possible, but White can still press with Nb3 and target d4.

notes.explains: Black's queenside castling is risky but sharp. White missed the chance to take on d5 earlier; now the position is complex.
notes.teaches: When your opponent castles into an attack, you must act quickly but accurately; slow buildup can be punished if you miss tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Play Nb3 to pressure d4, then consider a4 to open lines on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's c5 weakens d5 but also opens lines. White's knight on b3 is passive; rerouting it to d2 or c1 is better.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim are grim; if a knight has no future on b3, redeploy it to a better square like d2 or c1.
notes.plans: Play Nbd2, aiming for c4 or e4, and keep the tension on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's Nf4 is a mistake; it opens the e-file and allows White's queen to become active. The correct move was Rh6, defending and preparing counterplay.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, do not give up key squares without compensation; Nf4 weakens control of e6 and invites White's rook to e5.
notes.plans: Play Re5! immediately, attacking the knight and threatening to win the bishop on e6.

notes.explains: Re5 is a brilliant move, attacking the knight and threatening to capture on e6. The rook is untouchable due to the pin on the knight.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is to place a piece en prise if capturing it leads to a decisive advantage. Here Re5 exploits the overworked knight.
notes.plans: If the knight moves, capture on e6 and ruin Black's pawns; if ...Bxc4, recapture and then build up slowly with Ra1, Nc1-d3, and eventually b4.

notes.explains: After …Ne6, White has a positional advantage. Black's pieces are passive, and White can slowly improve.
notes.teaches: When you have a static advantage (better pawn structure, active pieces), do not rush; improve your worst piece and then break through.
notes.plans: Play Ra1, then Nc1-d3, and finally b4 to open lines on the queenside.

notes.explains: After improving all pieces, b4 is the decisive pawn break, opening the b-file and creating threats.
notes.teaches: When all pieces are optimally placed, use a pawn break to create new invasion points. Here b4 forces weaknesses in Black's camp.
notes.plans: After ...cxb4, play Nxb4 threatening Nc6+; if ...Nxb4, then Rxb4 and double on the b-file.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and has a strong attack. Black's queen is active but White's rooks dominate.
notes.teaches: In the attack, keep pieces coordinated; here the rook on b1 and the queen on f3 work together to threaten mate.
notes.plans: Play c5 to open the diagonal, then Re7 or Nf6 to deliver mate.

notes.explains: White's attack is overwhelming. Black's king is exposed, and White has multiple threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is trapped, use checks and threats to force mate or win material.
notes.plans: Play Qf4+ and then Nb4 to cut off the queen's defense, leading to mate on b7.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and has a winning endgame. The extra pawn and active rook ensure victory.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, simplify by trading queens and use your extra pawn to promote.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn, trade rooks if possible, and promote.

notes.explains: Black's d6 is passive, blocking the bishop and giving White everything it wants. The Vienna Gambit aims for Black to take the pawn, giving White central control with d4 and opening the f-file for attack.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing the f-pawn in the Vienna Gambit gains central space and opens lines against Black's king. The open f-file is a double-edged sword but can be a powerful attacking avenue.
notes.plans: Develop pieces naturally, aiming to build an attack. Do not go pawn-hunting prematurely.

notes.explains: After Nc3 Nc6, Bb5 is a Ruy Lopez-style move putting pressure on e5. Black's Bd7 is a reasonable response.
notes.teaches: In the Vienna, developing the bishop to b5 can be strong, but avoid immediate pawn grabs like Bxc6 then Nxe5, as Black can reply Qd4 forking the knight and king.
notes.plans: Instead of capturing, retreat the bishop to c4 or a4, preparing to castle and attack.

notes.explains: After Bc4 Be6, trading bishops on White's terms is good. Bb3 (or Bxe6) is a typical way to recapture with the a-pawn, improving the pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Trading on your own terms means forcing the opponent to capture your piece in a way that benefits your structure or activity.
notes.plans: After Bxe6 fxe6, White can play positionally with Nxe5 or aggressively with Ng5. The e6 pawn is a target.

notes.explains: After Ng5, Black's fxe5 allows d4 with tempo, then Ng6. White's center is strong, and the knight on e6 is a powerful outpost.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn majority and an outpost, use pawn breaks like d5 to secure the outpost and restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Play d5 to cement the knight on e6, then follow up with Bg5 hitting the knight on f6. Black's position is paralyzed.

notes.explains: In the position with a knight on e6 and Black's king stuck in the center, White can win with simple tactics. Nxd5 (or exd5) opens lines, and the f-file becomes deadly.
notes.teaches: When you have a huge positional advantage, look for tactical finishes. The open f-file and exposed king lead to quick checkmates.
notes.plans: Nxd5 exd5, then Qh5+ or Qf3, with threats of mate. Black's king is helpless.

notes.explains: If Black accepts the gambit with exf4, it's a mistake. Unlike the King's Gambit, White's knight on c3 supports e5, chasing the knight back to g8.
notes.teaches: In the Vienna, exf4 is bad because White can play e5, forcing the knight back and gaining a huge lead in development. Develop with Nf3 and d4 to recover the pawn.
notes.plans: Play Nf3 (not d4 immediately to avoid Qh4+), then d4. White will win back the pawn with a big development advantage.

notes.explains: In some sharp lines, White can sacrifice more material for a devastating attack. For example, after exf4 d6 d4, White can play Bc4 and later sacrifice a knight on f7 or similar.
notes.teaches: When you have a development lead, sacrifices to expose the king are often justified. Look for patterns like bishop g5 distracting the knight, then knight f7+ winning the queen.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with piece sacrifices, forcing the king into the open. Castle with check and deliver mate.

notes.explains: The best response to the Vienna Gambit is d5, countering in the center. This leads to theoretical lines where Qf3 is strong.
notes.teaches: Meet flank attacks with central counterplay. d5 is a principled move that challenges White's center.
notes.plans: In the d5 line, White plays Qf3, creating threats. Black must be careful.

notes.explains: After Black plays d6 and develops passively, White has a clear positional advantage. Black's bishops are passive, White has more central control and active pieces.
notes.teaches: The Vienna Gambit can lead to a positional edge even without tactics. Compare piece activity and central control to assess the advantage.
notes.plans: Continue developing, possibly with Kh1 to avoid Qd4 tricks, then slowly improve the position.

notes.explains: In the game, after Bc4 Be6, White traded bishops and later played Ng5. Black's Qd7 allowed fxe5, and then White sacrificed the exchange with Rxf6 to remove the defender of h5.
notes.teaches: When calculating sacrifices, look for the defender of a key square. Removing the defender can enable a decisive queen check or fork.
notes.plans: After Rxf6, if Kd8, Qf8+ wins the rook. If Ke7, Qf7? is a mistake; instead Qf6+ forks king and rook. Always check intermediate moves like bishop checks on c5.

notes.explains: After the exchange sacrifice, White must be careful of Black's counterplay on the diagonal. Bc5+ is an intermediate move that can be dangerous.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, always consider intermediate checks and captures. They can turn the tables.
notes.plans: If Bc5+, White can play Qf3 or Rf2 to consolidate. Two pieces for a rook is a material advantage.

notes.explains: After Nxc5 d4, White played d5 to secure the e6 outpost for the knight. This is game over; Black has no moves.
notes.teaches: When you have a knight outpost, support it with pawn advances to make it permanent. The knight on e6 paralyzes Black's position.
notes.plans: If Black moves the bishop, Nxg7 wins. Otherwise, simply improve pieces and deliver mate.

notes.explains: In the final position, after Kf7 g6, the fastest win is to remove the defender of g6 with a sacrifice, then check and win the rook.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for the most direct tactical finish. Removing the defender is a common motif.
notes.plans: Play a move like Bxg6+ hxg6, then Qxg6+ Kf8, and Qf6+ winning the rook.

notes.explains: After Nc3 d5, Black has many equalizing options. The most forcing and principled response is …c5, directly attacking the d4 pawn and exploiting White's knight on c3, which prevents the standard c2-c3 defense.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, Black should target the d4 pawn immediately with c5, as White cannot reinforce it with c3 due to the knight on c3.
notes.plans: After c5, Black can capture on e4 with the knight, forcing trades and leading to a queen check on a5, which is a topical line.

notes.explains: After Nc3 d5 Bf4 c5 e4 dxe4 Nxe4 Nxe4 dxc5 Qa5+ c3 Qxc5 Qa4+ Nc6 Qxe4, Black should develop harmoniously. Playing …Nc6 is better than …Bd7 because the bishop belongs on f5 or e6 later.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to develop with tempo if it misplaces a piece; instead, choose the most harmonious development, even if it seems slower.
notes.plans: Black aims to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop with g6 and Bg7, creating a threat of Bxc3+ winning the rook on a1.

notes.explains: After …g6 Bc4 Bg7, White must prevent Bxc3+. The best defense is Rd1 (type 2 prophylaxis), moving the rook off the a1-h8 diagonal. The inferior Bd2 physically blocks the threat but is passive.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis can be type 1 (physically preventing a threat) or type 2 (taking the sting out of it). Type 2 is often more active and flexible.
notes.plans: After Rd1, Black castles and develops with Bf5 or Be6, maintaining a solid position with slight pressure.

notes.explains: Black develops bishops to e7 and b6, which are invulnerable squares. Be7 prevents Ng5, and Bb6 reinforces the knight. This is solid and avoids tactics like Bg4 which would allow Nxe5.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on squares where they are not easily attacked and serve defensive roles. Avoid advanced bishop placements that create tactical vulnerabilities.
notes.plans: Continue improving position, possibly with a5 to prevent b4, then Qd7 to connect rooks.

notes.explains: f6 is safe here because White has no bishop on the a7-g1 diagonal, and Black's own bishop can reposition. It reinforces e5 and prevents Ng5.
notes.teaches: f6 is not always weakening; evaluate what it actually weakens. If the opponent cannot exploit the diagonal, it can be a solid defensive move.
notes.plans: Play Qd7, eyeing h3 and preparing potential sacrifices.

notes.explains: h4 weakens g4, allowing Black to place a bishop on g4 with queen support. Earlier Bg4 was bad because of Nxe5 tactics, but now the queen on d7 defends the bishop and the queen on c1 is misplaced.
notes.teaches: Re-evaluate candidate moves when circumstances change. A move that was bad earlier can become good if the opponent's piece placement changes.
notes.plans: Play Bg4, possibly followed by h5 to secure the bishop, exploiting White's passivity.

notes.explains: f5 reopens the bishop's diagonal, attacks h4, and defends the bishop on g4. It also prevents Nxe5 tactics.
notes.teaches: When defending a piece, consider moves that also create counterplay. f5 serves multiple purposes.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring White's kingside.

notes.explains: Bf6 defends the e5 pawn with the least valuable piece, freeing the rook for other tasks. This is more flexible than immediately playing Re8.
notes.teaches: Accomplish defensive tasks with the least valuable piece possible, keeping rooks and queen for more important duties.
notes.plans: Follow with Re8, completing development, then consider breaks like f4 or e4.

notes.explains: Black takes on g4 to prevent White from occupying e4 with a knight. Although it gives up the bishop, it avoids a strong knight outpost.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must part with a good piece to deny the opponent a key square. Evaluate the trade concretely.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, attacking the queen and starting active play.

notes.explains: f4 is a concrete attempt to break White's kingside defense, even though it gives up the e4 square. The attack should be worth the concession.
notes.teaches: When you sense the time is right, press the attack even if it means sacrificing a positional plus. Trust your feeling after improving your pieces.
notes.plans: After f4, aim to open the f-file by moving the bishop from f6.

notes.explains: Nf5 is the only logical square, pressuring White's kingside and threatening sacrifices like Bxh4.
notes.teaches: When attacking, place knights on squares that maximize pressure on the opponent's king.
notes.plans: Consider rook lifts or further sacrifices to break through.

notes.explains: After Nxg3 and Nxh4, Black wins a pawn and exposes White's king. The attack has paid off.
notes.teaches: When the attack yields material, take it and continue pressing. An exposed king is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Consolidate and exploit the weakened king position.

notes.explains: After Nf4 forces Bxf4, Black recaptures with the pawn, attacking the knight on g3. The bishop retreats to d8 again, staying out of the rook's way.
notes.teaches: After a trade, reassess the position. New ideas (like rook lifts) become possible. Retreat bishops to keep them safe and not block rooks.
notes.plans: Prepare to lift the rook to h6 or target the d3 pawn.

notes.explains: b6 prevents Nc5, which would fork the rook and queen. This allows the rook lift to h6.
notes.teaches: Identify your top priority (rook lift), find the obstacle (Nc5), and make it disappear with a prophylactic move.
notes.plans: Play Rh6, then continue the attack.

notes.explains: Be7 repositions the bishop to a better diagonal, preparing to bring the rook to d8 to pressure d3.
notes.teaches: Don't hesitate to reposition pieces to improve their activity. The bishop is still useful from e7.
notes.plans: Play Rd8, targeting the weak d3 pawn.

notes.explains: c4 provokes d4, which isolates the knight on e4 by removing its pawn support. Black then redirects pressure onto the knight.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you provoke a pawn move to weaken the opponent's piece support. Then shift your attack to that piece.
notes.plans: After d4, play Re8 to x-ray the knight, then maneuver to create a pin or win the knight.

notes.explains: Bxa3 exposes the attack on the knight on e4. It's a discovered attack, not a sacrifice, as the knight is undefended.
notes.teaches: Look for discovered attacks when a piece moves away. Even if it seems risky, calculate concretely.
notes.plans: Follow up by doubling rooks or taking the knight.

notes.explains: Kh8 is prophylaxis against knight checks on f6, but it walks into backrank issues. Better to play h6 first for luft.
notes.teaches: When playing prophylactically, also consider new weaknesses created. Always create luft when the backrank is vulnerable.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn to promote, while defending the c4 pawn.

notes.explains: Push the h-pawn, as it is far from White's knight and has good promotion chances. The d-pawn is blockaded.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, push the pawn furthest from the opponent's pieces. A single passed pawn can be very powerful.
notes.plans: Continue pushing h-pawn to promotion, while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White has a choice: Nxc6 wins a pawn but gives Black activity. It's better to avoid such 'cashing in' and instead maintain positional pressure.
notes.teaches: Don't be seduced by a flashy tactic that wins material if it allows the opponent to activate their pieces. Calculate deeper to see if the gain is worth the loss of initiative.
notes.plans: White should prefer developing moves like Bg2 or castling, keeping the tension and exploiting Black's weak pawns and passive pieces.

notes.explains: After castling, White has a pleasant position with active pieces and Black's queenside is weak. White should consider prophylactic moves like b4 to prevent Black's knight from reaching d4 via c5.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis is key: anticipate your opponent's best square for a piece and prevent it. Here, b4 stops ...c5 and ...Nc6-d4.
notes.plans: White plays b4, then develops the bishop to e3, and prepares f4 to control the center and restrict Black's pieces.
