notes.plans: After Nxd6, play Ba3 to threaten a discovered attack on the queen. The queen has only one safe square (Qb6), but then Nc4 or other moves win it.

notes.explains: White plays Ba3, threatening a discovered attack on the queen. Black's queen is trapped; after Qc3, Ne4 wins the queen.
notes.teaches: Use bishops to create discovered attacks against a trapped queen. Coordinate your pieces to maximize pressure on the opponent's most valuable piece.
notes.plans: Win the queen, then simplify and convert the material advantage. Push the d-pawn and centralize the queen.

notes.explains: Black blunders with Na7, leaving the pawn on b5 undefended. White can win a pawn, but there is a better move: d5! This piles pressure on the knight, opens the bishop, and wins the pawn in a much stronger version than immediate Nxb5.
notes.teaches: When an opponent's piece is undefended and under attack, look for a move that increases the pressure rather than capturing immediately. d5 here is more forcing and leaves Black's pieces passive.
notes.plans: Play d5, then after Black's response, capture on b5 with the bishop or knight, maintaining a dominant position.

notes.explains: After b4, White plays Qa4+ instead of capturing on a7. This check wins the pawn on b4 while attacking both queenside minor pieces. Black is forced to defend passively with Qb8, leaving a disastrous position.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is hanging, consider if a check or other forcing move can win it in a better way. Qa4+ wins the pawn while keeping the initiative.
notes.plans: After Qb8, prevent Black from castling by playing Nb5, trading knights to land the bishop on b5, pinning the knight on d7 and keeping the king in the center.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5, trading a good knight for Black's bad knight on a7. This seems to violate positional principles, but the concrete goal is to prevent Black from castling. After the trade, the bishop lands on b5, pinning the knight on d7 and trapping the king in the center.
notes.teaches: Concrete tactical goals can override general positional principles. Here, preventing castling is more important than preserving a good knight. Always prioritize the most forcing plan.
notes.plans: After Nb5 Nxb5 Bxb5, Black's king is stuck in the center. Follow up with Rc1, targeting the pinned knight and preparing a decisive attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7, protecting the knight and preparing to castle. However, the queen becomes vulnerable. White has a crushing tactical sequence: Bb6! uses the pin on the d7 knight, forcing the queen back, and then Rc1 wins material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is tied to defending a piece, look for a move that exploits the pin. Bb6 attacks the queen and the pinned knight simultaneously, winning at least a piece.
notes.plans: After Bb6 Qb8, capture on d7 with the bishop, forcing the king out, then deliver checkmate with Rc1+ and Rc7.

notes.explains: White captures on d7, transforming the pin into a direct attack on the king. After Kxd7, Rc1+ forces the king to the c-file, where it will be checkmated. This is the fastest path to victory.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, consider capturing the pinned piece if it exposes the enemy king. This can transform a material advantage into a mating attack.
notes.plans: After Rc1+, Black's king is forced to c6 or c7, and White delivers mate with Rc7 or Bc6.

notes.explains: Black retreats the bishop to g6 instead of trading, keeping the tension and threatening f5 to trap the bishop. White must respond with Nh4 to avoid losing the bishop.
notes.teaches: Sometimes maintaining the tension is better than trading; a threat like f5 can force the opponent into awkward moves.
notes.plans: After Nh4 Nxg6 hxg6, Black gets the pawn cube structure and can continue with Nb6 or Nf8.

notes.explains: After hxg6, Black has the pawn cube (pawns on f6, g7, h7). This structure is very safe for the king and allows Black to push f5 and g5 for attack without weakening.
notes.teaches: The pawn cube is a resilient structure: you can advance two pawns for attack while the king remains secure behind the remaining pawn.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to b6 or f8, then consider Bc7 and Qd6 to create a battery on the h2-b8 diagonal.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc7 and Qd6, creating a battery on the h2-b8 diagonal. If White plays g3 to block, then Rxe3 wins a pawn because the f2-pawn is overloaded (defending g3 and the bishop).
notes.teaches: A queen-bishop battery can create tactical threats; look for overloaded pawns that defend multiple pieces.
notes.plans: After Rxe3, Black wins a pawn and maintains pressure. If White avoids g3, Black can continue with Nd5 or other improving moves.

notes.explains: Black executes the tactic Rxe3, exploiting the overloaded f2-pawn. White cannot recapture because f2 defends both g3 and the bishop.
notes.teaches: When a pawn defends two pieces, capturing one can overload it; always check for such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After Rxe3, Black is a pawn up with a strong attack. Continue with fxe3 Qxe3+ and then bring the rook to the e-file.

notes.explains: Black has won a pawn and now must be flexible in converting the advantage. Instead of playing Rxe3 again (which would allow Kg2), Black drops the rook back to e8 or e4 to prepare for White's counterplay like c5.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be flexible; don't force a continuation if the opponent can escape. Look for ways to consolidate and take more pawns.
notes.plans: If White plays c5, Black can take on d4 with the rook, ending up with two extra pawns in an endgame. Otherwise, improve piece placement.

notes.explains: Black plays Re4, preparing to meet c5 with Rxd4, winning another pawn. This is a precise way to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, look for moves that secure material while preventing counterplay. Re4 both attacks d4 and prepares to capture if White pushes c5.
notes.plans: After c5 Rxd4, Black has two extra pawns and a winning endgame. If White doesn't play c5, Black can improve further.

notes.explains: White plays c5, and Black captures on d4 with the rook, winning a second pawn. The resulting endgame with two extra pawns is winning despite opposite-colored bishops.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, extra pawns are often decisive, especially if they are passed or can create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Black will have a material advantage and can aim to trade pieces or create passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black wins the queen for a rook and bishop, but more importantly, the pawn cube remains intact and Black has a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: Even after heavy exchanges, the pawn cube provides king safety and can be useful in the endgame for creating passed pawns.
notes.plans: Black will use the extra pawns and the active rook to win the endgame.

notes.explains: The pawn cube (pawns on f6, g7, h7) is a recurring theme. It allows Black to push pawns for attack without weakening the king, and even in endgames it can be useful.
notes.teaches: The pawn cube is a versatile structure: it provides king safety, supports pawn storms, and can be a asset in endgames due to its solidity.
notes.plans: In the middlegame, use the cube to launch an attack with f5 and g5. In the endgame, use the extra pawns to create passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black immediately plays d5, challenging the center and exploiting the weakness created by f4.
notes.teaches: Against the Grand Prix Attack (f4), the immediate d5 is the critical response, undermining White's center.
notes.plans: After d5, Black aims to recapture with the knight (Nf6) to put pressure on the d5 pawn on favorable terms.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6 instead of recapturing with the queen, keeping the tension and preparing to gambit the pawn.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the knight allows Black to play e6 next, forcing a trade and gaining compensation through control of d4 and pressure on White's weak f4 pawn.
notes.plans: Black will play e6, trade on d5, and then develop with active moves like Bc5 or Bd6, targeting the f4 pawn.

notes.explains: After the trades, White has a weak pawn on f4 and a bad bishop on f1, while Black has strong central control and active piece play.
notes.teaches: The f4 pawn becomes a long-term weakness; White's king safety is compromised because castling kingside doesn't fully solve the issues.
notes.plans: Black should develop actively, targeting the f4 pawn with moves like Bd6 and Qc7, piling up pressure.

notes.explains: White's a3 is a non-developing move that ignores the threats; Black can immediately punish by playing Bd6, attacking the f4 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes time, seize the initiative with active development and direct threats.
notes.plans: Play Bd6, then Qc7 to pile up on f4, and consider castling kingside to bring the rook into play.

notes.explains: Black captures the f4 pawn, opening the diagonal for the bishop and gaining material while maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: Taking free pawns is good, but ensure it comes with additional benefits like opening lines or creating threats.
notes.plans: After capturing, castle kingside to activate the rook and prepare further attacks, possibly with Ng4 targeting h2.

notes.explains: Black castles kingside, x-raying the queen and reinforcing control over d4. The rook on d8 adds pressure.
notes.teaches: Castling kingside in such positions is aggressive because it brings the rook to the d-file and supports central dominance.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ng4, threatening Bxh2 and aiming for e3 to create mating threats.

notes.explains: Ng4 creates threats of Bxh2 and the knight can go to e3, intensifying the attack on White's king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for knight maneuvers that create immediate threats and force weaknesses.
notes.plans: If White plays Bxf4, then Qd2, Black can play Nd4 to distract the knight on f3, followed by Be3+ and Qh2#.

notes.explains: White tries to trade queens with Qd2, but Black has a tactical refutation: Nd4, distracting the knight on f3.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers a queen trade, consider if you can use it to create a decisive tactical blow.
notes.plans: Play Nd4; if Qxd4, then Nxe2+ wins the queen. If not, Be3+ forces checkmate.

notes.explains: Nd4 exploits the weak d4 square tactically: it distracts the knight on f3, allowing Be3+ and Qh2#.
notes.teaches: A weak square can be used not only for positional outposts but also for tactical decoys to remove defenders.
notes.plans: After Nd4, if Nxd4, then Be3+ forces checkmate. If Qxd4, then Nxe2+ wins the queen.

notes.explains: White's alternative g3 creates weaknesses on the kingside; Black can respond with h5-h4 to open lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside, consider a pawn storm to exploit the exposed king.
notes.plans: Play h5, then h4 to open the h-file and launch an attack.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nbd7, allowing White to immediately push f4, entrenching the knight on e5. Black's position becomes difficult.
notes.teaches: When the Pillsbury knight is established, Black must undermine it immediately with ...c5 or ...g5, or risk being overrun.
notes.plans: White can now consider f5 to trap Black's bishop on e6, or castle queenside to prepare a direct attack.

notes.explains: White plays f5, attacking the bishop on e6. This wins a piece for two pawns, but also removes the powerful knight from e5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes tactical gains outweigh positional advantages; winning a piece for two pawns is often good in an open position.
notes.plans: After fxe6, recapture with the rook, then play d5 to gain tempo and open the center.

notes.explains: White castles queenside, deploying the rook quickly. Black has three pawns for the piece, but White's two bishops and open center give a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When ahead a piece in an open position, castling queenside can be safe and activate the rook faster than kingside.
notes.plans: Use the bishops to control diagonals and open files, targeting Black's king.

notes.explains: White plays Rhe1 to chase the queen away, then Bf5 to attack the rook and put pressure on Black's knights. Controlling the e-file is key.
notes.teaches: In open positions with a material advantage, controlling open files and activating pieces is more important than defending pawns.
notes.plans: After Bf5, Black's pieces are tied up; White can aim to trade on e6 and dominate the e-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd6, which is a blunder because the rook becomes trapped after Bg3. The game ends quickly.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to loose pieces and potential traps; a trapped rook can decide the game immediately.
notes.plans: Play Bg3, winning the rook. If Black tries Qc5, respond with Nxb5 to trade queens and win a pawn.

notes.explains: White plays Nxb5, attacking the queen and threatening to trade queens while winning a pawn. This is the most clinical continuation.
notes.teaches: When winning, look for moves that simplify while maintaining a decisive advantage. Trading queens when up material is often good.
notes.plans: After Qxb5, Bxd6 wins a rook. Black resigns shortly.

notes.explains: White sacrifices two pawns for a big lead in development and central control, aiming for a quick attack.
notes.teaches: In gambits, development and initiative often outweigh material; black must neutralize White's lead before cashing in the extra pawns.
notes.plans: Black should accept the gambit pawns but then carefully coordinate pieces to blunt White's attack and consolidate the material advantage.

notes.explains: White offers the first pawn with c3. Black can accept or decline; declining with d5 is a practical alternative that leads to equal but comfortable positions.
notes.teaches: Declining a gambit with a central counterstrike can take the fun out of White's attack and lead to a solid position.
notes.plans: After …d5, White's best is exd5; black recaptures with the queen, then develops with Nc6 and Bb4+, aiming for an endgame where White's isolated d-pawn is a weakness.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the knight, offering only one pawn. Black must avoid Nf6 due to e5; instead develop the dark-squared bishop to c5 and solidify with d6.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, delaying knight development can prevent tactical shots like e5. Prioritize bishop development and pawn solidity.
notes.plans: Play Bc5, d6, then Nf6 after White's e5 is neutralized. If White plays Qb3, counter with Qh4 attacking f2. After g3, drop back to f6, then e7 to stop Nd5 and prepare Nf6.

notes.explains: White offers a second pawn with Bc4. Black should accept with Nf6, not the old D5 line which gives White easy equality. After e5, check with Bb4.
notes.teaches: Accepting the second pawn is principled; the old D5 sacrifice is outdated. The check on b4 forces White to defend awkwardly.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then after e5, Bb4+. Against most White replies (Nc3, Nd2, Kf1), counter with d5. Against the best reply Bc3, play Qe7 pinning the e-pawn and preparing to redeploy the knight via g8-h6.

notes.explains: White blocks the check with Nc3, the most common move, but it loses on the spot. Black plays d5, counterattacking the center.
notes.teaches: When White's pieces are hanging, a central pawn break can exploit the lack of coordination. Here d5 attacks both the bishop and knight.
notes.plans: After …d5, if exf6, recapture with the queen (Qxf6) hitting both the knight and bishop. White cannot defend both, so Black wins at least a pawn with a winning position.

notes.explains: White moves the king. Black again plays d5, leading to an endgame where White gets a pawn on g7. Black's plan is to surround and win that pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a single extra pawn is often decisive if the opponent has no counterplay. Patience and accurate technique are required.
notes.plans: After exf6, play Qxf6, then develop with Nc6, Bf5, and rook to g8. Target the g7 pawn with moves like Nd7, f6, and Bg6. White's king is exposed, giving Black additional attacking chances.

notes.explains: White blocks with the bishop, the best but rare move. Black should not play d5 here; instead play Qe7, pinning the e-pawn and guarding the bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's best move is rare, it's still essential to know the correct response. Pinning a pawn can prevent a dangerous advance.
notes.plans: Play Qe7. If White takes on b4, recapture with the queen and then play Nd2-e4 with initiative. If White plays Qe2, retreat the knight to g8 and redeploy to h6, then castle and aim for d6 to trade off the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's Bb4+ pins the knight and threatens d5, but White's bishop on b2 eyes g7. Blocking with Nbd2 is natural but clogs the center; Kf1 is more aggressive, keeping the diagonal open.
notes.teaches: When deciding between blocking a check with a piece or moving the king, consider which option preserves your attacking potential. Here, Kf1 avoids blocking the bishop's diagonal and keeps the queen's mobility.
notes.plans: White aims to complete development and maintain pressure on g7, possibly with Qb3 or e5 later.

notes.explains: Black's f6 blunts the bishop but creates permanent weaknesses on the kingside, especially the diagonal a2-g8. The knight on g8 is undefended (type 2 undefended piece).
notes.teaches: Pawn moves that weaken the king's pawn shield are often irreversible. Exploit such weaknesses by targeting undefended pieces and building pressure along the weakened diagonals.
notes.plans: Play Qb3, attacking f7 and the undefended bishop on b4, forcing Black to respond and further disrupt his development.

notes.explains: After Qb3, Black trades bishop for knight with check, then White recaptures with the king. White's king is safe in the center because Black has no pieces developed to attack it. White now has a lead in development and pressure on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Moving the king early can be acceptable if the opponent cannot exploit it. Here, the king on d2 is safe and actually helps control key squares, while White's pieces are active.
notes.plans: White will castle kingside, then push e5 to open lines and exploit Black's weak f6 pawn.

notes.explains: White plays e5, opening the position. Black cannot capture the bishop on e5 because of the pin along the e-file (Re1 would skewer the queen). White's bishop on e5 is well-placed, but its job is done; it can now be redeployed.
notes.teaches: A piece that has fulfilled its purpose (here, preparing e5) can be repositioned to a more active square. Don't cling to a piece's current location if it can do more elsewhere.
notes.plans: Play Ba3, targeting f8 and preventing Black from castling, while preparing to bring the knight to d6 via c4.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop and castle. White's knight wants to reach d6, but the bishop on c4 is in the way. White needs to move the bishop to a square that keeps pressure on the diagonal and clears c4 for the knight.
notes.teaches: When planning a piece maneuver, consider intermediate moves that improve your position. Here, Bd5 centralizes the bishop and keeps the diagonal, while allowing the knight to go to c4 and then d6.
notes.plans: Play Bd5, then Nc4, aiming for Nd6. If Black takes on e5, White recaptures with the bishop and supports the knight with Bxc5.

notes.explains: The knight reaches d6, a powerful outpost. Black cannot easily dislodge it. White's pieces are active, and Black's king is stuck in the center. The knight on d6 controls key squares and restricts Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: An outpost knight, especially one that cannot be attacked by pawns, is a huge asset. It restricts the opponent's pieces and often leads to a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: White will continue to pressure Black's position, possibly with Rfd1 to x-ray the king, and look for tactical blows like Bxc6 or discovered checks.

notes.explains: White plays Rfd1, x-raying the king on e8. This is a preparatory move: it sets up tactics like discovered checks or pins. The choice of rook matters: putting the f-rook on d1 leaves the a-rook free to go to c1 if the king moves to c7.
notes.teaches: When placing a rook on an open file, consider where the other rook will go. Anticipate the opponent's likely response and place your rooks accordingly to maximize their activity.
notes.plans: If Black takes on e5, White can recapture and then use the discovered check. If Black moves the king to c7, White can play Rac1 to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black moves the king to c7 to escape the x-ray. White responds with Rac1, now x-raying the king again. The queen on e7 is also under pressure. White's pieces are perfectly coordinated.
notes.teaches: X-ray attacks (aligning a piece with the opponent's king through another piece) are powerful. By placing rooks on d1 and c1, White creates multiple threats and keeps the king in the crosshairs.
notes.plans: White will look to open lines, e.g., by Bxc6 or by playing a discovered check. The immediate threat is Nb5+ or Nd6+? Actually, the knight is already on d6; White can consider moves like Bxc6 or Qb3 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5+, forcing the king to the b-file. This clarifies the situation: the king cannot go back to d8 because of the rook on d1. The knight check also opens up possibilities for discovered attacks.
notes.teaches: A check can force the opponent's king to a worse square, especially when combined with x-ray threats. Always consider checks that restrict the king's options.
notes.plans: After the king moves to b8 or b7, White can play Bxc5, opening the b-file and threatening discovered check. The queen on e7 is x-rayed by the rook on c1, so Black must be careful.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop on c5 to open the b-file and create a discovered check threat. Black captures, but now White's queen and rook are aligned against the king. The pawn on b6 is gone, so the b-file is open.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you need to sacrifice material to open lines for an attack. Here, the bishop sacrifice removes the b-pawn, allowing a devastating discovered check or a direct attack on the king.
notes.plans: White can now play a discovered check by moving the knight, e.g., Nd6+ or Nc7+. The queen on e7 is also under attack, so Black's position is critical.

notes.explains: Instead of immediately playing a discovered check, White plays Nd4, improving the knight and x-raying the queen on e7. This is a patient move that maintains the tension and avoids premature complications.
notes.teaches: When the immediate tactical blow doesn't work (e.g., the discovered check leads to a defense), it's often better to improve your pieces and keep the pressure. Potential energy can be more valuable than cashing in too early.
notes.plans: White threatens Bxc6, attacking the queen and threatening checkmate on c7. Black must respond, and White can then win the queen or deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8, threatening checkmate on e1. White responds with h3, creating luft for the king and preventing back-rank mates. This is a necessary prophylactic move.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of back-rank threats. Creating luft (a pawn move to give the king an escape square) is often essential before launching a final attack.
notes.plans: After h3, White can continue the attack with Bxc6, winning the queen or delivering checkmate. Black's threats are neutralized.

notes.explains: White plays Bxc6, attacking the queen and threatening checkmate on c7. Black's queen is overloaded: it must defend c7 and cannot capture the bishop because of the x-ray from the rook on c1.
notes.teaches: An overloaded piece cannot defend two threats simultaneously. Here, the queen on e7 must defend c7 and cannot capture the bishop on c6 because that would lose the queen to the rook on c1.
notes.plans: After Bxc6, Black's queen is lost. White will capture the queen and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: White wins the queen for a rook and bishop, leaving Black with a rook and two pieces for the queen. However, White's remaining pieces are active, and Black's king is exposed. White can continue the attack.
notes.teaches: Even after winning the queen, the game isn't over. Keep attacking the exposed king and use your queen's mobility to pick off pawns and create threats.
notes.plans: White will play Qg3 or g6, threatening checkmate and forcing Black to give up more material. The king is safe on h2, and White's pawns are solid.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nf3 d5 Bf4, White's Nc3 instead of c3 exerts pressure on d5. Black's c5 is a mistake because dxc5 leaves Black struggling to regain the pawn without falling behind in development. a3 prepares b4 to secure the c5 pawn, and after e5 Bg5, Black must waste a tempo with Be6 to prevent Bxf6 Nxd5. b4 then secures the pawn, leaving White up a pawn with no compensation.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, the knight on c3 changes the character of the London system, allowing aggressive pawn grabs like dxc5. The move a3 is a key prophylactic idea to support the c5 pawn and prepare b4.
notes.plans: White should continue development with Nf3 and Be2, aiming to consolidate the extra pawn and restrict Black's piece activity.

notes.explains: After Qd7, Na4 becomes effective because it threatens Nb6, forking the queen and bishop. This increases pressure on Black's position and exploits the queen's placement.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen moves to d7, a knight jump to a4 can create tactical threats (Nb6 fork). This is a common motif in the Jobava London.
notes.plans: White should aim to play Nb6, forcing Black to deal with the fork, and then continue developing while maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's Qe8 is a brilliant move that sets up the threat of Ne4. If White castles, Black can play Ne4, and after Bxe7 Qxe7, the knight on c3 is undefended, leading to tactical complications. White's best response is Na4, which takes the sting out of Ne4 by moving the knight away from the vulnerable square.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's hidden threats. Qe8 prepares Ne4, exploiting the undefended knight on c3. Prophylactic moves like Na4 can neutralize such ideas.
notes.plans: White should play Na4, then continue development, keeping the extra pawn and avoiding the tactical trap.

notes.explains: After White castles, Black plays Ne4, leading to a sequence where White ends up with a rook and two pawns for two minor pieces. This is a typical material imbalance. The evaluation depends on piece activity: White's rook needs to become active immediately.
notes.teaches: When you have a rook for two minor pieces, prioritize rook activity. Place the rook on an open file and aim to dominate the minor pieces with long-range threats.
notes.plans: White should play Rfd1, putting the rook on the only open file, and then look to double rooks or occupy the d6 outpost. The rook on d6 can serve as an anchor point.

notes.explains: White's rook on d6 is well-placed, but Black's Qg5 is a strong move targeting g2. White prevents it with Qh5, and then both sides make useful moves: h3 creates luft, and Rf8 is a slight inaccuracy as it wastes time. Black should have played Qf6 immediately to pressure White.
notes.teaches: In rook vs. minor pieces, the side with the rook should seek to activate the rook and create luft for the king. The side with the minor pieces should aim to keep the opponent's pawns immobile and target weaknesses.
notes.plans: White should continue improving piece placement, possibly preparing c4 to break through on the queenside. Black should have played Qf6 to attack f2 and keep pressure.

notes.explains: After Qxb7, White has a rook and two pawns for two minor pieces, with a passed b-pawn. Black's queen is active, but White's king is safe. The key idea is to trade queens or rooks to reduce Black's defensive resources. A rook trade favors the side with the rook because minor pieces are poor at multitasking.
notes.teaches: In rook vs. minor piece endgames, trading rooks often benefits the side with the rook because the minor pieces struggle to defend multiple weaknesses. Similarly, trading queens can leave the minor pieces unable to stop a passed pawn.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade queens, e.g., with Qd5, and then push the b-pawn. If Black avoids the trade, White can use the rook to support the pawn's advance.

notes.explains: After Bc4, Black's queen is undefended on d8. White threatens d5, which would open the center and attack the queen. Black cannot easily defend because ...Nc6 allows d5 with tempo.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays passively, look for pawn breaks that open lines and create threats. d5 is a powerful central break here.
notes.plans: Prepare d5 by developing further, or play d5 immediately if Black cannot defend adequately.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne7, connecting the rook and queen. White considers d5 but it may be premature. Instead, finishing kingside development with Nf3 and then Ne2 is flexible, as Ne2 connects knights and prepares Nf4 to pressure e6.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to open the center if the opponent can defend. Sometimes a flexible developing move is better than an immediate break.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then Ne2, keeping an eye on d5 and e6. If Black plays d5, White can recapture and use the knight on f4.

notes.explains: After exd5 exd5, White plays Bb3. Black may try to close the center with c6, but White's bishop is well-placed. White's goal is not to win in 5 moves but to get a solid middlegame advantage.
notes.teaches: Against weird openings, don't expect a quick knockout. Aim for a plus-two advantage and convert patiently.
notes.plans: Continue developing, pressure e6, and keep the center open. Avoid allowing Black to play e5 and d6, which would close the center.

notes.explains: White plays Ne2, connecting knights and preparing Nf4 to pressure e6. The e6 pawn is a soft spot because White's bishop on b3 and knight on f4 can target it. Black cannot easily play d6 because then exd6 opens lines.
notes.teaches: Identify weak pawns in the opponent's camp and target them with your pieces. A knight on f4 can be very annoying.
notes.plans: Play 0-0, then consider Nf4 or d6 to maintain pressure. Prevent Black from playing e5 at all costs.

notes.explains: Black castles by hand with Kg7. White can win a pawn by dxe6, but it may be better to start with Nf4 to keep queens on the board and create more threats.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two good lines, consider which keeps more tension and attacking chances. Keeping queens on can increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play Nf4, threatening to win the e6 pawn. If Black plays Bxc3, White can recapture with the d-pawn and maintain a strong attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxc3, and White recaptures with the d-pawn. Now White has a strong center and pressure on e6. The knight on f4 is well-placed.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with a pawn can give you a strong pawn center. Don't always recapture with a piece if the pawn structure is beneficial.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring e6. Consider dxe6 or Nxe6 to win the pawn. Keep the queens on for attacking chances.

notes.explains: White plays dxe6, winning a pawn. Black cannot recapture because of the pin on the e-file. White now has a material advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, don't rush to trade pieces if you can maintain pressure. Keep the position complex.
notes.plans: After dxe6, Black may play fxe6. Then White can play Nxe6, winning another pawn. Alternatively, play Qg4 or Bxe6 to maintain the attack.

notes.explains: White plays Nxe6+ and then Nxc7, winning a second pawn. White now has a large material advantage and the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for ways to win more material without compromising your position. The knight fork is a common tactic.
notes.plans: After Nxc7, White has a winning position. Continue developing and consolidate. Avoid unnecessary risks.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd6, attacking the knight on c7 and threatening to trade queens. White must be careful not to lose the knight.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks your piece, consider retreating to a safe square or defending. Sometimes a retreat is best to maintain the advantage.
notes.plans: Play Nb5, attacking the queen, or retreat the knight to a safe square. Alternatively, play Bxe6 to keep the knight defended.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5, forcing queen trade. After Qxd1 Rxd1, White has a rook and two pawns for a knight, plus the bishop pair. The d-file is open for the rook.
notes.teaches: Trading queens can be beneficial when you have a material advantage and an open file for your rook. Don't be afraid to simplify.
notes.plans: Play Bxe6, winning the exchange. Then develop the bishop to e3 and connect rooks. The endgame is winning.

notes.explains: White plays Bxe6, winning the exchange. Now White has a rook and two pawns for a knight, a clear material advantage. The rook on e6 is active.
notes.teaches: Winning the exchange (rook for bishop/knight) is a common way to convert a material advantage. Keep your pieces active.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e3, connect rooks, and then target Black's weak pawns. The endgame is winning.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, completing development and connecting rooks. The d-file is controlled by White's rook. Black's position is passive.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, connect your rooks and control open files. Development is still important even with few pieces.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the d-file or target Black's weak pawns on a7 and c6. The bishop pair gives long-term advantage.

notes.explains: White plays h4, creating a second front and attacking the pawn chain. The idea is to open the h-file for the rook after g3, Kg2, and Rh1.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, creating a second front can increase pressure. Opening a file for the rook is a common attacking idea.
notes.plans: Play h4, then if Black takes, recapture with the bishop to open the h-file. Then play g3, Kg2, and Rh1 to activate the rook.

notes.explains: White plays Bxh6, opening the h-file. After gxh6 Rxh6, White has a rook on the open h-file and a material advantage.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a bishop to open a file can be worth it if it activates your rook and creates mating threats. This is a common tactical pattern.
notes.plans: Play g3, Kg2, and Rh1 to double rooks on the h-file. Then infiltrate with the rook and create mating threats.

notes.explains: White plays g3, Kg2, and Rh1, preparing to trade rooks. The idea is to exchange rooks and enter a winning pawn endgame.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, trading rooks can simplify to a winning pawn endgame. Use your king actively.
notes.plans: Play Rh1, offering a rook trade. If Black accepts, the pawn endgame is winning due to White's extra pawns and active king.

notes.explains: White trades rooks on h1, entering a pawn endgame with two extra pawns. The king is active and can support the pawns.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, an active king and extra pawns are decisive. Use your king to escort pawns and create passed pawns.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn and use the king to support it. Black's king is passive and cannot stop all the pawns.

notes.explains: White pushes the a-pawn, creating a passed pawn. Black's king is too far away to stop it.
notes.teaches: Create passed pawns whenever possible. They are a decisive advantage in the endgame.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn to promotion. Use the king to support it and block Black's king.

notes.explains: White plays Bc1, trapping the rook on b2. The bishop on b3 and the king on g2 prevent the rook from escaping. This is a common trapping pattern.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, look for ways to trap enemy pieces. A bishop and king can cooperate to dominate a rook.
notes.plans: Play Bc1, threatening to capture the rook. Black must give up the rook or lose it for nothing.

notes.explains: White plays Bh6+ and then Bxa7, winning a third pawn. Now White has three extra pawns and a winning position.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, continue to pick off free pawns. But don't be greedy if it compromises your position.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn to promotion. The endgame is trivial.

notes.explains: After Bb5+ and Bxc6, Black's bishop is pinned and the queen's contact with d6 is blocked, allowing Qxd6 to win a pawn.
notes.teaches: Intermediate moves like Bb5+ can improve the effectiveness of a capture by creating a pin or blocking defenders.
notes.plans: After Qxd6, Black may try to counter with Qa5+; White can block with Nc3, maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's queen move Qb6 loses another pawn and leaves his king exposed. White is now two pawns up with a dominating position.
notes.teaches: When you are underdeveloped, avoid trading queens if it leaves your king vulnerable or drops more pawns.
notes.plans: White can continue to develop and target Black's exposed king.

notes.explains: Black's king has been forced to f6, a very exposed square. White has many attacking options.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for checks and forcing moves, but also consider non-checking moves that bring more pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: e5+ is a natural check, but also consider Ng5+ or even O-O to bring the rook into the attack without rushing.

notes.explains: After e5+ Kxe5, Ng5+ forces fxg5, and then Qg4 threatens mate. If Black avoids the knight capture, Nc4 forks king and queen.
notes.teaches: When you can't find a forced mate, look for forks like Nc4 that win material and simplify the win.
notes.plans: If Black plays Kf6 instead of taking the knight, Nc4 wins the queen. Otherwise, Qg4 leads to a quick mate.

notes.explains: Castling is a powerful non-checking move that brings the rook into the attack. The king is so exposed that White doesn't need to rush.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is in the open, a quiet move that brings another piece into the attack can be more effective than a direct check.
notes.plans: After O-O, White threatens Re1+ and Qf3+ etc. The rook on e1 will be decisive.

notes.explains: Black blunts the bishop with e6 and develops solidly. White's Ng5 threatens nothing and Black can simply play h6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks prematurely, a simple developing move that defends the threat is often best.
notes.plans: Black can play h6 to drive the knight back, then continue development. The position is comfortable for Black.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black's king is in the center but safe for now. White has no immediate attack.
notes.teaches: Trading queens can relieve pressure, but be aware of king safety. Here Black's king is not in danger.
notes.plans: Black can continue development with Bd6, Nge7, and eventually castle manually. The doubled pawns on f6 are not a weakness.

notes.explains: White plays Bxf7, but Black can simply recapture with the king. White has no follow-up because his pieces are undeveloped.
notes.teaches: A sacrifice without sufficient development is usually unsound. Make sure you have enough pieces in the attack before sacrificing.
notes.plans: Black recaptures with the king and is fine. White's attack fizzles out.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the king and is safe. White has no compensation for the sacrificed bishop.
notes.teaches: When your opponent sacrifices, don't panic. Accept if you can defend, and trust your development.
notes.plans: Black is up a piece and can consolidate. The king on f7 is not in danger.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nc3, Black's standard reply is …d6. This avoids the Grand Prix Attack and keeps options open.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Sicilian, ...d6 is a flexible move that prevents White from playing Bb5+ and prepares to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Nf6, g6, Bg7, and 0-0, aiming for a Dragon-style setup.

notes.explains: White's Bb5+ is a sideline; the more common move order is e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+. Here, White has committed the knight to c3 early, which limits options like c3 or c4.
notes.teaches: Committing the knight to c3 early in Canal-type positions restricts White's ability to play c3 or c4 (Morozi bind setups), making the line less flexible.
notes.plans: Black can equalize with …Bd7, exchanging bishops and reaching a comfortable position.

notes.explains: After exchanging bishops, Black develops with ...Nc6 and ...g6, aiming for a Dragon-style setup. White's queen on d3 is well-placed.
notes.teaches: In these positions, Black should develop with g6 and Bg7, avoiding ...e6 which can be passive. The structure is balanced.
notes.plans: Black will play Nf6, Bg7, 0-0, and possibly ...d5 or ...e6 later, depending on White's setup.

notes.explains: White's Nd5 is a typical idea, pressuring the knight on f6. Black can equalize by trading minor pieces.
notes.teaches: When White plays Nd5, Black can simplify with ...Nxd5, ...Bg5, or even ...Ne8 to prepare ...e6, chasing the knight away.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Nxd5 exd5, then ...Bf6 to trade bishops, or ...Ne8 followed by ...e6 and ...f5 for counterplay.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ne8, a passive but purposeful move, preparing ...e6 to kick the knight from d5. The knight on e8 defends d6.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a passive-looking move like ...Ne8 is necessary to prepare a pawn break (e6) and gain tempi for a kingside attack with ...f5.
notes.plans: After ...e6, Black will play ...f5, creating a strong pawn center and active play.

notes.explains: White plays f4 without the light-squared bishop (traded on b5), which weakens the Grand Prix setup. The bishop is crucial for the attack.
notes.teaches: The Grand Prix Attack relies on the light-squared bishop for attacking chances; trading it off before playing f4 makes the setup innocuous.
notes.plans: Black can adopt a Dragon setup with ...Nc6, ...g6, ...Bg7, and ...d6, or the Botvinnik setup with ...e6 and ...Nge7.

notes.explains: Black adopts the Botvinnik setup with ...e6 and ...Nge7, solidifying the center and preparing ...f5 or ...d5.
notes.teaches: The Botvinnik setup neutralizes White's f5 push and prepares counterplay in the center.
notes.plans: Black will complete development, then consider ...f5 or ...d5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: White's knight on f7 is trapped. Black can play ...Rh7, not castling, to keep the knight stuck.
notes.teaches: When a knight is deep in enemy territory and defended only by a rook, look for an interception tactic like ...Rh7 to trap it.
notes.plans: After ...Rh7, Black will play ...Nf5, attacking the knight and winning material.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nd7 instead of ...Bd7, which is slightly less accurate. The engine prefers ...Bd7 for easy equality.
notes.teaches: In this line, ...Bd7 is the safest and most precise move, leading to a comfortable game. ...Nd7 is playable but may give White a small edge.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Ngf6, ...g6, ...Bg7, and ...0-0, but White's a4 and a5 can create queenside pressure.

notes.explains: White plays a4, a positional move preparing a5 to clamp down on Black's queenside expansion.
notes.teaches: a4 is a common prophylactic move in many openings (e.g., King's Indian) to prevent ...b5 and create long-term weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black should respond with ...Ngf6 and develop kingside, not automatically ...a6. If White plays a5, Black can still play ...b5 later, accepting a weak a6 pawn for activity.

notes.explains: White plays f4, a more tactical approach. Black should continue developing with ...a6 and ...b6, fianchettoing the light-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: In these positions, Black's plan is to develop with ...a6, ...b6, ...Bb7, and ...e5 or ...d5 to challenge the center.
notes.plans: Black will play ...a6, ...b6, ...Bb7, and then consider ...e5 or ...d5, depending on White's setup.

notes.explains: Black plays ...b6, intending ...Bb7 to pressure e4. However, this allows White's Bf3, threatening e5 and creating problems.
notes.teaches: Be careful with ...b6 when White can play Bf3, threatening e5. Sometimes ...g6 is more accurate, preventing Bf3 and preparing a Dragon setup.
notes.plans: If White plays Bf3, Black must respond with ...e5 to prevent e5, leading to a slightly worse but playable position.

notes.explains: White plays Bf3, threatening e5. Black must play ...e5 to prevent e5, otherwise White's e5 wins material.
notes.teaches: When White threatens e5 with a bishop on f3, Black must counter with ...e5, even if it creates a hole on d5. The hole is less important than being crushed.
notes.plans: After ...e5, Black will develop with ...Bb7, ...Be7, and ...0-0, accepting a slightly passive position but with counterplay.

notes.explains: Black has played ...e5, creating a hole on d5 but preventing White's e5. The position is roughly equal, with White having a slight space advantage.
notes.teaches: In such structures, Black must be careful about the d5 square, but White cannot easily exploit it because Black's pieces cover it well.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Nc5, ...Qe7, and possibly ...Rad8, aiming for ...c4 or ...f5 breaks.

notes.explains: White plays g4, a committal kingside attack. Black should respond by striking in the center with ...exf4, opening the e5 square for the knight.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks on the flank without completing development, counter in the center. Here, ...exf4 opens lines and gives the knight a great outpost on e5.
notes.plans: After ...exf4 Bxf4, Black will play ...Ne5, creating a strong knight on e5 and preparing ...Ned7 or ...Qd7.

notes.explains: Black has a strong knight on e5, and White's kingside pawns are overextended. Black's position is comfortable.
notes.teaches: A knight on e5 in the Sicilian is often a permanent outpost, dominating the center and supporting attacks.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Qd7, preparing ...0-0-0, and then ...g5 to challenge White's knight or ...Ned7 to reroute.

notes.explains: White plays g5, attacking the knight. Black must retreat to e8, not g8 (which loses to Bg7).
notes.teaches: When your knight is attacked by a pawn, calculate carefully. Retreating to e8 is safe; g8 blunders the rook to Bg7.
notes.plans: After ...Ne8, Black will reroute the knight via c7 to e6, pressuring g5 and central squares.

notes.explains: Black plays ...f5, creating a protected passed pawn and reactivating the knight via f7. The pawn on f5 also restricts White's bishop.
notes.teaches: The move ...f5 serves multiple purposes: it creates a passed pawn, opens lines for the knight, and restricts the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: After ...f5, Black will play ...Nf7, pressuring d5 and preparing ...f4 or ...e4 breaks.

notes.explains: White plays Bg2, preserving the bishop pair. Black should have recaptured with the bishop on f6 to create the threat of ...Bh4, pinning the knight.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider the resulting threats. Recapturing with the bishop on f6 would have created a pin on the knight, forcing White to defend awkwardly.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Bh4, pinning the knight and creating pressure. White may have to bail into an endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nh5, sacrificing a pawn to open the g-file and target White's king if it castles kingside.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn to open a file against the enemy king is a common attacking technique, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: After ...Nh5, Black will play ...Bxh5, opening the g-file, and then ...Rg8, putting pressure on White's king.

notes.explains: Black has sacrificed a pawn but gained the open g-file and active pieces. White's king is stuck in the center, making Black's practical chances good.
notes.teaches: Even when objectively worse, keeping the opponent's king in the center and creating practical difficulties can compensate for a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Rg8, ...Bf6, and ...b5, aiming to open the queenside and attack White's king.

notes.explains: Black plays ...b5, opening the queenside. White's a5 pawn becomes a target, and Black's queen and bishop create mating threats on a1.
notes.teaches: When attacking, use pawn breaks to open lines. Here, ...b5 opens the a-file and creates a target on a5, while the bishop on f6 eyes a1.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Qc7, threatening ...bxa5, and then ...Bxd4, creating unstoppable mate threats on a1.

notes.explains: Black's attack culminates in a forced checkmate. The key was the pawn break ...b5 and the sacrifice ...Nc4 to remove defenders.
notes.teaches: In mating attacks, use sacrifices to eliminate key defenders and open lines. The knight sacrifice on c4 forced White to capture, allowing ...Bxd4 with mate threats.
notes.plans: Black's plan was to open the queenside, create mating threats on a1, and then deliver checkmate with queen and rook.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black fianchettoes the bishop (g6, Bg7) to clamp down on d4. This is a classic setup against the Closed Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Fianchettoing the bishop in the Sicilian gives multiple pieces control over the d4 square, a key outpost.
notes.plans: Complete development with d6, Nf6, and castle kingside, aiming for an accelerated dragon setup.

notes.explains: White's Qe2 and g4 are premature. Black is already castled with coordinated pieces, while White's king is still in the center and his pieces are uncoordinated. The g4 push creates weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has lagged in development and created weaknesses, look for immediate tactical blows. A pawn storm without proper preparation can backfire.
notes.plans: Consider Nxg4 sacrifice to open lines, or play Rb8 followed by b5-b4 to dislodge the knight and open the b-file.

notes.explains: White played Qd1 instead of accepting the queen sacrifice for three pieces. This is a typical mistake: overvaluing the queen and underestimating the power of three minor pieces.
notes.teaches: Three minor pieces can be stronger than a queen, especially when the opponent's king is exposed and the pieces coordinate well. Evaluate imbalances concretely, not by rote.
notes.plans: Capture the rook with Bxf1, keeping the pieces on dominant squares and heading for a quick checkmate.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, Black can push f5 to open the f-file for the rook. White has no counterplay on the kingside, so Black's king is safe.
notes.teaches: When attacking, involve all available pieces. Opening a file for a rook can be decisive. Don't fear weakening your own king if the opponent has no attacking pieces.
notes.plans: Play f5, opening the f-file, then bring the queen to h4 via e5, and deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White's best response to the Closed Sicilian is g3 and Bg2, transposing to a standard setup. Instead, Nf3 and Bd2 are too passive.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Sicilian, fianchettoing the king's bishop is essential for a tenable position. Passive bishop development (like Bd2) leaves White without counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing with d6, Nf6, and castle kingside, aiming for a typical Dragon setup.

notes.explains: After White castles long, Black's bishop on g7 aims at b2. The immediate plan is to open the b-file with b5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent castles into your fianchettoed bishop, a pawn storm on that side (b5-b4) can open lines for a direct attack on the king.
notes.plans: Play b5 immediately. If White takes, play Rb8 and then b4 to dislodge the knight. If White doesn't take, push b4 anyway, then follow with Qa5 or Qb6.

notes.explains: If White responds to the pawn storm with b3, the attack shifts to exploiting the weakened dark squares (like a3 and b4).
notes.teaches: Pawn storms are not rigid; you must adapt to the opponent's defensive moves. When a pawn advance creates weaknesses, redirect your attack to exploit those squares.
notes.plans: Play Qb4 or Qa6, aiming to get the queen to a3 or the knight to b4, threatening checkmate.

notes.explains: Playing a5 instead of b5 is a mistake because White can reply a4, blocking the pawn storm, or a3, wasting Black's time. The pawn storm should aim to open files, not just push pawns.
notes.teaches: Pawn storms must have a clear purpose: opening lines for pieces. Don't advance pawns without a concrete plan; sometimes a single pawn push or a piece sacrifice is more effective.
notes.plans: Prefer b5 over a5. If the knight doesn't take, continue with b4 and then Qa5, putting pressure on the b-pawn.

notes.explains: After b5 b4, if White plays a3, Black can sacrifice with bxa3, threatening to promote on a1. The resulting queen on a1 is powerfully placed.
notes.teaches: Pawn sacrifices can create devastating passed pawns or open lines. Always consider the promotion threat when the opponent's pawn structure is compromised.
notes.plans: Play bxa3, then after Bxa3, the pawn on a2 threatens to queen, and the new queen will dominate the board.

notes.explains: After e4 c5, White's Bc4 is a harmless move because Black can later play e6 to block the bishop's diagonal to f7.
notes.teaches: Developing the bishop to c4 against the Sicilian is ineffective when Black can play e6, shutting the bishop out.
notes.plans: Black should develop naturally with Nc6 and Nf6, then prepare d5 to challenge the center.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Bc4 Nc6 Nf3 a6 a3 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Ba2 d5, Black has a comfortable position with central control.
notes.teaches: When facing sidelines, following basic principles (develop, control the center) often yields a good position.
notes.plans: Black can continue with Be7, 0-0, and later consider expanding or piece play.

notes.explains: After exd5 exd5 Nf3, Black should consider Bg4 to prevent White from playing d4. This violates the usual priority of kingside development but is active and stops d4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a developing move that prevents the opponent's central break is more important than castling immediately.
notes.plans: If White castles, Black can play Be7 and then consider Nd4 or other central breaks.

notes.explains: After …Bg4 9.0-0 Be7 h3, Black can play Bh5, inviting g4. If White pushes g4 and g5, the king becomes exposed, and Black can sacrifice the d5 pawn for long-term compensation.
notes.teaches: Do not fear minor material sacrifices when the opponent's king becomes vulnerable. The long-term weakness of the king outweighs a pawn.
notes.plans: After Bh5 g4 Bg6, Black can play h6 to prevent g5, or castle and later use the open lines.

notes.explains: After d3 h6 12.0-0, Black should consider Queen D7 to connect rooks and prepare central play, but must be aware of the threat g5 with tempo, putting pressure on d5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a pawn storm on the kingside, be careful about moves that allow them to gain tempo and increase pressure.
notes.plans: Black might consider Bd6 to neutralize the bishop on f4, or play Rfe8 and keep the tension.

notes.explains: After Bf4 Qd7 Rfe1, White's Knight F4 threatens the bishop on g6. Black should retreat the bishop to h7, then play b5 and c4 to shut down White's bad bishop on a2.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to restrict the opponent's bad pieces. A restricted bishop is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: After Bh7 Nf4, play b5 and c4, then continue with Rfd8 or other improving moves.

notes.explains: After Bh7 Nf4 b5 c4, Black has locked White's bishop on a2. Now Black can consider Queen C8, a retreating move that takes the sting out of Ne5 and creates an x-ray against White's queen.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves can be just as important as advancing ones. They improve the position without creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Qc8, Black can play Rfd8, then look for tactical opportunities like Ne4 if White's rook leaves d1.

notes.explains: After Qc8 Rd2, Black can play Ne4. If dxe4 dxe4, White's best is Nxd5, but then Black has Rxd5 followed by Rd8, exploiting the undefended rook on d1.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, always update which pieces are undefended. A seemingly quiet move like Rd2 can create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After Ne4, if White avoids the line, Black can continue with Nxg3 or other threats.

notes.explains: After Ne4 dxe4 dxe4, White played Nxg3 instead of the stronger Ng5. Ng5 would have opened the d4 square for a fork, but Black is still better.
notes.teaches: Retreating knight moves can be very powerful, especially when they open up key squares for forks.
notes.plans: After Nxg3, Black recaptures and continues with positional pressure.

notes.explains: After hxg3 d4, White's d4 is a mistake because it opens the diagonal for Black's bishop and gives Black the e4 square. Black can play Qb8, then Be4, dominating the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a bad bishop, do not open the position for it unless you have concrete compensation.
notes.plans: Black plays Qb8, Be4, then Rfe8, and eventually pushes a5-b4 to attack the queenside.

notes.explains: After Qb8 Rfe8 Be4 c3, Black's a5-b4 push breaks through on the queenside. White cannot take on b4 because of the fork threat e3.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a pawn break on the queenside can be decisive. Always check for tactical details like pawn forks.
notes.plans: After bxa5, Black plays b4, then Ba6, winning the bishop on b1.

notes.explains: After bxa5 b4 Bb1 Ba6, Black wins the bishop. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Consistent pressure forces the opponent to make mistakes. The collapse often happens in one or two moves.
notes.plans: Black takes the bishop, then simplifies to a winning endgame or checkmates.

notes.explains: Black trades the bishop on f3 to prevent Ng5, which would threaten f7 and create complications. After the trade, Black castles queenside, getting the king out of danger.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must give up the bishop pair to neutralize a specific threat. Here, eliminating the knight on f3 prevents a dangerous knight sortie to g5.
notes.plans: After castling, improve the king's safety with Kb8, and consider h5 to restrict White's queen and create a potential outpost on g4.

notes.explains: White plays e5, opening the center. Black should capture on e5, leading to a double-edged position. The knight can go to g4, and Black has tactical ideas involving Qd4+ and Bf6.
notes.teaches: When the center opens, be alert for tactical opportunities. Here, Black can use the exposed white king and the rook on f7 to create threats.
notes.plans: Capture on e5 with the knight or bishop. If the rook takes on f7, consider Qd4+ followed by Bf6 to intercept the rook's defense of the queen.

notes.explains: White plays g4, attacking the knight. Black should capture on e5 with the bishop, not the knight, because the bishop can later give check on d4 and the knight can retreat to f6 to eliminate White's centralized knight.
notes.teaches: When choosing which piece to capture with, consider the resulting piece activity. The bishop on e5 can deliver a check, while the knight on g4 is unsafe. Also, trading off White's strongest piece (the knight on c3) simplifies the position favorably.
notes.plans: Play Bxe5. If White plays h3, retreat the knight to f6 and exchange it for White's knight on c3. This leaves Black with a superior bishop and a simplified position.

notes.explains: Black plays h5, securing the knight on g4. Now Black should fix the remaining problems: the bishop on f4 restricts the king, so Black prepares e5 to challenge it.
notes.teaches: Identify and fix the biggest issues in your position. Here, the bishop on f4 is annoying, so Black prepares e5 with f6, a multi-purpose move that also threatens g5.
notes.plans: Play f6, preparing e5 to kick the bishop. This also gives the king breathing room and prevents any back-rank mates.

notes.explains: f6 is a game-winning move. It prepares e5, which will shut down White's bishop and give Black's king safety. White has no good response.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for moves that completely neutralize the opponent's counterplay. f6 does that by preparing a pawn break and improving the king's safety.
notes.plans: After f6, play e5 to chase the bishop. Then trade queens and convert the advantage.

notes.explains: Black wins a rook and now has a decisive material advantage. The rest is technique: keep the king safe, trade queens if possible, and avoid traps.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, stay disciplined. Look for queen trades to simplify, and always check for opponent's threats (like back-rank mates or forks).
notes.plans: Play Qd4 to offer a queen trade and attack b2. Then play e5 to close the center, and finally crash through with Rc8.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 dxc3 Nxc3, Black's a6 is an improvisation. White should respond with the normal setup: Bc4, aiming for a standard Morra development.
notes.teaches: In gambit openings, stick to the standard developing moves; don't improvise just because the opponent does.
notes.plans: Develop naturally: Bc4, Nf3, O-O, and later push e5 to open lines and create threats.

notes.explains: Black's combination of e6 and g6 (the 'Swiss cheese defense') is a classic mistake. It leaves d6 weak and White can quickly plant a knight there, as shown in the game.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, avoid playing both e6 and g6 unless you have a specific setup that covers the dark squares. The d6 square becomes a permanent weakness.
notes.plans: White should immediately target d6 with e5 and Ne4, aiming to get a knight to d6.

notes.explains: White plays e5 not to keep the pawn, but to sacrifice it to get the knight to d6. After e5 f6, White plays Ne4, sacrificing a second pawn. The knight on d6 will be worth more than the material.
notes.teaches: In gambits, be willing to sacrifice material for positional domination. A knight on a powerful outpost like d6 can outweigh two pawns.
notes.plans: Play Ne4, then Nxd6 (or Nc7) to establish the knight on d6, then bring other pieces to attack.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches d6, White needs to coordinate the other pieces. The idea of b3 and Ba3 is fast (only two moves) and threatens discovered checks along the a3-f8 diagonal, forcing the king to f6.
notes.teaches: Use the 'three-move rule' to evaluate if a plan is too slow: if it takes three or more moves, it's often too slow; two moves is fast enough.
notes.plans: Play b3 and Ba3 to create threats against the black king, forcing it into a vulnerable position.

notes.explains: With the king on f6, White reshuffles knights: Ng5 (retreating the knight from d6) then Nd6+ again, forcing the king back to e7 or f8, both on the a3-f8 diagonal, losing the queen.
notes.teaches: Retreating knights can be part of a regrouping maneuver to force the opponent's king into a worse position. Don't be afraid to move a piece backward if it sets up a stronger threat.
notes.plans: Play Ng5 (the other knight) to give check, then Nd6+ to drive the king onto the diagonal where Ba3 wins the queen.

notes.explains: After winning the queen, White should open the position to bring the queen into the attack. Even if Black gets a fork (e.g., d5), White can sacrifice material because being up a queen allows blasting through.
notes.teaches: When you are up significant material, simplify by opening lines and trading down. Don't be afraid of tactical complications if you have a material advantage.
notes.plans: Play e5 to open lines, then use the queen to deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White has a queen and rook against scattered black pieces. The simplest win is to go directly for checkmate with Rfd1 and then queen invasion.
notes.teaches: When winning, choose the most direct and safe plan. Avoid unnecessary captures that give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Rfd1, then Qf7+ or Qd6 to force mate or win more material.

notes.explains: If Black declines the Morra with Nf6, White can transpose into the Alapin (c3 Sicilian) with e5, which is a solid alternative. This makes the Morra a win-win: if Black accepts, White gets attacking chances; if Black declines, White gets a good positional game.
notes.teaches: Choosing an opening that can transpose into another familiar system gives you flexibility and reduces the amount of theory to learn.
notes.plans: After e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 Nf6, play e5 to transpose into the Alapin.

notes.explains: The Morra is not objectively bad; even with perfect play, Black is not better. At club level, opponents often mishandle it by playing as in the Open Sicilian, which leads to quick defeats.
notes.teaches: Don't dismiss gambits as unsound. Many are perfectly playable and can be very effective against unprepared opponents.
notes.plans: Learn a few key ideas and traps, such as the e5 push after Bc4 and Nf6, which can win the queen.

notes.explains: In the famous game against Van Wely, White played Bc4 even though it 'bites on granite' against e6. The idea is that tactics outweigh positional considerations: White later sacrifices a knight on d5 to open lines.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, tactical opportunities can override normal positional rules. Be alert for sacrifices that open up the opponent's king.
notes.plans: After Bc4, Nc6, Nf3, e6, castling, and Black's knight goes to e7, play Bg5 to induce f6, then retreat to e3, and later sacrifice on d5.

notes.explains: After the knight sacrifice on d5, White plays Rxd5, locking in Black's bishop on f8 and opening the e-file. Then f4 opens the position further, and Bg5 prevents castling and sets up a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, use pawn breaks and piece sacrifices to open files and diagonals for a direct attack.
notes.plans: Play f4 to open the e-file, then Bg5 to stop castling, followed by Qd2 and doubling rooks on the e-file.

notes.explains: The final combination in the Van Wely game: Rxc6 blasts through, and after Black recaptures, Bg5 wins because Qe7+ leads to mate. This shows the power of the bishop on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for sacrifices that remove defenders and create unstoppable threats. The bishop on g5 can be decisive.
notes.plans: Play Rxc6, then after dxc6, Bg5 threatening Qe7+ and mate.

notes.explains: The teacher recounts a personal game where he, as Black, played e6 and g6 and was punished by White's Qd6, threatening Nc7. This shows the danger of neglecting the d6 square.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of the opponent's threats to occupy weak squares. A knight on d6 can be devastating, especially if it forks the queen and rook.
notes.plans: If you have a weak square, try to prevent the opponent's piece from landing there, or prepare to trade it off.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played f6, which was the losing move. Better was f5 to prevent Ne4, or g4 to stop the knight from reaching d6. But even then, White's compensation is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, you must be precise. Allowing the opponent to establish a knight on a key outpost like d6 is often fatal.
notes.plans: If Black plays f5, White can play Bg5 and Qd6, still maintaining strong pressure.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches d6, White's b3 and Ba3 is the final nail in the coffin. It threatens discovered checks and forces the king into a mating net.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominant piece, bring your other pieces to support it. A bishop on a3 can be deadly when combined with a knight on d6.
notes.plans: Play b3, Ba3, then use the knight to give check and force the king onto the a3-f8 diagonal.

notes.explains: The knight reshuffling (Ne4, Nfg5, then Nd6+) is a key maneuver to drive the king onto the deadly diagonal. This idea can be hard to see but is essential in such positions.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to retreat knights to regroup. A temporary retreat can set up a decisive double attack or check.
notes.plans: Play Ne4, then Nfg5, then Nd6+ to force the king to e7 or f8, winning the queen.

notes.explains: The main line of the Morra accepted often involves e6 and a6, with White playing Qe2 and Rd1. This is a standard setup that gives White good compensation.
notes.teaches: In the Morra, a typical plan is to put the queen on e2 and rook on d1, supporting the center and preparing e5.
notes.plans: Develop with Qe2, Rd1, and then push e5 when ready.

notes.explains: White's e5 is a mistake; it gives Black an ideal French setup with the bishop on f5 and knight on c6. Black should not rush with Bf5 but can play Nc6 first.
notes.teaches: When White plays e5 in this structure, Black gets a French-like position with the bishop outside the pawn chain, which is very comfortable. Develop naturally with Nc6 and Bf5.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, Bf5, e6, and then Qb6 to pressure d4.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, completing the French pawn chain. White may try g4, but Black can respond with h5 to prevent overextension.
notes.teaches: In this setup, White's aggressive pawn pushes like g4 are not dangerous if Black responds correctly with h5, creating weaknesses for White.
notes.plans: Continue with Qb6, then develop the knight to f5 via h6 or g6.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, pressuring d4. Unlike in the French, the bishop on f5 is already developed. The knight on g8 needs a home; options include Nh6 or Bg6 followed by Nf5.
notes.teaches: Qb6 is a standard French idea to pressure d4. Here, the bishop on f5 is a bonus. The knight on g8 can be developed to f5 via h6 or g6, often after Bg6.
notes.plans: Play Bg6, then Nh6 or Nf5, and later castle kingside or queenside.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh6, not fearing Bxh6 because White's dark-squared bishop is a key defender of d4. If White takes, Black gets the g-file and pressure on b2.
notes.teaches: Do not fear Bxh6 in such positions; White's dark-squared bishop is important for defending d4. Losing it weakens White's structure and gives Black attacking chances.
notes.plans: If White takes on h6, play gxh6, then use the g-file and pressure on b2. Otherwise, continue with Bg6 and Nf5.

notes.explains: Black completes the regrouping: Bg6 vacates f5 for the knight, and Nf5 gives the knight a strong outpost. All pieces are developed except the king.
notes.teaches: When pieces compete for squares, a timely retreat (like Bg6) can free up a better square for another piece. This is a common maneuver in cramped positions.
notes.plans: Castle, then prepare f6 to break open the center and increase pressure on d4.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to open the center and increase pressure on d4. White's knight on b5 is a target; Black can retreat the queen to b6 or b8, but b6 pins the knight to the pawn.
notes.teaches: f6 is a typical break in French-like structures to challenge the center. It opens lines and increases pressure on the d4 pawn.
notes.plans: After f6, if White takes, recapture with the bishop and target d4. If White doesn't take, consider a6 to drive the knight away or take on e3 later.

notes.explains: Black retreats the queen to b6, pinning the knight to the pawn and reinforcing pressure on d4. The position is ripe for a breakthrough.
notes.teaches: Retreating the queen to b6 pins the knight and adds pressure. Always consider pins to increase the effectiveness of your attack.
notes.plans: Prepare to take on e5 or e3, depending on White's response. The knight on b5 is a liability.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, a mistake. Black can now win material by taking on e5 or e3. The key is to calculate carefully: after exf5, Bxf5, Bxf5, Qxf5, the knight on b5 is hanging.
notes.teaches: When calculating captures, always note undefended pieces at the end of the line. Here, the knight on b5 is hanging after the sequence, winning a piece.
notes.plans: Play exf5, then after Bxf5, take on e3 or e5, exploiting the hanging knight on b5.

notes.explains: After the sequence, Black wins a piece because the knight on b5 is hanging. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Always check for hanging pieces at the end of a tactical sequence. This is a common source of blunders.
notes.plans: Capture the knight or the bishop on e3, winning material.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, trying to transpose into a Sicilian. White can punish Black's extra pawn moves by pushing d5, creating a Benoni-like structure where Black has wasted tempi.
notes.teaches: When opponent makes many pawn moves, seize the center with d5 to gain space and punish the loss of time.
notes.plans: Play d5 to fix the center and exploit Black's lag in development.

notes.explains: White pushes d5, reaching a Benoni-like structure. Black's a6 and c5 cost time, giving White a lead in development.
notes.teaches: In such structures, White's space advantage and development lead are key. Don't rush to attack; consolidate first.
notes.plans: Defend the d5 pawn with Nc3, and avoid premature moves like Ng5 that drop pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, defending the c5 pawn. White now has a choice between positional (a4) and tactical (dxe6) approaches.
notes.teaches: With a lead in development, the tactical approach (opening the center) is often more punishing. The positional approach (a4) is also good but less direct.
notes.plans: White chooses dxe6 to open the center and attack Black's weakened pawn structure.

notes.explains: White captures on e6, opening the center. Now White considers Ng5 with a specific aim: to eliminate Black's light-squared bishop and attack the weak e6 pawn.
notes.teaches: Ng5 is not just a 'cool' move; it has a concrete goal: trade the bishop on e6 and then target the pawn on e6 with Bc4. Only play such moves when you have a clear follow-up.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, threatening to take on e6. If Black moves the bishop, Bc4 will be crushing against f7.

notes.explains: White plays Ng5, threatening Nxe6. Black should not play h6 because White wants to take the bishop anyway; h6 weakens the diagonal and invites Bg4.
notes.teaches: Don't play weakening pawn moves like h6 when the opponent wants the trade. Instead, develop with Nc6 or consider b5, though risky.
notes.plans: If Black plays Nc6, White takes on c6 and then plays Bc4, targeting the e6 pawn.

notes.explains: White executes the plan: Nxe6 eliminates the bishop, and Bc4 targets the weak e6 pawn. White is clearly better.
notes.teaches: When you have a specific plan, execute it consistently. The e6 pawn is a permanent weakness.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring e6 and develop the rest of the pieces. Black's pawn structure is damaged.

notes.explains: Black blunders with h6, allowing Nxe6 winning a piece. This is a common mistake at lower levels.
notes.teaches: Always consider if your opponent's threat is real. Here, Ng5 threatens Nxe6, and h6 doesn't prevent it; it just loses time.
notes.plans: White takes on e6 and wins a piece. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: After Nxe6, Black tries Qe7 attacking the knight. White can play Qh5, pinning the pawn on e6 and threatening multiple things.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for the most accurate move. Qh5 pins the pawn and keeps the attack going, rather than simplifying immediately.
notes.plans: Play Qh5, then if Qf6, play g5! to open lines and win the queen.

notes.explains: White plays Qh5, pinning the e6 pawn and threatening Nc7+ or simply winning material. Black's position collapses.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple winning moves, choose the one that maintains the most pressure and limits counterplay.
notes.plans: After Qf6, play g5! to open the f-file and win the queen.

notes.explains: White plays g5, attacking the queen and opening lines. If Qe6, Nc7+ wins the queen. This is a typical tactical motif.
notes.teaches: Pawn pushes like g5 can open lines and create decisive threats. Always consider such advances when the opponent's queen is exposed.
notes.plans: After g5, Black's queen must move, and White wins material.

notes.explains: Nc7+ forks king and queen, winning the queen. The game is over.
notes.teaches: Always look for forks and checks that win material. This is a classic knight fork.
notes.plans: Take the queen and convert the endgame.

notes.explains: White wins the queen with Nc7+. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, stay alert for tactical finishes. Don't relax until the game is won.
notes.plans: Capture the queen and simplify to a won endgame.

notes.explains: The game ends with White winning a queen. Black's opening play was poor, and White punished it effectively.
notes.teaches: This game illustrates how to punish unusual early pawn moves with principled development and a concrete attacking plan.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3 to prevent Black from developing his bishop to f5. Black's bishop has no good square, and White's position is already excellent.
notes.teaches: In positions where Black has played ...h5, Bd3 is often the most precise move—it stops ...Bf5 and prepares natural development.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nf3 and h3, reinforcing the center and preparing to exploit Black's passive setup.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the d4 pawn. White can play a3, a useful waiting move that also defends the pawn indirectly. If Black takes on d4, White traps the queen with Be3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is active, look for ways to trap it. Here a3 is both a useful defensive move and a trap—if Black grabs the pawn, the queen gets caught.
notes.plans: Play a3, then h3 to kick the bishop, and if Black takes on f3, recapture with the queen and then Be3 traps the queen on d4.

notes.explains: Black falls into the trap: after Qxf3, Black takes the d4 pawn, and Be3 traps the queen. Black's queen is lost, giving White a decisive advantage.
notes.teaches: Don't settle for winning a piece when you can win the queen. Always look for the most punishing continuation.
notes.plans: After trapping the queen, simplify and convert the material advantage. Keep pressure on Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black tries Ng5 to create counterplay, but White simply retreats the queen to e2, keeping the trap intact. Black's queen is still trapped.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to complicate, stay calm and find the simplest refutation. Don't panic and give up your advantage.
notes.plans: Continue to exploit the trapped queen; eventually Black will have to give up material.

notes.explains: White castles queenside, and the position is winning. Black's queen is still trapped, and White has a huge material advantage.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify and trade down. Keep your king safe and avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Use the extra queen to attack Black's weakened pawns and king. The knight on d6 is a strong outpost.

notes.explains: White grabs the a7 pawn, winning material. Black's position collapses.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for direct captures that maintain or increase your lead.
notes.plans: Continue to attack Black's weaknesses; the knight on d6 is a powerful outpost.

notes.explains: White plays Nc5, threatening mate on b7. Black's knight on b6 is the only defender; once it moves, mate follows.
notes.teaches: When looking for mate, identify the key defensive pieces and target them. Here the knight on b6 is the main obstacle to Qb7#.
notes.plans: If Black moves the knight, play Qb7#. Otherwise, continue pressuring the knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Rb8, but White takes on b7 with checkmate. The game ends.
