notes.teaches: Always be alert for checkmate patterns. Here the queen and knight combine for a simple mate on b7.

notes.explains: After winning a piece, White must avoid moves like Bb5+ that allow c6, leading to unnecessary complications. Instead, retreat the bishop to b3.
notes.teaches: When up material, avoid giving the opponent counterplay. Choose simple, solid moves that maintain your advantage.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b3, then play d3 to eliminate the e4 pawn and open lines for the dark-squared bishop.

notes.explains: Black's c5-c4 push does nothing because c4 is defended by the bishop. White's priority is to complete development and remove the e4 pawn, which is a hindrance.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is 'hanging over' your position, removing it (e.g., with d3) can improve piece coordination and open lines.
notes.plans: Play d3, then develop the dark-squared bishop to g5 or f4, and eventually castle queenside to bring the rook to the d-file.

notes.explains: After trading bishops and queens, White's king is safe, and the knight on d5 is a powerful outpost. Castling queenside brings the rook to the open d-file.
notes.teaches: When up material, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. An outpost like d5 for the knight is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f4 (safe square), then castle queenside and double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black's c4 push opens the d4 square for the knight. White castles queenside, defending the knight with the rook and preparing to double rooks.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is pushed, look for new squares for your pieces. Doubling rooks on an open file is a standard way to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play Rd2, then Rd1 to double rooks, then move the knight away from d4 to open the file for the rooks.

notes.explains: White doubles rooks on the d-file, then moves the knight to f5 (an ideal square). The e4 pawn is defended, and Black has no threats.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, you don't need to grab every pawn. Focus on activating your pieces and simplifying.
notes.plans: After Nf5, trade bishops if possible, then trade rooks and create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: White uses the rook to win pawns and create a passed c-pawn. The rook cuts off the black king, allowing the pawn to promote.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, cutting off the enemy king with your rook is a powerful technique to promote a pawn. Always be careful not to stalemate.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn, use the queen to drive the king to the back rank, and deliver checkmate with the rook.

notes.explains: The king on d1 is vulnerable. Black should develop with Nf6, not rush to capture on d3, and aim to trade on favorable terms.
notes.teaches: Develop pieces before capturing pawns, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, developing and threatening e4. If White takes, recapture with the knight after trading queens.

notes.explains: Bd2 unpins the knight and reinforces e4, forcing Black to trade on d3. After Bxd3, Black can castle, and the f4 pawn becomes a long-term weakness for White.
notes.teaches: A pawn that looks supportive can become a target once the opponent's king is safe and the position opens.
notes.plans: Take on d3, castle, then target the f4 pawn.

notes.explains: After castling, Black should immediately challenge the knight on e5 with Nbd7, aiming to trade it off before White can solidify it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a well-placed knight, trade it off quickly before it becomes a permanent outpost.
notes.plans: Play Nbd7, threatening to exchange on e5.

notes.explains: Black is up the exchange. The immediate priority is to activate the rook on a8 and bring it into play. The queen can wait; moving the rook to e8 is a low-hanging fruit.
notes.teaches: When ahead material, activate all pieces before rushing with the queen. Look for simple improvements.
notes.plans: Play Rae8, putting the rook on an open file.

notes.explains: White has two bishops on the d-file, but they cannot both move at once. Black can safely play Rae8, and when the bishop on d2 moves, the queen can go to c7 or a5.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pieces on a file if they block each other; you can wait for them to move before committing your queen.
notes.plans: Wait for the bishop to move, then place the queen on c7 or a5.

notes.explains: The position offers multiple good plans. One strong idea is to trade pieces with Nf5, aiming to exchange on d5 and simplify. If White avoids the trade, Black should not fear threats to h7; g6 is a simple defense.
notes.teaches: When ahead, simplify by trading pieces. Don't be afraid of mating threats if you have a simple defensive move like g6.
notes.plans: Play Nf5, threatening to trade on d5. If White doesn't take, continue with g6 to defend h7.

notes.explains: After Nxd5, White recaptures with the rook. Black should not automatically recapture with the pawn; instead, look for a better move: Rxe1+ forces a rook trade, and then Qxd5 wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: Always look for checks and captures that improve your position before making automatic recaptures.
notes.plans: Play Rxe1+ first, then Qxd5.

notes.explains: Black is up a pawn and has a winning endgame. White plays Qh3, threatening h7. Black must create luft; g6 is better than h6 because the bishop on d3 controls h7.
notes.teaches: When making luft, consider which squares the opponent's bishop controls. g6 is often safer than h6 against a bishop on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Play g6 to block the bishop's diagonal.

notes.explains: Black can win the a2 pawn with Qa5+ followed by Qxa2. But first, activating the rook with Re8 is even better; it creates a hidden threat of Qa1# if the d2 square is controlled.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate all pieces before grabbing pawns. A rook on an open file can create mating threats.
notes.plans: Play Re8, threatening Qa1# after controlling d2. Then pick up the a-pawn.

notes.explains: White cannot prevent the mate threat. If White plays Qh6, then Re2 controls d2, forcing Bxe2 and Qa1#. Other defenses also fail.
notes.teaches: When you have a coordinated attack, look for quiet moves that set up unstoppable threats.
notes.plans: After Re8, if Qh6, play Re2, then Qa1#.

notes.explains: After d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7, the 'trap' is Bf4 (or Bg5) allowing Qb4+ forking king and bishop. But Bd2 Qxb2 Nc3 Bb4 Rb1 Qa3 Nd5 is strong: the knight attacks c7 and threatens Bxb4. Black's queen is deep in White's camp with no development.
notes.teaches: In gambits, accepting material and then returning it to gain a development lead is often correct. Don't fear 'traps' if you know the refutation.
notes.plans: After …Qa5 Nxb4 Nxb4, play e4 to open lines and develop. Then Nd4 covers e6 and centralizes. Finally, cover b2 with Qc1 to trap the queen after Ra1.

notes.explains: After …Bxe5, White should play e3 (or e4) to solidify the center. The computer novelty g4! is even stronger, preparing g5 to chase the knight and fianchetto the bishop.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for prophylactic or aggressive pawn moves that restrict the opponent's pieces and prepare further development.
notes.plans: Play g4, then Bg2, and develop the knight to c4. Black's queen is a distant memory; White's attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: After trapping the queen, White's pieces cooperate perfectly: the knight on d4 covers e6, the bishop on f5 covers escape squares, and the rook on a1 finishes the job. Black is completely undeveloped.
notes.teaches: When you have a large development lead, you can afford to invest several pieces in a trapping net. Methodically cover all escape squares.
notes.plans: If Black tries to free the queen with ...c5, simply play Rb1 and continue the squeeze. The queen is doomed.

notes.explains: After Nb5 and Nd6+, White gets a monster pawn on d6 that cramps Black's position. Black's dark-squared bishop is gone, so the d6 pawn is hard to attack.
notes.teaches: A knight on d6 supported by a pawn is a powerful outpost. Don't be afraid to sacrifice a pawn if you get such a strong positional trump.
notes.plans: Defend d6 with Bf4 after eliminating the knight on c6 (Nxc6). Then Black's lack of dark-squared bishop makes d6 a permanent weakness.

notes.explains: Black castles, which opens the h-file for White's attack. The pawn on d6 restricts Black's king escape squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent castles into a weakened kingside, consider rook lifts (e.g., Re3) and queen maneuvers to the h-file. The d6 pawn prevents the king from fleeing to the center.
notes.plans: Play Ng5 to prevent f6 (which would loosen White's grip). Then lift the rook to e3 and bring the queen to g4 or h4 for a mating attack.

notes.explains: After Qg4, Black's best defense is f6, but then g5 is a strong reply, leading to a messy but winning attack for White. The key is that the g6 pawn is crucial; if it falls, Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, don't rush; consider prophylactic moves like Re3 to support the e6 pawn and enable doubling on the e-file. The immediate Qg4 was actually winning, but the preparatory Re3 was also good.
notes.plans: After f6, play g5 to open lines. If Black takes on g5, Qxg5 followed by Rh3 creates mating threats. The bishop on f4 covers c1, preventing back-rank counterplay.

notes.explains: In this line, Black's only move to avoid immediate loss is g5, but after Qf5 and Rh3, White threatens mate. Black must find Rf8, but White still has a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When the g6 pawn is captured, the h-file becomes lethal. The d6 pawn prevents the king from escaping to e7, making the mating net effective.
notes.plans: Continue with Rh3 and Qh5, threatening Qh7#. If Black defends, consider sacrificing the knight on e6 to open lines.

notes.explains: The engine shows that even in complex lines, White maintains an advantage. The bishop on f4 is crucial for covering c1, preventing Black from forcing a draw by repetition.
notes.teaches: Never rush a move. In this position, a3 (threatening Qxd5) was even stronger than Bf4, winning a pawn and simplifying. Always consider if you can improve your position before committing to a 'natural' move.
notes.plans: If you have time, look for ways to win material without compromising your attack. Here, a3 followed by Qxd5 would have been clean.

notes.explains: Black's …Nf6 is a blunder. White plays Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ forking king and bishop, winning two pawns and leaving Black's king exposed. Black's best defense was …Nd7 to cover e5.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's tactical resources. A seemingly natural developing move like Nf6 can be punished by a combination that exploits the weakened f7 square.
notes.plans: White is two pawns up with a shattered black kingside. Continue developing (e.g., Nc3, O-O) and prepare to attack down the f-file or along the a2-g8 diagonal.

notes.explains: After …Ke8 Nxg4, Black plays …Nd7 to block the e5 square. White is two pawns up and can choose between materialistic play (Nc3 protecting e4) or rapid development (O-O). Castling is fine; White should not fear ...Bxc3 because the dark-squared bishop is valuable for the attack.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, avoid one-move threats that neglect development. Moves like c3 (threatening Qb3) can be tempting but may allow Black to consolidate. Instead, prioritize piece activity and king safety.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then consider e5 to dislodge the knight on f6, opening lines for the queen and rook. The immediate threat is Qe6# after ...Nxe5 Qxe5.

notes.explains: White plays e5, attacking the knight on f6 and threatening Qe6#. Black cannot defend f6 with a piece because the rook on f1 controls the file. This pawn push uses the central pawn to dislodge Black's only defender, creating a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Use central pawn advances to open lines and create direct mating threats. When the opponent's king is exposed, every tempo counts—don't waste time on slow maneuvers.
notes.plans: After …Nxe5 Qxe5, Black cannot block the f-file (e.g., ...Qf4? Rxf4). The threat of Qe6# is unstoppable, leading to a quick win.

notes.explains: Black's correct response to Bc4 is …Nd7, covering e5. After O-O, Black can play ...Ngf6 to cover the rook on f1. White then typically plays c3, intending Qb3, creating a battery on the b3-f7 diagonal and attacking b7. Black must be precise to survive the sharp complications.
notes.teaches: In sharp lines, knowing the correct defensive moves is crucial. Black must be willing to enter complex positions where one mistake can be fatal. The Fantasy Variation is a practical weapon because it forces Black to know theory.
notes.plans: White can consider h3 to provoke ...h5? (then g4) or play c3 and Qb3. Black should aim to castle quickly and challenge White's center.

notes.explains: After O-O Ngf6, White's queen should not go to f6 (to cover the rook) because that exposes the queen to tactical ideas. Instead, develop the knight to c3 and prepare c3 and Qb3. The queen belongs on b3, where it attacks b7 and creates a battery with the bishop.
notes.teaches: Avoid using the queen to do a knight's job. The queen is a valuable piece that should not be placed in front of a rook where it can be targeted by discovered attacks.
notes.plans: Play c3, then Qb3. If Black castles, White can consider taking on b7, but must be careful not to fall behind in development. The position remains sharp with mutual chances.

notes.explains: White's c3 prepares Qb3, creating a battery on the b3-f7 diagonal. This is a good idea because it attacks b7 and the f7 square simultaneously. Black must respond accurately, e.g., with ...Bd6 or ...Qc7.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, the queen-bishop battery on b3-f7 is a key attacking idea. It pressures Black's queenside and kingside at the same time.
notes.plans: After c3, play Qb3. Black may castle, and then White can consider taking on b7 or continuing development with Bg5. The center remains fluid, and both sides must navigate tactical complications.

notes.explains: After …Bd6 Qb3 O-O, White can consider taking on b7, but this is risky because White is underdeveloped. The pawn on b7 is poisoned; Black gets active play. White should instead continue development with Bg5 or h3.
notes.teaches: Material gain is not always worth the cost of development. When the opponent has active piece play, it's often better to consolidate and maintain the initiative rather than grab a pawn.
notes.plans: Play h3 to prevent ...Bg4 and prepare g4, or play Bg5 to pin the knight. The position remains sharp, and White should aim to keep the pressure without overextending.

notes.explains: White plays h3, threatening g4 to chase the knight on f6. If Black retreats ...Bh5, then g4 traps the bishop. If Black plays ...h5, White can play g4 anyway, opening lines. This is a typical way to gain space and create attacking chances on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In closed positions with a space advantage, use pawn advances to cramp the opponent and create weaknesses. h3-g4 is a common plan to expand on the kingside.
notes.plans: After h3, if Black plays ...Bh5, then g4 wins the bishop. If Black plays ...h5, White can play g4 anyway, opening the h-file. White should continue developing and look for tactical blows.

notes.explains: After …Bh5, White plays g4, trapping the bishop. Black must give up the bishop or allow a decisive attack. This is a direct consequence of the h3-g4 plan.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is pinned to the edge of the board, a pawn advance can trap it. Always be alert to such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After g4, Black's bishop is lost. White will be up a piece and can continue the attack. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: If Black retreats ...Bg6, White can continue with h4-h5, trapping the bishop again. The bishop on g6 is a target, and White can win it with accurate play.
notes.teaches: Once you have a bind on the opponent's piece, keep the pressure on. Use pawn advances to force the issue and win material.
notes.plans: Play h4, threatening h5. Black may try to escape with ...f6, but White's attack is overwhelming. The bishop is doomed.

notes.explains: White plays h4, threatening h5 to trap the bishop. Black cannot prevent it, and the bishop will be lost. This is the culmination of the kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: A consistent pawn storm can decisively win material. Once the opponent's piece is trapped, don't give them a chance to escape—push the pawns.
notes.plans: After h4, Black's bishop is lost. White will be up a piece and can convert the win.

notes.explains: White plays h5, winning the bishop. Black cannot save it because ...Bxh5 allows Rxh5, and ...f6 allows exf6. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear winning plan, execute it without hesitation. Don't look for fancy alternatives when a simple pawn push wins material.
notes.plans: After winning the bishop, White is up a piece and can simplify or continue the attack. The win is straightforward.

notes.explains: After …Bxh5 Rxh5, White has won a piece. Black's kingside is shattered, and White has a rook on the h-file. The attack continues.
notes.teaches: Winning material is good, but don't stop there. Keep the pressure on the exposed king and look for further tactical blows.
notes.plans: White can bring the queen to the h-file or play Qg3, threatening mate. Black's position is hopeless.

notes.explains: White plays Qd2, preparing to double on the h-file or play Qh6. The queen joins the attack, and Black has no defense. The game is over.
notes.teaches: Coordinate your pieces for the final assault. Once the opponent's king is exposed, bring all available pieces to the attack.
notes.plans: Play Qh6, threatening Qxh7#. Black can only delay with ...f6, but White's attack is decisive.

notes.explains: After …f6 exf6 Rxf6, White plays Qh6, threatening Qxh7#. Black's rook on f6 is pinned by the bishop on c4, and there is no defense. The game ends in a few moves.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create an escape, use the pin to maintain the mating threat. The bishop on c4 is a powerful attacking piece even in the middlegame.
notes.plans: After Qh6, Black's only move is ...Rf7, but then Qxh7+ Kf8 Qh8#. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qh8#. The entire sequence from h3 to mate is a model of how to conduct a kingside attack in the Fantasy Variation.
notes.teaches: A well-executed pawn storm followed by piece coordination can lead to a quick checkmate. The Fantasy Variation is a dangerous weapon that rewards aggressive play.
notes.plans: The game is over. White wins by checkmate.

notes.explains: This game illustrates the key ideas of the Fantasy Variation: rapid development, targeting f7, and a kingside pawn storm. Black's early mistake (…Nf6) was punished immediately, but even with correct play (…Nd7), White has a sharp attacking game.
notes.teaches: The Fantasy Variation is a practical and underrated weapon against the Caro-Kann. It leads to sharp, tactical positions where knowledge of the key ideas gives White excellent winning chances. Black must be precise to survive.
notes.plans: If you play the Fantasy Variation, study the main lines after …Nd7, including the h3-g4 plan and the queen-bishop battery. If you face it as Black, be prepared to defend accurately and know the critical defensive moves.

notes.explains: After …Nc6, the natural d5 closes the center and lets Black's knight retreat. Taking on c3 with Nxc3 opens the center and leaves Black's knight on e5 unsupported.
notes.teaches: When a central pawn capture opens lines and leaves an opponent's piece without pawn support, it is often better than pushing past. The knight on e5 looks active but is vulnerable to attack.
notes.plans: Develop flexibly with Nc3, keeping options open. Avoid committal moves like Nf3 or f4 until Black's intentions are clearer.

notes.explains: Black's …Nf6 develops a knight without moving a pawn, leaving his knights unstable. Now f4 is strong because it attacks the knight on e5 and is followed by e5, kicking the knight back to g8, gaining time and central space.
notes.teaches: When the opponent develops knights without pawn support, pawn advances can harass them and win tempi. A weakening move like f4 becomes justified if it leads to a strong follow-up like e5.
notes.plans: Play f4, then e5, forcing the knight back to g8. Continue developing with Nf3 and Bc4, exploiting Black's lost time.

notes.explains: Black plays …d6, breaking White's pawn center. White should not fear the pin on the knight after ...Bg4 because the knight is protected by a pawn, reducing the urgency. Allowing ...Bxf3 doubles White's pawns, but Black loses the dark-squared bishop and White gains the bishop pair and open lines.
notes.teaches: Pins where the pinned piece is defended by a pawn are less dangerous. Doubled pawns are not always bad; they can be acceptable if they come with compensation like the bishop pair or open files, especially away from the king.
notes.plans: Ignore the pin and develop naturally with Bc4, castling, and centralizing the knight. Do not play passive moves like Bd2 to break the pin.

notes.explains: After …Nxe5, White can recapture with Nxe5, forking Black's pawns and centralizing the knight. This is better than recapturing with the pawn because it keeps the initiative and exploits the specific position.
notes.teaches: When choosing a recapture, consider not only material but also piece activity and tactical opportunities. A recapture that centralizes a piece and creates threats is often superior.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, then follow up with Bc4 and Bg5, pinning the knight and preparing a decisive attack.

notes.explains: White has a development advantage and Black's king is exposed. Instead of forcing immediate tactics, White improves piece placement with Nd5, attacking the bishop on c5 and centralizing the knight. This is a simple, strong move that maintains the initiative.
notes.teaches: When you have an initiative, you don't need to find the flashiest move. Improving your pieces with simple, active moves can be just as effective and safer than speculative attacks.
notes.plans: After Nd5, follow up with Bg5 to pin the knight, then look for a breakthrough like Nf6+ forking king and bishop.

notes.explains: White's pieces are all active, and Black's are passive. The disparity in piece activity is so great that White can look for a tactical transformation. The move Nf6+ forks the king and bishop, forcing Black to capture and allowing White to recapture with the bishop, pinning the knight and setting up a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a large positional advantage (development, piece activity, central control), look for ways to convert it into a direct attack. A fork or other tactical blow can be the payoff for superior piece placement.
notes.plans: Play Nf6+, then recapture with the bishop (Bxf6) to keep the knight pinned and prepare Qd2 followed by Qh6 or Qg5, threatening mate on g7.

notes.explains: After Bxf6, the knight on c6 is pinned and cannot move. White threatens Qd2 and Qh6/Qg5 with mate on g7. Black is helpless despite being up a piece because White's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: A pinned piece can be a decisive weakness. When the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces coordinate well, a material deficit may not matter. Focus on the attack, not the count.
notes.plans: Play Qd2 (or Qc1) threatening Qh6. If Black defends, continue with Rf3 or other reinforcements. The mate threat is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black strikes in the center with d5, aiming to exploit White's awkward knight development. After exd5 Qxd5, White's knight cannot go to c3, and Qa4 is the main line.
notes.teaches: In the Ponziani, d5 is a thematic central strike that challenges White's setup and can lead to active play.
notes.plans: Black prepares to develop rapidly and target White's uncastled king.

notes.explains: After the sequence, Black has a lead in development and White's queen on f3 is awkward, vulnerable to ideas like ...e4.
notes.teaches: A centralized queen can become a target if the opponent has active pieces.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing with ...e4, opening the center and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays c6 to keep the knight on d5, maintaining central control. Alternatives like Nb6 develop with tempo but decentralize the knight.
notes.teaches: When deciding between centralization and development, consider which piece is more valuable in the current position.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...Bd6 and castle, keeping pieces near the center.

notes.explains: Black plays f5, a safe move that defends the e4 pawn and prepares to develop the bishop. Castling is also possible, but f5 is solid.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is vulnerable, defending it solidly is often better than sacrificing it without clear compensation.
notes.plans: Black will continue development, possibly with ...Qc7 or ...Bf5, maintaining a strong center.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 to defend the b7 pawn and prepare long castling, while also creating a threat against h2. This is a practical defensive move that addresses White's threats.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that was previously suboptimal becomes the best option due to changed circumstances. Prioritize defense when under attack.
notes.plans: Black will castle long or short depending on White's play, with a solid position.

notes.explains: White plays g3, creating a hook on the kingside. Black should immediately think of exploiting this with ...h5-h4 or preparing ...f4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates a pawn hook, look for ways to attack the kingside by advancing pawns or opening lines.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Be6 to defend the knight on d5, then consider ...O-O-O or ...O-O and prepare ...f4.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 to dislodge the bishop on c4, making the f4 break even stronger. This is a patient preparatory move that removes a key defender.
notes.teaches: Before launching a direct attack, consider removing the opponent's defensive pieces first. This can make the breakthrough more effective.
notes.plans: After ...b5, Black will play ...f4 with greater effect, as White's bishop on c4 is no longer defending key squares.

notes.explains: Black plays f4, breaking open the kingside. The bishop on d5 is well-placed, as it defends the e4 pawn and eyes the kingside. If gxf4, then Nxf4 defends the bishop and attacks.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, a well-placed bishop can serve both defensive and offensive roles. The f4 break is a typical way to open lines against the castled king.
notes.plans: After ...f4, Black will continue with ...Nf4 or ...Bxf4, maintaining pressure. The attack is overwhelming due to White's lack of development.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the knight on f4, defending the bishop on d5 and threatening ...Nd3. The e4 pawn is valuable as it defends f3 and anchors the knight.
notes.teaches: In an attack, keep your pawns and pieces supporting each other. The e4 pawn is a key asset that should not be given up without a clear mating sequence.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Nd3 or ...Rf6, bringing more pieces into the attack. The king on h1 is vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black plays Bd5, keeping the f-file open and preparing to exploit the bishop's potential energy. If the pawn on e4 ever moves, the bishop becomes a monster.
notes.teaches: A bishop that appears passive can have great potential energy if the pawn structure changes. Keeping the f-file open is important for the attack.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Nd3 or ...Rf6, maintaining pressure. The bishop on d5 is a key defensive and offensive piece.

notes.explains: Black plays Rf6, threatening Rg6 to pin the queen to the king. This rook lift brings another piece into the attack.
notes.teaches: Rook lifts are a powerful way to bring rooks into the attack, especially when the opponent's queen is exposed.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Rg6, winning the queen or delivering mate. The attack is decisive.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd3, threatening Nxf2 and opening the bishop's diagonal. This is a direct and incisive move that forces White to defend.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for knight forks and direct threats to force a win.
notes.plans: Black will capture on h2 or f2, leading to a decisive material advantage or mate.

notes.explains: Black plays Rxf2, a clean capture that wins material. The attack is overwhelming, and many moves win.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, don't overcomplicate. Simple captures that maintain pressure are often best.
notes.plans: Black will continue to threaten mate or win more material. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg1, a replacement sacrifice idea. If White captures the bishop, the queen delivers mate on h2. If White doesn't capture, the bishop on g1 blocks the king's escape.
notes.teaches: A replacement sacrifice involves offering a piece to clear a square for a mating attack. The idea is that whichever piece is captured, the other delivers mate.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...Qh2# or win the queen. The concept is common in attacking positions.

notes.explains: Black delivers checkmate with Qh2# after the replacement sacrifice. The king is trapped by its own pawns and the bishop on g1.
notes.teaches: Recognizing mating patterns like the replacement sacrifice can lead to quick finishes.
notes.plans: The game is over. Black's attack succeeded due to White's lack of development and the open kingside.

notes.explains: Black's queen retreats to d8 (the John Bartholomew setup), a solid but passive system. White should occupy the center with d4 and develop naturally and actively.
notes.teaches: Against passive setups, the most principled approach is to seize the center and develop with maximum activity, aiming for rapid piece play.
notes.plans: Play d4, Nf3, Bc4, targeting f7, and continue with natural development like 0-0 and Re1.

notes.explains: Black's h6 is a wasted tempo; it doesn't address White's threats and delays development. White can punish this by playing Bc4, aiming at f7.
notes.teaches: Every tempo matters in the opening. Unnecessary pawn moves like h6 give the opponent a free developing move and can be exploited by direct threats.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, threatening f7. If Black plays Bf5, then Ne5 intensifies the pressure on f7.

notes.explains: Black has played e6 to block the bishop's diagonal, but the pressure on f7 remains. White can consider a tactical idea: Qf3, threatening Nxf7 and Qxf5.
notes.teaches: When you see a potential sacrifice on f7, calculate the follow-up. Here Nxf7 Kxf7 Qxf5 wins a pawn and exposes the king, a common tactical motif in many openings.
notes.plans: Play Qf3, threatening Nxf7. If Black takes on d4, Qxd4 keeps the attack alive. The key is to break down the tactic: pressure on f7, the loose pawn on e6, and the queen's safety after the sacrifice.

notes.explains: White plays Qf3, a risky but thematic move. Black can take on d4, but White has a tactical follow-up: Nxf7 Kxf7 Qxf5, winning a pawn and destroying Black's king safety.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid of tactical complications if you have calculated clearly. The queen is safe because the bishop on c4 defends it after the sacrifice, and Black cannot both capture the queen and break the pin.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Qxd4, then Nxf7! Kxf7 Qxf5, winning a pawn and leaving Black's king vulnerable. White can then continue developing with tempo.

notes.explains: Black captures the bishop on c4, but White can take the rook on h8, winning the exchange. However, the knight on e5 is now trapped after ...g5 and ...Bg7, so White must be careful.
notes.teaches: When calculating a sacrifice, consider not only immediate gains but also the safety of your own pieces. Here, the knight might get trapped, so a safer approach (like castling) might be better if you want to avoid complications.
notes.plans: White can play Qxh8, but must then rescue the knight. Alternatively, White could have chosen a quieter move like 0-0 or Bf4 to maintain pressure without risk.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange but the knight on e5 is trapped. Black can play ...g5 and ...Bg7, winning the knight. White's position is still good due to development lead, but complications remain.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the most forcing line isn't the best. If you have a comfortable position, avoid unnecessary complications. A simple developing move like 0-0 or Bf4 might be more effective.
notes.plans: White should try to activate the rook and queen, perhaps with Qe5 or Qh5, while keeping the knight safe. But the position is messy; a mature player would have chosen a simpler path.

notes.explains: White's queen is on h7, pressuring e6 and supporting the attack. Black's king is exposed. White should keep the queen on h3 (supporting actress) rather than moving it to e5 where it can be attacked by ...Nd7.
notes.teaches: In attacks, the queen often works best from behind the front lines, supporting the heavy pieces. Avoid putting the queen in the middle of the action where it can be chased away by developing moves.
notes.plans: Keep the queen on h3, pressuring e6. Prepare to break with d5 or play Bf4 to increase pressure. Castle queenside to bring the rook into the attack.

notes.explains: Black blunders the e6 pawn with ...Kg7. White takes it, winning a free pawn and collapsing Black's position. The attack is now overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is under pressure, they often make mistakes. Be alert to capture hanging pawns and keep the initiative.
notes.plans: After Qxe6, White can play Be5 to pin the knight to the king, or simply bring the rook to d1. The position is winning; any reasonable attacking move will do.

notes.explains: White plays Be5, pinning the knight on f6 to the king. This is a strong move that prevents Black from defending effectively. The x-ray from the rook on d1 against the queen on d8 is also a factor.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful attacking tools. Look for opportunities to pin enemy pieces to the king or queen, especially when you have a lead in development.
notes.plans: After Be5, White can consider d5 to open lines and exploit the x-ray. If Black plays ...c5, push d6 to trap the bishop. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: White pushes d5, opening the diagonal for the bishop and exploiting the x-ray against the queen. Black's position crumbles.
notes.teaches: When you have an x-ray (a rook staring at the queen through pieces), try to open lines to exploit it. A pawn break like d5 can be devastating.
notes.plans: After d5, if Black plays ...cxd5, then Rxd5 wins the queen. If Black plays ...c5, then d6 traps the bishop. White's attack is decisive.

notes.explains: White captures on d5 with the rook, threatening the queen. Black is forced to give up the queen or lose material. The attack is winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive attack, look for the most forcing continuation. Here, Rxd5 wins material immediately.
notes.plans: After Rxd5, Black's queen is attacked. If Black moves the queen, White can capture the knight on f6. The rest is technique.

notes.explains: White wins the queen for a rook. The position is completely winning. White can now simplify and convert.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, simplify the position by trading pieces, especially queens, to reduce counterplay.
notes.plans: White can play Bxf6 to trade bishops, then bring the rook to the seventh rank for a mating attack. The simplest plan is to target the king.

notes.explains: White has a queen and rook against a bishop and knight. The simplest plan is to trade the last remaining defender (the bishop on b7) and then get the rook to the seventh rank.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, focus on the fastest path to checkmate. Here, trading bishops and placing the rook on the seventh rank is the most efficient.
notes.plans: Play Bb5 to trade bishops, then Rd7+ followed by Qe7 or Rh7 with mate threats. Use the whole board to bring pieces to the attack.

notes.explains: White trades bishops and then plays Rd7+, forcing the king to g8. Qe7 threatens mate on g7 or h7. Black is helpless.
notes.teaches: Use checks and threats to force the king into a mating net. The rook on the seventh rank is a powerful attacking piece.
notes.plans: After Qe7, Black cannot prevent mate. The simplest is Rh7 followed by Qxh6# or Qg7#.

notes.explains: White plays Rh7, threatening Qxh6#. Black's only move is ...h5, but then Qg7# is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and a strong attack, look for the quickest mate. Here, the rook on h7 and queen on e7 create a simple mating threat.
notes.plans: Play Qg7# next move. The game is over.

notes.explains: After the trade, White's knight on f5 is ideally placed, attacking d6 and limiting Black's piece activity. Black's position is cramped and worse.
notes.teaches: A knight on f5 in the Open Sicilian is a powerful outpost that restricts Black's development and creates long-term pressure.
notes.plans: White will aim to consolidate with O-O, then possibly play e3 and Nd5, or prepare a pawn break with g4.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the b2 pawn. White should not panic and defend passively; instead, active development is better.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked, consider whether the opponent's threat can be ignored in favor of a more active move, especially if you have a lead in development.
notes.plans: White can play Bg5, pinning the knight and preparing Nd5, or simply castle and continue development, accepting the pawn sacrifice if necessary.

notes.explains: Bg5 pins the knight on d7, threatening Nd5 which would attack the queen and rook. This is more active than Bg5, which would only attack the queen.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a bishop, consider which square best supports your long-term plan (e.g., pinning a defender) rather than just creating a threat.
notes.plans: After Bg5, White threatens Nd5. If Black takes the knight, White recaptures with the queen, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: Black captures on e4, hoping to complicate. White must choose carefully: Nd5 is best, centralizing the knight and exploiting the pin.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, moving a knight to a central outpost can create multiple threats and often wins material or forces a favorable trade.
notes.plans: After Nd5, if Black takes the knight, White recaptures with the queen, threatening the rook on d8 and the pawn on d6.

notes.explains: Nd5 is the correct move. It threatens the queen and the rook, and if Black captures the knight, White recaptures with the queen, maintaining a strong attack.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pin, centralizing the knight can create a decisive double threat. Avoid the temptation to grab material immediately if it allows counterplay.
notes.plans: After Qxd5, White threatens Qxd8+ and Qxd6. Black's king is exposed, and White's pieces coordinate well for an attack.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, White has a rook on d5, a knight on f5, and a bishop on g5. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White has a winning attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent's king is exposed, trading queens can simplify into a winning endgame or middlegame with a strong initiative.
notes.plans: White will bring the rook to d1, double rooks, and target the d6 pawn. The knight on f5 and bishop on g5 restrict Black's pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd8, attacking the rook. White should not retreat but instead play Rd1, doubling rooks and increasing pressure on d6.
notes.teaches: When your rook is attacked on an open file, doubling rooks is often a strong response, especially when the opponent's king is vulnerable.
notes.plans: After Rd1, White threatens Rxd6, and Black's knight is pinned. White can then play Bxf6 or advance the attack.

notes.explains: White doubles rooks on the d-file, threatening to capture on d6. Black's knight is pinned, and White's pieces dominate.
notes.teaches: Doubling rooks on an open file is a classic way to increase pressure, especially when the opponent has a pinned piece.
notes.plans: White will play Rxd6, then continue with the attack, possibly involving the bishop on g5 or the knight on f5.

notes.explains: Black defends with Rc7. White can now play Bxf6, forcing gxf6, then Qxf6, but Black has Kc7 and the rooks connect. Instead, White should play Rd5 with tempo, attacking the queen.
notes.teaches: When calculating, consider intermediate moves that improve your position with tempo. Rd5 attacks the queen and prevents Black from consolidating.
notes.plans: After Rd5, Black must move the queen, allowing White to double rooks or capture on d6. The attack continues.

notes.explains: Rd5 attacks the queen on b6 and threatens Rxd6. Black's queen must move, and White gains time to bring the other rook to d1.
notes.teaches: Using a rook to attack the queen with tempo is a common tactic to gain time and improve your position.
notes.plans: After the queen moves, White plays Rd1, doubling rooks, and then captures on d6 or delivers checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb5, defending the rook on c7. White should not panic; instead, play Rd6, threatening Rxd6 and keeping the pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent defends, look for ways to increase the pressure without allowing counterplay. Rd6 attacks the pawn and prepares Rd1.
notes.plans: After Rd6, White will play Rd1, doubling rooks, and then capture on d6 or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White doubles rooks on the d-file, threatening Rxd6 and checkmate. Black's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: Doubling rooks on an open file with a pin is a decisive attacking pattern. The opponent's pieces are paralyzed.
notes.plans: White will play Rxd6, then continue with the attack, possibly involving the bishop on g5 or the knight on f5.

notes.explains: Black captures the rook, but White recaptures with the queen, sending the king back to d8. Then White can trade queens and win all of Black's pawns.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, forcing it back with a queen check can lead to a winning endgame where you pick off pawns.
notes.plans: After Qxd6+, Kd8, White plays Qxd7+ and Qxd7, then captures pawns with the rook and knight.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, White has a rook and knight against a rook. White's pieces are active, and Black's king is exposed. White can win by capturing pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity and king safety are crucial. White's rook on the seventh rank and knight outpost give a winning advantage.
notes.plans: White will capture Black's pawns, starting with d6, then advance the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: White plays Bc1, aiming to swing the bishop to a3 and then play Rd7, checkmating or winning the rook.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, look for patterns like swinging the bishop to a distant diagonal to support a rook invasion on the seventh rank.
notes.plans: After Ba3, White plays Rd7+, forcing the king to c8, then Rc7+ and Bc5+ leads to checkmate or material gain.

notes.explains: White plays Rd7+, forcing the king to c8, then Rc7+ and Bc5+ leads to checkmate or winning the rook.
notes.teaches: A bishop on a3 can support a rook checkmate on the seventh rank. This is a classic pattern in rook endgames.
notes.plans: After Kc8, White plays Rc7+ Kb8, then Bc5+ Ka8, and Rc8#.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Rc8#, a classic pattern with bishop and rook on the seventh rank.
notes.teaches: This checkmate pattern (rook on c7, bishop on c5, king on a8) is a common finish in rook endgames.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, and Black now develops the bishop to g4. This is a flexible approach: Black waited to see where White's bishop went before committing. If White had played Be2, Black would have played Bf5 instead.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can delay developing a piece to see your opponent's setup, then place your piece optimally. This is a form of 'prophylaxis' or 'waiting move' strategy.
notes.plans: After Bg4, Black pins the knight on f3. The next move is Nbd7, completing development and preventing White's knight from reaching e5.

notes.explains: White plays Qb3, attacking b7 and the knight on e4 simultaneously. This is a mistake because Black can simply play Nd6, defending b7 and threatening the bishop on f4. White's king is exposed, and if White takes on d6 and then b7, Black delivers checkmate with Qg5+ and Qf4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes an impatient move that creates multiple threats, look for a defensive move that also creates counter-threats. Here Nd6 defends and threatens the bishop, while the king safety becomes paramount.
notes.plans: Play Nd6, forcing White to deal with the threat to the bishop. If White takes on d6, Black's queen and rook will deliver a quick checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays Nxd6, capturing the bishop. White recaptures with cxd6, but then Black has Qg5+ followed by Qf4, threatening Qxh2#. White's king is trapped and cannot escape.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, a check can drive it further into the corner, making checkmate easier. The sequence Qg5+ then Qf4 is more clinical than Qh4 immediately, as it prevents the rook from escaping.
notes.plans: Deliver checkmate with Qg5+ Kh8 Qf4, threatening Qxh2#. White's only delay is to play Rg8, but then Qxh2 is still mate.

notes.explains: After d5, Black plays Nb4 attacking c2 and gaining a tempo. The bishop on f5 supports this threat.
notes.teaches: Use piece activity to create threats and gain time; Nb4 exploits the loose pawn on c2.
notes.plans: If White defends with Nd4, Black can consider retreating the knight to a6 and redeploying to c5.

notes.explains: White plays Nd4 defending c2 and attacking the bishop on f5. Black's best response is to retreat the knight to a6, which is not a disaster.
notes.teaches: Don't fear retreating a knight to a6; it can be redeployed to c5 later. Avoid forcing complications when a simple retreat is fine.
notes.plans: Play Na6, then reroute to c5 via b8 or c7. Meanwhile, improve the rook and prepare to pressure d5.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to a6. White's best plan is a3 to restrict the knight and prepare b4, while Black must avoid getting the queen trapped.
notes.teaches: When a knight is stuck on a6, White can restrict it with a3 and b4. Black must keep the queen safe and seek counterplay.
notes.plans: Black can consider an exchange sacrifice on c3 to activate the pieces and ruin White's pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange on c3 to destroy White's pawn center and gain long-diagonal pressure. This is a classic idea in many openings, especially the Sicilian.
notes.teaches: The exchange sacrifice on c3 is a thematic idea to undermine White's center and activate Black's pieces. It often provides sufficient compensation.
notes.plans: After Rxc3, Black recaptures with the pawn, then builds a battery on the long diagonal with Qa8 and Bg7, pressuring g2.

notes.explains: After Bxf7+, Black plays Nf6 as a good intermezzo. White must stay energetic; Qe6 is strong because the queen and knight form a powerful tandem, targeting f7.
notes.teaches: The queen and knight are a deadly duo; sometimes the queen should join the attack directly even if it violates the principle of keeping the queen behind the front lines.
notes.plans: Play Qe6, threatening Qf7+, and be ready to castle and bring the rook to d1.

notes.explains: Black plays Nxd4 with tempo, but White ignores it and plays Qf7+ anyway, then after Kd7, Black threatens Nxc2. White castles to get out of the fork and prepares Rd1.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is attacked but you have a bigger threat, ignore the pawn and continue the attack. Castling can be a strong defensive and offensive move simultaneously.
notes.plans: Castle, then play Rd1, threatening skewer if Black takes on c2.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne2+ hoping for a back-rank mate if White takes, but White simply moves the king to f1, attacking the queen and defending the rook.
notes.teaches: Always check if the opponent's tactic is sound; here the discovered check is not dangerous because the king can move to safety while creating threats.
notes.plans: Play Kf1, winning material as Black's queen is attacked and the rook is defended.

notes.explains: After winning the queen, White is up material but must complete development to convert efficiently. Bf4 and Rd1 are natural developing moves that also create threats.
notes.teaches: When converting an advantage, don't neglect development. Even with a queen up, your other pieces matter.
notes.plans: Play Bf4 and Rd1, then target Black's weak pawns and king.

notes.explains: White plays Qc4, pinning the rook and preparing to bring the queen closer to the kingside for checkmate. The pin is not dangerous because White threatens discovered check.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a pin is not a problem if you have counterplay; here the queen is well-placed for a mating attack.
notes.plans: Follow up with Bb6+ and then look for a back-rank mate.

notes.explains: The idea behind openings that lose tempi (like the Scandinavian) is that Black trades the e-pawn early, reducing White's central mobility and creating a solid structure. This is similar to the French Rubinstein, Caro-Kann, and Petroff.
notes.teaches: Trading the e-pawn early can be a valid strategy to limit White's central space and create a solid defensive setup.

notes.explains: White castles and plays f4 to open the position, targeting Black's king stuck in the center. The f-pawn push is less weakening than g4 or h4 because Black has no kingside pieces.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling, you should start a pawn storm on the side where your opponent's king is. f4 is a safe way to open lines when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Continue with a4, b4, b5 to break open the queenside. Develop the knight to a3-c4-e5 to put pressure on e5.

notes.explains: Black's play is suspiciously accurate, with every move being a top engine choice. Moves like Qe8 (unpinning the queen) and Bc8 (anticipating f6) are inhumanly deep.
notes.teaches: When an opponent consistently plays top engine moves with little time, especially moves that are hard for humans to find, it may indicate cheating. Look for a pattern of inhuman accuracy.
notes.plans: In this game, White tries to create complications to test the opponent, but the cheating is evident. The game ends with a blunder by the cheater.

notes.explains: After gxf6, Black's king is exposed on the open g-file. White's rook lift to g3 creates direct threats, and the d4 pawn is well-defended, freeing the bishop to capture on h6. The knight on f7 blocks the queen's access to h6, but after Qf4 and Nd6, the h6 square opens, allowing Qh6+ winning the queen.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, identify the open file and lift a rook to that file to create threats. Look for ways to open squares for your pieces as the opponent's pieces move.
notes.plans: Play Qh6+ to win the queen, as the knight's departure from f7 opens h6. The king cannot escape due to the rook on g3 and bishop on d3.

notes.explains: After Nxf6+, Black must recapture with the pawn (gxf6) because recapturing with the rook would allow White to trade rooks and keep the kingside pawn structure intact. The resulting open g-file is a major weakness for Black.
notes.teaches: When forcing captures on f6, consider the recapture: if the opponent recaptures with a pawn, it may open lines to the king. Prioritize keeping your own pawn structure intact while exploiting the opponent's weaknesses.
notes.plans: White will now use the open g-file to attack Black's king, starting with a rook lift to g3.

notes.explains: Ne4 is strong because it attacks the bishop on f6, and if Black trades bishops, d4 is no longer under pressure. White can then focus on other improvements without worrying about defending the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop pins your knight or pressures a central pawn, consider centralizing a knight to challenge that bishop. Trading it can relieve defensive duties and free your pieces.
notes.plans: White intends to capture on f6 at a convenient moment, but first improves the rook placement with Rdf1 to maintain pressure on the f-file.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 is inaccurate because it allows White to play Ne4, pressuring the bishop on f6. The bishop on g4 also relinquishes control of e4, a key square for White's knight.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing bishops on g4 in such positions if it allows the opponent to centralize a knight with tempo. Control of e4 is important for White's central dominance.
notes.plans: White will play Ne4 next, attacking the bishop and preparing to trade on f6 to relieve pressure on d4.

notes.explains: After f6, White has a clear advantage due to better central control and Black's backward pawn on e6. White's pieces are well-placed, and the plan is to connect rooks and improve piece coordination.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage and a backward pawn, focus on improving your pieces without rushing. Connect rooks and prepare to double on open files.
notes.plans: White will play Qd2 to connect rooks, then place rooks on c1 and d1, and look for opportunities to increase pressure on Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: White declined the gambit with e3, but Black already has a lead in development and a good center.
notes.teaches: When your opponent declines a gambit, you often get a comfortable position with active pieces.
notes.plans: Develop quickly and maintain central control.

notes.explains: The knight maneuver to g6 via ...Ng7 is preferred to get the knight to a good square and allow the bishop to develop.
notes.teaches: In many positions, the knight on g6 supports kingside play and keeps options open.
notes.plans: Follow up with ...Bg7 or ...Bc5, then ...d6.

notes.explains: Playing ...Bc5 even though it seems to bite on granite is fine because it has potential energy; if White plays e4, the bishop becomes active.
notes.teaches: A piece that appears passive can become powerful after a pawn push; this is 'potential energy' in chess.
notes.plans: Wait for White to push e4, then the bishop will target the kingside.

notes.explains: After ...a6, if White plays b4, the bishop retreats to a7 where it is just as good, and White's queenside expansion is not scary.
notes.teaches: Don't fear pawn advances like b4; the bishop can retreat to a7 and remain strong, while White's pawns may become targets.
notes.plans: Continue development with ...d6 and ...Re8, provoking e4.

notes.explains: The knight maneuver ...Ng4 and ...Nh6 aims to provoke h3, which acts as a hook for a later bishop sacrifice on h3, and also clears the path for the queen to go to h4 or g5.
notes.teaches: Provoking weaknesses like h3 can create attacking chances; the knight may seem misplaced but serves a greater purpose.
notes.plans: After ...Nh6, consider ...f5 to push pawns and open lines, or ...Qh4 to join the attack.

notes.explains: With the knight on d2 gone, ...Qh4 is safe because ...g3 would drop the h3 pawn. The queen is well-placed on h4, threatening ...Bxh3 and supporting ...f5.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for the queen, consider whether it can be chased away; a safe queen on the kingside can be a powerful attacking piece.
notes.plans: Keep the queen on h4 and prepare ...f5 or ...Bxh3 if the timing is right.

notes.explains: After ...Qh4, ...f5 is played instead of ...Bxh3 because after ...Bxh3 gxh3 Qxh3, White has the defensive resource f3, which brings the queen into defense and blocks the knight on h6.
notes.teaches: Before sacrificing, check if the opponent has a strong defensive move that refutes the sacrifice; sometimes it's better to push pawns first.
notes.plans: Play ...f5 to open lines and keep the queen on h4 for pressure; later ...f4 may reopen the diagonal for the bishop.

notes.explains: After ...f5, White's queenside play is slow because Black's structure is solid (a6 prevents Nb5). The queen on h4 remains useful even if the diagonal is closed.
notes.teaches: A queen on h4 can be a standalone attacking piece; it doesn't need to be part of a specific sacrifice to be effective.
notes.plans: Continue with ...e4 to gain space and use the e5 square for the knight, or ...f4 to reopen the diagonal.

notes.explains: After ...e4 and ...Ne5, the rook lift ...Rf6 and ...Rg6 brings the rook into the attack, a slow but powerful maneuver since the center is closed.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you can take time to bring all pieces into the attack; rook lifts via the sixth rank are a common attacking motif.
notes.plans: Play ...Rf6, ...Rg6, and then consider ...g5 or ...f4 to break open the kingside.

notes.explains: After White's Nd4, Black plays ...c6 to prevent Nb5 and also prepares ...Kh8 and ...Bb8 to reroute the bishop to a better diagonal.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you need to make prophylactic moves to stop opponent's ideas, and then reposition pieces to the optimal squares.
notes.plans: Play ...Kh8, ...Bb8, and then ...Nf3 to sacrifice on f3 and open up White's king.

notes.explains: The move ...Nf3 sacrifices the knight to shatter White's kingside; after ...Qxh3, Black threatens ...Qh2# or ...Rg8+.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a knight on f3 can be a powerful way to break open the king's position, especially when the queen and rook are ready to deliver mate.
notes.plans: Follow up with ...Rg8 and ...Qh2# if White doesn't defend accurately.

notes.explains: In the analysis, the line ...Rf6 (to lift the rook to g6) followed by ...c4 (to open the bishop's diagonal) is a beautiful attacking idea. After ...Ng4, White cannot play f3 because of ...Bxe3+ and Qh2#.
notes.teaches: Combining rook lifts with pawn breaks like ...c4 can open lines for the bishop and create decisive threats. Always look for ways to activate all pieces.
notes.plans: Play ...Rf6, ...Rg6, then ...c4 to open the bishop, and ...Ng4 threatening mate.

notes.explains: a5 forces White to deal with the threat of ...a4, which would undermine the b4 pawn and prepare c5.
notes.teaches: Use pawn moves to challenge the opponent's pawn chain and create weaknesses before striking in the center.
notes.plans: After b4, play c5 to open the center; if White takes on c5, recapture with the c-pawn to create a passed pawn and attack the knight.

notes.explains: White took on c5, but Black cannot recapture immediately because the bishop on b2 x-rays the c5 pawn. Instead, Black plays Qa5, pinning the bishop.
notes.teaches: When a direct recapture is problematic, look for intermediate moves that create threats and maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: After Qa5, White must retreat the bishop to b2; then Black recaptures on c5 with the queen, winning a pawn and keeping the attack.

notes.explains: Black has won a pawn and now has a strong attack. White's king is stuck in the center, and the d-file is the main avenue.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is uncastled, open files and diagonals to launch a direct attack. The d-file is the natural target.
notes.plans: Play dxc4 to open the d-file, then bring rooks to d8 and use the knight on d4 to create threats.

notes.explains: After opening the d-file, Black's rook checks on d8. White's king is exposed and the attack is decisive.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, prefer checks and threats that force the king into the open. Avoid crowding the king with your own pieces, as they can become targets.
notes.plans: Continue with checks and threats; if White tries to trade queens, consider keeping the queens on to maintain attacking chances.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the bishop on a3 to deliver a discovered check with the knight. White's king is helpless.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be willing to sacrifice material if it exposes the enemy king and leads to a decisive attack. The bishop on a3 is no longer needed.
notes.plans: After Nxe4, White cannot avoid checkmate or loss of material. The simplest finish is Qb4+ followed by Rd1#.

notes.explains: The final checkmate: Qb4+ forces Kc1, then Rd1#. The attack succeeded because White never developed kingside pieces.
notes.teaches: A simple, direct checkmate pattern: queen check on the b-file followed by rook delivering mate on the back rank.

notes.explains: White has achieved the ideal center with c3 and d4. Black's queenside pawns are still weak, and his bishop on e7 is passive. White is clearly better.
notes.teaches: A central pawn duo (d4+e4) supported by pieces is a huge asset. Black's structural weaknesses on the queenside remain even after undoubling with cxd4.
notes.plans: White can play Bg5, Qd2, and consider e5 at the right moment to open lines. Black struggles to find a plan.

notes.explains: Qa4 is an ideal square: it attacks c6, is out of the way, and cannot be easily harassed. The queen is well placed on the edge when it still controls key diagonals.
notes.teaches: Place the queen on squares where it is safe and active. The edge of the board can be a good hiding spot if the queen still participates in the attack.
notes.plans: White will develop the knight to a3-c4 or use g5 to harass Black's bishop. The c6 pawn is a permanent target.

notes.explains: Na3 prepares Nc4, attacking the queen and defending the b2 pawn. However, Nc4 is often premature because of ...Qb5, forcing queen trades and fixing Black's pawns.
notes.teaches: Do not rush to place the knight on c4 if it allows Black to trade queens and repair his pawn structure. Always check if the opponent has a tactical refutation.
notes.plans: Instead of Nc4, consider Ng5 to chase the bishop from e6, or play Bd2 and Rc1. Patience is key.

notes.explains: Ng5 chases the bishop from e6, gaining a tempo and further weakening Black's control of the center. White's pieces become more active.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a passive piece, harass it to gain time. Every tempo counts in a positional squeeze.
notes.plans: After the bishop moves, White can play Nc4 with more effect, or simply continue developing with Bd2 and Rac1.

notes.explains: Black's pawn structure is now a disaster: doubled e-pawns and weak queenside pawns. White has a clear positional advantage.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has multiple weaknesses, do not rush. Methodically increase pressure. Every exchange that fixes the opponent's structure is a small victory.
notes.plans: White can play Qc4, targeting e6, or develop the bishop and double rooks on the c-file. Black's pieces are passive.

notes.explains: Qc4 attacks e6 and is safe. Black cannot easily defend the pawn. This is better than Nc4 because it avoids ...Qb5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a tactical trick (like ...Qb5), choose a different move that still attacks weaknesses. Concrete thinking overrules general principles.
notes.plans: White will continue with e5 to drive the knight away, or simply pile up on e6. The position is winning.

notes.explains: After exd6+ (discovered check), Black must block with the bishop, and then dxc7 forks the queen and rook. Black loses a rook.
notes.teaches: Discovered checks are powerful because they force the opponent to deal with the check while the moving piece can capture something. Always consider changing the move order to maximize tactics.
notes.plans: White is up a rook and should consolidate. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: Black plays …f4, closing the kingside and blunting White's dark-squared bishop. This pawn is well-defended and prepares a pawn storm with ...g5, ...h5, ...g4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes closing the position is better than opening it, especially when you have a clear attacking plan on one side. The f4 pawn cramps White and gives Black a target.
notes.plans: Black will launch a kingside pawn storm with ...g5, ...h5, ...g4, supported by the bishops.

notes.explains: Black starts the pawn storm with …g5, preparing ...h5 and ...g4. White's knight retreats to d1, avoiding the vulnerable c3 square.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage on one side, advance your pawns to cramp the opponent and create attacking chances. The pawn storm is a typical plan in such structures.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...h6, ...h5, and ...g4, opening lines against White's king.

notes.explains: Black plays …h6, a preparatory move that prevents ...Ng4 and prepares ...h5. It also gives the queen access to g6.
notes.teaches: When attacking, make preparatory moves that improve your pieces and prevent counterplay. h6 is flexible and doesn't commit to a specific plan.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...h5, ...g4, or ...Qg6, depending on White's response.

notes.explains: White captures on c5. Black must decide between recapturing with the bishop or the pawn. Taking with the pawn (…dxc5) solidifies f4 and prepares the pawn storm, but weakens the queenside. Taking with the bishop (…Bxc5) keeps the structure sound but may allow White counterplay.
notes.teaches: When choosing between recaptures, consider which piece is more valuable and what your strategic goals are. Here, taking with the pawn prioritizes the kingside attack over queenside weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black chooses …dxc5, keeping the f4 pawn strong and focusing on the kingside attack.

notes.explains: White plays Qh5, attacking the kingside. Black must deal with the queen. The plan is to chase it away with ...Bf7, then play ...h5 and ...g4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen enters your position, look for ways to chase it away with tempo, using bishops or pawns.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Bf7, forcing the queen to move, then continue with ...h5 and ...g4.

notes.explains: White plays h4, trying to stop the pawn storm. Black captures …gxh4, opening the g-file and creating a passed h-pawn. The queen now has access to g5, threatening ...Qg5 and ...Qxg2.
notes.teaches: When your opponent blocks your pawn storm, be flexible. Capturing opens new lines and creates new threats. Here, ...gxh4 opens the g-file and gives Black a dangerous queen sortie to g5.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Qg5, threatening to trade queens or attack g2. If White avoids the trade, Black will use the g-file with ...Kh7 and ...Rg8.

notes.explains: Black plays …Kh7, a flexible move that gets the king off the g-file and prepares ...Rg8. It also avoids potential checks.
notes.teaches: When attacking, improve your king's safety and prepare to use the open file. Kh7 is a useful, non-committal move that doesn't hinder your attack.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Bf6, ...Rg8, and ...Bg4, trapping the queen or delivering mate.

notes.explains: Black plays …Bf6, protecting the h4 pawn and preparing ...Rg8. The bishop is well-placed, eyeing the kingside.
notes.teaches: In an attack, coordinate your pieces. Bf6 defends the pawn and prepares to join the assault.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rg8 and ...Bg4, trapping the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays …Qd7, preparing ...Bg4 to trap the queen. This move also defends the e5 pawn and avoids tactics.
notes.teaches: When preparing a trap, ensure your pieces are well-defended. Qd7 is a flexible move that supports the attack and prevents counterplay.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Bg4, trapping the queen, or ...Rg8, piling on the g-file.

notes.explains: White retreats the queen to f3. Black now has a winning attack. The g-file is open, and Black can play ...Rg8, ...Bg4, or ...Qg7.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive attack, keep up the pressure. The queen's retreat shows White is struggling.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rg8, doubling on the g-file, and then ...Bg4 or ...Qg7, threatening mate.

notes.explains: Black plays c5 to pressure the d4 pawn and open the c6 square for the knight, following the typical Caro-Kann plan of contesting White's center.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, black's main idea is to challenge White's pawn chain with c5, aiming to undermine the d4 pawn.
notes.plans: Continue developing with Nc6, Qb6, and possibly Bb4, keeping pressure on d4.

notes.explains: Black's queen on b6 attacks the b2 pawn and puts pressure on d4, forcing White to defend carefully. White's knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, making d4 weak.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a weak pawn, focus your pieces on it. Defending a pawn with pieces ties them down; prefer pawn defenses.
notes.plans: Black can continue pressuring d4 with moves like Nf6, Bg4, and eventually castle kingside.

notes.explains: Black has developed harmoniously and maintains pressure on d4. White's knight on c3 is misplaced, blocking the c-pawn and weakening the pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Avoid blocking your own pawns with pieces unless necessary. The c-pawn could defend d4 or advance to c4 for counterplay.
notes.plans: Black can consider Bg4 to pin the knight, or simply continue with Rac8 and Qb6 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight on f3 with Bg4, increasing pressure on d4. White must decide whether to break the pin or allow it.
notes.teaches: Pinning a defender of a weak pawn is a common technique to increase pressure. Delay committing to exchanges until necessary.
notes.plans: Black can follow up with Qb6, Rac8, and possibly e5 to open lines.

notes.explains: Black wins the d4 pawn after the exchange on f3, as White's queen recaptures but the pawn is undefended.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, wait for the right moment to capture. Here, after h3, the bishop had to move, but taking on f3 was correct because it wins a pawn.
notes.plans: Black is up a pawn and can consolidate with moves like Nc6, Qb6, and castle.

notes.explains: Black has won two pawns and the queen is active. White's king is exposed, but Black is winning easily.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading queens if possible, but avoid unnecessary risks. Keep pieces active to prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: Black can develop the rook to d8, play b6, and eventually push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black is three pawns up and has a winning endgame. White's king is exposed, but Black's material advantage is decisive.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, avoid unnecessary complications. Trade pieces to reduce counterplay, but don't give back material without good reason.
notes.plans: Black can centralize the king, activate the rook, and push the passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black pushes c4, blocking the bishop on a2 and attacking d5. White must play e4 to defend, but this creates a target.
notes.teaches: Pushing c4 in Benoni positions slices off the bishop's defense of d5 and vacates c5 for a knight outpost.
notes.plans: After e4, play Re8 to prepare against Bh6, then Nfd7 and Nc5 to pressure white's center.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2, which is a mistake as it walks into e6. Black can now open the center with e6, activating the bishops.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen moves away from defending key pawns, consider opening the center to exploit the loose pieces.
notes.plans: Play e6 to open the center; after dxe6, recapture with the rook to maintain pressure on e4 and activate the light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices a pawn to activate pieces. After Nxe4, black has strong coordination and threats against white's king.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for piece activity and initiative is often worth it when the opponent's king is exposed and pieces are uncoordinated.
notes.plans: Continue with Rc8 to pressure the knight on c4, or consider Nd4 to attack the queen and rook.

notes.explains: White plays Nd4, attacking the queen and rook. Black must respond carefully; Rc8 is bad because Nxe6 wins the queen. Instead, Re8 is correct to keep the diagonal open.
notes.teaches: When a piece attacks two of your pieces, check if counterattacking the queen works; sometimes the capture creates additional threats.
notes.plans: Play Re8, maintaining pressure. If white plays Nf5, look for tactics exploiting the overloaded queen defending both knights.

notes.explains: White plays Nf5, but the queen is overloaded defending both knights. Black can exploit this with Rc8, attacking the queen and winning a piece.
notes.teaches: The queen is a poor defender because it often has to defend multiple pieces; look for moves that attack the queen to overload it.
notes.plans: Play Rc8, attacking the queen. If the queen moves to b3, take on d5 and then Rc5 to win the knight on d4.

notes.explains: Black wins a piece: after Qb3, Bxd5, Qxd5, Rc5 attacks the queen and wins the knight on d4.
notes.teaches: When the queen is overloaded, a simple rook move to attack it can win material. Always consider if the opponent's queen can defend all its pieces.
notes.plans: After winning the piece, simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black has an isolated queen pawn (IQP) structure with a blockading knight on d5, which is favorable for Black. The move Nb4 attacks the d4 pawn and targets White's light-squared bishop, the key attacking piece for White's kingside play.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the blockade is important, but also attacking the pawn and eliminating White's attacking bishop can be even more effective.
notes.plans: Black aims to eliminate White's light-squared bishop to neutralize the kingside attack, then continue developing and pressuring the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays f5 to chase the bishop, then Bc6 to maintain the blockade on d5. The e6 pawn becomes weak, but Black gains compensation through control of d5 and the prospect of activating the bishop via a6.
notes.teaches: Moves with drawbacks can be good if the strengths outweigh them. Here, weakening e6 is acceptable because White cannot easily exploit it and Black gets a strong blockade.
notes.plans: Black will continue to blockade d5, aim for Bc8-a6 to pressure White's queen, and eventually complete development.

notes.explains: After queen trade, Black has an endgame with a weak e6 pawn but active pieces. The knight on b5 can be improved, and Black's rook will come to b6 to overprotect e6 and prepare b6-b5 expansion.
notes.teaches: In endgames, overprotecting weaknesses and improving piece coordination is key. The rook lift to b6 serves both defensive and offensive purposes.
notes.plans: Play Rb8-b6 to defend e6, then consider pushing b5 to open lines on the queenside. The king can later move to f7 to support.

notes.explains: Black's bishop finally reaches b7, completing development. The knight on c5 is a nuisance, but Black's pieces are well-coordinated. The plan is to expand on the kingside with g5 and create mating threats.
notes.teaches: Patience in improving pieces and waiting for the right moment to strike is crucial. The bishop on the long diagonal can become a powerful attacking piece.
notes.plans: Play g5 to open lines against White's king, aiming for Rook h8 and potential checkmate. If White trades on g5, Black's attack becomes very dangerous.

notes.explains: Bc4 looks passive but is correct to support a future Nd5 sacrifice. The bishop may later relocate to the b1-h7 diagonal.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best square for a piece is not the most obvious one; anticipate future sacrifices and piece coordination.
notes.plans: Prepare Nd5 after castling and Re1, aiming to exploit the d5 outpost.

notes.explains: After 0-0 d6, White plays Qe2 to centralize the queen and prepare Rd1, putting pressure on d6. The queen is well-placed on e2, protecting the bishop and keeping central influence.
notes.teaches: In positions with a weak pawn (d6), centralize the queen and double rooks on the d-file to maximize pressure.
notes.plans: Play Rd1, then Bf4 to provoke e5, creating a hole on d5 for the knight.

notes.explains: Black's passive Nd7 and Qc7 allow Bf4, which provokes e5. If Black plays e5, it opens the diagonal for the bishop and creates a permanent outpost on d5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is passive, provoke pawn advances that create weaknesses; use the threat of e5 to gain a strong square.
notes.plans: After e5, play Nd5 with tempo, exploiting the hole and the queen's position on c7.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, which opens the diagonal for the bishop and creates a hole on d5. White must calculate carefully; the immediate Bxf7 sacrifice is tempting but requires precise follow-up.
notes.teaches: When a sacrifice is available, calculate deeply and consider the opponent's best defenses; sometimes a preparatory move (like Ng5) is better than the immediate capture.
notes.plans: Consider Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+ Ke8 Nb5, attacking the queen and threatening Nc7, or the immediate Nd5 if Black's king is exposed.

notes.explains: Bxf7+ is a thematic sacrifice to expose the king. After Kxf7, Ng5+ Ke8, White has two promising ideas: Nd5 (attacking the queen) or Nb5 (double attack on the queen). Nb5 avoids the resource Nxd5, which would give Black rook and two pieces for the queen.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing, look for alternatives that avoid the opponent's best defensive resources; a double attack on the queen can be more effective than a direct capture.
notes.plans: After Ng5+ Ke8, play Nb5, threatening Nc7+ and attacking the queen. If the queen moves, Nc7+ wins material.

notes.explains: After Nb5 Qc1, the intermediate Nxd6+ is crucial: it wins a pawn and opens the d-file, maintaining the attack. Black's king is exposed and pieces uncoordinated.
notes.teaches: Intermediate checks can improve the position before recapturing; opening files against a exposed king is worth more than material.
notes.plans: After Nxd6+ Bxd6, play Qc4, threatening Qf7# and Qe6+, forcing Black to defend both threats.

notes.explains: Qc4 creates a double threat: Qf7# and Qe6+. Black cannot defend both; the attack is decisive.
notes.teaches: After a successful sacrifice, look for double threats that target the king and other pieces; forcing moves often lead to mate or material gain.
notes.plans: Play Qf7+ Kd8, then take on d6, winning material and maintaining the attack.

notes.explains: After Qf7+ Kd8, Qxd6 wins a piece and the game is effectively over. Black's king is exposed and White has a decisive material and positional advantage.
notes.teaches: Converting an attack into a material advantage while keeping the king exposed is a common winning technique.
notes.plans: Continue with Be3 to activate the last piece, or simply take on g7 to win the knight.

notes.explains: Be3 activates the last piece and threatens to take the knight on f6. It's a calm but powerful move that maintains all threats.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, activate all pieces; a quiet developing move can be more effective than flashy checks.
notes.plans: After h6, take on g5 and then deliver mate with Bb6+ and Qc7#.

notes.explains: The final mating sequence: Bb6+ forces Kc8, then Qc7#. The pattern is a classic queen-and-bishop mate.
notes.teaches: Recognize common mating patterns; once you identify the target square, work backwards to clear the path.

notes.explains: White plays d3, Nbd2, Ngf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, aiming for a flexible setup against the French. The knight on d2 blocks the bishop but is essential to avoid early queen trades after ...dxe4.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian Attack, the knight belongs on d2 (not c3) to prevent Black from forcing a queen trade after ...dxe4. The setup is a system, not a forced line.
