notes.plans: Close the center with e5, then reroute the knight via f1-h2-g4 to attack the kingside. Develop the bishop to f4 after rook e1.

notes.explains: After e5, Black's knight on h7 is poorly placed. White plays h4 to prevent ...Ng5 and create a transit square for the knight on h2.
notes.teaches: When a knight is stuck on h7, restrict it with h4 to keep it out of play and prepare the rerouting maneuver Nh2-g4.
notes.plans: Continue with Re1, then Nf1-h2-g4, targeting h6 or f6. If Black plays ...f5, take en passant to keep the kingside open.

notes.explains: Black plays ...d4, weakening the c4 square. White's knight jumps to c4, an outpost that cannot be attacked by pawns.
notes.teaches: When the opponent pushes a pawn in the center, look for outpost squares for your knights. A knight on c4 dominates the position.
notes.plans: Exploit the d5 weakness and the c4 outpost. If Black plays ...Bg4, consider Re4 to attack the bishop and prepare an exchange sacrifice.

notes.explains: In the Fischer game, the setup is identical: e4, d3, Nd2, Ngf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, e5, Re1, Nf1, h4, Bf4. The h4 pawn serves two purposes: preventing ...g5 and creating a transit square for the knight via h2.
notes.teaches: The h4 push is a key prophylactic move in the King's Indian Attack. It stops Black from kicking the bishop with ...g5 and opens a path for the knight to reach g4.
notes.plans: After h4, continue with Nf1-h2-g4, aiming for a sacrifice on h6 or f6. The bishop on f4 supports the attack.

notes.explains: Fischer plays Bf4, then a3 to slow Black's queenside attack. Later, he retreats the knight to f1 and then to d2, eventually rerouting it to e4 via d2.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you have time to reroute pieces. Don't be afraid to retreat a knight to a worse square if it can later reach a better one. Patience is key.
notes.plans: After Nf1, the knight goes to d2 and then e4, targeting f6 or d6. Meanwhile, the bishop on h3 pressures e6, and the queen goes to h5.

notes.explains: Fischer plays Bg2, a mysterious move that later enables a checkmate. After h5, Rh4, and Qh6, the bishop on g2 delivers mate on h7.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a seemingly passive retreat sets up a future combination. The bishop on g2 controls the long diagonal and becomes deadly when the h-file opens.
notes.plans: Open the h-file with h5-h6, then bring the rook to h4 and queen to h6. The bishop on g2 delivers mate or wins material.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: After the trades, black has a slight development lead and the bishop on g7 is powerful. White's queenside is undeveloped. Black chooses Re8 over the simpler Nxd4 Qxd4 Be6, to keep tension and complicate.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between simplifying and keeping tension, prefer the latter against higher-rated opponents. Forcing them to make decisions increases the chance of error.
notes.plans: Play Re8, targeting e4, and prepare d5 to open the center while White's queenside is still undeveloped.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: White retreats the knight to f3, a slight inaccuracy. Black now pushes d5, opening the center. After e5, the knight goes to e4, a classic outpost. Black's better development and active pieces give a small edge.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is underdeveloped, open the center. A knight on e4 in such structures is often a powerful outpost, even if temporarily sacrificed.
notes.plans: Play d5, meet e5 with Ne4, and then consider trades to exploit White's weak queenside and exposed king.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black's knight on e4 is well-placed, attacking d2 and c3. White's queenside is still undeveloped. Black's plan is to trade on d4 and then target White's pawns and king.
notes.teaches: In open positions with a lead in development, centralize your pieces and create threats. The knight on e4 is a classic outpost that restricts White's options.
notes.plans: Trade on d4, then use the bishop on g7 and rook on e8 to pressure e4 and the queenside. Consider moves like Bb6, Qd7, and Rac8.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: After trades, black has a knight on d5 and bishop on g7 vs White's bishop on c2 and undeveloped queenside. Black's pieces are more active. White's queen is misplaced on d1.
notes.teaches: In positions with an isolated pawn (d6), active piece play can compensate. The knight on d5 is a strong outpost, but must be defended carefully.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f5 or b6, bring the rook to c8 or e8, and target White's weak b2 pawn and the knight on b1.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black plays Qd7, preparing to meet Bg5 with ...Bxb2? but also avoiding the pin. White's knight on a3 is awkward. Black's pieces are active; White's queenside is still undeveloped.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis: anticipate the opponent's threats (like Bg5) and prepare a response. Qd7 both develops and prevents a pin.
notes.plans: Continue developing, possibly with Re8 or Rac8, and look for opportunities to exploit White's weak b2 pawn and uncoordinated pieces.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black plays Ncb4, defending the knight on d5 and threatening Nd3. White's queen on d1 is passive. Black keeps the tension, avoiding queen trades.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, avoid unnecessary trades that relieve pressure. Keep the opponent's pieces tied down.
notes.plans: Prepare to play Nd3, targeting the queen, or consider moves like Rc8 to activate the rook. White's queenside is still undeveloped.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black wins a pawn after a series of trades. White's bishop on b3 is offside. Black's queen and rook are active; White's king is slightly exposed.
notes.teaches: When you win a pawn, ensure your pieces remain active. Don't make concessions just to grab material; keep the initiative.
notes.plans: Consolidate the extra pawn, activate the rook (e.g., Re8), and target White's weak pawns. Avoid allowing White counterplay.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black plays Bc2, forcing the trade of bishops. This is a slight inaccuracy; Bc4 was better to avoid the weakening g4 push. However, White misses g4, and Black remains a pawn up.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, even simple tactics can be missed. Always double-check your candidate moves; don't tunnel vision on one idea.
notes.plans: After the bishop trade, Black has a pawn-up endgame. Activate the rook, trade queens if favorable, and push the passed pawns.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: After queen trade, Black has a rook endgame with an extra pawn. White's king is cut off on the e-file. Black's plan is to activate the king and rook, create a passed pawn, and force a rook trade.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, the king's activity and pawn structure are crucial. Cut off the opponent's king and use your rook to create threats.
notes.plans: Play Re8, then bring the king to e5. Use the rook to attack White's pawns and force a favorable rook trade, leading to a winning king-and-pawn endgame.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black's rook on c6 forces a rook trade because White's rook has no safe squares. After the trade, Black's king is active and the pawns are unstoppable.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, look for ways to force a rook trade when your king is more active. A rook trade often leads to a winning king-and-pawn endgame.
notes.plans: Play Rc6, forcing Rxc6 Kxc6, then advance the king and pawns to promote.

notes.explains: Black's f6 weakens the diagonal to his king and creates a target on e5. The pawn on e5 is not hanging because of the threat of Qh5+.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays a weakening move like f6, prioritize exploiting the weakened diagonals over immediate checks. Develop with tempo, e.g., Bc4, to prevent castling.
notes.plans: Play Bc4 to pressure f7 and prevent black from castling kingside. Follow up with Nf3 and 0-0, maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: After Ne7, black's king has no escape squares: f7 is covered by the bishop, and the knight blocks e7. This triggers a mating idea.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is trapped with no squares, look for forcing sequences that lead to checkmate. Induce a pawn move (g6) to remove support from a key defender.
notes.plans: Play Qh5+ to force g6, then exf6, threatening mate on f7. If black takes the queen, f7# is mate.

notes.explains: If black had played fxe5 instead of f6, white can win with Qh5+ because the pawn on e5 is now black's, allowing a fork after g6 Qxe5+.
notes.teaches: A common tactical theme: after f6 and ...exf6? (or similar), Qh5+ g6 Qxe5+ forks king and rook. This is a classic idea from the Damiano Defense.
notes.plans: After Qxe5+, black's king is exposed; if Ke7, Bg5+ leads to mate or heavy material loss.

notes.explains: After exf6, black is busted: the knight on e7 is pinned to the king by the bishop, and the rook on h8 is undefended. White can increase pressure with Nh4, threatening Nxg6# or simply winning the pinned knight.
notes.teaches: When a pinned piece is defended only by a pawn, look for ways to attack it with pieces that also threaten other targets (e.g., the undefended rook). This overloads the defense.
notes.plans: Play Nh4, threatening Nxg6# and also attacking the pinned knight. Black cannot defend both threats.

notes.explains: White has a massive center and a kingside attack underway. Black's queenside counterplay is slow because Black has no pieces there. The g6 pawn is the key weakness; placing the queen on g6 would be crushing.
notes.teaches: When attacking, identify the weakest squares (here e6 and g6) and ask which piece would be most devastating on that square. Then find a way to get it there.
notes.plans: Play Qg2, threatening Qxg6, which cannot be defended. After capturing, follow up with Bh3 and Be6 to deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: If White plays Bd3, Black can either take or play Ne7, trading on favorable terms. The position is equal.
notes.teaches: When White plays a passive move like Bd3, Black has multiple equalizing options; choose based on preference.
notes.plans: If Black takes on d3, the position simplifies; if Ne7, Black keeps the bishop pair.

notes.explains: Against Qb3, Black plays Rb8. The queen is tied to attacking the b7 pawn, while the rook defends it. This is a favorable trade of roles.
notes.teaches: Don't fear a queen attacking a pawn if the defender is a rook; the queen is often more valuable and can be tied down.
notes.plans: After Rb8, Black continues development; avoid b6 as it weakens c6.

notes.explains: Black develops Nd7 before Nf6 to prevent Ne5. This small move order prevents White from gaining a tempo with Ne5.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, prevent enemy knight outposts; Nd7 first stops Ne5, then Nf6 completes development.
notes.plans: Castle, then aim for Ne4 or Nd5, maintaining a solid pawn chain.

notes.explains: Black maneuvers the knight to d5, a semi-outpost. The knight controls many squares and prevents b4.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight doesn't need an immediate threat; its value is in control and flexibility.
notes.plans: After Nd5, prepare a kingside attack or maintain pressure; avoid c5 as it opens the center prematurely.

notes.explains: Black plays a5 to prevent b4. If White plays b4 anyway, Black can take en passant, keeping the queenside closed.
notes.teaches: Prevent opponent's pawn breaks with your own pawn moves; a5 stops b4 and maintains the closed center.
notes.plans: Prepare a kingside attack with moves like Rfe8, Qg6, or f6-f5.

notes.explains: Black lifts the rook to e6, preparing to double on the g-file or support a kingside pawn push.
notes.teaches: Rook lifts are a common way to transfer a rook to an active file, especially when the center is closed.
notes.plans: After Re6, Black can play Rg6, or prepare f5-f4 to open lines against the white king.

notes.explains: Black's rook reaches g6, putting pressure on the kingside. White's knight can go to g3, but Black has resources.
notes.teaches: When the opponent blocks a file, look for alternative ways to continue the attack; here Black can sacrifice the exchange on g3.
notes.plans: If White plays Ng3, Black can play Rxg3, winning a pawn and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: White retreats the knight to h2. Black can now play f6 to prevent Ne5, then h5 to chase the knight further, and finally f5 to open the g-file.
notes.teaches: To push a knight away, first block its escape squares (f6 prevents Ne5), then attack it with pawns (h5).
notes.plans: Play f6, then h5, then f5. After f5, the g-file opens and Black's rook and knight become very active.

notes.explains: After f6, h5, and f5, Black has opened the g-file and the knight on d5 is ready to join the attack. White's knight is stuck on h2.
notes.teaches: A patient pawn storm can create a winning attack; the knight on d5 becomes a hero once the position opens.
notes.plans: Play f4 to break through; if exf4, Nxf4 gives Black a devastating attack.

notes.explains: Black's knight on f4 threatens Rxg3 and other tactics. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight becomes extremely powerful when the position opens; it can fork, attack, and support breakthroughs.
notes.plans: Play Rxg3, then Nxg3+ and Qxd4, winning two pawns and a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black wins two pawns and enters a winning knight endgame. The rest is technique.
notes.teaches: When converting an advantage, trade pieces to reduce counterplay and push passed pawns. Keep the king active.
notes.plans: Push the queenside pawns, bring the king to the center, and promote.

notes.explains: Black should not castle queenside in this structure because the pawn on c6 creates a hook for White's attack. White's queenside attack would be faster.
notes.teaches: When considering castling, look at pawn structure hooks; a pawn on c6 can be a target for a queenside attack.
notes.plans: Castle kingside and attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: The Carlsbad structure (cxd5 exd5) leads to a minority attack for White: b4-b5 to undermine Black's pawn chain. Black should aim for active piece play.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad, Black's plan is to develop the bishop to b7 (not d6) and prepare counterplay in the center or kingside.
notes.plans: Black can play ...b6, ...Bb7, and ...c5 or ...e5 breaks.

notes.explains: The Maroczy Bind (pawns on e4 and c4) controls d5, making it hard for Black to break with ...d5. If Black mishandles it, the position becomes cramped and passive.
notes.teaches: A bind is a pawn structure that restricts the opponent's central break. The Maroczy Bind specifically prevents ...d5, so Black must find other ways to generate counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should aim for piece activity and pawn breaks like ...b5 or ...f5, rather than forcing ...d5.

notes.explains: After …d6, Black prevents e5 and prepares to develop the bishop to g7. This is a standard way to handle the Maroczy Bind.
notes.teaches: In the Maroczy Bind, Black should avoid allowing e5, which would cramp the position. ...d6 is a solid prophylactic move.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g7, castle kingside, and look for breaks like ...b5 or ...f5.

notes.explains: If White plays f3 instead of Nc3, Black can consider ...Bg7, allowing e5, because White's poor development makes the e5 pawn hard to hold.
notes.teaches: Sometimes allowing an apparent cramping move like e5 is acceptable if the opponent's development is lagging; the center pawn can become a target.
notes.plans: After e5, Black can play ...d6 and attack the e5 pawn with ...Bg7 and ...Nf6, exploiting the pin on the queen.

notes.explains: In the position after e5, Black should not rush to attack the e5 pawn directly. Instead, developing moves like ...Be6 are more practical, keeping the tension and improving piece activity.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a central pawn that appears weak, it's often better to improve your pieces first rather than lashing out immediately. The threat of ...d6 or ...Qa5 can be held in reserve.
notes.plans: Play ...Be6, controlling d5 and pressuring c4, then decide how to break the center.

notes.explains: After ...Be6, Black threatens ...d6 and ...dxe5, and also eyes the c4 pawn. White's queen on d4 is vulnerable to discovered attacks.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, the fianchettoed bishop and the knight on f6 often combine to create threats against the white queen on d4. Keeping the tension can lead to tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Continue development with ...0-0, then consider ...d6 or ...Qa5 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: When White plays h4, threatening h5, Black should not panic. The h5 push can be met by ...Nxh5, and if White plays g4, the knight returns to f6. Black's king is safe, and White has weakened his own pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Attacks on the kingside without sufficient development are often bluff. Black can call the bluff by capturing the pawn and trusting that White's lack of piece coordination prevents a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Take on h5 with the knight, and if g4, retreat to f6. Then aim for a queen trade with ...Qb8 to simplify into a favorable endgame.

notes.explains: After ...Nxh5, White may try g4, but Black can play ...Nf6, and if White continues with Qh2, the h7 pawn is well defended. Black is simply a pawn up.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplifying by trading queens is often the most effective way to convert. Look for moves that force or invite a queen trade.
notes.plans: Play ...Qb8, threatening to trade queens. If White avoids the trade with Qg5, then ...Qg3+ forces the exchange.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black has an extra pawn and a superior bishop (White's bishop is bad due to the c4 pawn). The knight on h5 can jump to f6 or g3, and the bishop on e6 controls key squares.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a bad bishop (blocked by its own pawns) is a significant weakness. Black's bishop is active and can dominate.
notes.plans: Trade rooks to reduce White's counterplay, then use the kingside pawn majority to create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nxd4 Qxd4 d6, Black has a solid position. The main line continues with ...Bg7 and ...0-0.
notes.teaches: This is the standard Maroczy Bind setup for Black. The d6 pawn prevents e5, and Black will develop harmoniously.
notes.plans: Play ...Bg7, ...0-0, and then consider ...Be6 or ...Qa5 to pressure White's center.

notes.explains: If White plays Bg5, Black should not fear the pin. The standard response is ...Be6, threatening ...Nxd4, and if White drops the bishop back to d2, Black plays ...Qa5.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, Black's setup is resilient. The bishop on e6 is a key piece, controlling d5 and supporting queenside play.
notes.plans: Play ...Be6, then ...Qa5, putting pressure on c3 and the center. If White plays Bh6, trade bishops and exploit the weakened dark squares.

notes.explains: A common trap in the Accelerated Dragon occurs when White plays Bc4 and tries to play a normal Dragon setup. Black can play ...Qb6, attacking the undefended bishop on e3.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to undefended pieces. The move ...Qb6 is a classic tactic that exploits the bishop on e3 and can win material.
notes.plans: After ...Qb6, if White plays Nf5, take on b2. If White defends with Bb3, then ...Nxc4 wins a pawn.

notes.explains: If White plays Qd2 in response to ...Qb6, Black can play ...Nxc4, because after Qxc4, Black has ...Qxb2, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: When the queen moves to d2, it no longer defends the c4 pawn. This is a common tactical motif in the Accelerated Dragon.
notes.plans: Play ...Nxc4, and if Qxc4, then ...Qxb2. If White recaptures with the bishop, Black wins the exchange.

notes.explains: After ...b5, if White plays cxb5, Black can recapture with the pawn and then play ...Rxc3, sacrificing the exchange for two pawns and a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing the exchange for two pawns and active pieces is often favorable, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Play ...axb5, then ...Rxc3, and follow up with ...Qxb5 or ...Nxb5, depending on the position.

notes.explains: Another common break is ...f5, challenging White's center and opening lines for the bishop on g7.
notes.teaches: The ...f5 break is a typical Accelerated Dragon idea. It attacks e4 and can lead to a powerful kingside initiative.
notes.plans: Play ...f5, and if exf5, then ...Bxf5, putting pressure on c2 and e4. If White ignores, ...f4 can cramp White's position.

notes.explains: In positions where White has played a4 to prevent ...b5, Black can target the b3 pawn with ...Qb6 and ...Nd7-c5.
notes.teaches: When White weakens the queenside with a4, the b3 pawn becomes a long-term target. Maneuver the knight to c5 to pressure it.
notes.plans: Play ...Nd7, then ...Nc5, and if White defends with b4, the knight can go to a4, attacking c3.

notes.explains: White plays Bb5, pinning the knight and preparing to recapture on e5 with the pawn. If Black takes on e5, White can recapture with the pawn, opening the f-file and keeping the queen trade optional.
notes.teaches: In open positions, a queen trade is not always bad; the remaining pieces can still have a strong initiative. Pinning the knight with Bb5 is a flexible way to maintain pressure.
notes.plans: After dxe5, recapture with the pawn (fxe5), then castle and use the f-file for attack.

notes.explains: After castling, Black captures on e5 and White recaptures with the pawn. The f-file is open, and Black's knight on f6 is pinned by the pawn on e5. Black's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: An open file near the opponent's king, combined with a pawn center that restricts enemy pieces, creates a powerful attacking platform.
notes.plans: Use the f-file to pile pressure on f7, with moves like Ng5 and Rxf7.

notes.explains: Black plays Qe7, which invites the tactical idea Nd5. However, because the f-pawn is gone, there is a diagonal from c5 to f2. White must calculate carefully: Nd5 Qc5+ seems to fork the bishop, but then Nxc7+ forks the queen and rook, and the queen is trapped.
notes.teaches: When you see a tactical pattern (like a fork), calculate one move further to check for counter-tactics. In positions with a development lead, there are often hidden resources.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, and if Qc5+, then Nxc7+ forking queen and rook, winning material.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd4, unpinning with check. White retreats the knight to c3, maintaining the pin on the knight on d4. The bishop on b5 x-rays the king, and the knight on d4 is pinned and will be won.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is on the same file as your queen, look for x-ray attacks. Retreating a piece to maintain a pin can be stronger than capturing.
notes.plans: Win the pinned knight on d4, then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: After a sequence of captures, White plays e6, a discovered check that also opens the diagonal for the bishop. This move threatens the queen and creates a double attack.
notes.teaches: Discovered checks can be combined with clearing a square for another piece. Look for ways to use a pawn move to open lines and create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Play e6, forcing Black to deal with the discovered check and the threat to the queen, winning material.

notes.explains: After e6, Black captures, and White recaptures with the bishop, giving check. Black's king is forced to d8, and White can take on f8 with check, then take on f7, winning a rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use checks and captures to win material. The rook on f8 is undefended and can be taken with check.
notes.plans: Continue the attack, picking up the rook on f8 and then the pawn on f7, remaining with a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: White plays Qg4, threatening the pawn on g7 and keeping the pressure. Black's rook is still trapped, and White will win it.
notes.teaches: After winning material, continue to attack the opponent's weaknesses. The queen can harass the king and pawns while the rook remains trapped.
notes.plans: Win the rook on f8, then convert the material advantage in the endgame.

notes.explains: White wins the bishop on g7 and then the knight on h6, leaving White with queen and pawns against a lone king.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a queen is often enough to force checkmate or win more material.
notes.plans: Use the queen to checkmate or promote a pawn.

notes.explains: White has a queen and pawns against a lone king. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: Convert a queen endgame by centralizing the queen and advancing pawns.
notes.plans: Checkmate or promote a pawn.

notes.explains: The game is over; White has a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning position, play accurately to avoid counterplay.
notes.plans: Deliver checkmate or promote a pawn.

notes.explains: Black challenges the London with c5, then plays Qb6 to pressure b2. White trades queens, giving Black doubled b-pawns but a semi-open a-file. Black follows up with b5, threatening b4 to break through White's queenside defense.
notes.teaches: In the London System, Black can fight for initiative by contesting the center with c5 and using the queen to create tension. The semi-open a-file after queen trade is more valuable than White's doubled pawns.
notes.plans: Black aims to push b4, exploiting the undefended rook on a1. If White moves the rook, Black can later target the b2 pawn with a rook lift.

notes.explains: White prematurely opens the center with e4, but Black's development and space advantage make e5 a strong reply, exploiting White's uncastled king and uncoordinated pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and space, opening the center (e5) punishes the opponent's lagging king safety and piece coordination.
notes.plans: After e5, Black's bishops become powerful in the open position, and White's king remains vulnerable. Black can castle to activate the rook.

notes.explains: Black supports the e4 pawn with f5, creating a pawn chain. The e5 pawn is now a target, and Black will win it after further pressure.
notes.teaches: Supporting a pawn chain with f5 solidifies the center and creates a target (e5) that White cannot easily defend.
notes.plans: Black will play h5 to prevent White from trapping the bishop, then follow up with e3 and f4 to create a powerful pawn wedge.

notes.explains: Black plays Bh6, which looks passive but defends the crucial f4 pawn. The bishop and pawn form a 'megapiece' — removing either collapses the structure.
notes.teaches: A 'bad' bishop defending a key pawn is not a weakness; it is part of a defensive unit. Evaluate pieces in context, not isolation.
notes.plans: Black will later capture on e5, castle to activate the rook, and bring the knight to d3 for a decisive attack.

notes.explains: After capturing the knight, Black plays c5, opening the g-file for White. White should reorient toward attacking the king. Queen e4 is a strong square because it eyes the kingside and avoids the x-ray from Black's bishop on c8.
notes.teaches: When the g-file opens, consider centralizing the queen on e4 to support a kingside attack while avoiding tactical tricks like ...d5.
notes.plans: Play Qe4, threatening mate and preparing Bd3. Avoid Qg4 because of ...d5.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, which blocks f5 but also opens lines. White should play Re1 first to increase pressure, then Bd3, as f5 is no longer possible due to en passant after exf6.
notes.teaches: Use prophylactic moves like Re1 to increase attacking potential before committing the bishop. The en passant rule can prevent defensive pawn moves.
notes.plans: Play Re1, then Bd3, threatening Qxh7#. Black cannot play ...f5 because of en passant.

notes.explains: After h6, there is a forced mate in three. The elegant line is Rxg7+ Kxg7, then either Qh7+ and Qg6# or Qg6+ and Qh7#.
notes.teaches: When the king is exposed, look for sacrificial breakthroughs on g7 to deliver mate. Symmetrical mating patterns can arise.
notes.plans: Play Rxg7+ Kxg7, then Qh7+ Kg8, Qg6# (or Qg6+ Kh8, Qh7#).

notes.explains: White plays Bb5+ to force an exchange that ruins Black's pawn structure. Black can avoid this by playing ...Qb6 before ...e6, so that after Bb5+, Black recaptures with the queen, preserving the pawn structure.
notes.teaches: When White threatens to exchange on c6, prepare to recapture with a piece (queen) to avoid doubled pawns. ...Qb6 is a prophylactic move that also attacks b2.
notes.plans: Play ...Qb6, then ...e6, and develop the kingside. If White plays Bb5+, recapture with the queen.

notes.explains: Black has a flexible setup. The knight on c6 and pawn on e6 create a solid center. Black can develop the kingside with ...g6 and ...Bg7, but here the bishop is on e7. A creative idea is ...h5, ...Nh6, ...Bg6, and ...Nf5, which prevents White from playing g4 and gives the knight a strong outpost on f5.
notes.teaches: In structures with a pawn on e5, the knight often belongs on f5. The pawn push ...h5 prevents g4 and prepares ...Nh6-f5. This setup is common in the Caro-Kann and similar positions.
notes.plans: Play ...h5, ...Nh6, ...Bg6, ...Nf5. The knight on f5 is powerful, and ...h5 stops White from kicking it with g4.

notes.explains: White plays c4, which weakens the d4 square. Black should not immediately take on d4; instead, bring the knight to f5 to control d4 and prepare Bc5. The dark-squared bishop is valuable because White has many weak dark squares.
notes.teaches: When White creates a hole on d4, control it with a knight rather than exchanging pieces. The dark-squared bishop is often more important than a knight in such positions.
notes.plans: Play ...Nf5, then ...Qb6, threatening ...Nxd4 and ...Bc5. Avoid trading the dark-squared bishop for a knight.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bc5, threatening to win a pawn on d4. White is tied up. The key is to intensify pressure rather than cash in immediately.
notes.teaches: When you have a bind, increase pressure gradually. Threatening to win material can force concessions without committing to exchanges.
notes.plans: Play ...Bc5, threatening ...Nxd4 and ...Bxd4. If White defends, continue with ...Qb6 and ...Rac8.

notes.explains: After winning the pawn on c4, Black has a clear advantage. The compensation for the pawn earlier in the game was based on three factors: the backward d-pawn and weak d4 square, the open king (due to f4), and White's bad bishops (both bishops are blocked by pawns).
notes.teaches: When evaluating compensation for a pawn, consider structural weaknesses (backward pawns, holes), king safety (open king), and piece activity (bad bishops). These factors can outweigh a material deficit.
notes.plans: Consolidate by developing and exploiting White's weaknesses. The knight on f5 and queen on c5 are well placed.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, blocking the rook's line to f7 but leaving the bishop on d6 undefended. White simply captures the bishop.
notes.teaches: When your opponent defends one threat, look for other weaknesses; here the bishop on d6 becomes vulnerable.
notes.plans: White takes the bishop on d6, winning a piece.

notes.explains: White captures the bishop on d6. Now Black's king and queen are a knight's move apart, setting up a fork.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king and queen are close, look for knight forks.
notes.plans: White will play Ng5+ and then Ne6+ forking king and queen.

notes.explains: White plays Ng5+; Black blocks with Nxg5, but then Qxg5 wins the queen. White is now up a queen for a piece.
notes.teaches: A knight check can force a trade that wins the queen; always calculate captures carefully.
notes.plans: White will consolidate and trade pieces to simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to support the d4 pawn and maintain the center. Black cannot take on d4 because of tactics.
notes.teaches: When up material, protect your pawns and avoid unnecessary weaknesses.
notes.plans: White will complete development, trade pieces, and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: White trades bishop for knight, then develops the knight to d2. This simplifies the position and reduces Black's counterplay.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, trade pieces to reduce the opponent's attacking chances and make the win easier.
notes.plans: White will aim to occupy the weak f5 square with a rook or knight.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, creating a weak square on f5. White immediately occupies it with the rook, attacking the e5 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens pawns, occupy the resulting outpost with a rook or knight to increase pressure.
notes.plans: White will use the rook on f5 to target e5 and create threats.

notes.explains: Black captures on d4. Instead of recapturing, White plays e5, forking the bishop on d6 and knight on f6, while the rook defends the pawn.
notes.teaches: Always look for intermediate moves; a pawn fork can win material when pieces are undefended.
notes.plans: White will win a piece with the fork.

notes.explains: White plays Qxe5+ check, then captures the knight on e5. Now White has a queen and knight for a rook and bishop, with a winning attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, use checks to force the king into a vulnerable position.
notes.plans: White will deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: White plays Qd6+ forcing the king back, then captures the knight. White is now up a queen and knight with a mating attack.
notes.teaches: Use intermediate checks to improve your position before capturing material.
notes.plans: White will deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qa3#. The king is trapped by the rook on f5 and the knight on e5.
notes.teaches: A queen and rook can deliver checkmate when the king is confined to the edge.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6 instead of e5, keeping flexible. White's Bc4 is not dangerous because Black hasn't committed the e-pawn yet.
notes.teaches: When facing Bc4 without e5, you can delay d5 and develop first. The bishop is less effective if Black can later play e6 to blunt it.
notes.plans: Develop the knight, possibly lure White into playing e5, then play d5 to grab center control.

notes.explains: Black's queen to f6 is premature and leaves the queen exposed. White has two good approaches: trade queens on favorable terms with Be3, or decline the trade and place the queen on an active square.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers a queen trade, you can decline if you have a better square for your queen that supports your plan.
notes.plans: Castle queenside quickly to exploit Black's lack of development. The queen on e3 protects f2 and prepares Bd2 and O-O-O.

notes.explains: Black's b6 weakens the c6 square. White can immediately exploit this by playing Ba6, attacking the weak c8 bishop and threatening to win a pawn after Bb7.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens a square, immediately target it with your bishop to create pressure or win material.
notes.plans: Play Ba6, then Bb7 to win the pawn on c6, or consider other active options like f4 or Qd3.

notes.explains: Bb5 is a provocative move that sets up Nd5, threatening to jump to the powerful outpost. If Black captures the bishop, the pawn on c6 is pinned, so Nd5 is still possible.
notes.teaches: When you have a piece sacrifice in mind, check if the opponent's capture would leave a pin that still allows your main idea.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, forcing the queen back to d8, then blast open the center with e5, exploiting Black's lack of development.

notes.explains: With the knight on d5 and the center opened by e5, Black is completely overwhelmed. White's pieces are active while Black has none developed.
notes.teaches: After establishing a knight outpost, immediately open the center to maximize the activity of your pieces and exploit the opponent's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Continue the attack; for example, Nc7+ forcing the king to d7, or the quiet Bg5 to set up a discovered attack.

notes.explains: Nc7+ wins the queen after Kd7? Nxa8, but even if Black avoids that, White is up material. Simpler is just to take the queen on c8 after the knight check.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning tactical shot, don't overcomplicate; sometimes the simplest capture is best.
notes.plans: Take the queen on c8 and then consolidate; White is up a queen and the game is over.

notes.explains: After winning the exchange and a pawn, White is up a queen. The simplest continuation is to take the bishop on c8 and then the pawn on e5, leaving Black helpless.
notes.teaches: After winning material, simplify by trading pieces and consolidating your position.
notes.plans: Play Re1 to activate the rook, then target Black's weak pawns and king.

notes.explains: Black's king is exposed and White's queen dominates. Qe6+ forces the king to f8, then Qxc8 wins the rook, and Black resigns.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use checks to force it into a worse position and win material.
notes.plans: No further plan needed; Black resigned.

notes.explains: Now White strikes with d4. If Black plays …Nxd5?, then dxc5! wins a pawn because the knight on d5 is pinned and the pawn on c5 cannot be recaptured (the knight on d7 is pinned). If …cxd4, then Qxd4! and the queen is well-placed behind the pawn on d5, which acts as an umbrella. Black will struggle to recover the pawn.
notes.teaches: Opening the center at the right moment can exploit pinned pieces and leave the opponent's pieces misplaced. The queen can be safely placed behind a pawn shield.
notes.plans: White should aim to maintain the extra pawn or trade it for a lead in development. The pawn on d5 is a strong asset.

notes.explains: Black plays …a6, which is the correct move. White should not retreat the bishop to a4 (too stubborn) or c4 (allows Black to expand with ...b5 and fianchetto). Instead, White should drop the bishop back to e2, a modest move that keeps the pawn on d5 as a bargaining chip and continues development.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn but the opponent has counterplay, it's often better to give back the pawn for a lead in development rather than cling to it stubbornly. A quiet retreat can be more effective than an aggressive one.
notes.plans: White should develop naturally (Nf3, Nc3, O-O) and aim to use the d5 pawn as a wedge. The bishop on e2 is well-placed to support the center.

notes.explains: After Be2, White has a solid position. The pawn on d5 is a strong central wedge. Black's knight on d7 is passive, and White's pieces are ready to develop. White should consider playing c4 to drive the pawn to d5, creating a Benoni-like structure.
notes.teaches: In such structures, the pawn on d5 gives White a space advantage. Playing c4 can be a principled way to solidify the center and restrict Black's counterplay.
notes.plans: White should develop knights to c3 and f3, castle, and then consider pushing c4 to fix the pawn on d5. Black may try ...b5 or ...g6, but White's space advantage is clear.

notes.explains: Black plays ...g6, fianchettoing the bishop. White should continue developing with Nc3 and Nf3, not worrying about ...Ng4 (which is not a threat). The position is pleasant for White due to the space advantage and clear development.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, focus on completing development and not overreacting to minor threats. The extra space will make Black's pieces cramped.
notes.plans: White should castle, then consider moves like h3 (to prevent ...Ng4) or a4 (to prevent ...b5). The bishop can go to e3 or g5, and the queen to d2.

notes.explains: Black plays ...b5, a Benko-like pawn sacrifice to generate counterplay. White should accept the sacrifice with cxb5 axb5 Bxb5, as the pawn is weak and Black's compensation is insufficient. White has already castled and developed, while Black's knight on d7 is passive and the c5 pawn is weak.
notes.teaches: In Benko-style positions, accepting the pawn sacrifice is often correct if you have a lead in development. Black's compensation relies on open files and active pieces, but here White's pieces are well-placed to defend.
notes.plans: After accepting the pawn, White should aim to trade pieces and consolidate. The connected passed pawns on the queenside are a huge asset.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to b7, threatening ...Nb6 to attack the d5 pawn. White must not play Bc6? because …Qb6! attacks the bishop and the queen, and after trades, Black's queen on b7 becomes very strong, pressuring d5 and b2. Instead, White should play a move like Be3 or Bf4, which ties Black to the c5 pawn and prepares to meet ...Nb6 with d6.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are undefended, be wary of moves that allow the opponent to improve their piece placement. A seemingly active move like Bc6 can backfire if it helps the opponent's queen reach a powerful square.
notes.plans: White should play Be3, threatening to take on c5 if ...Nb6. If ...Nb6, then Bxc5! gives White connected passed pawns on the queenside. Alternatively, Bf4 with the same idea.

notes.explains: Black captures on d5, and White recaptures with the knight. Now White has two connected passed pawns on the queenside. The key is to trade pieces to simplify into a winning endgame. White should play Nxd5 Bxd5 Bd4!, threatening to trade bishops and leave Black with a weak king and passive pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage (especially connected passed pawns), trading pieces is usually beneficial. The endgame is easier to win with fewer pieces on the board.
notes.plans: White should aim to trade bishops with Bd4. If Black avoids the trade, the knight on d7 is passive. White can then push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays …e5, a creative move to avoid the bishop trade. White should not panic. The idea is that after Bxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Qg5, Black threatens ...Qxg2 and ...Nf4. But White has a tactical resource: Bc6! attacking the bishop on b7. If …Bxc6, then Nxc6 and Black's attack fizzles. If …Qxe5, then Bxb7 and White is two pawns up.
notes.teaches: When facing a tactical blow, calculate calmly. Look for counterattacks that exploit the opponent's undefended pieces. A move like Bc6 can turn the tables by attacking the bishop and threatening to win material.
notes.plans: After Bc6, Black's best is to trade, leaving White with two extra pawns. White should then consolidate and push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: After Bxb7, White is two pawns up. Black may try …Nf4, threatening checkmate on g2. White can simply play Qf3, defending g2 and attacking the knight. Black has no further threats, and White's extra pawns will decide.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, don't be afraid of one-move threats. Calmly defend and consolidate. The extra pawns will eventually win.
notes.plans: White should play Qf3, then bring the rooks into play and push the queenside pawns. Black's initiative will die out.

notes.explains: Black plays …Qf6, luring White into Nd7? which appears to win the exchange. But after …Qg5!, White's bishop on c6 is no longer available, and if Nxf8? then …Ne3! with a double attack on g2 and the queen, winning. Instead, White should play Qf3!, a counterintuitive move that puts the queen under the bishop's nose. The key is that the bishop on b7 is undefended, so a pin is a two-way street. Black cannot exploit the queen's position because the bishop is also vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Pins and x-rays are two-way streets. If the piece giving the pin is undefended, the queen can often move into the line of fire safely. Always consider that the opponent's piece may be just as vulnerable as yours.
notes.plans: After Qf3, Black's best is …Rfc8, defending the bishop. White can then play a4, supporting the bishop and preparing to push the pawn. The bishop on b5 is crucial as it defends the knight on e5.

notes.explains: White plays a4, a quiet but strong move. It supports the bishop on b5, prepares to push the a-pawn, and also enables ideas like Nb6 (forking the rooks) because the bishop is now defended. Black has no threats, so White can improve the position calmly.
notes.teaches: In positions with no immediate threats, look for quiet moves that improve your position and support your pieces. A move like a4 can be more effective than rushing into tactics.
notes.plans: White's plan is to push the a-pawn, trade queens with Qg3, and eventually simplify into a winning endgame. The bishop on b5 is a key defender.

notes.explains: Black trades queens and plays …Bc8, threatening to trap the bishop on b5. White must be careful: Bc6? allows …Ra5!, attacking the knight on e5. If the knight moves, Black's rook defends the other knight. Instead, White should play Rfc1!, defending the knight and preparing to meet ...Ra5 with Bc6 anyway, now that the knight is defended.
notes.teaches: When your calculation shows a move fails, don't force it. Look for alternative improvements. Here, Rfc1 is a natural developing move that also defends the knight and takes the sting out of ...Ra5.
notes.plans: After Rfc1, White threatens Bc6. Black's best is to retreat the bishop, but White remains with a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: White plays Nd2 instead of Nc3 to avoid Bb4 pin and keep the center intact with c3 if Black plays c5.
notes.teaches: The knight on d2 supports d4 and unblocks the c-pawn, allowing c3 to reinforce the center.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, keep the center, and prepare to meet ...c5 with c3.

notes.explains: After Bh6 and Bf8, White has strong dark-square control. Black's g6 weakens f6 and h6, and White's queen on g4 eyes g7.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pawn sacrifice, maintain the initiative by controlling key squares and preventing the opponent from consolidating.
notes.plans: Keep the queen active, consider Bh6 to force ...Bf8 (a concession), and prepare to open lines on the kingside with h4-h5.

notes.explains: Qf4 keeps the queen active and avoids trades. Black's ...Bxh6 would give up the dark-square bishop, a serious concession.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, avoid unnecessary piece trades that dilute your pressure. Keep the tension.
notes.plans: Maintain the queen on h6 or f4, prepare h4-h5 to break Black's pawn cover, and double rooks on the c-file.

notes.explains: h4-h5 is a thematic pawn break to destroy Black's kingside pawn cover. Black's g6 pawn is a primary target.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to chip away at the opponent's pawn shell when your pieces are well placed. A pawn storm can open lines for infiltration.
notes.plans: Push h5, if ...gxh5 then Nxg5 with tactical threats; if ignored, take on g6 and exploit the weakened dark squares.

notes.explains: After the tactical sequence, White wins back the piece and Black's king is exposed. The c-file infiltration with Rc7 wins the queen.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, combine direct threats with infiltration on open files to win material. Do not tunnel vision on checkmate.
notes.plans: Play Rc7, forcing ...Qxc7, then Qxc7+ followed by Rc1 to mate or win more material.

notes.explains: g5 attacks the bishop on d7, forcing it to move and securing the bishop pair for White. If Black takes on b3, White should recapture with the bishop (not the pawn) to keep the bishop pair and maintain a solid pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Prioritize the bishop pair over opening lines when the pawn structure is not yet fixed. Recapturing with the bishop keeps the c-pawn ready to advance (c4) and forces Black's hand.
notes.plans: After Bxb3, play c4 to challenge Black's knight and maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the pawn opens the a-file, giving White pressure on a7 and potential rook activity. However, Black can play Bf5, which leads to complications after d6? e6 Nxe5? and Black has D5! interfering and trapping the knight. White's best is to accept the bishop pair with Bxb3 instead.
notes.teaches: Opening a file is not always beneficial; concrete tactics can punish premature pawn recaptures. Always calculate forcing sequences before committing.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bf5, White should avoid the d6 trap and instead play Na3, rerouting the knight to b5 or c2.

notes.explains: Black has taken on d5 with the knight. White plays g4 to attack the bishop on f5 and create complications. The move exploits the fact that Black's knights are defending each other; chasing the bishop away can overload the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When two enemy knights defend each other, a pawn attack on one can force a favorable concession. In endgames with queens off, king safety is less of a concern, so pawn advances like g4 are less risky.
notes.plans: After Bf5 retreats to e6, play Nc2 to prepare d4 and clear the a-file for the rook.

notes.explains: White pushes d4, opening the center while Black's kingside is undeveloped. Black's bishop on f5 was a mistake; better was Bh3, intending e6. After Bxd5, Black loses the exchange because the rook on d8 has no safe squares (Ne3 forks rook and bishop).
notes.teaches: In positions with a development lead, open the center to exploit the opponent's lack of coordination. Always consider captures that win material or force a favorable transformation.
notes.plans: After Bxd5, play Ne3 to win the exchange, then take on f7 and push d5 to prevent Black from playing e6.

notes.explains: White plays Bf4, paralyzing Black's position. The bishop covers e5 and prevents g6 (because Be5 would trap the rook on h8). Black has no useful moves; the kingside is completely locked.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is paralyzed, take your time to improve your position. Prophylactic moves that prevent the opponent's only freeing ideas can be game-winning.
notes.plans: Play Rxa6 or other improving moves; Black cannot develop and will eventually lose material.

notes.explains: White converts the advantage by slowly improving the pieces, trading rooks, and pushing the d-pawn. The final blow is Bg8, preparing d6, which traps the rook on h8. Black resigns.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, avoid unnecessary risks. Simplify when ahead, but keep the opponent's counterplay in check. Use prophylactic moves to prevent freeing breaks.
notes.plans: Push the kingside pawn majority, trade rooks, and then advance the d-pawn with the bishop supporting it.

notes.explains: Black has blunted White's light-squared bishop with e6 and now strikes in the center with d5, solving all opening problems and gaining a larger share of the center.
notes.teaches: Against Bc4 in the Sicilian, e6 followed by d5 is a classic equalizing plan. The pawn on e6 makes the bishop ineffective, and d5 challenges White's center.
notes.plans: Continue development with Be7 and castle, or consider dxe4 to force an endgame. Avoid closing the center with d4, as that benefits the side with less space.

notes.explains: After dxe4, White can recapture with the queen, giving check. Black must be careful not to lose the bishop pair or allow a favorable trade for White.
notes.teaches: In endgames resulting from early queen trades, pawn structure becomes more important than king safety. Here Black's isolated pawns are a long-term weakness, so avoiding this trade is preferable.
notes.plans: Instead of dxe4, develop with Be7 and castle, keeping the queens on and maintaining a healthy pawn structure.

notes.explains: White pins the knight with Bg5, but Black can unpin with Be6 or Qc7, maintaining the bishop pair and central control.
notes.teaches: When your knight is pinned, look for ways to break the pin without losing material. Here Be6 or Qc7 are safe, while Bd7 would surrender the bishop pair unnecessarily.
notes.plans: Play Qc7, preparing to meet Bf4 with Bd6, unpinning the queen and creating tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: Black unpins with Bd6, threatening to capture on f4 and also eyeing the h2 pawn. White's bishop on b5 is misplaced and can become trapped.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's bishop is on b5, you can often trap it with a4-a5 or by attacking it with pawns. Here, after Bd6, White's bishop is vulnerable.
notes.plans: After Bd6, consider dxe4 to open lines, or play 0-0 and prepare e5 to activate the light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a knight on d5, but Black can win a piece by capturing on f4 and then defending the knight on d5. The key is to avoid panic and calculate accurately.
notes.teaches: When your opponent sacrifices material, remain calm and calculate. Here, Bxf4 wins a piece because the knight on d5 is pinned and cannot recapture.
notes.plans: Capture on f4, then defend the knight on d5 with Qd6 or Be6, consolidating the extra piece.

notes.explains: After a forced sequence, Black emerges with an extra piece but damaged pawn structure. However, the extra piece is more important than the pawn weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, pawn structure becomes secondary. Focus on consolidating your advantage and simplifying to an endgame.
notes.plans: Castle, develop the remaining bishop, and aim to trade queens or launch an attack using the extra piece.

notes.explains: Black is a piece up but must complete development. White's king is safe, but Black's bishop on c8 is hemmed in. The plan is to activate it via e5 and Be6.
notes.teaches: When up material, prioritize completing development and activating your pieces. Don't rush to attack; instead, improve your position step by step.
notes.plans: Play e5 to open the diagonal for the bishop, then Be6. If White plays Bf4, meet it with Ng4, forcing h3 and then Nxe3, ruining White's kingside pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd8, attacking the queen and forcing it to a worse square. This intermezzo (in-between move) improves Black's position before playing Ng4.
notes.teaches: Look for intermezzo moves that improve your position before committing to a tactical sequence. Here, Rd8 forces the queen to a square where Ng4 is even stronger.
notes.plans: After the queen moves (e.g., Qd3), play Ng4, forcing h3, then Nxe3, leaving White with a ruined kingside pawn structure. Then develop the bishop to e6 and infiltrate with Rd2.

notes.explains: Black wins a bishop and White's kingside is shattered. Black's extra piece and White's weak pawns make the win straightforward.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pawn structure is compromised, use your extra piece to target weaknesses. Here, White's f2 and e3 pawns are vulnerable.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e6, then infiltrate with Rd2, attacking the e3 pawn. Trade queens if possible to simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black's rook infiltrates the second rank, attacking the e3 pawn and threatening further damage. White's queen is misplaced on a4.
notes.teaches: Infiltrating the opponent's second rank with a rook is often decisive. Here, Rd2 attacks the weak e3 pawn and creates mating threats.
notes.plans: Capture the e3 pawn, then bring the other rook to d8 or b8, targeting b2. Use the extra bishop to support the pawns and create passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black trades rooks to simplify, then brings the other rook to d8, attacking the d3 pawn and preparing to push the c-pawns.
notes.teaches: In endgames with an extra piece, simplify by trading pieces while keeping pawns. Here, the rook trade reduces White's counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Rd8, then capture on d3 or b2. Use the bishops to support the passed c-pawns and promote.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn and now has a material advantage of a piece and a pawn. The endgame is winning.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, target the opponent's weakest pawns. Here, the d3 pawn was vulnerable.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawns, using the bishops to protect them and restrict White's king. Aim to promote one of the pawns.

notes.explains: Black's passed pawns are unstoppable. The bishops control key squares, and White's king is helpless.
notes.teaches: In endgames with passed pawns, use your pieces to shield them and prevent the opponent's pieces from blocking. Here, the bishop on c3 protects the c4 pawn and eyes the promotion square.
notes.plans: Push the c4 pawn to c2, then promote. Use the bishops to defend the pawn and attack White's king if necessary.

notes.explains: Black promotes the c-pawn to a queen, winning easily. The extra bishop ensures the promotion.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, use your pieces to clear the path and protect the promotion square. Here, the bishop on d4 controls c1, forcing White's rook to capture and then Black recaptures with the bishop.
notes.plans: Promote the pawn, then use the queen and bishop to checkmate White's king.

notes.explains: After e4 exd5 exd5, White has a space advantage and Black is cramped. White should develop naturally, not rush to trade pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, avoid unnecessary trades. Develop pieces to active squares and squeeze the opponent.
notes.plans: Develop Bd3, Nf3, O-O, then consider f4 or Bf4 to increase pressure. The d6 pawn is a long-term target.

notes.explains: Black's Ng4 aims for e5, but White should not overreact. Castle first, and later chase the knight away with f4.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight is not automatically good if it can be easily chased away. Calculate a few moves ahead to see if it's a threat.
notes.plans: Castle, then if Ne5, play f4 with tempo. Drop the bishop back to e2 to avoid tactics, then f4 kicks the knight.

notes.explains: White plays f4, chasing the knight and gaining space. The f-pawn push is relatively safe because the king can tuck on h1.
notes.teaches: Pushing the f-pawn is less weakening than g4 or h4 because it doesn't expose the king as much. Always consider king safety when advancing pawns.
notes.plans: After f4, Black's knight retreats. White can continue with Be3, Qd2, and prepare to open the center or attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, completing development. Simplicity is key; there's no need for fancy sacrifices. Black's position remains cramped.
notes.teaches: Part of a positional style is knowing when to play simple, solid moves. Don't always look for flashy tactics; sometimes just develop and improve your position.
notes.plans: After Be3, White can consider taking on e6 to open the d-file and target the backward d6 pawn. The plan is Qd2, Rfd1, and pressure on d6.

notes.explains: After Bxe3 fxe3, White's pawn structure is slightly damaged but the d-file is open. The backward d6 pawn becomes a clear target.
notes.teaches: When the center opens, look for weak pawns. A backward pawn on an open file is a major liability. Coordinate your pieces to attack it.
notes.plans: Play Qd2, Rfd1, and pressure d6. The rook on d1 and queen on d2 create strong pressure. Black will struggle to defend.

notes.explains: White brings the rook to d1, increasing pressure on d6. Black's position is very difficult; the d6 pawn is weak and White's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: After opening the d-file, double rooks on the file and use the queen to support. This is a classic way to exploit a backward pawn.
notes.plans: Continue pressure with e5, breaking through. If Black defends, White can play Nxd5 or other tactical blows. The game is strategically winning.

notes.explains: Black has played b6 and e6, intending Bb4. White defends e4 with Nc3, then plays Bd3 and Ne2 to connect knights and avoid weakening the e4 pawn. After Black takes on c3, White recaptures with the b-pawn, getting the two bishops. Qg4 is a strong move, anticipating a kingside attack and putting pressure on Black.
notes.teaches: In the Owen's Defense, developing the knight to e2 instead of f3 keeps the e4 pawn solid and prepares to recapture with a pawn if Black trades on c3, giving White the bishop pair. Qg4 can be an annoying move when Black has castled kingside, as it creates immediate threats.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qg4, forcing Black to respond. The queen on g4 eyes g7 and can support a kingside pawn storm.

notes.explains: After Black plays Nf6, White plays Bg5. This is more effective than earlier because Black's knight on f6 blocks the queen's pressure on g7, and Bg5 pins the knight. If Black plays h6, White can take on h6, forcing the queen to e8 and exposing the weakness of the c7 pawn.
notes.teaches: Timing matters: a move like Bg5 can be ineffective in one position but strong in another. Here, the pin on the knight and the threat to the h6 pawn create concrete weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Bg5, if h6, Bxh6 forces Qe8, then White can target the undefended c7 pawn with ideas like Nb5 or Qb3.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5, attacking the c7 pawn. Black cannot defend it easily because the queen is on e8 and the rook is on f8. If Rc8, White takes on a7 and returns to b5, or simply takes on c7. The knight on b5 is excellent, freezing Black's position.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is forced to a passive square, look for undefended pawns to attack. A knight on b5 can be a powerful outpost, tying down Black's pieces.
notes.plans: White will capture the c7 pawn, gaining material, then consolidate and improve the position before launching a decisive attack.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and now plays e5, opening the center and creating a passed pawn. Black's position is cramped and passive.
notes.teaches: After gaining material, it's important to slow down and make general improving moves. Pushing the e-pawn opens lines and restricts the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: White will continue to improve piece placement, perhaps with Rae1, and target Black's weaknesses. The pawn on e5 is a strong asset.

notes.explains: White plays h4, preparing to kick the knight. This is better than f4 because it doesn't weaken the f4 square and keeps the bishop on h4 active.
notes.teaches: Not all weakening moves are equal. h4 is less weakening than f4 because it doesn't open the king's diagonal. Consider whether the opponent can exploit the weakness in the near future.
notes.plans: White will continue with h5, forcing the knight to move, then build up pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, a good move that challenges White's center. White responds with Bc4+, exploiting the weakened diagonal, and then Nd5, bringing the knight back to a central outpost.
notes.teaches: When an opponent pushes a pawn, look for weakened diagonals and checks. Every pawn move has a drawback. Here, e5 weakened the f7-b3 diagonal, allowing Bc4+.
notes.plans: White will continue with Nd5, threatening to take on f6 and open the e-file. The bishop on e6 will be a monster.

notes.explains: White plays Nd5, a strong centralizing move. The knight on d5 is powerful, and White threatens to take on f6 with the pawn, opening the e-file and x-raying the queen.
notes.teaches: In positions with a material advantage, bring pieces to central outposts. Nd5 is a classic square that controls key squares and supports a kingside attack.
notes.plans: White will play f5 to open lines, or simply improve piece coordination. The bishop on e6 is well-defended and controls the long diagonal.

notes.explains: Black takes on h4, but White has Bxd7, winning a pawn. Black's rook on d8 defends the knight, but White's c7 pawn is still undefended? Actually, White's c7 pawn is already gone. The point is that Black's pieces are disorganized.
notes.teaches: When pieces are hanging, calculate carefully. Here, White's bishop on h4 is semi-hanging, but the trade works in White's favor because of the weak c7 pawn (already captured).
notes.plans: White will continue to consolidate, perhaps with f5 or Rf3, and use the extra pawn to win.

notes.explains: White plays Nxf6, winning the exchange and a pawn. The knight on d5 was powerful, and now White has a clear material advantage.
notes.teaches: Centralized knights can create tactical opportunities. Here, the knight on d5 supported the capture on f6, winning material.
notes.plans: White will simplify to a winning endgame or continue the attack with the extra material.

notes.explains: Black has played d5 to challenge White's center, a principled and ambitious response to the passive Anti-Sicilian setup. White's bishop on b3 is slightly misplaced, and Black's central pawn break gains space.
notes.teaches: When facing passive or unusual openings, the most principled response is often to strike in the center with d5, claiming space and punishing slow development.
notes.plans: After d5, Black can recapture with the knight to preserve pressure on d3, then develop with b6 and Bb7, targeting the d3 pawn.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the knight on d5 is counterintuitive but strong. It keeps the d3 pawn under pressure and allows Black to develop the light-squared bishop to b7, creating a compact, harmonious position.
notes.teaches: In pawn structures where the opponent has a backward pawn on d3, recapturing with a knight can maintain tension and prepare a long-term siege of that pawn.
notes.plans: Follow up with b6 and Bb7, then double rooks on the d-file and aim to play Nc6-e5 to increase pressure on d3.

notes.explains: b6 serves two purposes: it defends the c5 pawn and prepares Bb7, which will target the d3 pawn and support the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When developing, look for moves that accomplish multiple objectives: defense of a pawn and preparation of a strong piece placement.
notes.plans: After Bb7, Black will complete development with Qc7 and Rad8, piling up on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black has completed development and now has a clear plan: double rooks on the d-file and bring the knight to e5 to increase pressure on the d3 pawn. White's position is passive and lacks counterplay.
notes.teaches: When converting an advantage, have a clear plan (here: attacking d3) and make every move serve that plan, either by improving your position, simplifying, or directly advancing the attack.
notes.plans: Play h6 to prevent any back-rank tricks, then Ne5, and if White defends d3, activate the bishop via a5 and Ba6 to force c4, creating further weaknesses.

notes.explains: Ba6 forces White to play c4, which creates a permanent hole on d4 and weakens the d3 pawn further. The bishop has done its job and can later retreat to b7.
notes.teaches: Use a bishop to provoke a weakening pawn move (c4) that creates an outpost for your knight and makes the target pawn more vulnerable.
notes.plans: After c4, the knight can go to d4 or b4, and the rook can occupy d4. The bishop can return to b7 to pressure e4.

notes.explains: With c4 played, the knight jumps to b4, attacking the bishop on a6 and the pawn on d3. White must move the bishop, and Black wins the d3 pawn.
notes.teaches: When a weakness is created, immediately target it with your pieces. The knight on b4 is perfectly placed to exploit the hole on d4 and the weak pawn.
notes.plans: After winning d3, the position collapses. Black can then centralize the queen and rook for a decisive attack.

notes.explains: Black wins the d3 pawn. Now the bishop on a6 is no longer useful (it bites on granite), so it should be redeployed. The plan shifts to attacking the king.
notes.teaches: After achieving a material gain, reassess the position. A piece that has fulfilled its purpose should be moved to a more active square. Here, the bishop returns to b7 to pressure e4.
notes.plans: Retreat the bishop to b7, then prepare an invasion with the queen and rooks. White's king is exposed, and Black can aim for a checkmate or further material gain.

notes.explains: Black has won a pawn and now has a decisive attack. The queen and rook coordinate to threaten mate. White's king is exposed, and Black's pieces dominate.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate your king and centralize your pieces. Here, the queen on d6 attacks h2 and prepares to double rooks or deliver checkmate.
notes.plans: Play Re1 to force the rook trade, then the queen infiltrates. If White blocks with the queen, Black can take on b2 or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5 d5 exf6 dxc4 fxg7 Bxg7 O-O Nd7, White has a choice. The main line is Re1 O-O Bxc6, but here White played Nbd2, which is less common. Black should not panic; the immediate threat is not serious.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar line, stay calm and look for natural developing moves. Don't waste time on unnecessary pawn moves like a6; instead, castle or develop a piece.
notes.plans: Black can consider f6 to challenge the e5 pawn, or the solid Nd7-b8 to reinforce the knight and prepare c5. Both are playable.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to challenge the e5 pawn, which is a key structural point. The pawn on e5 restricts Black's pieces and cuts off the sixth rank. Removing it is a logical priority.
notes.teaches: A pawn that cramps your position is a target. Sometimes it's worth investing a tempo to eliminate it, even if it opens lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: After exf6 Bxf6, Black has a comfortable position with active bishops and pressure on d4. The d4 pawn is a potential target.

notes.explains: Black plays Nxe5, attacking the queen and threatening to win the e6 pawn. White's king is exposed and White's pieces are poorly coordinated. Taking on e5 twice would be a mistake.
notes.teaches: Don't be seduced by material gains if your king is unsafe and your pieces are undeveloped. Activity and king safety often outweigh a pawn.
notes.plans: Black aims to exploit White's weak king and undeveloped pieces. The e6 pawn is a target, but the main idea is to build an attack.

notes.explains: Black plays g6 to avoid a tricky line where White plays Nf5, Bxe6, and then f4-f5 trapping the bishop. This is a practical decision to keep the game complex.
notes.teaches: When calculation reveals a dangerous forced line, it's often better to deviate even if the alternative is less clear. Practical chances matter.
notes.plans: Black will try to consolidate and eventually win the e6 pawn. The king goes to g7 to avoid knight forks.

notes.explains: In this endgame, Black is down the exchange but has a powerful passed pawn on d3. The key is to keep the pawn alive and active pieces. White's rook is passive because Black's knight on c2 controls e1 and a1.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn is a huge asset, especially in the endgame. Keep it protected and use it to tie down enemy pieces. Piece activity is often more important than material.
notes.plans: Black aims to push the d-pawn further, activate the king, and create threats against White's king. The knight on c2 is a star, restricting the rook.

notes.explains: Black's king becomes very active, marching to d4. White's king is stuck on f1, and Black's pieces dominate. The passed pawn on d3 is a constant threat.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate your king! A centralized king is a powerful piece. Use it to support pawns and attack enemy weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will try to create a second passed pawn or force a decisive penetration. The immediate threat is mate or winning the rook.

notes.explains: a5 pushes the pawn to create pressure on Black's queenside, especially targeting the b6 pawn. Black's ...c5 weakened d6 and b6, making a5 even stronger.
notes.teaches: Advancing a pawn to the fifth rank can cramp the opponent and create targets; combine with rook lifts or piece pressure.
notes.plans: After a5, consider Rfd1 to support the center and prepare d5 or tactical blows like Nc6.

notes.explains: Rfd1 is an improving move that x-rays the queen, supports the center, and increases tension without changing the pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Place rooks on open or semi-open files that also support central pawns; such flexible moves maximize pressure.
notes.plans: Wait for Black to commit; if ...Ne8, then a6! wins the exchange due to the rook on d1.

notes.explains: Black's ...Ne8 cut the rooks' connection, making a6! winning the exchange because the rook on a8 is undefended and the pawn on b7 is pinned.
notes.teaches: Pressure creates tactical opportunities; wait for the opponent to weaken their coordination before striking.
notes.plans: After winning the exchange, convert by centralizing pieces and exploiting Black's shattered pawn structure.

notes.explains: After Bd2, Black may try Qe5+ forking king and rook, but White has Qe2 pinning the black queen to the king, forcing a queen trade and winning.
notes.teaches: When the e-file is open, always consider checks on e2/e7 and pins that can force favorable queen trades.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, pinning the queen; if Black takes the rook, the king is in check, so Black must trade queens, leaving White up a piece.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2, pinning the black queen. Black cannot take the rook because the king would be in check. The queen trade is forced, leaving White with a winning material advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin that forces a queen trade, do it; simplifying when up material is a key winning technique.
notes.plans: After Qe2, Black must trade queens or lose the queen; White then consolidates and wins.

notes.explains: After queen trade, White's king is in the center. Black's king is still on e8, and White can castle long to activate the rook and keep the king safe.
notes.teaches: In endgames with queens off, centralizing the king is often good, and castling long can be efficient to activate the rook.
notes.plans: Castle long (O-O-O) to bring the rook to the d-file and keep the king safe.

notes.explains: Black plays Qe7+ to force a queen trade. White can take and then castle long, activating the rook. Black's king is stuck in the center with no development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no development, centralizing your king and activating rooks can lead to a quick win.
notes.plans: After Kxe7, castle long (O-O-O) and then attack the exposed black king.

notes.explains: White castles long, centralizing the rook on d1. Black's king is exposed and Black has no developed pieces. White can now deliver checkmate threats.
notes.teaches: In endgames, activating the rook via castling can be more efficient than moving the king manually.
notes.plans: Play Bb4+ to force the king to e8, then Re1+ and continue the attack.

notes.explains: White wins the rook on b7. Black's king is still exposed, and White has multiple checkmate threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for concrete wins of material or checkmate; don't overcomplicate.
notes.plans: Continue the attack; for example, play Bc5+ or other checks to force mate.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Re8#. The bishop on c5 cuts off f8, the rook on e8 gives check, and the king has no escape squares.
notes.teaches: Pattern recognition: when the king is trapped on the back rank with limited squares, a rook check along the e-file can be mate.

notes.explains: In the Danish Gambit, the main line for Black is ...d5, sacrificing back a pawn to accelerate development. After Bxd5, Nf6 attacks the bishop, and White must be careful not to lose it.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, returning a pawn for quick development is a common equalizing strategy.

notes.explains: A tricky line: after Bxf7+ Kxf7, Qb3+ wins back the bishop, but Black can play ...d5 and develop with tempo, leaving White's queen misplaced.
notes.teaches: Changing the order of moves can give the opponent extra defensive resources; always check if the opponent has a strong reply.

notes.explains: After ...Qe7, White can play Qe2 to break the pin and renew the threat of exf6. If Black plays ...d5, then exf6 wins a piece because the queen on e2 attacks the knight.
notes.teaches: When your opponent pins a piece, look for ways to break the pin with a queen move that also creates threats.

notes.explains: In the endgame after queen trade, Black's king is stuck in the center with no development. White's active pieces and central king give a winning attack.
notes.teaches: Even in endgames, an exposed king can be mated if the opponent has no developed pieces.

notes.explains: Black blunders with b5, allowing White to win a pawn. White recaptures with the knight (not the queen) to keep the queen on d3, which eyes h7 and supports a future rook lift.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider piece placement. The queen on d3 is centralized and creates tactical threats along the diagonal.
notes.plans: After Qd3, look to bring the knight to f5 via the maneuver Nb5-d4-f5.

notes.explains: The knight goes to f5, the ideal square, pressuring g7. Even if Black plays g6, Nf5 is still strong because after gxf5, Rg3 is devastating.
notes.teaches: The knight on f5 is a classic attacking outpost. Don't be afraid to sacrifice it if the resulting attack is decisive.
notes.plans: After Nf5, prepare to sacrifice on g7 or lift the rook to g3.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop on g7 to open the king. After Bxg7, Kxg7, then Rg3+ forces the king to f8, and Rg8+ deflects the king to g8, allowing Qg7#.
notes.teaches: The deflection sacrifice on g7 is a classic attacking pattern. Sacrifice to open the king's shelter and then deliver mate.
notes.plans: After Bxg7, play Rg3, then Rg8+ to force mate.

notes.explains: The game ends with a classic mate: rook sacrifice on g8 forces the king to g8, then queen delivers mate on g7.
notes.teaches: This is a standard attacking idea: sacrifice the rook to deflect the king, then mate with the queen.

notes.explains: White's c3 is mediocre because it reinforces the knight but takes the c3 square away from the knight, leading to passive development.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, black develops naturally with Nf6, castling, and then d5 in one go, often skipping d6.
notes.plans: Black will fianchetto the bishop and apply pressure on white's center.

notes.explains: White's Be3 is a common setup. Black should immediately consider the tactical idea of Ng4, attacking the bishop and threatening Qb6, hitting f2 and b2.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a bishop on e3, always be alert for Ng4 and Qb6 double attacks. This is a standard tactical motif in Sicilian structures.
notes.plans: Play Ng4, then Qb6 to put pressure on f2 and b2, exploiting the absence of the c-pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, forking b2 and f2. White must defend f2, so Black captures on b2. The queen is safe on b2 because it has multiple escape routes (a3, c5, etc.) and cannot be trapped easily.
notes.teaches: When deciding to grab a pawn with the queen, assess escape squares. If the queen has multiple retreats and the opponent cannot cut them off in one move, the risk is often worth it.
notes.plans: After taking on b2, consolidate the queen by moving it to c5 or d6, or bring the knight back to e5 to centralize.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng5, hitting the bishop and centralizing the knight. This is better than keeping the knight on g4 where it is loose. The queen on c5 defends e7.
notes.teaches: When your knight has done its job on the rim, bring it back to the center. Centralized knights are more powerful and less vulnerable.
notes.plans: Prepare to consolidate with d6 or h6, chasing away white's active pieces.

notes.explains: Black finally plays d6, now that e7 is defended. This opens the light-squared bishop and solidifies the center. White's h4 is a strong attacking move, opening the kingside.
