notes.teaches: When Black plays e6, the knight on b5 becomes a powerful outpost. It threatens Nc7+ and forces Black to react.
notes.plans: Play Na3, then Nb5. If Black plays Qd8, then Qxd4 or Nxd4. If Black plays Na6, then White has a pleasant endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, a solid move that prepares kingside development (Be7, O-O) and leaves the c8 bishop for later. White now has a choice: standard development or the aggressive Na3.
notes.teaches: Against e6, White's most promising plan is Na3, with three ideas: (1) Nb5 threatening Nc7 fork, (2) preparing Bc4 with tempo, and (3) if Black plays a6, Nc4 targets the weak b6 square.
notes.plans: White plays Na3, intending Nb5 or Nc4 depending on Black's response. If Black allows Nb5, White follows with Bf4 to pressure c7.

notes.explains: After dxc5 Qxd1+ Kxd1, White has an extra pawn but the king is in the center. Black's best is e5 or Bg4. The endgame is tricky but favorable for White due to the c5 pawn and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to enter an endgame with the king exposed if you have a pawn advantage and active pieces. The king can often find safety later.
notes.plans: Develop quickly, aiming to secure the c5 pawn or trade it for positional gains. Na3 and Nb5 is a common plan.

notes.explains: e5 is a common move, trying to challenge White's center. White should play b4, gaining space and threatening to develop with tempo. If Black plays e4, the knight can go to d4.
notes.teaches: When Black pushes e5, respond with b4 to gain space on the queenside. This is a typical Alapin idea.
notes.plans: Play b4, then develop the bishop to e3 or b5. The king can go to c1 or b2 for safety.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight. White's best is Be3, developing and protecting the c5 pawn. If Black plays Nc5, then Bxc5 is possible, but the engine prefers Bc4.
notes.teaches: When Black pins the knight, develop the bishop to e3 to support the center and the c5 pawn. Be aware of tactical nuances like ...Nxe3 fxe3.
notes.plans: Play Be3, then consider h3 to drive the bishop away. If Black takes on f3, recapture with the pawn and use the open g-file.

notes.explains: Bd2 is a passive but recently popular move; White intends to recapture on c3 with the bishop to preserve queenside pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black often trades the bishop for the knight on c3 to weaken White's control over e4.
notes.plans: Black will develop with b6, Bb7, d6, and Nbd7, creating a solid, flexible setup.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, preparing Bb7 and a solid setup. This is a standard Nimzo-Indian plan, avoiding d5 which would be less thematic.
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian setup with b6, Bb7, d6, and Nbd7 is solid because it creates no weaknesses and gives Black easy development.
notes.plans: Continue with Bb7, d6, Nbd7, then consider either Qe7 followed by e5, or the more aggressive Ne4 and f5.

notes.explains: Black puts a knight on e4, a natural outpost. This is a typical idea in many openings, often followed by f5 to support the knight and start a kingside attack.
notes.teaches: A knight on e4 supported by f5 is a classic attacking structure; it pressures White and can lead to a kingside initiative.
notes.plans: After Ne4, play f5 to reinforce the knight and prepare further kingside expansion.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes the bishop to g7, but this is slow and the bishop will bite on White's pawn chain. White has several good moves, including Nc3 or Bc4. Bc4 forces Black to decide between retreating the knight or playing e6, which weakens dark squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is fianchettoed against a pawn chain, it often becomes a 'granite biter'—less effective. Exploit slow development with active piece play.
notes.plans: Play Bc4 to pressure f7 and force Black to weaken the dark squares. If Black plays e6, target the weakened d6 and f6 squares.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2 to avoid queen trades and support the center. This move also prepares to meet Bg4 with a tactical sequence: Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+ Kg8 Qxg4, winning a pawn and exposing Black's king.
notes.teaches: A queen move to e2 can simultaneously support the center, avoid trades, and set up tactical threats against a pin.
notes.plans: After Qe2, continue development with O-O and h3 to prevent Bg4. Then aim to build pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: After both sides castle, White plays h3 to prevent Bg4, which would pin the knight and threaten the center. The knight is an integral defender of the d4 and e5 pawns.
notes.teaches: Prevent pins that target key defenders of your pawn center. A pawn move like h3 can be more important than developing a queenside piece.
notes.plans: After h3, continue with Rook to d1 to support the d4 pawn and prepare to meet Qc7 with Bf4, developing and defending e5.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 attacking e5. White defends with Bf4, which develops the bishop, protects the pawn, and sets up an x-ray against Black's queen. The bishop can later retreat to h2 if needed.
notes.teaches: When defending, look for moves that accomplish multiple tasks: development, defense, and setting up future threats.
notes.plans: After Bf4, develop the queenside with Nc3, and consider Rd1 to pressure the queen. If Black plays Bf5, White can consider g4 to chase the bishop away, but a solid approach is Nc3.

notes.explains: Black plays Rfd8, a mistake. The rook on f8 was protecting f7, so White can now play Bxf7+ Kxf7, followed by e6+ discovering an attack on the queen. Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of which pieces are defending critical squares like f7. Moving a defender can create tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: After Bxf7+, if Kxf7, play e6+ forking king and queen. If Kh8, retreat the bishop to b3, sacrificing the exchange to keep the light-squared bishop active for the attack.

notes.explains: Nbd7 looks like it blunders a pawn (cxd5 Nxd5 Bxd8 Bb4+), but it's a famous trap that wins a piece if White falls for it.
notes.teaches: Setting traps in the opening can punish automatic captures. Always check if the capture leads to a discovered attack or check.
notes.plans: If White avoids the trap with e3, Black develops normally with Be7 and castles.

notes.explains: Be7 unpins the knight and prepares kingside castling. White's bishop on g5 pins the knight, so Black must address the pin before developing further.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are pinned, prioritize unpinning before continuing development. The pin on the knight threatens to win a pawn if not resolved.
notes.plans: Castle short, then decide on the development of the light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: c6 looks passive and hems in the bishop, but it's part of a solid system. Black waits for White to move the light-squared bishop before capturing on c4, winning a tempo.
notes.teaches: Sometimes playing a 'passive' move is part of a deeper plan. Delaying captures until the opponent commits can gain time.
notes.plans: After White moves the bishop (e.g., Bd3), capture on c4 and then play Nd5 to trade dark-squared bishops.

notes.explains: e5 is a key pawn break that frees Black's light-squared bishop and challenges White's center. Black must first capture on c3 to avoid leaving the knight underprotected.
notes.teaches: Pawn breaks like e5 are essential to activate passive pieces and create counterplay. Always ensure your pieces are coordinated before breaking.
notes.plans: After e5, Black will develop the bishop to e6 or f5 and aim for full equality.

notes.explains: Be6 develops the bishop and neutralizes White's bishop. Black has equalized; the position is solid with no weaknesses.
notes.teaches: A position with no weaknesses is hard to crack, even if it looks passive. Solid development and piece coordination are more important than space.
notes.plans: Complete development with Rad8, then consider active play or an endgame.

notes.explains: Black's Nc6 is a slight inaccuracy because after d4 cxd4 cxd4, White threatens d5, kicking the knight. Without pawn support, the knight lacks a foothold and can be driven back or trapped.
notes.teaches: In the opening, pawns should lead the way; bringing out knights before supporting pawns allows the opponent to chase them with tempo.
notes.plans: White will push d5 to gain space and displace the knight, then develop with Nf3 and Nc3.

notes.explains: Black's best response is d5, counterstriking in the center. After exd5 Qxd5, White must defend the d4 pawn with Nf3, not Nc3 (which hangs d4).
notes.teaches: When the queen appears early, prioritize protecting your central pawn over attacking the queen; Nf3 develops and defends d4 simultaneously.
notes.plans: After Nf3, White will develop Nc3, gaining a tempo on the queen, and then push d5 to create an isolated queen pawn (IQP) structure.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bg4, threatening to win the d4 pawn. The intuitive Be2 is too slow; White must play Nc3 immediately, forcing the queen to move.
notes.teaches: When the queen is on d5, Nc3 forces it away, and if it retreats, d5 becomes a devastating pawn push, kicking the knight and opening lines against the uncastled king.
notes.plans: Play Nc3, and if the queen moves, push d5 to gain space and create threats like Bb5+ or Qa4+.

notes.explains: Black's queen retreats to a5. White should immediately push d5, kicking the knight, because delaying allows black to play e6, blunting the pawn push.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the pawn push d5 is a critical lever; play it before black can solidify with e6.
notes.plans: Push d5, forcing the knight to move, then exploit the open lines with Bb5+ or Qa4+ to harass the black king.

notes.explains: Black's knight goes to e5. White can play Bb5+ to force the king to move or block, exploiting black's lack of development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, checks and tempo-gaining moves can create a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Play Bb5+, forcing either Kd8 (disastrous) or a block that weakens black's position further.

notes.explains: Black's king is forced to d8, a terrible square. White has a massive lead in development and can continue with Qe2 or Nxe5, opening lines.
notes.teaches: When the king is forced to the center, every tempo counts; bring out pieces quickly and avoid trading queens unless it wins material.
notes.plans: Develop with Qe2 or Nxe5, then castle and bring rooks to open files to attack the exposed king.

notes.explains: Black castles queenside, but the king on c8 is vulnerable due to the open c-file. White can play Bd2 to unpin the pawn and set up an x-ray against the queen.
notes.teaches: Queenside castling in an open c-file is risky; use the open file to attack the king with rook to c1.
notes.plans: Play Bd2, threatening to win the queen or force a favorable trade, then bring the rook to c1.

notes.explains: Bd2 unpins the d5 pawn and threatens Nxb5, attacking the queen. Black must deal with this threat, often by moving the queen or playing e6.
notes.teaches: Simple developing moves with a threat are often stronger than flashy tactics; they maintain pressure without risk.
notes.plans: After black responds, continue developing with Bc4 or O-O, preparing to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: Black exchanges bishop for knight. White can recapture with the queen (Qxf3) or the g-pawn (gxf3). Qxf3 is positionally sound, keeping pawn structure intact, while gxf3 opens lines for attack.
notes.teaches: When deciding between recaptures, consider pawn structure and king safety; gxf3 can be aggressive but weakens the kingside.
notes.plans: If Qxf3, centralize the queen to e4 or f5, pressuring the knight and preventing counterplay. If gxf3, use the open g-file for attack.

notes.explains: Black's knight jumps to e5, attacking the queen. White can play Qe4 or Qf5, both centralizing the queen and threatening the knight.
notes.teaches: Centralize the queen to active squares where it cannot be easily attacked; avoid giving the opponent tempo with pointless queen moves.
notes.plans: Play Qe4, covering c2 and attacking the knight; if the knight retreats, continue developing with Bd3 or O-O.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to d7. White should avoid automatic moves like Bb5, which allows black to trade queens and ease the defense. Instead, play Bd3, developing and preparing Nxb5.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, prefer simple, solid moves that maintain pressure; avoid trades that relieve the opponent's congestion.
notes.plans: Play Bd3, reinforcing the threat of Nxb5, then castle kingside and bring the rook to e1 to attack the black king.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop and castle. White should continue developing with O-O, then bring the rook to e1, targeting the e7 pawn and the king.
notes.teaches: Patience is key; keep building pressure with simple moves like castling and rook activation. The opponent will eventually crack under the strain.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then play Re1, threatening to open the e-file. If black castles, the e-file attack remains strong.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes and is close to castling. White must prevent this. A good move is Be3, forcing the queen to a worse square, or Re1, doubling on the e-file.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is about to complete development, use prophylactic moves to disrupt their plans. Blocking the e-file with Be3 can be counterintuitive but effective if it forces the queen to a bad square.
notes.plans: Play Be3, attacking the queen. If the queen moves to b6 or d8, follow with Bd4, dominating the long diagonal and pressuring the knight.

notes.explains: Black's queen goes to b6. White can play Bd4, attacking the queen and threatening to win the knight on d7. The bishop on d4 is powerful on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on long diagonals where they pressure the opponent's pieces and restrict the king's escape.
notes.plans: Play Bd4, forcing the queen to move. If the queen takes on b2, White has tactical resources like Qc7 or Rc1 to win material.

notes.explains: White plays a3 as a waiting move, avoiding commitment of the dark-squared bishop. Black can choose between e6 or e5 setups; here Black opts for a Dragon-style setup (g6, Bg7) to exploit the potential weakness on a3.
notes.teaches: A waiting move like a3 can be met by switching to a different system that targets the new weakness. The 'Dragodorf' (Najdorf + Dragon) uses the a3 pawn as a hook for queenside play.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Bg7, d6, Nbd7, and prepare queenside expansion with b5, while keeping the king flexible.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne4, the principled response, challenging the bishop immediately. White often replies h4 (Hodgson variation), intending to recapture with the h-pawn if Black takes on g5, opening the h-file and freezing Black's kingside pawns.
notes.teaches: In the Trompowsky, Ne4 is a sharp, principled move that forces White to commit. If White plays h4, Black should not take on g5, as that plays into White's plan.
notes.plans: Black should aim to undermine White's center and exploit the weakened kingside. A simple plan is to play d5, then retreat the knight to f6, reaching a solid Queen's Gambit Declined structure.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to f6 after provoking h4. White's extra tempo has been spent on a weakening pawn move, so Black's piece maneuver is justified. The position resembles a reversed Queen's Gambit Declined.
notes.teaches: Moving the same piece multiple times is acceptable if you provoke a weakness (like h4) and the center remains closed. The extra tempi spent by the opponent on weakening moves offset the loss of time.
notes.plans: Black will play e6 and then c5 to contest the center, exploiting White's passive development. The light-squared bishop can be developed later via d7 or b7.

notes.explains: After Bb5+ Bd7 Be2 Nxd5, Black's bishop on d7 is awkward, cutting communication between Black's pieces. White is already up a pawn with no compensation.
notes.teaches: A check followed by a retreat can force the opponent into a passive setup, especially when the bishop blocks its own pieces.
notes.plans: White should develop naturally with d4, Nf3, and castle, maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: White has played d4 and developed naturally. Black's last move Nc6 threatens ...Nb4, but White can defend with c3. The move c4 would be risky due to ...Bg4 pinning the knight and tactics on d4.
notes.teaches: When the center is fluid, avoid weakening pawn moves like c4 that create targets. Instead, solidifying with c3 protects the d4 pawn and restricts Black's knight.
notes.plans: Play c3 to secure d4, then continue development with Bg5 or Nbd2, followed by Rfe1.

notes.explains: White chooses the Tarrasch Variation (Nbd2) over the main line Nc3 to avoid excessive theory while still fighting for an advantage.
notes.teaches: The Tarrasch Variation strikes a balance between theoretical depth and practical venom, making it suitable for players who want a manageable but dangerous repertoire.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, aiming for a closed center and a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After castling, White has a small but stable advantage. The knight on f3 supports d4 and prepares kingside play.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece activity and central control matter more than space. White's setup is flexible and can transition to attack or positional play.
notes.plans: Prepare to meet ...f6 with Re1, and consider maneuvering the knight to g3 via Nf1.

notes.explains: Black's ...a5 and ...Nb4 aim for queenside play, but White's bishop retreats to b1, keeping pressure on h7 and preparing a rook lift via a3.
notes.teaches: A retreating move can be strong if it maintains long-range influence. The bishop on b1 still targets h7 and enables future attacking ideas.
notes.plans: Play Nf1 to reroute the knight to g3, then consider h4 and Ng5 to build a kingside attack.

notes.explains: White maneuvers the knight from d2 to f1, heading for g3. This unclogs the position and brings the knight closer to the kingside.
notes.teaches: In closed centers, you have time for slow maneuvers. The knight on g3 can jump to h5, threatening sacrifices on g7 or f6.
notes.plans: Continue with Ng3, then consider h4 and Ng5 to open the h-file and launch a mating attack.

notes.explains: Black plays ...f6 to open the center and challenge White's kingside plans. White must respond accurately, balancing attack and defense.
notes.teaches: When the opponent strikes in the center, you must decide whether to maintain tension or capture. Here, exf6 is correct to avoid losing the e5 pawn.
notes.plans: After exf6, consider Bg5 to pressure the e5 square and prepare a positional squeeze, or look for tactical opportunities like a Greek gift sacrifice.

notes.explains: White plays b4 to lure Black's c-pawn away from c5, aiming to occupy the center with d4. This gambit is dubious; Black can achieve an advantage with accurate play.
notes.teaches: In gambits, the key is to accept the pawn when it doesn't compromise your development, but be wary of moves that give White extra tempos.
notes.plans: Black should consider capturing with the pawn (cxb4) rather than the knight, to avoid allowing White to gain time with c3.

notes.explains: After cxb4, White typically plays d4. Black must avoid being overrun in the center. The immediate d5 by Black is natural, but it can lead to a queen sortie that White can harass.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, contesting the center early is crucial, but be careful not to expose your queen to attacks that lose time.
notes.plans: Black can play d5, but after exd5 Qxd5, White may play c4 attacking the queen. Black should be ready to retreat the queen or find a safe square.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, but this can lead to positions where White's pawns become powerful. An alternative is d6, which is more modest but avoids sharp theory and forces White to think for themselves.
notes.teaches: When you are unfamiliar with the theory of a sharp line, a solid, slightly inferior move can be a practical choice to avoid prepared lines.
notes.plans: After d6, Black aims to develop pieces and keep the center closed, preventing White's pawns from advancing too quickly.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, a modest move that prevents White's e-pawn from advancing easily. White has only one piece developed, so Black is not far behind in development.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet move that stops the opponent's plans is better than a flashy one that opens lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: Black will develop the knight to f6, fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, and castle kingside, aiming to neutralize White's center later.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to b2, eyeing the long diagonal. Black's pawn on d6 is a weakness, but Black should not play f6 as it hinders development.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening pawn moves that impede your piece development. Instead, focus on developing with threats.
notes.plans: Black should play Nf6, attacking e4 and forcing White to react. This is a natural developing move that also creates counterplay.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. White may respond with Qd4, attacking the knight and the g7 pawn. Black must be careful not to lose the g7 pawn.
notes.teaches: When your opponent threatens multiple things, prioritize the most dangerous threat. Here, defending g7 is crucial to avoid king-side collapse.
notes.plans: Black should retreat the knight to f6 (or possibly d6) to defend g7. Then continue development with g6 and Bg7.

notes.explains: Black played Nd7, a passive developing move that doesn't challenge White's center. White can close the center with e5, leading to a favorable French-like structure where Black's knight on d7 is poorly placed.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a passive move, consider closing the center to deny them counterplay and exploit their poor piece placement.
notes.plans: Solidify the pawn chain with c3 and f4, then develop naturally with Nf3 and Bd3.

notes.explains: Black attacks the base of the pawn chain with c5. White reinforces with c3 to prevent the chain from dissolving, which would leave White's position vulnerable.
notes.teaches: In closed center positions, protect your pawn chain with pawns to maintain structural integrity and prevent your opponent from undermining it.
notes.plans: Continue with f4 to support the chain and open a developing square for the knight.

notes.explains: White plays f4 to solidify the pawn chain and prepare Nf3. The bishop on c1 can later develop to e3 or d2, supporting the center.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, prioritize reinforcing your pawn chain and developing pieces to natural squares. Not every piece needs to be active immediately.
notes.plans: Develop Nf3, then Bd3, and consider Be3 or Bf2 to overprotect d4.

notes.explains: After d4 d5 e4 dxe4, White often plays f3 to try to regain the pawn, but the best response for Black is to counterstrike in the center with e5.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, counterattacking in the center is often the best way to refute it, rather than passively defending.
notes.plans: If White takes on e5, Black recaptures with the queen, leaving White uncastled and Black with quick development. If White doesn't take, Black can develop naturally.

notes.explains: After d4 d5 e4 dxe4 Nc3 Nf6 f3, Black should not take on f3 immediately. Instead, Black should develop with Nc6, counterattacking the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, it's often better to ignore the offered pawn and focus on development and counterplay, rather than grabbing material at the cost of activity.
notes.plans: Black plays Nc6, threatening the d4 pawn. If White pushes d5, the knight slides to e5, a strong outpost. Black can then continue developing with Bf5 or e6.

notes.explains: White played Bf4 instead of the better d5, allowing Black to take the pawn on d4. White's center collapses and Black gets a clear material advantage.
notes.teaches: When your opponent insists on sacrificing a pawn without compensation, take it. Don't be afraid to accept material when there's no clear compensation.
notes.plans: Black captures on d4, then develops naturally. White's knight on b5 is a mistake; Black can trade pieces and simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Bf5 looks good because it develops and defends the e4 pawn, but it's vulnerable to pawn advances. White can play g4 and g5, attacking the bishop and winning the e4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Developing pieces without moving pawns can make them targets. Be wary of pawn storms that can trample your pieces, especially when they are not supported by other pawns.
notes.plans: White plays g4, forcing the bishop to move, then g5, winning the e4 pawn. Black is still okay but has no reason to allow this.

notes.explains: After White's mistake of Nb5, Black can play c6, attacking the bishop and preparing to develop. Black is up two pawns and has a dominant position.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for moves that consolidate your position and prevent counterplay. c6 attacks the bishop and prepares development.
notes.plans: After c6, Black can play Bd7 or even Ke8 to move the king away from the center, then develop the other bishop and rook.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, attacking the e4 pawn. White can take on e5, but the knight on e4 looks strong. However, it can be attacked with moves like Bc4 or Qe2.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight can be intimidating, but it's vulnerable if it can be attacked by pawns or pieces. Look for ways to challenge it rather than fear it.
notes.plans: White plays Bc4, preventing d5 and threatening Qd5. If Black plays c6, White can play Qe2, pinning the knight and preventing d5.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6 to immediately target the d4 pawn. The idea is not to take on c4 (which allows d5), but to apply indirect pressure by attacking the defenders of d4.
notes.teaches: Attacking a pawn can mean either direct pressure or indirect pressure on the pieces that defend it.
notes.plans: Follow up with e5 or Bg4 to challenge the knight on f3 and weaken White's pawn structure.

notes.explains: Bg4 pins the knight on f3, threatening to take it and ruin White's pawn structure, which weakens the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Pinning a defender to weaken a key pawn is a common tactical motif.
notes.plans: After Bxf3, recapture with exf3 to double White's pawns and create a target on d4.

notes.explains: After cxd5, Black recaptures with the queen (Qxd5) rather than the knight, because Nxd5 would allow Nc3 with tempo. Qxd5 attacks d4 and forces White to defend it.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece is more active or creates threats. The queen recapture keeps pressure on the center.
notes.plans: Follow up with e5 to challenge the d4 pawn further, or develop with Nf6 and Bb4.

notes.explains: Black captures on d4, opening the c3 square for White's knight. White refrains from the tempting Bc4 because of Qe4+; instead, Nb5 is the correct intermezzo, threatening Nc7 fork.
notes.teaches: When a fork is threatened, do not automatically recapture. Look for intermediate moves that maintain or increase the threat. Here Nb5 is stronger than Bc4 because it keeps the fork alive.
notes.plans: After Nb5, Black must defend c7. If Black plays Bd6, White can respond with Bc4, exploiting the pin on the d-file and threatening to win material.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, a patient developing move that maintains the pressure. Black's queen on e4 is vulnerable, and the bishop on d6 is still hanging due to the fork threat. White will recapture on d4 after Black deals with the threats.
notes.teaches: Patience in attack is crucial. Instead of forcing immediate tactics, complete development while maintaining threats. Be3 is both developing and keeps the pressure on Black's disorganized pieces.
notes.plans: White will soon recapture on d4 with the knight, gaining a huge lead in development. Black's king is stuck in the center, and White's pieces coordinate perfectly.

notes.explains: Black plays Ke7, a desperate move to unpin the bishop and avoid the fork. White now has the simple Nxd6, winning the bishop pair and driving the king to d6, where it remains exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, exchanging to win the bishop pair is often strong. The king on d6 is a permanent target, and White's lead in development becomes decisive.
notes.plans: White plays Nxd6+ Kxd6, then Nxd4, threatening Nf5+ and a devastating attack. Black cannot take on g2 due to Nf5+ leading to mate.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d4 with the knight, threatening Nf5+. Black's king on d6 is a sitting duck. White now castles to unpin the bishop and bring the rook into play.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by castling and activating rooks. Do not rush for a knockout; instead, improve your position and let the opponent's weaknesses tell.
notes.plans: White castles, then plays Re1 to harass the queen and open the e-file. The immediate threat is Nf5+, but White must first unpin the bishop on e3.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, hoping to dislodge the knight. White responds with Bg5, pinning the knight on f6 and forcing the queen to move. The queen has few safe squares that keep contact with e5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create counterplay, use pins and threats to maintain pressure. Bg5 is strong because it forces the queen away while also pinning the knight.
notes.plans: After Bg5, Black's queen must move to g6 or g4. White then captures on e5, forcing the king back to f8, followed by Ne6+ forking the rook on d8 and leading to mate.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, which is not the most challenging move. Black now recaptures with the knight on d5, achieving the goal of the line: a comfortable recapture without exposing the queen.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with a knight instead of the queen can be advantageous when the queen would become a target. Always consider piece development and king safety when choosing recaptures.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming for a solid IQP structure if White plays d4.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, putting pressure on the knight on d5. Black responds with Nb6, stepping back to force the bishop to commit and increasing control over the d5 square.
notes.teaches: Retreating a piece can be a strong positional move if it improves control over key squares. Here, Nb6 prepares for an IQP structure by dominating d5.
notes.plans: Black will develop the light-squared bishop to f5 before playing e6, then bring the b8 knight to c6. The order prevents White from playing d5 in response to Bf5.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to b5, putting pressure on the knight that defends the e5 pawn. This indirectly attacks the pawn and is the start of the Spanish Game.
notes.teaches: Develop your pieces to active squares where they exert pressure. A bishop on b5 can target the knight and, indirectly, the pawn it defends.
notes.plans: Black will play a6 to ask the bishop what it intends to do.

notes.explains: White captures on c6, entering the Exchange Variation. Black must recapture wisely: taking with the d-pawn opens the bishop and prepares queen d4, which punishes any greedy Nxe5 by forking the knight and pawn.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider opening lines for your pieces. The 'capture toward the center' rule is a guideline, not an absolute; weigh the concrete consequences.
notes.plans: After dxc6, Black will play f6 to defend e5, a solid old main line.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, violating the 'never play f6' rule. However, here it is justified because Black needs to keep the center closed and avoid opening lines for White's pieces, given Black's lag in development.
notes.teaches: General principles like 'don't move f-pawn' can be broken when the specific needs of the position demand it. Here, keeping the center closed outweighs the king safety concern.
notes.plans: Black will aim to keep the center closed and trade queens to reduce White's attacking chances.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight on f3 with Bg4. This is a strong response because it prevents White from opening the center with dxe5 and also develops a piece.
notes.teaches: Pins are a powerful tactical weapon. A bishop pinning a knight to the queen restricts the knight's movement and can be used to maintain tension.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming to castle and then consider how to handle the pin.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to d6, defending the e5 pawn and preparing to castle. This is the old main line, solid and simple.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize development and king safety. Bd6 is a natural developing move that also protects the pawn.
notes.plans: Black will complete development with Nf6 (or Nh6) and castle.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to h6, which looks awkward but is necessary to allow castling. Knights on the rim are generally worse, but here it's a temporary measure.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must accept a suboptimal piece placement to achieve a more important goal, like castling. The knight can later be rerouted.
notes.plans: Black will castle next move, then consider how to improve the knight.

notes.explains: When White pushes h3, Black retreats the bishop to h5 instead of exchanging. The pin on the knight is valuable, so preserving it is correct.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves are not inherently bad. If a piece is doing a useful job (like pinning), it's often better to retreat than to trade it away.
notes.plans: Black will continue development and castle, maintaining the pin.

notes.explains: White plays Qb3, setting up an x-ray against the black king and unpinning the knight. Black must address both the threat of Nxd6+ and the pressure on e5.
notes.teaches: An x-ray attack can be as dangerous as a direct threat. When the opponent unpins a piece, be alert for discovered checks or other tactics.
notes.plans: Black should find a move that simultaneously protects e5 and blocks the x-ray. Bf7 is one idea, but it allows Ng5. The best move is to trade queens or defend accurately.

notes.explains: Black plays Bf7 to block the x-ray and defend e5, but White responds with Ng5, attacking the bishop and threatening Nxf7. Black must find a way to avoid losing material.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks a defender, you need to either move the defender, defend it, or counterattack. Here, Black can play b5 to attack the knight and force White to capture on f7.
notes.plans: Black plays b5, forcing White to take on f7. After Rxf7, Black recaptures with the pawn to improve pawn structure.

notes.explains: White plays e3 and Bc4, neglecting central pawn control. Black immediately strikes with d5, attacking the bishop and gaining space.
notes.teaches: Balance pawn control and piece development. Overemphasizing development without a solid pawn center leaves pieces vulnerable to pawn attacks.
notes.plans: After d5, Black can develop naturally with Nf6, Bd6, and castle, aiming to exploit White's weak center.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to f6, supporting the d5 pawn. White's bishop retreats to b3. Black should avoid overextending with c5 and instead focus on piece play.
notes.teaches: Controlling the center is a balance between pawns and pieces. Don't overextend with too many pawns; develop pieces to support them.
notes.plans: Play c6 to solidify the pawn chain, then Bd6, supporting e5 and preparing kingside attacks. The knight can go to d7 if c6 is occupied.

notes.explains: Black plays c6, defending d5 with a pawn and preparing Bd6. This follows the principle of using the least valuable piece for defensive tasks.
notes.teaches: When supporting a pawn, prefer a pawn over a piece if possible. This keeps pieces flexible for more important roles. A pawn chain is robust.
notes.plans: Follow with Bd6, then castle. The knight can go to d7 if needed; c6 is not a concession.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to d6, supporting e5 and eyeing the kingside. White plays Ng5, a typical but harmless move since f7 is not under threat.
notes.teaches: Don't fear a knight on g5 if it doesn't threaten anything. Often it becomes a target. Ignore it and continue development; you can attack it later with h6 when it gains more.
notes.plans: Castle kingside. If White plays e4, Black can play h6 attacking the knight, then capture on e4 with advantage.

notes.explains: Black castles, ignoring the knight on g5. White plays e4, trying to expand, but Black can now attack with h6, winning a tempo.
notes.teaches: Reserve moves like h6 for when they gain something. Playing it immediately might not be as effective. Timing is crucial.
notes.plans: Play h6, forcing the knight to move. Then capture on e4, as the pawn is now undefended. Black's pieces are active, White's king is stuck in the center.

notes.explains: Black captures on e4, simplifying. White's pieces are uncoordinated, and Black has a strong center. The queen is hemmed in on d1.
notes.teaches: When unsure about a tactical sequence, a simple capture can be a good practical choice. Avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Play Bg4, attacking the queen. White must either retreat the knight or play f3, weakening the kingside. Either way, Black gains a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight and attacking the queen. White's queen has no safe squares, leading to material loss.
notes.teaches: Exploit an opponent's undeveloped queenside by attacking the queen. A hemmed-in queen is a major weakness.
notes.plans: After White's response (e.g., f3), capture on f3, opening lines. Black's attack is overwhelming.

notes.opening: Four Knights Scotch, Deferred Latvian Gambit
notes.explains: Black's early f5 creates permanent kingside weaknesses. White should not play passively (like d3) nor accept the gambit with exf5, which gives Black a tempo. The correct response is d4, opening the center to exploit Black's weak king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn push like f5, the best way to punish it is to open the center immediately, not to play defensively or grab material.
notes.plans: After d4, if exd4 then Nxd4; if fxe4 then Nxe5. In either case, White gains a strong attack.

notes.opening: Four Knights Scotch, Deferred Latvian Gambit
notes.explains: After Nxd4, Black may try Nxd4? but then Qxd4 leaves the queen powerfully centralized. If Black instead plays fxe4, White should not recapture immediately but play Nxe5, offering a knight trade to keep the attack rolling.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, recapturing a pawn automatically can be a mistake. Look for intermediate moves that maintain or increase the initiative.
notes.plans: After Nxe5, if Black recaptures, White's queen checks on h5 and the attack continues. If Black doesn't recapture, White has a big development lead.

notes.opening: Four Knights Scotch, Deferred Latvian Gambit
notes.explains: Black's best try is Nf6, sacrificing the e4 pawn for development. White should not grab the pawn but instead play Bc4, threatening mate on f7 and keeping the pressure.
notes.teaches: When attacking a weak king, developing with threats is often more important than winning material. A simple developing move like Bc4 can be devastating.
notes.plans: After Bc4, Black must defend f7, e.g., with Qe8. White can then continue with simple attacking moves like O-O and Rfe1, gradually increasing the pressure.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense, Four Pawns Attack
notes.explains: Black plays e5 to challenge the center immediately, a sideline that can throw White off if unprepared.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, Black can deviate from main lines with e5 to create immediate tactical complications.
notes.plans: After e5, Black aims to induce weaknesses in White's center and prevent White from castling.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense, Four Pawns Attack
notes.explains: White takes on e5, but this is a mistake because it opens lines for Black. Black should not recapture immediately but instead play c5 to attack the d4 pawn and undermine the knight on c3.
notes.teaches: When White captures on e5, Black should counterattack the center with c5, targeting the d4 pawn which defends the knight on c3. Removing that defender exposes the knight to tactics.
notes.plans: Play c5 to force d4 to move, then follow up with Rook e8 to pressure the e-file and prevent White from castling.

notes.opening: King's Indian Defense, Four Pawns Attack
notes.explains: Black plays c5, attacking the d4 pawn. White's best response is d5, blocking the center and creating a pawn on d5 that can become a target.
notes.teaches: The d5 pawn in such structures is a blockading target. Black should aim to occupy the d6 square with a knight, which can both blockade the pawn and pressure c4 and e4.
notes.plans: After d5, develop the knight to d7 and then to d6 via e8, or play Rook e8 to pressure the e-file. The knight on d6 is an ideal blockader.

notes.explains: Black can respond to the Bishop's Opening by playing Nf6, exploiting that White hasn't played Nf3. After d3, Nc6, Nf3, Black can transpose into an Italian with Bc5 or play the solid Bb7 (Hungarian Variation).
notes.teaches: When White plays Bc4 instead of Nf3, Black should consider Nf6 to challenge the center and avoid automatic Nc6.
notes.plans: Develop solidly with Bb7, d6, and castle, aiming for a symmetrical but slightly passive position with no weaknesses.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 d4 d6, White can take on e5 and then on d8, but trading queens reduces the impact of Black losing castling rights. Black's king can find safety on c7 after c6, and the pawn on c6 limits White's knight on c3.
notes.teaches: Trading queens diminishes the advantage of preventing castling; the king can often 'castle by hand' to safety.
notes.plans: White should avoid queen trades to keep attacking chances; develop with Nf3 instead.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 pins the knight and is a mistake because it allows White to play Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5, violating the principle of not moving a piece twice early. White then gets a strong attack with Bc4 and Qb3, threatening mate and forking pawns.
notes.teaches: Moving a piece twice in the opening without necessity can lead to a development disadvantage and tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: White plays Bc4 threatening Scholar's Mate, then Qb3 attacking b7 and f7, forcing Black to lose a pawn or worse.

notes.explains: Black's …c6 is poor because it blocks the knight's natural development square and does not defend the e5 pawn. White simply takes the pawn, and Black's attempt to win it back with Qa5+ is met by Nc3, developing with tempo.
notes.teaches: Pawn moves that hinder piece development should be avoided in the opening. Developing with tempo is a key advantage.
notes.plans: After Nc3 and Nf3, White has a large development lead. Attack with Ng5 and Bc4, targeting f7.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 attacking the bishop. White should not immediately take on f7 with the knight because after Nxf7 Qe7, taking the rook allows Black to trap the knight. Instead, White can play Bb3 first, then take the rook at leisure.
notes.teaches: When calculating, do not assume a move is forced. Go back to the last decision point and consider alternatives. Uncouple emotions from analysis.
notes.plans: Play Bb3, then Nxh8, remaining up material with a strong position.

notes.explains: Bf7+ is also strong. After Kd8, White notices the king and queen are a knight's move apart. White can move the bishop away with gain of tempo (e.g., Bxe8) and then continue the attack. If Black plays h6, White retreats the knight to f3, attacking the queen, and Black's king remains exposed.
notes.teaches: When unsure, make simple developing or improving moves like castling. Use the queen as a 'punching bag' to gain tempi.
notes.plans: Castle, then if h6, play Nf3 attacking the queen, followed by Bb3 and further pressure.

notes.explains: Nxf7 is objectively strong. If Black moves the queen (e.g., Qe7), White plays Bb3, protecting the knight, and then takes the rook on h8. Black may win the knight later but White remains up an exchange and pawns.
notes.teaches: When a tactical line seems messy, check if intermediate moves (like Bb3) improve the outcome before committing to captures.
notes.plans: After Nxf7 Qe7, play Bb3, then Nxh8, consolidating the material advantage.

notes.explains: If Black plays d5, attacking the bishop and opening the diagonal, White should not panic. Simply retreat the bishop (e.g., Bb3) and castle. Black's d5 pawn is actually a weakness because it allows White to open the e-file later with exd5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a noisy move that attacks a piece, respond calmly. The move may create long-term weaknesses that you can exploit.
notes.plans: Retreat the bishop to b3, castle, and then consider opening the center with exd5, using the e-file for attack.

notes.explains: Black played Bc5 and then dxc3, which is a mistake. The correct response is Nf6, transposing to the Italian after cxd4 Bb4+. Falling for the trap Bxf7+ forces the king out and White picks up the bishop on c5 with Qd5+, leaving Black much worse.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch Gambit, Black should not cling to the extra pawn on d4 with dxc3; instead, develop with Nf6 and accept the pawn sacrifice for active play.
notes.plans: After Bxf7+, Black must choose the safest king retreat. Kf8 is best because Ke8 leaves the king exposed on the e-file and makes d6 a hook for e5.

notes.explains: After Kf8, Black must develop quickly and aim to castle by hand. The immediate plan is to play h6, then Kf7, Rf8, and Kg8, using the bishop on c8 to cover checks on the light squares.
notes.teaches: When the king is exposed, prioritize castling by hand over material. Do not cling to extra pawns if they compromise king safety.
notes.plans: Play h6 to prevent Nxg5, then Kf7, Rf8, and eventually Kg8. Develop the knight to f6 and bishop to g4 or e6.

notes.explains: The move d4 opens the center, forcing both sides to develop actively. This teaches beginners the importance of piece activity and exposes mistakes quickly.
notes.teaches: Open centers reward rapid development and punish passive play. The Scotch is ideal for learning to coordinate all your pieces.
notes.plans: Continue developing knights and bishops to active squares, aiming to control the center and prepare for an attack.

notes.explains: White plays d4, challenging Black's center. This is a natural move in the Alekhine's Defence, leading to open positions.
notes.teaches: In the Alekhine's Defence, White often plays d4 early to challenge Black's pawn on e5. Black's best response is usually ...d6 or ...exd4.
notes.plans: White will continue with d5 or Nc3 depending on Black's response.

notes.explains: d6 is passive because it opens the light-squared bishop but blocks the dark-squared bishop, which can only develop to e7—a less active square.
notes.teaches: When developing, avoid moves that block your own pieces. Prefer moves that free both bishops.
notes.plans: White should continue developing with Nc3 and Bc4, putting pressure on f7.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, a standard move in the Alekhine's Defence. White now has several options, including the Four Pawns Attack with c4.
notes.teaches: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 d6, White can choose the Four Pawns Attack with d5 and then c4. This is a sharp line that requires precise play.
notes.plans: White will play d5 next, gaining space and forcing Black's knight to move.

notes.explains: g6 is a mistake because it takes two moves to fianchetto the bishop, allowing White to launch a quick attack. Black should have played Be7 to castle quickly.
notes.teaches: In open positions, you cannot afford to spend extra tempi on slow development. Prioritize castling and rapid piece activation.
notes.plans: White can now exploit Black's lagging development with a tactical sequence: Nxc6, e5, and Bxf7+ if Black recaptures.

notes.explains: After e3 Nf6 Nf3 g6 d4 Bg7 Bd3 d6 5.0-0 0-0 b3, Black plays …e5 immediately because White's b3 leaves the long diagonal unguarded, making the tactical sequence dxe5 dxe5 Nxe5 Ng4 possible. If …Nxe5? Bxg7 Kxg7 Qxd8 Rxd8 Nxe5, White wins a pawn. Instead …Ng4 attacks the knight twice; if Nxg4 Bxa1, Black wins the exchange.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's bishop is not yet fianchettoed, you can often play an early e5 in King's Indian setups, exploiting the tactical vulnerability of the e5 pawn.
notes.plans: After …Ng4, Black threatens ...Nxe5 and ...Bxa1. White's best is e4, leading to a reversed French structure where Black has comfortable play.

notes.explains: White plays e4, reaching a reversed French structure. Black should not rush with ...e5 again because after …e5? dxe5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nxe4 Nxf7? (a common mistake) is met by …Bxc3! (check) winning the knight. The correct approach is …c5, pressuring d4 and transposing to a Benoni-like setup.
notes.teaches: In reversed openings, beware of copying plans blindly; concrete calculation matters. Here, the absence of a knight on c3 makes ...e5 risky.
notes.plans: After e4, play …c5. If d5, then …e6 with a Benoni structure; if dxc5, recapture with the knight and develop naturally.

notes.explains: Black plays …Nh5, defending e5 and threatening ...Nf4. The knight on f4 is a classic outpost, pressuring d3 and the kingside. White's best response is Bc4 or Bb5, aiming to trade queens and reduce Black's attacking potential. Instead, Nc3? allows …Bxg4 Qxg4 Nf4, and Black's knight dominates.
notes.teaches: A knight on f4 (or f5) is often a powerful outpost, especially when the opponent lacks a dark-squared bishop to challenge it. Prophylaxis against such knights includes trading queens or forcing the knight away with g3, but g3 weakens light squares.
notes.plans: Black's plan is to play ...Nf4, then possibly ...Bg4 to pin the knight on f3, and later ...Qe7 or ...Qg5 to increase pressure. White should consider Bc4 to offer a queen trade.

notes.explains: White has set up the Maróczy Bind with pawns on e4 and c4, both aiming at d5. This structure prevents Black from playing the freeing ...d5 break, which is the main idea of the Accelerated Dragon.
notes.teaches: The Maróczy Bind is a pawn structure that restricts Black's central counterplay. Black must find alternative ways to generate activity, often on the queenside or via piece play.
notes.plans: Black should delay ...Bg7 and instead play ...Nf6 to challenge e4 immediately, then recapture on d4 with the knight to lure White's queen to d4.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nf6 instead of the automatic ...Bg7, challenging the e4 pawn. After ...Nxd4 and Qxd4, Black plays ...d6 to prevent e5 and prepare ...Bg7. The queen on d4 is exposed to future discovered attacks.
notes.teaches: Delaying the fianchetto can be a practical way to avoid main lines. The queen on d4 becomes a target after Black develops, gaining a tempo.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Bg7, castling, and then look to trade the dark-squared bishops or create pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, which is a mistake because it allows Black to play ...Ng4, trading the knight for White's dark-squared bishop. This leaves Black with an uncontested dark-squared bishop, which is very powerful in Sicilian structures.
notes.teaches: Trading the opponent's dark-squared bishop for a knight is often favorable for Black in the Accelerated Dragon, as it gives Black control over dark squares and a powerful bishop.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Ng4, forcing the trade, then recapture with ...Bxg4, leaving Black with a dark-squared bishop monopoly.

notes.explains: After the trade, Black has an uncontested dark-squared bishop. The next challenge is where to place the light-squared bishop. Options include ...Bd7 (preparing ...b5) or ...Be6, which is more active and puts pressure on c4.
notes.teaches: In the Maróczy Bind, the light-squared bishop often goes to e6 to pressure the c4 pawn and restrict White's knight. Avoid fianchettoing it to b7, as White can play f3 and make it passive.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Be6, then consider queenside expansion with ...a6 and ...b5, or immediate pressure with ...Qa5 and ...Rfc8.

notes.explains: Black has completed development with ...Be6. The position is balanced, but Black has clear plans: pressure on c4 and queenside expansion. White's queen on d2 is awkward and may need to move.
notes.teaches: In the Maróczy Bind, Black's plan is to undermine White's pawn chain on the queenside with ...a6, ...b5, or ...a5 to gain space and create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Qa5, putting pressure on the knight and a2 pawn, then follow with ...Rfc8. Alternatively, ...a5 to grab space and then ...Qa5 is also good.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qa5, a non-committal move that improves the queen, connects rooks, and keeps pawns flexible. The queen is safe here and can later go to c5 or e5.
notes.teaches: When possible, prefer piece play over pawn moves. ...Qa5 is flexible and avoids committing to a specific pawn structure prematurely.
notes.plans: Black will follow with ...Rfc8, putting pressure on the c-file. If White plays a3 and b4, the c4 pawn becomes weak and the a3 pawn may hang.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rfc8 (keeping the rook on a8 for tactical reasons). White's a3 weakens the queenside. Black now threatens ...Bxc3 and ...Rxc4, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Maróczy Bind, the rook on a8 is often better kept to support the a-pawn in lines where White captures on b7. The rook on f8 is more active on the c-file.
notes.plans: Black can play ...Bxc3 to cripple White's queenside pawns, then ...Rxc4. Alternatively, ...Rxc4 immediately is also strong.

notes.explains: Black captures on c3 and then on c4, winning a pawn. White's queenside is shattered, and Black has a clear advantage. The opposite-colored bishops in the middlegame are not a drawing factor; they actually give Black attacking chances.
notes.teaches: Opposite-colored bishops in the middlegame are often an advantage for the attacking side, as they can control squares the opponent cannot defend. Do not fear them.
notes.plans: Black will consolidate, target the a2 pawn, and push the a-pawn. The rook on a8 is useful to support the a-pawn's advance.

notes.explains: Bb5+ develops with tempo, forcing Black to choose between Bd7 or Nc6. This is a standard way to gain time in IQP positions.
notes.teaches: Use checks to develop pieces while forcing the opponent to make less useful moves. This gains a tempo that can be used for further development.
notes.plans: After Black's response, continue developing naturally. If Nc6, follow up with Nf3 and later capture on c5 only after Black moves the dark-squared bishop.

notes.explains: White has castled and Black has played Nf6. The IQP structure is set. White's next moves should aim to control d4 and pressure the pawn.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, develop pieces to active squares. The knight often goes to b3 to challenge the bishop on c5 and later to d4. The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6.
notes.plans: Play Bg5 to pin the knight, then Nbd2 followed by Nb3 to target the bishop on c5 and prepare Nd4. Avoid premature checks like Qe1+ which can expose f2.

notes.explains: White plays Bxc6, exchanging the light-squared bishop for a knight. This removes the IQP and creates hanging pawns on c6 and d5. In return, White gains a powerful initiative.
notes.teaches: Transforming a positional advantage (IQP weakness) into a dynamic one (piece activity) is a key skill. Don't be afraid to give up a static plus for a more active one.
notes.plans: After bxc6, place a knight on e5 to attack c6 and threaten d7. Follow up with Bxf6 to ruin Black's kingside pawns if possible. The initiative should lead to material gains.

notes.explains: After Bxf6 gxf6, White captures on c6 with the knight. Black's pawn structure is damaged, and White has a material advantage. The knight on c6 threatens e7 and forks.
notes.teaches: Knights on c6 often target e7, a common tactical motif. When a piece is trapped, consider sacrificing it for maximum material rather than panicking.
notes.plans: If Black plays Qe8 to trap the knight, respond with Nxa7 to create a three-pawn majority on the queenside. Push the a-pawn and keep the bishop passive.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to create a pawn chain that blunts Black's dark-squared bishop on g7. The downside is that the knight loses the c3 square, but it can later develop to d2, similar to the London System.
notes.teaches: When facing the Modern Defense, c3 is a solid, positional setup that limits Black's bishop and allows for slow, patient development.
notes.plans: Develop with Bd3, Nf3, and later Nbd2-f1-e3-g4, aiming to occupy the f6 square.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, which is a strategic mistake because it weakens the dark squares. White should close the center with e5, not capture on d5, to exploit those weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens dark squares, closing the center with e5 gives you a clear target and a long-term plan.
notes.plans: Play e5, then develop with Nf3, and later maneuver the knight to f6 via d2-f1-e3-g4.

notes.explains: Black plays c4, further locking the center. This gives White a free hand to attack on the kingside, as Black's dark-square weaknesses become permanent.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, you can safely maneuver pieces without fear of immediate counterplay. The 'three-move rule' is less relevant in closed positions.
notes.plans: Prepare the knight maneuver Nbd2-f1-e3-g4 to target f6, and eventually attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: f3 looks anti-developmental, but the point is to prepare e2-e4, seizing a massive center. Black's most common reply Nc6 allows White to execute the plan.
notes.teaches: Sometimes violating development principles is justified if it sets up a powerful central pawn duo. The key is to have a concrete follow-up.
notes.plans: Play e4, then after dxe4, interpose d5 to kick the knight, then recapture on e4 with a pawn mass.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, a move the teacher doesn't know. White must choose between dxe5, exd5, or f4. f4 is tempting to chase knights and create a pawn chain, but it weakens the king.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar move, rely on general principles but stay flexible. f4 is a natural-looking pawn lever, but concrete calculation is needed.
notes.plans: Consider f4 to push e5 later, or exd5 to win a pawn but risk development issues.

notes.explains: f4 is played, but Black responds with Ng4, attacking the queen and threatening to exploit White's weak dark squares. White's king is exposed and development lags.
notes.teaches: A pawn chain is only good if your king is safe and pieces are developed. Here f4 created weaknesses without sufficient compensation.
notes.plans: White must defend against Ng4 threats and try to catch up in development. Options include Qxd5, Be2, or h3.

notes.explains: Black's queen on e7 blocks the bishop and is vulnerable. White has a lead in development and should not rush sacrifices.
notes.teaches: Developing the queen early can obstruct piece development and create targets. Complete development before launching attacks.
notes.plans: Castle, then consider Nxc3 or Rxe1 to exploit the queen's position.

notes.explains: White pushes h4 to dislodge the knight on g3 (or g6 in similar positions). This is a common idea to gain space and open lines.
notes.teaches: Pushing the h-pawn can be used to kick away a knight that blocks a bishop or to create attacking chances, even if it weakens the king's pawn shield. Evaluate concretely, not by dogma.
notes.plans: After h5, if the knight moves, the bishop on f5 becomes active. If the knight captures on h5, recapture with the bishop and attack.

notes.explains: Black's Qb6 pins the pawn on b2 and threatens Nxg5. White must respond carefully; moving the king to h1 is safe.
notes.teaches: When your pawn push is met with a counterattack, don't panic. A king move can defuse the pin and maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: After Kh1, continue with the plan to dislodge the knight or sacrifice on h7.

notes.explains: Black's b5 is an obscure pawn sacrifice, not a standard Benko Gambit. White should simply accept the pawn and develop naturally without overthinking the opponent's intentions.
notes.teaches: When facing offbeat openings, prioritize sound development and material advantage over trying to refute the opponent's idea immediately.
notes.plans: Take the pawn on b5 with cxb5, then develop knights to c3 and f3, and bishops to f4 and d3, maintaining a solid center.

notes.explains: Bishop to f4 is better than g5 because it pressures the backward c7 pawn and avoids the trade after ...Be7. The b5 pawn restricts Black's ...c6 break, which would allow White to liquidate the b-pawn and remain a pawn up.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on squares where they exert pressure on weak pawns and cannot be easily traded off without compensation.
notes.plans: Continue with e3, Bd3, Nf3, and h3 to prevent ...Nh5 harassment, then centralize with moves like Qc2 and Ne5.

notes.explains: h3 is a useful prophylactic move that prevents ...Nh5 attacking the bishop on f4. White can afford this tempo because Black has played passively.
notes.teaches: In quiet positions, a preventive move like h3 can save future headaches and is justified when the opponent has no active counterplay.
notes.plans: After h3, continue with Ne5, Qc2, and castle, maintaining central pressure and preparing to exploit Black's cramped position.

notes.explains: Ne5 centralizes the knight and discourages ...Nc4 by adding a defender to the c4 square. The knight is well-placed here, supported by the pawn on d4.
notes.teaches: Centralized knights are powerful; place them on outposts where they cannot be easily chased away and where they support your strategic goals.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qc2 to create a battery on the c-file, then consider Be5 or Bg5 to target the knight on f6.

notes.explains: Instead of immediately playing Nc6, which looks tempting but can be undermined by ...a6 and ...Bb7, White should consider Be5. This move threatens to ruin Black's kingside pawn structure after Bxf6, and the bishop is untouchable because ...gxf6 would trap the knight on c4.
notes.teaches: Look for moves that create concrete threats and force weaknesses, rather than just placing pieces on seemingly good squares without a clear follow-up.
notes.plans: Play Be5, threatening Bxf6. If Black avoids the capture, follow up with Qf3 to increase pressure, then castle and bring rooks to the center.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3, which can lead to a Grand Prix Attack or a Closed Sicilian, but also keeps the option of transposing into an Open Sicilian with d4 later. Black's response depends on which Sicilian variation they play against Nf3.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, choose your move based on your preferred Sicilian setup against Nf3. For Najdorf players, d6 is recommended; for Sveshnikov or Accelerated Dragon players, Nc6; for Kan or Taimanov players, e6.
notes.plans: Black should develop harmoniously, aiming for a flexible setup.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nc3, White has not committed to an open Sicilian. Black's choice of response depends on which open Sicilian variation they intend to play.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, the move you choose should align with your intended open Sicilian repertoire. Accelerated Dragon players play …Nc6; Najdorf players should play …d6 to avoid being move-ordered into an unfavorable line.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...g6 and ...Bg7 to reach the Accelerated Dragon setup, or with ...d6 and ...Nf6 for the Najdorf.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3, a common anti-Sicilian move that can transpose into an Open Sicilian if White follows up with Nf3 and d4.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, play the same system you would against the Open Sicilian. If you play the Najdorf, play d6; if you play the Taimanov, play e6. This avoids being move-ordered into an unfamiliar line.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, preparing b5 to expand on the queenside and fianchetto the light-squared bishop. This is an underrated response that works well against the Grand Prix Attack and the Closed Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Early queenside expansion with b5 can be a good way to counter White's setup, gaining space and activating the bishop on b7.
notes.plans: Follow up with b5, Bb7, and then develop kingside pieces, keeping the center flexible with d6 and e6.

notes.explains: Black builds a hedgehog-like structure with pawns on d6 and e6, controlling central squares. The queen on c7 connects rooks, controls e5, and prepares for action. The knight on d7 is preferable to c6 as it doesn't block the bishop.
notes.teaches: In such setups, the queen often goes to c7 to support the center and connect rooks. The knight belongs on d7 to keep the c-file open for the bishop and to avoid blocking the bishop's diagonal.
notes.plans: Castle kingside or keep the king in the center if both flanks are dangerous. Prepare to counter White's kingside expansion with h5 if needed.

notes.explains: Black plays h5 to prevent White's g4 expansion, keeping the kingside closed. This is risky because it weakens the kingside, but it forces White to reconsider their plans. The king remains in the center for now.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to prevent the opponent's expansion even at the cost of weakening your own pawn structure. Keeping the king in the center can be safer than castling into an attack.
notes.plans: If White plays a4, respond with b4 to keep the queenside closed. Consider castling queenside if the center remains closed.

notes.explains: White plays c3, weakening the d3 pawn. Black notices that the pawn on d3 is now vulnerable to undermining with c4, rather than direct attack.
notes.teaches: A weak pawn can be exploited not only by attacking it with pieces but also by using your own pawns to undermine the opponent's pawn structure. Here, c4 attacks the base of White's pawn chain.
notes.plans: Play bxc3 first to avoid dropping the b4 pawn, then play c4 to attack d3. Follow up with Nc5 to put more pressure on d3.

notes.explains: Black accepts the gambit but plans to return the extra piece to avoid deep theory. By playing Ng6 and then sacrificing the knight back, Black gains development and a solid position.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit you haven't studied, returning the material can simplify the position and reduce White's attacking chances. Development and activity can compensate for the sacrificed piece.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, castle, and aim for a solid middlegame with equal chances.

notes.explains: After d4 exd4, Black castles. White can play Nxe4 (Max Lange) or d6 (solid but passive). Here Black chooses the principled Nxe4.
notes.teaches: In the Max Lange, Black can accept the pawn on e4. White gets compensation with pressure on the e-file and a lead in development.
notes.plans: After Nxe4, White plays Re1, forcing d5. Black must be careful: the knight on e4 is pinned, and the queen must move after Bxd5 Nxd5 Nc3.

notes.explains: Black's bishop g4 is a mistake because it leaves b7 and f7 vulnerable. Qb3 hits both targets and is more forcing than Bxf7.
notes.teaches: When attacking f7, consider queen checks or queen attacks that also target other weaknesses. The queen can often create more threats than a piece sacrifice.
notes.plans: After Qb3, if Black plays Bh5, White has Qb5+ exploiting the a4-e8 diagonal; if Black plays Bb6, White trades queens and wins a pawn.

notes.explains: Bb5 is an anti-Sicilian that resembles a Rossolimo but is inferior because the knight on c3 does not protect d4. Black's best response is …Nd4, challenging the bishop and establishing a strong outpost.
notes.teaches: When a bishop pins your knight on c6, the principled counter is to attack it immediately with ...Nd4, gaining time and central control.
notes.plans: After …Nd4, Black threatens to capture the bishop and will follow up with ...a6 and ...d6 to consolidate.

notes.explains: After Bb5, the standard reply is …Nxd4, but …g6 is a practical alternative that avoids theory. If White takes on c6, Black recaptures with the b-pawn, accepting doubled pawns in exchange for the bishop pair, the b-file, and quick access to d5.
notes.teaches: Accepting doubled pawns is often fine when you gain compensating dynamic factors like the bishop pair and central control. Don't fear structural damage if you get active play.
notes.plans: After Bxc6 bxc6, Black aims to push d5 or d6, develop the kingside, and use the bishop pair in a semi-open position.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black should not automatically play ...a6. The knight on b5 is not immediately dangerous. Instead, Black can consider ...d6 or ...Nf6, but the most practical is …a6, chasing the knight to c3 and transposing to a Najdorf-like setup.
notes.teaches: Do not assume a forcing move like ...a6 is necessary. Evaluate the actual threats; sometimes delaying development is fine if the opponent's pieces are not well placed.
notes.plans: After …a6 Nc3 d6, Black prepares ...Nf6 and ...g6, aiming for a comfortable Najdorf structure.

notes.explains: White's d3 is passive, blocking the bishop. Black can strike in the center with d5, which is principled and beneficial if trades occur.
notes.teaches: When White plays passively, Black should challenge the center immediately with d5.
notes.plans: Play d5, and if White takes, recapture with the knight, then develop naturally.

notes.explains: After Nxd5, Black should not take on c3, as that pawn structure is not bad for White. Instead, develop the knight to c6.
notes.teaches: Avoid releasing tension with captures that improve the opponent's pawn structure; develop pieces first.
notes.plans: Continue development, aiming to place bishops on safe squares.

notes.explains: After d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 a6, Black prepares b5. White's g3 fianchetto is a Catalan-style approach, often sacrificing the c4 pawn for dynamic play.
notes.teaches: In the Slav, g3 can lead to rich, imbalanced positions where piece activity compensates for a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: White develops with Bg2 and may play Qb3 to pressure Black's queenside, or simply complete development and open the center.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 is dubious because White can immediately play h3, forcing the bishop to retreat to h5, after which Qb3 creates strong pressure on b7 and d5.
notes.teaches: When an opponent's bishop pins a knight on f3, look for h3 to gain a tempo and follow up with Qb3 to attack the center and queenside.
notes.plans: After Bg4, White plays h3, then Qb3, targeting b7 and d5, forcing Black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White plays e4 to blast open the center. Black's underdevelopment makes this aggressive push especially strong, as White's pieces are more active.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, opening the center with pawn breaks like e4 can expose the opponent's king and create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: White aims to open lines for the bishops and rooks, while Black struggles to catch up in development.

notes.explains: Black's early e5 weakens the d5 square, giving White total control over it.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening key central squares like d5 without good reason, especially in gambit lines where development and square control matter most.
notes.plans: Develop normally with Bc4, then put pressure on f7 with Qb3.

notes.explains: Qb3 is better than Bxf7+ because after Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Black can play d5, using the tempo to push the pawn and gain counterplay. Qb3 keeps the pressure on f7 and avoids giving Black time.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prefer moves that maintain pressure and force concessions over flashy sacrifices that give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: After Qb3, if Qd7, take on b4 with the pawn to keep the battery on f7 and prepare Ba3+.

notes.explains: White has played the Scotch Gambit. Black can choose sharp theory (Nf6 or Bc5) or a quieter approach.
notes.teaches: When you sense your opponent knows the main line better than you, you can play a solid, slightly passive move to avoid being blown off the board.
notes.plans: Play d3 to prevent White from building a dominant center, accepting a slightly worse but safe position.

notes.explains: After d3, White can play c3, threatening to take the d-pawn. Black cannot recapture with dxc3 due to Qd5 threatening mate on f7.
notes.teaches: When a pawn capture leads to a tactical disaster, consider sacrificing the pawn back on your own terms to complete development.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, allowing e5, then d3 to force White to capture, or play d3 immediately to keep the pawn.

notes.explains: Black played Nf6 and d5, entering main line theory. White now has a strong center and attacking chances.
notes.teaches: The Scotch Gambit is dangerous for Black if you don't know the theory; White gets a pawn on e5 and active pieces.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development and challenge White's center with ...c6 or ...d6.

notes.explains: Black played ...Ba6 to attack the c4 pawn, but this was a mistake. The correct move was ...Bb7, which supports a central break with ...d5 after ...exf5. With the bishop on a6, ...d5 is less effective because White can reply Ng5, threatening f6 and creating a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When choosing a square for a bishop, consider how it supports your central pawn breaks. Compare ...Ba6 vs ...Bb7: the latter directly supports ...d5, while the former leaves the center vulnerable.
notes.plans: Black should have played ...Bb7, then after ...exf5, play ...d5 to open the center and activate the pieces.

notes.explains: Black's Bb4 is a passive move that doesn't challenge the Vienna setup. It resembles an inverted Trompowsky, but the natural response Nd5 is unstable because Black can chase it with c6.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar move, stay calm and ask what your opponent wants. Here, Bb4 doesn't interfere with f4, so keep the opening's spirit.
notes.plans: Play f4 anyway, maintaining the aggressive Vienna structure.

notes.explains: Black's h6 reveals his plan: g5 to build a pawn chain and keep the f4 pawn. If White plays d4 now, Black replies g5 and White gains nothing. The correct response is to ignore the pawn and develop rapidly, punishing Black's slow play.
notes.teaches: Read your opponent's intentions. When they waste time on pawn moves, accelerate your development rather than reacting mechanically.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, a calm developing move, and see how Black arranges his pieces before deciding on further action.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, a solid move. White should not play e5 immediately because Black replies d5, opening the center and exploiting the pin on the c3-knight. Instead, castle first to safeguard the king.
notes.teaches: When in doubt, develop and castle. Premature central pushes can backfire if your king is still exposed.
notes.plans: Castle, then consider e5 after Black's king is committed.

notes.explains: White's setup with Nc3 and exd5 blocks the c-pawn, preventing c3 or c4. This makes d4 a static weakness rather than a dynamic center.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, White's ideal is to maintain tension with c3 or c4. Blocking the c-pawn with Nc3 after exd5 is a common inaccuracy.
notes.plans: Black develops naturally (Nc6, Nf6, Bg4/Bf5) and aims to keep the pawn chain intact.

notes.explains: Black is not worried about Bxf6 because the doubled f-pawns can actually strengthen the center, and White loses time.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pawns if they come at the cost of opponent's development; they can be a structural asset.
notes.plans: If Bxf6, recapture with gxf6 and maintain the center.

notes.explains: Black develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain (Bg4) rather than locking it in with e6. This is a luxury because White hasn't played c3 or c4.
notes.teaches: When White's center is not dynamic, you can often develop the bishop outside the pawn chain for more activity.
notes.plans: Continue development, possibly with e6 later, but keep the bishop active.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc5, which prevents d4 but has a flaw: the fork trick Nxe5. If Black takes on f2, White gets central control and king safety despite losing castling.
notes.teaches: When facing Bc5 in the Four Knights, Nxe5 is a strong reply because Black's bishop is vulnerable and the fork trick can be dangerous if Black takes on f2.
notes.plans: After Nxe5, if Black plays Bxf2+, respond with Kxf2, then play d4 to control the center. The king will hide on g1, and White's development advantage compensates for the exposed king.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, which loses a queen to Bg5! because the bishop on c4 guards the only escape square. This is a tactical trick that arises from natural development.
notes.teaches: Play moves that are good in themselves but also contain a threat. Here, Bc4 is a strong developing move that also sets up a trap. Always look for such dual-purpose moves.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, trapping the queen. After winning the queen, convert the extra material without unnecessary complications. Simplify only when convenient; don't give up your best pieces.

notes.explains: The correct response to Nxe5 is Bd6, not Bxf2+. Bd6 wins back the pawn and keeps the bishop pair. Black is slightly worse due to White's center control and development lead, but it's much better than the losing line with Bxf2+.
notes.teaches: In the fork trick position, don't give up your bishop for a pawn. Play Bd6 to regain the pawn and maintain piece activity. Giving up the dark-squared bishop early is a major concession.
notes.plans: After Bd6, White can play f4 or Bd3 to maintain an advantage. Black should aim to complete development and challenge White's center.

notes.explains: Retreating the bishop to e2 (instead of a4) avoids being chased by b5 and then Nc5, which would trap the bishop. From e2, the bishop is safe and can later go to f3.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically retreat a bishop to a4 after a6; consider the opponent's counterplay. Preserve your active pieces by retreating to a square where they remain useful.
notes.plans: Black will likely play Nb6 to attack the d5 pawn. White should complete development with Nf3 or Ne2 and d4.

notes.explains: Playing d4 controls the center and prepares to develop the knight. Black's knight on b6 attacks d5, but White can defend or trade.
notes.teaches: In the opening, central control is paramount. Even when behind in material, completing development and controlling the center gives compensation.
notes.plans: After Black recaptures on d5 (e.g., Nxd5 or Qxd5), White can develop with Nf3 or Ne2 and Bf3, aiming for a slight advantage.

notes.explains: After Qxd5, White has a choice: develop the knight to f3 or play Bf3. Bf3 puts the bishop on the long diagonal, eyeing b7, and then the knight can go to e2.
notes.teaches: Be flexible with knight development. Ne2 is a legitimate square; the knight can later go to g3 or c3. Don't be afraid to put knights on non-standard squares to improve other pieces.
notes.plans: Play Bf3, then Ne2, castle, and aim to pressure b7. Black will struggle to develop the c8-bishop without losing the b7 pawn.
