notes.explains: Black's queen on b5 defends b7 and threatens to develop the bishop. White should not play a4 immediately because the queen can drop back to b6, and the threat is not meaningful. Instead, continue development with Ne2.
notes.teaches: Don't make a move just because it creates a threat. The threat must be meaningful; if the opponent can easily sidestep it, you may waste time. Focus on your own plans.
notes.plans: Play Ne2, castle, and later consider a4 when the king is safe and the bishop on f3 pressures b7.

notes.explains: After castling, the situation changes: the king is safe, and the bishop on f3 pressures b7. Now a4 becomes a meaningful threat because the queen is the only defender of b7, and it can be chased away.
notes.teaches: Re-evaluate tactical ideas as the position evolves. A move that was bad earlier (a4) can become good later when conditions change (king safety, piece placement).
notes.plans: Play a4, then a5, then Nc3 to chase the queen and win the b7 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's e6 is a third-tier response to e4, often transposing to the French Defense after d4 d5 e5. White can avoid the advance French by capturing on d5.
notes.teaches: Against e6, white has the option to take on d5 and reach a different pawn structure, avoiding the main lines of the French.
notes.plans: White can play exd5, leading to a queen recapture and a position where white develops naturally.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, heading for the French Defense. White intends to play the Gionatus Variation but Black plays a6, an unusual move.
notes.teaches: When facing unusual early pawn moves, simply develop your pieces. Don't try to punish immediately; principled development is best.
notes.plans: Develop with Nf3, preparing to play c3 later if needed.

notes.explains: After exd5, black recaptures with the queen, leading to a unique pawn structure unlike the isolated queen pawn positions from the Alapin.
notes.teaches: Queen recaptures on d5 change the nature of the position; white should develop naturally and look for active knight maneuvers.
notes.plans: White plays Nf3, Nf6, and then considers the aggressive Na3, heading for b5 or c4.

notes.explains: White plays Na3, a typical Alapin developing move aiming for b5, threatening Nc7 forking queen and rook. This is dangerous for black if imprecise.
notes.teaches: Na3 is a venomous move that can yield a quick win if black errs, but even against best play white retains an edge. The knight heads for an outpost.
notes.plans: If black plays a6, the knight reroutes to c4, eyeing b6 and e5. White should not fear b5 as the knight can go to e5.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, preventing Nb5. White's knight goes to c4, a more sustainable square than Bc4, which would block the knight and be vulnerable to b5.
notes.teaches: When a knight's intended outpost is denied, look for another forkable square. Nc4 is strong because it eyes b6 and e5, and cannot be easily chased.
notes.plans: White continues development with Bd3, castles, and prepares to open the center with dxc5.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to d3, aiming at h7, and castles. Black's queen retreated to d8, a common but slightly passive move.
notes.teaches: Develop the bishop to the most active square, especially if castling kingside. Bd3 targets h7 and supports a future dxc5 with tempo.
notes.plans: White can now play dxc5, forcing the bishop on e7 to move again, gaining a tempo. Then prepare to open the center with Rd1 and Qe2.

notes.explains: After e4 d5 e5 d4, Black's d-pawn counterattacks the knight on c3, which is the cleanest path to equality.
notes.teaches: Counterattacking the opponent's pieces is often more effective than simply retreating.
notes.plans: After …d4, White may capture on d4, leading to mutual destruction with ...Qxd2+ allowing Black to survive.

notes.explains: White starts with b3, a hypermodern opening that avoids occupying the center with pawns, instead fianchettoing the bishop to attack the center from a distance.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, you don't need to occupy the center immediately; you can control it with pieces and later strike with pawns.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b2, then play e3 or c4 to support the center, and eventually d4 to open lines.

notes.explains: White fianchettoes the queen's bishop, aiming to pressure Black's center hypermodernly. The idea is to attack Black's e5 pawn without building a pawn center.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, you don't occupy the center with pawns but attack it with pieces from a distance. The bishop on b2 targets e5.
notes.plans: Play Bb5 to pin the knight and threaten the e5 pawn. Develop knights to e2 instead of f3 to avoid e4 with tempo, and prepare f4 to open lines.

notes.explains: Black's h5 is an unusual move that weakens the kingside, especially the g6 square. White should not react to such provocation but instead continue with solid development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays dubious moves, focus on your own development and central control rather than reacting to threats.
notes.plans: Play e3, then develop the knight to f3, and later occupy the center with d4.

notes.explains: Black's a5 aims to undermine White's pawn structure with a4. White can neutralize this with a3, preparing b4 if Black plays a4.
notes.teaches: Against a5, a3 is a good prophylactic move that keeps the pawn structure flexible and prevents Black from gaining space on the queenside.
notes.plans: After a3, continue development with Nf3, then d4, and later consider c4 if needed.

notes.explains: Black played d6 instead of the critical d5, leaving White with a full center and the c3 square for the knight. White's position is already very pleasant.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, Black must play d5 to fight for the center; otherwise White gets a dominant center and easy development.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, keeping the center intact. Consider h3 to restrict Black's light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: White develops the knight to c3 first. Nf3 would allow Bg4, giving Black extra options. By playing Nc3 first, White can follow with h3 to restrict the bishop.
notes.teaches: When two moves are equally good, choose the one that limits the opponent's options. Here, Nc3 avoids Bg4 and allows h3 to force Black's bishop to a passive square.
notes.plans: Play h3, then Nf3, developing with the bishop on e3 or d3, keeping the center solid.

notes.explains: After h3 and Nf3, Black has fianchettoed. White considers d5 but prefers simpler development. d5 would open the fianchetto bishop and require precise follow-up like Bg5 to neutralize the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: Don't overextend the center unnecessarily. Simple development (Be3, Bd3) keeps the position solid and avoids creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play Be3 (not Bf4, which is vulnerable to e5 or Nh5), then Bd3, castle, and prepare queenside or kingside play.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to d3 instead of c4. Bc4 is tactically bad because of Nxe4! d5 winning back the piece, and positionally bad because b5 can chase it away. Bd3 reinforces the center and is safe.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing bishops on c4 in the Alapin when Black has a knight on c6; the tactical trick Nxe4 is a common pitfall. Prefer d3 for solidity.
notes.plans: Complete development with O-O, then consider queenside expansion with a4 or kingside play.

notes.explains: White plays a4 to provoke b4, creating a weakness on b4 and a hole on b5. This restricts Black's queenside counterplay and gives White freedom to operate on the kingside. The knight can later maneuver to g3 via c3-e2-g3.
notes.teaches: Provoking pawn weaknesses can be a strategic tool. a4 forces b4, which becomes a target and gives White the b5 square for a bishop or knight.
notes.plans: After b4, maneuver the knight to g3, then play Qd2 and Bh6 to trade Black's fianchetto bishop, followed by kingside attack.

notes.explains: In a similar position, a4 is not always correct. Playing a4 automatically can create a hole on b4 for Black's knight. It's often better to allow b5 and keep the queenside solid.
notes.teaches: Don't play a4 automatically to prevent b5. Consider the downsides: it weakens b4, which can become an outpost for Black's knight. Sometimes allowing b5 is safer.
notes.plans: If Black plays b5, consider maneuvers like Nc3-e2-g3 to attack on the kingside, or simply continue development and wait for Black to overextend.

notes.explains: Black voluntarily ruins his pawn structure with Nf6, leading to the Tartakower after exf6 exf6. This opens the bishop on c8 and gives Black dynamic chances.
notes.teaches: Accepting a compromised pawn structure can be worthwhile if it activates your pieces and creates attacking chances.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with Bd6, O-O, and then pin White's knight with Bg4 to create pressure.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the e-pawn, creating a 'pawn cube' on f6, g7, h7. This structure is solid defensively and allows Black to push f- and g-pawns for attack without exposing the king.
notes.teaches: The pawn cube (three pawns on f6, g7, h7) provides king safety and attacking potential; pushing two pawns leaves the king still well-protected.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to d7, then consider rerouting it to f8 or b6 to reach d5 or e6.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bg4, a very annoying move for White. White's typical responses (h3 or Be2) are either weakening or passive.
notes.teaches: Pinning a knight to the queen or king can be a powerful developing move that disrupts the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: Complete development with Nd7, then consider Bh5 to maintain the pin, or trade on f3 if beneficial.

notes.explains: Black's f6 is a serious mistake because it weakens the kingside and allows White to play Nxc3, winning a rook after Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+ and Qxa8.
notes.teaches: In open gambits, accepting material and then exploiting the opponent's weakened king safety is often decisive.
notes.plans: After Bxf7+ Kxf7, Qd5+ followed by Qxa8 leaves White with a rook and pawn for a bishop and knight, a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black pins the knight on c3 to prevent e4 and control the center from a distance. White's e4 is a mistake because it allows Black to take on c3 and win a pawn.
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian is a hypermodern opening where Black controls the center with pieces rather than pawns, and the pin on the knight is a key idea.
notes.plans: After e4, take the pawn on e4 with the knight, then later take on c3 with the knight to win a pawn and ruin White's structure.

notes.explains: When White plays Nf3 in the Caro-Kann, Black has the extra option of Bg4 instead of the usual Bf5, because the queen no longer controls g4. This pins the knight and puts pressure on d4.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, if White plays Nf3 early, consider Bg4 to pin the knight and create pressure, as the queen no longer defends that square.
notes.plans: Play Bg4, then e6, c5, and Nc6 to develop and challenge the center.

notes.explains: The Carlsbad pawn structure arises after White captures on d5 early, releasing central tension. White gets an e-pawn versus Black's c-pawn, creating a structural imbalance that defines the middlegame.
notes.teaches: Releasing central tension early can create a fixed pawn structure with clear strategic plans for both sides.
notes.plans: White aims for a minority attack on the queenside (b4-b5) or a central break with f3 and e4, depending on piece placement.

notes.explains: Playing Qc2 early prevents Black's bishop from coming to f5, which can be annoying. It's a useful prophylactic move with no downside.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves that prevent opponent's active options are often worth including, even if they seem slow.
notes.plans: Continue development with Nf3 or Ne2, then castle and decide on the minority attack or central break.

notes.explains: In the Carlsbad, White can develop the knight to f3 or e2. Here Nf3 is chosen because Ne2 runs into the tricky idea ...Bxh2+ and ...Ng4+ after castling, which is messy.
notes.teaches: Knight development in the Carlsbad depends on specific tactical nuances; both f3 and e2 are viable but have different pros and cons.
notes.plans: Prepare to play Ne5 (Pillsbury knight) supported by f4, or go for the f3-e4 central break if the knight is on e2.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on d6 is less accurate than e7 because it doesn't address the pin on the knight and weakens control over e5.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad, Black's dark-squared bishop is usually best on e7 to support the kingside and avoid weakening key squares.
notes.plans: White can now aim for Ne5 (Pillsbury knight) since Black's bishop doesn't contest e5.

notes.explains: White establishes a Pillsbury knight on e5, supported by pawns on d4 and f4. This knight is very strong and hard to dislodge.
notes.teaches: The Pillsbury knight (knight on e5 supported by f4) is a powerful attacking formation in the Carlsbad, often leading to a kingside crush.
notes.plans: Play f4 to entrench the knight, then decide on castling direction. If Black plays ...Nbd7, push f4 immediately.

notes.explains: Black has played the Bongcloud (Ke2), a deliberately bad opening. White must avoid impulsive checks like Qh5+ or Bc4+ which allow Black to gain time with g6 or e6.
notes.teaches: Against troll openings, develop pieces first before trying to attack. The most flexible developing move is best.
notes.plans: Start with Nc3, developing the queenside. Follow with Bc4, aiming to open the center with d5 later.

notes.explains: Black's passive development and h6 are serious weaknesses. White has a space advantage and can now consider opening the center.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays passively, look for the right moment to open the center and exploit their lack of development.
notes.plans: Consider Bb5+ to force a pin on the bishop, then take on e6 to leave Black's bishop pinned and vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black's h6 is a serious mistake. Instead, Black should have played e5 to close the center and limit White's development advantage.
notes.teaches: When underdeveloped, closing the center with e5 can reduce the opponent's attacking chances. Avoid weakening pawn moves like h6.
notes.plans: If Black plays e5, White is still better but the advantage is smaller. White can reroute the knight to c4 and prepare f4.

notes.explains: White's f3 is premature and weakens the kingside. Black should focus on development rather than immediately exploiting the weakness.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to exploit a weakness if it means neglecting development. The weakness will remain; develop first and exploit later.
notes.plans: Black plays Bf5, developing with pressure on the knight. Later, the weakness of f3 can be targeted.

notes.explains: Immediate g6 is an underrated response to Nc3, especially for Accelerated Dragon players. It avoids the Rossolimo (Bb5) lines that arise after Nc6.
notes.teaches: If you play the Accelerated Dragon, consider g6 against Nc3 to sidestep the Rossolimo. The downside is that White can play d4 and Qxd4, but theory considers that equal.

notes.explains: White plays the Grand Prix Attack with f4, aiming for a quick kingside assault. Black should respond with the same setup as against the Closed Sicilian: Bg7, Nc6, and later d6 or e6.
notes.teaches: The Grand Prix Attack and Closed Sicilian are similar; the main difference is that in the Grand Prix, White often puts the bishop on c4 to attack f7. Black's standard setup works against both.

notes.explains: White plays Bb5, a topical move that pressures the knight. Black's best response is Nxd4, offering a knight trade to eliminate White's light-squared bishop, which is a key attacker in the Grand Prix.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, the light-squared bishop on c4 (or b5) is often White's most dangerous piece. Trading it off can defuse the attack.
notes.plans: Play Nxd4, then after Bxd4, recapture with the knight. This removes White's bishop and leaves the knight on b5 vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black captures on b5. Now Black should not rush to play a6; the knight on b5 is not immediately dangerous and can be left alone. Instead, complete development with d6 and Nf6.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically chase away a knight that isn't threatening anything. Delaying a6 keeps the knight on an awkward square and avoids helping it return to c3, where it controls d5.
notes.plans: Play d6, then Nf6, developing kingside pieces before dealing with the knight on b5.

notes.explains: White plays Qe1, preparing Qh4 and a kingside attack. Black should avoid castling kingside, as White's queen and pawns can create a dangerous mating attack. Instead, consider queenside castling.
notes.teaches: In the Grand Prix Attack, castling kingside can be risky because White's queen on h4 and pawns on f4 and g4 can launch a direct assault. Queenside castling is a viable alternative to avoid the attack.
notes.plans: Play Bg4 to pin the knight and prepare Qd7, then castle queenside. This removes the king from danger and allows counterplay on the queenside.

notes.explains: White plays c4 to contest the d5 square immediately, but Black should still play d5. This often transposes into the Panov-Botvinnik Attack or an IQP position.
notes.teaches: When White plays c4 in the Caro-Kann, Black should not be deterred from playing d5. The resulting structures often lead to an isolated queen's pawn (IQP) position, which is comfortable for Black.
notes.plans: Black will develop naturally, aiming for an ideal French setup with the bishop outside the pawn chain.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, a rare move. White should continue developing with Nf3, not Nc3, to keep the option of c3.
notes.teaches: Avoid committing your knight to c3 if you want to play c3 later. Keep flexibility.
notes.plans: Develop naturally and wait for Black to reveal more intentions.

notes.explains: White plays f3 to maintain the center and prevent Black's light-squared bishop from developing to f5. This line is underrated but dangerous if handled correctly.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, White's main idea is to keep the center intact and not allow Black easy development. Flexibility is key—be ready to adapt your plans.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with Nc3, Be3, and consider castling queenside to exploit Black's potential overextension.

notes.explains: Black plays ...d5 and White advances e5, gaining space and kicking the knight. Black's knight on f6 is vulnerable, and White can now build a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When Black plays ...Nf6 in the Fantasy, e5 is a strong reply—it's not like the Advance Variation; here Black is nearly busted if he doesn't respond accurately.
notes.plans: After e5, if Black retreats to d7, play e6 with a gambit. If Black plays ...Nh5, continue with g4 or other aggressive moves.

notes.explains: Black's Nd4 is a premature centralization. With only one developed piece, Black cannot have a real trick here.
notes.teaches: A piece in the center is not automatically good if it lacks support and can be attacked. When the opponent has few developed pieces, you can safely capture pawns without fear of traps.
notes.plans: Capture on e5, then retreat the knight to f3 to attack Black's knight and consolidate the pawn.

notes.explains: Retreating Nf3 kills two birds: it moves the knight to safety and attacks Black's knight on d4. Black immediately blunders by exchanging knights, leaving White up a piece.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplify by trading pieces. Avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, complete kingside development, and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: c6 is a rare but tricky move, preparing d5 after Nf3, similar to the Caro-Kann idea. Black is slightly worse if White knows how to respond, but often Black gets good practical chances.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, unusual moves can create confusion and steer the game into less theoretical territory.
notes.plans: After Nf3, play d5, striking in the center.

notes.explains: After d5 exd5, pushing e4 gains space and attacks the knight on f3. White should take on e4, trade queens, and force the white king to d1, leaving it vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, trading queens can leave the king in a dangerous central position even without queens on the board.
notes.plans: Take on e4, trade queens, and exploit the king on d1.

notes.explains: If Black plays …d6 instead of Nc6, White has exd6 Bxd6 Bg5! pinning the knight and threatening Bxd6. After …Nf6 Bxd6 cxd6, Black has an isolated pawn and no compensation.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, look for intermediate moves that disrupt the opponent's development before capturing.
notes.plans: Play e3, develop pieces, and target the weak d6 pawn. White's advantage is structural and lasting.

notes.explains: The main line after …Qxc3 Bxb4 Nxb4 Rxb4 gives White rook and two pawns for two pieces. Black's bishop on c3 looks active but is vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Material imbalances (rook + pawns vs two pieces) require concrete play. The active bishop can be targeted with rook lifts and queen maneuvers.
notes.plans: Play Rb3 attacking the bishop, then Qa1 attacking the knight. If ...Nc4, take on g7; if ...d6, Rb5 hunting the bishop. The key is to force trades or win material.

notes.explains: After the sequence e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6, White has a comfortable position. The pawn structure is favorable for White, and Black's dark-squared bishop is bad because its counterpart on light squares is hemmed in.
notes.teaches: In the French Advance, the knight often goes to d2 and then b3, but here Nc3 is also strong because it threatens Na4 to eliminate Black's important dark-squared bishop. The Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+) is a tactical idea if Black castles kingside.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3, aiming for Na4 or Nb5 to pressure d6. If Black plays Qc7, Nb5 is a good option to target d6.

notes.explains: After a3, the queen on e7 x-rays the king on e1. If the e5 pawn were gone, a knight landing on d3 would be checkmate. Black plays Ncxe5, threatening Nxd3#.
notes.teaches: In gambits, rapid development and threats can create tactical motifs like smothered mate. Always look for x-ray attacks and checkmate patterns when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: If White avoids the trap (e.g., e3), Black can recapture the pawn on e5 and develop harmoniously with Bg7, d6, and rook to e8, enjoying easy play and no weaknesses.

notes.explains: White can defend against the smothered mate by playing e3 instead of a3. Then Black recaptures on e5 and develops with d6, Bg7, and O-O, reaching a position where White has the bishop pair but Black has no weaknesses and easy development.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, precise defense (like e3) can neutralize immediate threats. Black's compensation in such positions is based on active piece play and structural harmony, not material.
notes.plans: Black will fianchetto the bishop, play d6, and bring the rook to e8, aiming for kingside pressure. White should avoid h3, which drops the e5 pawn, and instead play e3 or Nc3.

notes.explains: Black played e5 without first playing a6, which is a mistake. The correct move order is a6 first, then e5, to prevent Bb5.
notes.teaches: In Open Sicilian lines, the move a6 is often essential to prevent a bishop check on b5 that would force the knight to a3, a poor square.
notes.plans: White can now play Bb5+ with tempo, forcing Black to block with the bishop or knight, then retreat to d3 or trade and follow with Nf5.

notes.explains: Bb5+ exploits Black's omission of a6. Black must block with Bd7 or Nbd7, after which White can trade bishops and place a knight on f5.
notes.teaches: A check on b5 in the Open Sicilian can force a favorable trade and secure the f5 outpost for the knight.
notes.plans: After Bxd7+ and Nf5, White's knight dominates, pressuring d6 and limiting Black's counterplay.

notes.explains: Black faces the unusual e5, which is not a main line but playable. The simplest equalizing response is d6, immediately trading the e5 pawn to avoid any opening advantage for White.
notes.teaches: When facing an unusual early pawn move, the simplest way to neutralize it is often to trade it off immediately, leading to a dry but equal position.
notes.plans: After dxe5 dxe5, Black has a symmetrical pawn structure with an extra tempo, so developing naturally with Nf6 and later d5 is fine.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, opening the diagonal for the bishop to d6. This leads to a symmetrical position where Black has an extra tempo, effectively playing White's role.
notes.teaches: In symmetrical positions, having an extra tempo can be a subtle advantage; you can often play as if you were White, pressing for small edges.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to d6 and continue with natural moves like 0-0, aiming for a comfortable middlegame.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5, pinning the knight. Black has several good responses: Bb7 to unpin, or more ambitiously Ne4 to centralize the knight and force White to resolve the tension.
notes.teaches: When your knight is pinned, you can either break the pin immediately or use the pin to create counterplay by centralizing the knight, forcing the opponent to make a decision.
notes.plans: Playing Ne4 is ambitious; if White takes, Black recaptures with the queen and has a comfortable game. If White doesn't take, the knight is well placed.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne4, centralizing the knight and challenging the bishop. White's best is to take on e7, but here White plays Bf4, which is passive and allows Black to maintain pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent avoids a trade that would simplify, you can often keep the tension and improve your position gradually. Patience is key.
notes.plans: Castle, then develop the bishop to g4 or f5 depending on White's bishop placement. The knight on e4 is strong and can be supported later.

notes.explains: Black plays c5 and Qb6 to lure the white knight to c3, a square London players dislike because they prefer a pawn on c3.
notes.teaches: In the London, Black can provoke Nc3 to create a structure where White's knight is awkwardly placed.
notes.plans: Black will fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, castle, and develop naturally.

notes.explains: After Nc3, Black plays d6 instead of taking on b2, avoiding a well-known trap where White can trap the queen.
notes.teaches: Do not take on b2 in this line; it leads to a dangerous trap for Black.
notes.plans: Develop the dark-squared bishop to g7, then castle and play Nc6.

notes.explains: Developing the bishop to g4 allows White to play h3 and force a trade, giving up the bishop pair unnecessarily.
notes.teaches: Avoid giving up the bishop pair early in these structures; prefer Bf5 or fianchetto.
notes.plans: Play Bf5 instead, keeping the bishop and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: The engine prefers a6 over d6, preparing Qxb2 by covering b5. This is a more accurate move order.
notes.teaches: a6 covers b5, preventing Nb5 after Qxb2, and is a flexible waiting move.
notes.plans: After a6, Black can play Qxb2 if White doesn't defend, or continue development with g6 and Bg7.

notes.explains: If White plays Rb1, Black can play d5 immediately, gaining a comfortable position.
notes.teaches: When White defends b2 passively, Black can seize the center with d5.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with g6, Bg7, Nf6, and castle.

notes.explains: Black's a6 prepares b5, which can be met by a4 to soften the queenside pawns or by Bc4 to develop and set a trap.
notes.teaches: When facing b5 ideas, a4 is a common response to weaken the queenside structure, while Bc4 develops and may provoke b5 for tactical shots.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with Nf3 and Bg4, avoiding premature d5 which blocks the bishop and weakens squares.

notes.explains: Black's Nc6 walks into d5, but d5 is not best because it blocks the bishop and weakens the d5 square, allowing the knight to jump to e5.
notes.teaches: Avoid pushing a pawn that blocks your developed piece and creates a target for the opponent's knight.
notes.plans: Instead of d5, play Nf3 and Bg4, maintaining pressure and development.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 is a blunder due to Bxf7+ winning a pawn and destroying Black's kingside, though Black can recoup the pawn later.
notes.teaches: Bxf7+ is a classic tactic that ruins Black's castling rights and kingside structure, often worth a temporary pawn sacrifice.
notes.plans: Play Bxf7+ immediately, then follow up energetically with queen and knight coordination.

notes.explains: The a6-b5 setup is a legitimate opening (St. George Defense). Karpov famously lost to Tony Miles in this line; it's not as bad as it looks.
notes.teaches: Offbeat openings can be playable if you understand the resulting structures. Here Black aims for a solid center with a pawn on d5 and pressure on White's e-pawn.
notes.plans: White should play naturally and avoid overpressing; Black's structure can be solid.

notes.explains: Black's a6 and b5 define the St. George's Defense. White should not automatically develop the knight to c3; instead, a flexible setup with Nf3, Bd3, and later c3 and Nbd2 is effective.
notes.teaches: Against a6/b5, avoid the standard Nc3 setup. Use Nf3, Bd3, and a pawn on c3 to maintain a solid center and prepare a4 to challenge Black's queenside expansion.
notes.plans: Castle, then play a4 to undermine Black's b5 pawn. If Black plays c6, the x-ray on a8 allows a4xb5 cxb5 Bxb5+ winning a pawn.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on f5 is well placed, pressuring the center. White's b3 weakens the c3 square, making the d4 pawn more vulnerable.
notes.teaches: In the Advanced Caro-Kann, Black's main plan is to pressure the d4 pawn with moves like c5 and queen to b6.
notes.plans: Play c5 to attack d4, then bring the queen to b6 to increase pressure. If White plays Nc3, consider taking on d4 immediately to avoid the knight jumping to a4.

notes.explains: Taking on d4 is good because it opens lines and prevents White from playing Na4, which would attack the queen on b6 and the pawn on c5.
notes.teaches: When your queen is on b6 and White has a knight on c3, be wary of Na4 attacking both queen and pawn. Taking on d4 can avoid this nuisance.
notes.plans: After cxd4, play Bb4+ to check and disrupt White's development, then Nc6 to cover the check and develop.

notes.explains: Both sides have castled, and White has a solid center with good piece activity. Black's bishops are somewhat passive, and White's space advantage gives long-term pressure.
notes.teaches: After castling, assess the center and piece activity. White's pawns on d4 and c4 give space, while Black's knights are awkwardly placed. Use your space to restrict Black's pieces.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qd2 to connect rooks and prepare for central or kingside operations.

notes.explains: b3 is a useful prophylactic move, preparing to develop the bishop to b2 and reinforcing control over the center. It also prevents Black from playing ...Bg4 pinning the knight on f3.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, develop the bishop to b2 after securing the center. b3 also prepares to challenge Black's dark-squared bishop and supports a future pawn expansion.
notes.plans: White will castle and then connect rooks, aiming for a kingside attack or central break.

notes.explains: Black has developed both bishops and knights, but White's center is strong. The bishop on e2 is well-placed to support the center and potentially recapture on f3 if needed.
notes.teaches: Develop naturally, but be aware of pins. Keeping the bishop on e2 allows it to recapture on f3 without losing the c4 pawn, as the knight on c3 defends it.
notes.plans: White will play b3 next to develop the bishop to b2 and prepare castling.

notes.explains: White castles, completing development. Black's bishop on g4 pins the knight on f3, but White's center is solid and the pin is not dangerous because the d4 pawn is well-defended.
notes.teaches: Castling is a priority to ensure king safety. Even with a pin, if the center is secure, the pin can be ignored or dealt with later.
notes.plans: White will continue with b3 and then develop the bishop to b2, connecting rooks.

notes.explains: Black develops the knight to f6, putting pressure on the center. White's bishop on e2 is well-placed to support the d4 pawn and avoid pins.
notes.teaches: Develop knights to active squares, but be mindful of the opponent's plans. White's setup with Be2 and Nc3 is solid and flexible.
notes.plans: White will castle next, then play b3 to develop the bishop.

notes.explains: White plays Be2, avoiding the pin on the knight. This is a key move: it defends the d4 pawn indirectly and prepares to castle. Black's bishop on g4 is now less effective.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, avoid Nf3 early because of ...Bg4 pinning the knight to the queen. Instead, develop the other knight and bishop first, then play Nf3 when it's safer.
notes.plans: White will castle next, then continue development with b3 and Bb2.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight on f3. This is a common idea, but White can respond with Be2 to break the pin and defend the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Pins can be annoying, but they are not always dangerous. White can often break the pin by developing a bishop to e2, which also defends the center.
notes.plans: White will play Be2 next, then castle and continue development.

notes.explains: White develops the knight to c3, supporting the d5 pawn and preparing to challenge Black's bishop on f5. Black's knight on g6 is somewhat passive.
notes.teaches: Develop knights to active squares that support the center. Nc3 is natural, reinforcing d5 and preparing for future operations.
notes.plans: White will continue with Be3, then consider Nf3 after Black's bishop moves or is traded.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to f5, a natural square. White's Be3 is a good response, defending d4 and preparing to develop the knight.
notes.teaches: Develop bishops to active squares, but be aware that White's setup with Be3 and later Nc3 is solid. Black's bishop on f5 can be challenged by g4 or Nc3-e4.
notes.plans: White will play Nc3 next, then consider Nf3 after Black's bishop moves or is traded.

notes.explains: White plays Be3, defending the d4 pawn and preparing to develop the knight. This is better than Nf3, which would allow ...Bg4 pinning the knight.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, prioritize developing the bishop to e3 over the knight to f3. This avoids the pin and keeps the center solid.
notes.plans: White will continue with Nc3, then develop the other knight after Black's bishop moves.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to g6, a typical maneuver in the Four Pawns Attack. The knight is somewhat passive here, but it defends e5 and can go to f4 or h4 later.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, Black often maneuvers the knight to g6 to challenge White's center. White should continue developing with Be3 and Nc3.
notes.plans: White will play Be3 next, defending d4 and preparing to develop the knight.

notes.explains: White plays c4, establishing the Four Pawns Attack. This is a sharp, aggressive setup aiming to dominate the center. Black's knight on e7 is a typical response.
notes.teaches: The Four Pawns Attack is a direct way to challenge Black's setup. White sacrifices some pawn structure for space and attacking chances. It's important to know the main lines to avoid falling into traps.
notes.plans: White will continue with Be3, then Nc3, and aim for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to e7, a typical move in the Four Pawns Attack. The knight will often go to g6 to challenge White's center.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, Black often retreats the knight to e7 to avoid the pawn push d5 and then redeploy to g6. White should continue developing with c4.
notes.plans: White will play c4 next, establishing the Four Pawns structure.

notes.explains: White pushes d5, gaining space and forcing Black's knight to move. This is a key idea in the Four Pawns Attack: gaining central space and restricting Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: In the Four Pawns Attack, the pawn push d5 is a typical way to gain space and challenge Black's knight. It's important to follow up with c4 to solidify the center.
notes.plans: White will play c4 next, establishing the full pawn center.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6, a natural developing move. White now has the option to play d4, entering the main lines of the Alekhine's Defence.
notes.teaches: Develop knights to active squares. Nc6 is standard, but White's next move d4 will challenge the center.
notes.plans: White will play d4 next, aiming for central control.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, a natural developing move. Black's best response is ...Nc6 or ...d6.
notes.teaches: Develop knights to f3 and c3 in the opening. Nf3 is standard, but in the Four Pawns Attack, White may delay Nf3 to avoid pins.
notes.plans: White will continue with d4 next.

notes.explains: Black responds with e5, the standard response to e4. White now has many options, including the Four Pawns Attack.
notes.teaches: …e5 is the most common response to e4, leading to open games. White can choose aggressive setups like the Four Pawns Attack.
notes.plans: White will play Nf3 next, developing and preparing d4.

notes.explains: White opens with e4, the most common first move. Black's response will determine the opening.
notes.teaches: e4 is a strong first move, controlling the center and opening lines for the bishop and queen.
notes.plans: White will continue with Nf3 or other moves depending on Black's response.

notes.explains: White has played a3 and still has not developed any kingside pieces. Black has a solid QGD setup with full development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent neglects development, the correct response is to open the center and exploit the lack of king safety.
notes.plans: Undermine White's queenside pawn structure with a5, forcing b4 or allowing c5 later.

notes.explains: Bb5 is not about pressuring e5 (there is no e5 pawn in the Sicilian). The point is to take the knight on c6 at a favorable moment, damaging Black's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo, the bishop on b5 is placed to provoke or accept a structural concession on Black's queenside. Do not confuse it with the Ruy Lopez.
notes.plans: White will often follow with 0-0, c3, and d4, aiming for a central pawn duo while Black's doubled c-pawns remain targets.

notes.explains: a6 is a waste of tempo because White is happy to take on c6 anyway. Black loses a move and still gets doubled pawns.
notes.teaches: Do not automatically play a6 against Bb5; it only helps White. The main replies are g6, e6, d6, or Nf6.

notes.explains: After Bxc6, Black can recapture with the d-pawn (dxc6) to keep the center solid, but the queenside pawns become a long-term target. White gets a nice center and easy development.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always bad, but here Black's c6 and a6 pawns are weak and accessible. White should target them with moves like Qa4 or Qc2.
notes.plans: White will play h3 to prevent Bg4, then develop with 0-0, Re1, and prepare d4. Black's bishop on c8 often has no good square.

notes.explains: h3 is a useful prophylactic move: it stops Bg4, which would pin the knight and annoy White. Black's bishop on c8 now has no obvious good square.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo structure, preventing Bg4 is often more important than rushing to develop. A piece without a good square is a positional asset.
notes.plans: White will continue with 0-0, Re1, and prepare d4. Black's bishop may remain passive for a long time.

notes.explains: White can also play a hybrid with c3 and d4, avoiding the main line. The key is to control the center and exploit Black's pawn weaknesses.
notes.teaches: There are many move orders in the Rossolimo. The core idea remains: damage Black's pawn structure and gain a central advantage.
notes.plans: White will develop naturally and target the c6 and a6 pawns. Black's bishop on g6 is misplaced.

notes.explains: f4 is the Vienna Gambit. White sacrifices the f-pawn to gain control of the center and rapid development. Black's best is to decline or counter-gambit with d5.
notes.teaches: A gambit is a pawn sacrifice for a lead in development or central control. The Vienna Gambit is especially effective against players who accept without understanding the follow-up.
notes.plans: If Black takes on f4, White plays e5, attacking the knight and gaining space. The knight has no good retreat except back to g8.

notes.explains: After e5, Black's knight is attacked. If it moves to g8, Black loses time. Black often tries to pin the e5 pawn with Qe7, but White can unpin with Qe2.
notes.teaches: When you have a development lead, open the center and attack the opponent's pieces. A pinned pawn can be unpinned by blocking the line with a piece of equal or lesser value.
notes.plans: White will play Qe2, threatening to take the knight. Black's queen on e7 is exposed and can be attacked with Nd5.

notes.explains: Qe2 unpins the e5 pawn and threatens Nxf4. Black's queen is now in the way and can be attacked with Nd5, forcing it back.
notes.teaches: When your pawn is pinned, move a piece of equal or lesser value into the line to break the pin. Here the queen blocks the pin and defends the pawn.
notes.plans: After Nd5, Black's queen must retreat, and White gains a tempo. White's development advantage becomes decisive.

notes.explains: Nd5 attacks the queen and threatens Nxc7+. Black's queen has no good square; retreating to d8 allows a discovered check with exd6, winning material.
notes.teaches: A knight fork on c7 is a common tactical motif. When the opponent's queen is exposed, look for ways to harass it with a knight or bishop.
notes.plans: White will play exd6+ (discovered check) or Nxc7+ depending on Black's response. Either way, White wins material.

notes.explains: Black chooses …d6 over …d5 to avoid the pawn becoming a target after e5. The d6 pawn supports c5 and keeps the center solid.
notes.teaches: In such structures, pushing d5 can weaken the c5 pawn if White plays e5. Sometimes a modest move like d6 is more resilient.
notes.plans: Black will develop, castle, and prepare counterplay on the kingside or center.

notes.explains: Instead of the natural …Nf6, Black plays …Nh6, preparing ...f5 to prevent White's f5 advance and blunt the dark-squared bishop. The knight will later go to f7.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Sicilian/Grand Prix, Black's standard Nf6 can lead to a quick kingside attack by White. Nh6 is an underrated prophylactic idea that stops White's f5 and prepares ...f5 oneself.
notes.plans: After ...f5, the knight retreats to f7, creating a solid pawn box and contesting the kingside.

notes.explains: Black immediately plays …f5, striking at White's center and freezing the f4 pawn. This prevents White from playing f5 and gaining space, while creating tension.
notes.teaches: When you have prepared a pawn break, execute it without delay if your opponent's move (like h3) is a tempo loss. Don't allow them to expand with g4.
notes.plans: After ...f5, Black will develop, castle, and later consider e5 to open the center favorably.

notes.explains: Black castles kingside, a natural move. White's queen on e2 eyes the center. Black must be aware of tactical tricks: if White plays e5, Black can play ...Nf7, and if White then castles queenside, ...dxe5 fxe5 Nxe5 Qd4+ wins a pawn due to the weakened a7-g1 diagonal.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical opportunities along diagonals weakened by pawn moves. The a7-g1 diagonal becomes a target after White's f4 and Black's ...f5.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...Nf7, ...Rb8, and prepare ...e5 to open the center.

notes.explains: The knight retreats to f7, a better square than h6. It controls key squares and prepares ...e5. If White plays e5 now, ...dxe5 fxe5 Nxe5 Qd4+ wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim are grim; find a better square for them when possible. Here f7 is ideal, supporting the center and kingside.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rb8, ...e5, and aim to open the center for the bishop pair.

notes.explains: Black plays …Rb8, a useful waiting move that doesn't weaken the position. It prepares ...b5 or ...Qb6 ideas and forces White to spend time.
notes.teaches: When you have no immediate threat, make a useful, non-committal move that improves your position or provokes a weakness. Rb8 is low-risk and can become important if the queenside opens.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...e5, opening the center for the bishops.

notes.explains: Black plays …e5, opening the center. After fxe5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Bxe5, Black has the bishop pair and pressure on h2. The loose knight on c3 is also a target.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair and the opponent's king is slightly exposed, opening the center is beneficial. The bishops become powerful on open diagonals.
notes.plans: After ...e5, Black will recapture with the knight, then aim to exploit the bishop pair and the weak c3 knight.

notes.explains: White's Bf4 is an unusual, London-like setup. Black must be flexible and not blindly follow Grünfeld lines.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays an offbeat move, adapt your opening plan rather than forcing your usual system.
notes.plans: Delay d5; consider a King's Indian setup with d6, c6, a6, and b5.

notes.explains: Black builds a queenside pawn triangle (c6, a6, b5) to expand and create space, while keeping the center solid.
notes.teaches: Queenside expansion with b5 is a standard King's Indian plan; it controls key squares and prepares piece development.
notes.plans: Play b5 to gain space; if white plays a4, respond with a5 and then Na6 to use the b4 outpost.

notes.explains: Black plays b5, threatening further expansion. If white plays e4, black can respond with b4, dislodging the knight and winning the e4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Flank expansion can undermine the opponent's center; a pawn on b4 can attack the knight and win a central pawn.
notes.plans: After b5, develop with Bb7 and Nbd7, preparing c5 or e5 depending on white's play.

notes.explains: After c5 and d5, a Benoni-like structure arises. Black's bishop on b7 is temporarily blocked but can be reactivated.
notes.teaches: In Benoni structures, the c5 pawn and d5 pawn create a tension; black often targets the d5 pawn and uses the c4 square as an outpost.
notes.plans: Play Nb6 to hit the bishop, then consider c4 to open the diagonal and use c5 as a knight outpost.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nf3 e6 Bc4 a6, Black's a6 is flexible. White should develop with Nf3 before Bc4 to keep options open.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, develop knights before committing bishops to maintain flexibility and wait for Black to reveal their setup.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then prepare a knight sacrifice on d5 after adequate development.

notes.explains: White plays c3 on move 5 instead of the immediate c3 on move 2, leading to a different structure than the standard Alapin. Black should develop naturally with Nf6, avoiding the trap Nxe4? Qa4+ forking king and knight.
notes.teaches: In the Delayed Alapin, black's first priority is development; the immediate Nxe4 is a common trap to avoid.
notes.plans: Develop knights and bishop, prepare to challenge d4 or allow it with a fianchetto setup.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: White's Bd3 (Kopec System) intends Bc2 to control d4. Black can allow d4 and play a Dragon setup with g6 and Bg7, or push e5 to clamp d4.
notes.teaches: Against the Kopec System, black has two main approaches: allow d4 with a fianchetto or prevent it with e5. Both are playable; choose based on style.
notes.plans: If playing e5, follow with Bg7 and prepare to meet d4 with exd4 and central play.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: Black plays e5, creating a clamp on d4 and discouraging White's d4 push. The pawn on e5 and bishop on g7 work together to control d4. The hole on d5 is less relevant because White cannot easily occupy it (the knight on f6 defends it).
notes.teaches: Think of the e5 pawn and the fianchettoed bishop as a unit controlling key central squares. A hole is only a weakness if the opponent can exploit it.
notes.plans: If White pushes d4, trade on d4 and open the center, using the bishop's long diagonal. If White plays d3, maintain the clamp and develop.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Delayed Alapin, Kopec System
notes.explains: White pushes d4 as expected. Black trades on d4 and recaptures with the e-pawn, opening the diagonal for the bishop on g7. The resulting structure (isolated d6 pawn, open e-file) is similar to certain Ruy Lopez lines; black has compensation in development and the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: When the opponent pushes d4 in this setup, trade and recapture with the e-pawn to activate the fianchettoed bishop. The isolated pawn is a target but not fatal if black has active pieces.
notes.plans: Develop the queen's bishop to b6 or e6, prepare to target e4 with Rook to e8, and consider d5 to open the center further.

notes.explains: After c5 and dxc5, Black has a hanging pawn structure on c5 and d4. The pawn on d4 opens the diagonal for the bishop on b7. Black considered tactical ideas like Bxf3, Rxc8, Qxe8, but rejected them because the attack fizzled. Instead, Black recaptured simply, keeping all pieces active.
notes.teaches: When calculating tactics, if the attack doesn't lead to a clear win, it's often better to keep the tension and improve your position rather than forcing complications. The threat can be stronger than the execution.
notes.plans: Recapture on c1 with the rook, then bring the knight to c5 or play Qa5 to increase pressure. Avoid premature sacrifices that trade off active pieces.

notes.explains: After Qb6, the theoretical move is Qd2. If Black takes on b2, White gets a rook on b7 and a strong center; the doubled f-pawns can even be useful for a kingside attack after queenside castling.
notes.teaches: In the Pirc with early c6, White can sacrifice the b2 pawn for development and attacking chances. The doubled f-pawns are not a weakness but can serve as battering rams.
notes.plans: Castle queenside and push f5, h4 to open lines against Black's king.

notes.explains: Playing Be7 before Nf6 prevents Bg5, avoiding annoying pin lines. If White plays Nf3, Black can still play Nf6, transposing to normal lines.
notes.teaches: Move-order tricks can avoid specific lines; Be7 is a flexible way to dodge Bg5 in the Queen's Gambit Declined.
notes.plans: After Be7, if White plays Nf3, Black can play Nf6; if White plays cxd5, Black recaptures with the pawn.

notes.explains: Playing c6 and later Bd6 (repositioning the bishop) is a setup used by strong players. It looks like a tempo loss, but the closed center allows it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you can spend tempi repositioning pieces; don't blindly follow development rules—assess the center first.
notes.plans: After c6, if White plays Bf4, Black plays Bd6, offering the trade of dark-squared bishops, which is good for Black.

notes.explains: After trading bishops, Black aims to develop the light-squared bishop to f5 before White can play Bd3. Bf5 is more active than Bg4, which is often overrated.
notes.teaches: Prioritize active bishop development; Bf5 prevents White from dominating the diagonal and is more flexible than Bg4.
notes.plans: Develop knights to d7 and f6, castle, and aim for a knight to e4 or d5.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 d4 exd4 c3 dxc3 Bc4 Nc6 Nf3, White has sacrificed a pawn for rapid development. Black's knight on c6 is not yet supported, so White can later push it away with d4 or f4.
notes.teaches: In gambit openings, rapid development and central control often outweigh the material deficit. The knight on c6 is not a threat without pawn support.
notes.plans: Develop flexibly, likely Nc3, and later decide whether to play f4 based on Black's setup.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, which is a mistake. White can now push the knight away with f4, followed by e5, forcing the knight back to g8. This gives White a big center and a development lead.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's knights are in no-man's land without pawn support, you can chase them away with pawn advances, gaining space and time.
notes.plans: Play f4, then e5, then develop with Nf3, keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: After e4 Nc6, White can play Nf3, which often transposes to the Four Knights Scotch if Black plays …e5. This avoids the Vienna but is a solid choice.
notes.teaches: Against …Nc6, Nf3 is a simple way to reach familiar territory, as Black's most natural reply …e5 leads to the Four Knights Scotch.
notes.plans: Develop naturally and aim for central control.

notes.explains: Black's Bb4 is an inaccuracy because it fails to play d6, allowing White to push e5 and gain space.
notes.teaches: In the Four Knights Scotch, Black must play ...d6 early to prevent White from gaining a spatial advantage with e5.
notes.plans: Play e5 immediately to drive the knight back, ideally to g8.

notes.explains: Black's knight on h5 is a typical mistake. The automatic reaction should be g4, trapping the knight, as a pawn is the best attacker against a piece.
notes.teaches: When a knight goes to h5 or a5, immediately consider g4 (or b4) to trap it. Pawns are superior attackers because they cannot be defended by another pawn.
notes.plans: Play g4, trapping the knight. Black cannot defend it with g6 due to the pawn structure.

notes.explains: White plays f4, the Accelerated Grand Prix. Black's best response is d5, immediately challenging the center. After exd5, Black recaptures with Nf6, not Qxd5, to develop with tempo.
notes.teaches: Against the Grand Prix Attack (f4), the move ...d5 is a strong equalizer. Recapture with the knight to maintain development and avoid queen exposure.
notes.plans: Play ...d5, and after exd5, Nf6, pressuring the pawn and preparing ...e6.

notes.explains: White plays f3 to defend the e4 pawn and preserve the pawn center, avoiding the main lines like Nc3 or exd5.
notes.teaches: The Fantasy Variation aims to keep a strong pawn center by supporting e4 with f3, rather than exchanging or advancing.
notes.plans: White will develop pieces quickly, aiming to build a pawn center with e5 and f4 later.

notes.explains: After e4 c6 d4 d5 f3, Black's most critical response is …e5, transposing into an awkward Alapin Sicilian where Black's c6-pawn is misplaced (it belongs on c5) and the semi-open f-file favors White. Moves like …Nf6 give White a comfortable advantage.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, Black must play ...e5 to challenge the center; otherwise, White gets a favorable version of the Alapin with extra tempi.
notes.plans: White aims to complete kingside development, castle, and pressure f7 via the f-file.

notes.explains: The Fantasy Variation (f3) challenges Black immediately, creating a threat of dxe4 and Qh4+. White must defend without weakening the kingside further.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, a move like f3 can be good if it creates concrete threats and fits a tactical repertoire, even if it looks anti-positional.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3 to reinforce e4 and prepare to meet Qh4+ with g3.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, challenging White's center. White cannot take on e5 because after dxe5, Black has Qh4+ forking the king and the e4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Avoid greedily capturing pawns in the opening if it allows the opponent to gain a tempo with a queen check or fork.
notes.plans: White should develop the knight to f3 to block the check and defend the e4 pawn.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to g4, pinning the knight. White cannot take on e5 because the knight is pinned to the queen.
notes.teaches: Pins can prevent captures; recognize when a piece is pinned and avoid moving it.
notes.plans: White should develop the bishop to c4, aiming at the weak f7 pawn, and prepare castling.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, aiming at the f7 pawn, the weakest square in Black's position. The rook on f1 also eyes f7 along the semi-open f-file.
notes.teaches: The f7 pawn is often a target in the opening; bishops on c4 and rooks on f1 create pressure on it.
notes.plans: White will castle and then look to sacrifice on f7 if Black does not defend adequately.

notes.explains: White castles, completing development and reinforcing the threat against f7. Black's bishop on d6 is a mistake because it does not defend f7.
notes.teaches: Castling is a key developmental move that also activates the rook; always consider the threat to f7.
notes.plans: White is ready to sacrifice the bishop on f7 to expose the black king.

notes.explains: Black played Bd6, a mistake because it does not defend f7. White now has a crushing sacrifice: Bxf7+.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is only defended by the king, a bishop sacrifice can expose the king and lead to a devastating attack.
notes.plans: White will play Bxf7+ Kxf7, then Ng5+ forking king and bishop, winning back the piece with a discovered check.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop on f7, forcing the king to capture. Then Ng5+ is a discovered check from the rook, forking the king and the undefended bishop on g4.
notes.teaches: A discovered check can win material; look for undefended pieces when delivering check.
notes.plans: After the fork, White will win the bishop and have a strong attack.

notes.explains: Black avoids the sacrifice by moving the king to f8, hiding behind the bishop. White cannot immediately deliver a discovered check without losing the queen.
notes.teaches: When the king hides behind a piece, you may need to reposition your pieces to continue the attack.
notes.plans: White plays Be6, sacrificing the bishop again to lure the king into the open or win material.

notes.explains: White plays Be6, threatening to take on f7 again. If Black captures, the king is exposed to the rook. Black's best is Bxf6, but then White recaptures and wins a piece.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a second sacrifice is needed to maintain the initiative; look for ways to force the king into the open.
notes.plans: After Be6, White will win material and continue the attack.

notes.explains: Qa4+ forces a piece to d7, cutting the queen's connection to the d5 pawn and making it harder for Black to recapture.
notes.teaches: Forcing a defender to an awkward square can disrupt the opponent's coordination and make it difficult to recover a sacrificed pawn.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qb3 to attack b7 and reserve c4 for the bishop.

notes.explains: Black's queen on b6 mirrors White's queen on b3. Neither side wants to capture because opening the a-file gives Black pressure on a2, but concrete analysis shows that recapturing with the pawn would allow b5, hitting the bishop and losing the d5 pawn.
notes.teaches: In queen standoffs on b3/b6, avoid releasing the tension unless concrete tactics justify it. Always consider recapture options carefully.
notes.plans: Develop with Bc4, reinforcing d5 and challenging Black to act.

notes.explains: Black's knight heads to c7 to pressure d5. White cannot easily stop Nc7xd5, so instead of clinging to the pawn, White should trade the material advantage for the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: When you cannot hold a material advantage, convert it into a lasting positional asset like the bishop pair.
notes.plans: Play g5 to attack the bishop on d7 and force a favorable endgame with the bishop pair.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3, Black should play …d5 to prevent White from playing e4, which is a key central advance.
notes.teaches: Against d4 and Nc3 (Veresov), Black's most solid response is d5, blocking e4 and transposing into a Queen's Gambit Declined structure.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop naturally, keeping the center closed and avoiding early weaknesses.

notes.explains: White's f3 is a weakening move that clearly intends e4. Black should strike in the center with c5, exploiting the fact that White can no longer develop the knight to f3, putting pressure on d4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a weakening flank move, meet it with a central pawn break to open lines and expose the weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play c5, challenging the d4 pawn. If dxc5, then d4 forks the knight and bishop. If White doesn't take, the d4 pawn remains under pressure.

notes.explains: After c5, White's best is e3, but even then Black is better. The move c5 is natural in d4 openings and exploits that Nc3 blocks the c-pawn.
notes.teaches: In many d4 openings, c5 is a standard way to challenge White's center, especially when the c-pawn is blocked by a knight on c3.
notes.plans: Continue developing with Nc6, putting more pressure on d4. If White takes on c5, d4 forks pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6 instead of taking on d4, keeping tension. Taking on d4 would allow Bxd4 centralizing the bishop. Nc6 also threatens e5 later.
notes.teaches: When attacking a pawn, use a piece of lesser value if possible, and avoid releasing tension prematurely if it helps the opponent.
notes.plans: After Nc6, Black can consider e5 or first capture on d4 to drag the bishop to d4, then play e5 to steamroll in the center.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, attacking the knight and preparing d4. This is a powerful central breakthrough, exploiting White's weak pawn structure.
notes.teaches: After building pressure, a timely central pawn push can overwhelm the opponent's position, especially when they have weaknesses.
notes.plans: Follow up with d4, pushing the knight away, and then exploit the long diagonal with checks or attacks.

notes.explains: After d4, White's knight is forced to e4, and Black develops Bf5. Now Black has a strong position with central control and active pieces.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are driven back, develop with tempo and maintain pressure.
notes.plans: Continue developing, perhaps with Qa5+ or Bb4+, exploiting the weak dark squares around White's king.

notes.explains: In the Benoni, after d4 Nf6 Nc3 c5 d5, Black's d6 is slightly passive. White should expand with e4, gaining space.
notes.teaches: In the Benoni, White's typical plan is to play e4, gaining central space and cramping Black. Compare structures to find the best move.
notes.plans: Play e4, then after exd5, recapture with the pawn to maintain symmetry and keep Black cramped. Develop with Bd3, Nf3, O-O.

notes.explains: After Nbd2, white sacrifices the d4 pawn to gain rapid development. Black can take on d4, but white will follow up with Bc4 attacking the queen and later Qb3 targeting b7 and f7.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, Nbd2 is a sharp alternative to Bb2. It prioritizes piece activity over material, sacrificing a pawn to create threats against the exposed black queen.
notes.plans: Play Bc4 with tempo, then Qb3 to pressure b7 and f7. If Black takes on f3, consider Qb3 ignoring the capture, as the queen cannot escape with check.

notes.explains: After Qb3, black's queen is attacked and cannot escape with check because the knight on c6, pawn on d4, and bishop on c4 control the escape squares. White ignores the bishop on f3 to maintain the initiative.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, consider ignoring the capture if the attacking piece can be trapped or if the initiative is more valuable than the material.
notes.plans: After black moves the queen, recapture on f3 with the knight, preserving queens and keeping the initiative. The black king will be stuck in the center.

notes.explains: Instead of Na5, black could try Bxg2, sacrificing the queen for material. After Bxd5 Qxb7, black has Nxd4 leading to wild complications. White should avoid rushing to take the queen and instead play f3 to break the connection between black's pieces.
notes.teaches: Don't fear queen sacrifices if they bring significant material and activity. When defending, look for ways to give up the queen for multiple pieces. When attacking, look for moves like f3 that sever defensive connections.
notes.plans: After Bxg2, play Bb5 threatening to take the queen. If black takes on h1, insert f3 to trap the bishop. White ends up with a winning position.

notes.explains: Black's Na5 attacks the queen and threatens to trap it. White must give check with the queen to avoid losing it. Qb5+ is better than Qa4+ because after Qd7, the queen on a4 would be undefended.
notes.teaches: When your queen is attacked, look for checks that can save it. Compare candidate squares: after Qa4+ Qd7, the queen is undefended; after Qb5+ Qd7, the queen remains defended by the bishop.
notes.plans: After Qb5+ Qd7, take on f3 with the knight. The position remains complicated but white has good compensation.

notes.explains: Black's Qc6 is a mistake because it allows Qxa5 with the threat of Bb5. Black cannot defend both the knight and the bishop on f3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes an unexpected move, reassess the position. Here, Qc6 leaves the bishop on f3 undefended and allows a double threat.
notes.plans: Play Qxa5, threatening Bb5. If black plays b6, continue Qa6 maintaining the threat. Eventually black will lose material.

notes.explains: After Qb7, white can simply take the bishop on f3, emerging a full piece up. Black's king is stuck in the center and white has a winning attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify by capturing undefended pieces. Don't overcomplicate; the simplest win is often best.
notes.plans: Take on f3, then play Bb5+ to keep the king in the center. Use the extra piece to attack.

notes.explains: White overprotects the e4 pawn with Nc3 and Bd3 to blunt Black's typical ...f5 break. Black's bishop on e7 is passive; better is ...Bb4.
notes.teaches: Overprotecting key central pawns with minor pieces neutralizes opponent's pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Develop normally with Nf3 or Ne2, then castle and prepare queenside expansion.

notes.explains: Qe2 prevents Black from playing ...d5 and ...Ne4, which would win a pawn if the queen were not defending e4.
notes.teaches: Anticipate tactical threats like ...Ne4 after ...d5 and preempt them with prophylactic queen moves.
notes.plans: After Qe2, continue development and prepare to meet ...d5 with e5, forcing the knight back.

notes.explains: Trading light-squared bishops with Ba6 weakens Black's queenside light squares, creating targets for white's pawns and pieces.
notes.teaches: Exchanging a bishop that attacks the kingside for one that defends the queenside can create lasting light-square weaknesses.
notes.plans: Follow up with a4-a5 to pressure Black's queenside pawns and exploit the weakened light squares.

notes.explains: Black accepted the gambit only partially by playing Nf6 instead of taking on b2. After Nxc3, White has a lead in development and must act quickly before Black consolidates.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, a lead in development must be exploited immediately; delaying allows the opponent to catch up and leave you down material.
notes.plans: Play e5 to open lines and attack, forcing Black to respond actively.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb4, pinning the knight. White must avoid the tempting e5 because Black has the counter d5, opening lines and attacking the bishop on c4.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is on c4, be aware of the ...d5 counterattack that can disrupt your plans.
notes.plans: Instead of e5 immediately, consider simple moves like taking on c3 to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Now e5 is correct because Black's d5 would be less effective after the knight is on c3. White must step on the gas before Black castles.
notes.teaches: Timing is crucial: a move that was bad one turn can become good after a key exchange.
notes.plans: Play e5 to open the center and attack the knight on f6.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, a common counter. White must decide how to recapture. The simplest move is to take with the bishop, but that may lead to complications.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, start with the simplest forcing move (capture, check, threat) to save time and reduce error risk.
notes.plans: Consider Bxd5 first; if that works, it's the best choice.

notes.explains: White captures the knight on f6. If Black recaptures with the queen, White can trade queens and enter an endgame with a strong passed pawn on g7.
notes.teaches: When ahead in development, trading queens can lead to a favorable endgame where your active pieces and pawn weaknesses matter more.
notes.plans: After exf6, if Qxf6, play Bxd5; if Black recaptures, consider fxe7 or other trades to reach a good endgame.

notes.explains: Black takes the bishop on c4. White can now take on d5 with the queen, and if Black forks with Bxc3, White has Bd2 to defend and remain a piece up.
notes.teaches: Always check for defensive resources like Bd2 that parry forks and maintain material advantage.
notes.plans: Play Qxd5, then after Bxc3, Bd2, leaving White up a piece.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4, White has set up the Jobava London. Black's most common response is ...e6, but White's immediate threat is Nb5, targeting c7. Black has three main defenses: ...Bb4, ...Na6, and ...Bd6. The most popular on Lichess is ...Bd6, which is actually the worst of the three.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, White often plays for a quick Nb5 to pressure c7. Black's most common reply is often suboptimal, so knowing the correct responses gives White an edge.
notes.plans: After ...Bd6, White can play e3 and then develop naturally, aiming to exploit Black's passive bishop placement.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4 Bf5 e3 e6 Nf3 Nbd7, Black's setup looks solid but is deceptive. White can immediately play g4, threatening h5 to trap the bishop on f5. If Black plays ...h6, White takes on f5, ruining Black's pawn structure and leaving the g6 pawn weak.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, the g4-h5 pawn advance is a common tactical idea to trap Black's light-squared bishop or destroy Black's kingside pawn structure.
notes.plans: After g4, if Black plays ...h6, White takes on f5 and then plays Qf3, pinning the king and threatening g5, with a winning attack.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 d5 Bf4, if Black plays ...Nc6, White has a winning tactic: Nb5! Black cannot defend c7 adequately. Similarly, ...Nbd7 also loses to Nb5.
notes.teaches: In the Jobava London, ...Nc6 and ...Nbd7 are immediate losing moves due to the threat of Nb5 attacking c7. Always be alert for such tactical shots.
notes.plans: Play Nb5, threatening Nxc7+ and winning material.

notes.explains: Black took the knight on d4, which is a mistake. After Qxd4, Black often plays c5, attacking the queen, but that weakens the center. The better move is d6, preventing e5.
notes.teaches: Don't play c5 just to attack the queen; it creates weaknesses. Instead, play d6 to solidify the center.
notes.plans: White will develop naturally, aiming for a positional game.

notes.explains: With d6, Black prevents e5 and prepares to develop. White should decide where to castle and develop the bishop. Bc4 is better than Bd3 because e4 is already well-defended, and the bishop on c4 eyes the kingside.
notes.teaches: Choose bishop development based on the pawn structure; don't overprotect already-defended pawns.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then develop the other bishop.

notes.explains: Instead of standard bishop moves like Bg5 or Bf4, fianchettoing the bishop to b2 is a strong idea. It creates an x-ray against g7 and avoids blocking the d-file.
notes.teaches: Fianchettoing is not just for the Nimzo-Larsen; it's a legitimate development scheme in many positions.
notes.plans: Complete development with Bb2, then improve piece placement.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight. White should not trade on e6 because that gives Black the f-file and more center control. Instead, ignore the pin and continue development.
notes.teaches: Keep the tension; don't trade pieces unless it benefits you. An opponent's pin is not always dangerous.
notes.plans: Play Re1 and Rd1, then consider f4 for kingside expansion.

notes.explains: White creates luft with h3 to avoid back-rank issues if the center opens. This is prophylactic, preparing for possible e5 breaks.
notes.teaches: Creating luft is a good habit, especially when the center might open and tactics arise.
notes.plans: Continue improving pieces, prepare f4.

notes.explains: Black prepares b5, so White plays a4 to prevent it. This is prophylactic, stopping Black's queenside expansion.
notes.teaches: Be proactive in preventing your opponent's plans. a4 is a common move to stop b5.
notes.plans: After a4, continue with the kingside attack.

notes.explains: White moves the rook to f1 to defend the f4 pawn, preparing a rook lift to the kingside. Nd5 is not good because Black can play c6 and chase the knight away.
notes.teaches: Don't centralize a knight if it can be easily chased away. Ensure the square is stable first.
notes.plans: Lift the rook to g3 or d3, then bring the queen to h4.

notes.explains: Black develops quickly with Nf6 and castles before pushing d6, preserving flexibility. White's Bc4 is met with O-O, avoiding premature commitment.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, prioritize rapid development and king safety over early pawn pushes. Delaying d6 keeps options open and can punish slow white play.
notes.plans: Continue development with d6 or d5 depending on white's setup, aiming for a quick queenside counterplay.

notes.explains: Black has transposed into the Accelerated Dragon by playing g6 and Bg7, delaying d6. This prevents White from entering the mainline Dragon with dangerous attacking chances.
notes.teaches: In the Accelerated Dragon, delay d6 to allow a quick d7-d5 break, avoiding White's queenside castling attack.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f6, castle kingside, then push d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: White's a3 is a waste of time; Black can proceed as if given a free move. Black should now castle before playing d5 to avoid the pin Bb5.
notes.teaches: Only play d5 after castling kingside to prevent a bishop pin on the knight.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then play d5 to open the center and exploit White's lagging development.

notes.explains: White's a3 is a wasted move. Black should play d5 immediately, but must be careful of Bb5 pin. Castling first is safer.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes a move, you can often seize the initiative by opening the center. But ensure your king is safe first.
notes.plans: Castle, then d5 to open the center and exploit White's lagging development.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, opening the center. White's a3 is a wasted move, leaving the king in the center and vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Punish slow development by opening the center when the opponent's king is uncastled.
notes.plans: After d5, Black has active pieces and pressure against White's center.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 c3, Black often plays …d5 or …Nf6, but knowing the follow-up is essential. The move …g6 is a decisive mistake because White gets Nc3 with tempo, chasing the queen and enabling d5.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, the key idea is to play d5 as quickly as possible after developing with tempo, exploiting Black's queen placement.
notes.plans: Play Nc3, then d5 (pre-move against most queen retreats) to seize the center and open lines for attack.

notes.explains: Black's queen to f6 is a common beginner mistake: it doesn't develop a minor piece and blocks the g8 knight's natural square.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes an early queen sortie, focus on gaining a lead in development and then open the center.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3, preparing d4 to open the center while the queen is vulnerable.

notes.explains: With two developed pieces to zero, it's time to open the center with d4. Black's queen becomes a target.
notes.teaches: When you have a development lead, open the center to exploit the opponent's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Play d4, and after exd4, recapture with the knight.

notes.explains: White's a4 is a poor move because it does nothing to challenge Black's control of d5. The knight on d5 is a powerful blockader, and White should have played Re1 to prepare against b6.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the side fighting the pawn must immediately contest the square in front of it. Leaving the blockader unchallenged gives the defending side a comfortable game.
notes.plans: Black will complete development with b6 and Bb7, then bring a rook to c8, aiming to pressure d4. The knight on d5 is stable and can later be redeployed to win the pawn.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes the light-squared bishop, a standard plan to complete development and add pressure on d4. The bishop on b7 eyes the center and supports the knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When facing an IQP, develop actively and aim to pressure the pawn. Fianchettoing the bishop is a common and effective setup.
notes.plans: After Bb7, Black will play Rc8, and later consider moves like Nc2 to trade off White's light-squared bishop, which is White's main attacking piece.

notes.explains: White's Ne4 is aimless; it does not threaten anything concrete and allows Black to continue developing. The knight on e4 is not well placed and may become a target.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, every tempo counts. White must generate active play or build a battery (Bc2, Qd3) to attack the king. Wasting time on pointless maneuvers gives Black the initiative.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Bb7, Rc8, and later consider Ncb4 to trade off White's bishop. White's lack of a plan allows Black to consolidate.

notes.explains: White's Nc3 in a Colle is positionally suspect because it blocks the c-pawn, which should go to c4. The d4 pawn becomes a target since White cannot support it with c3.
notes.teaches: In queen-pawn openings, Nc3 is often a positional mistake because it blocks the natural c4 break and weakens the d4 pawn.
notes.plans: Black should immediately challenge the center with c5, exploiting the weakness of d4.

notes.explains: After c5, Black is not afraid of dxc5 because recapturing with the bishop or queen is comfortable. There is no need to rush to win back the pawn; developing naturally is better.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to regain a pawn if it costs development. The pawn isn't going anywhere and can be won later with better piece activity.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to g4 or play e6, keeping flexible options. Avoid premature e5 which can create weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black recaptures on c5 with the bishop, developing with tempo. White's queen d3 is a meaningless move that doesn't threaten anything.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a lone queen sortie, don't panic. It rarely creates real threats if you just continue developing.
notes.plans: Defend the bishop (e.g., Qe7 or Bb6) and continue development. White's queen on b5 can be answered with Nbd7 or a6.

notes.explains: White plays Ne5, attacking the bishop on g4. Black must first deal with the threat to the bishop before addressing other issues like the attack on c6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a move, identify all threats. Don't get tunnel vision on one part of the board and forget about a hanging piece.
notes.plans: Take the bishop on g4 (Bxf3) and after White recaptures, play Rc8 to defend the knight on c6. Alternatively, Qc7 is also good.
